towards-a-framework-for-evaluation-of-sp.scientist: Subsea Inspection, Maintenance and Repair (IMR) interactions on underwater Oil & Gas infrastructure can have severe consequences in case of failure. Currently, these interactions are mainly carried out using Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) with attached robotic arms where operators assess the situation and make decisions. To allow for increased autonomy in operations on routine objects (valves, wires, hoses, tools), the ROV has to detect the objects and their pose before manipulation tasks can be performed. These tasks typically involve risks, and therefore it is desirable to estimate the probability of operation failure in order to provide decision-support to human operators during the mission. In this paper, we propose a framework using machine learning with a Gaussian Naive Bayes Classifier to estimate the failure-probability of robotic tasks based on the objects’ spatial uncertainties. As the uncertainty input-feature we use the 6 DOF standard deviation of the object’s pose-estimate. We show how prediction accuracy improves over time and how well the predictions match actual failure rates. We run 1000 simulated pick-and-place operations with different uncertainties and discuss how our method can improve decision-support during operation. We also include a small dataset collected by a 3D camera from real-world objects, test the transferability of simulation results to these data and a pose-estimation algorithm, and examine the impact of data quality.
towards-a-framework-for-evaluation-of-sp.student: Underwater maintenance on oil and gas infrastructure, often done by remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) with robotic arms, carries high risks if tasks fail. To increase autonomy, ROVs must first detect and locate objects like valves or hoses before manipulating them. This study proposes a machine learning framework using a Gaussian Naive Bayes Classifier to estimate the probability of task failure based on spatial uncertainties in the object’s position and orientation (6 degrees of freedom, or 6 DOF). The method uses the standard deviation of the object’s pose estimate as input. Results from 1000 simulated pick-and-place operations show that prediction accuracy improves over time and aligns with actual failure rates. A small real-world dataset from a 3D camera is also tested to assess how well simulation results transfer to real conditions and how data quality affects performance.
towards-a-framework-for-evaluation-of-sp.layman: Repairing underwater oil and gas equipment is risky and usually done by remote-controlled robots. To make these robots more independent, they need to recognize and locate objects before handling them. Researchers created a system that predicts how likely a task is to fail based on how uncertain the robot is about an object’s position. They tested this with 1000 computer-simulated tasks and a few real-world examples. The system gets better at predicting failures over time and works even when the data isn’t perfect.

digitalization-and-sustainable-manufactu.scientist: The manufacturing industry is facing massive changes driven by digitalization and sustainability. It is being redefined to meet the UN SDGs with the creation of new materials, processes and machinery. The drive for digitalization in order to use resources more effectively and efficiently adds to the complexity of this twin transition. This book presents results from 8 years of research with 15 industry partners, following the transition towards a digitalized industry 4.0 manufacturing and sustainable manufacturing paradigm. The selected chapters demonstrate how globally competitive manufacturing in high-cost countries such as Norway is enabled by AI-supported intelligent and flexible automation and the use of digital twins, as well as human-centred manufacturing. This book describes the interactions in innovative and sustainable organizations and changes in materials, products and processes, digital twins and AI-supported automated manufacturing processes. Supported by case studies and reflections from the manufacturing industry, this book evaluates how the combination of digitalization and sustainability enables competitiveness. With a focus on multi-material products and processes, robust and flexible automation and innovative and sustainable organizations, it provides a multi-disciplinary insight into the challenges and opportunities faced by manufacturing industries over time.
digitalization-and-sustainable-manufactu.student: The manufacturing sector is evolving due to digitalization and sustainability pressures, aligning with the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This book synthesizes eight years of research with 15 industry partners, exploring how high-cost countries like Norway can remain competitive by adopting Industry 4.0—advanced manufacturing that integrates digital technologies. Key enablers include AI-driven automation, digital twins (virtual models of physical systems), and human-centred approaches. The work examines how these innovations interact with new materials, processes, and organizational structures, using case studies to assess their impact on competitiveness. The focus is on multi-material products, flexible automation, and sustainable practices, offering a multidisciplinary view of the challenges and opportunities in modern manufacturing.
digitalization-and-sustainable-manufactu.layman: Factories are changing to use new technology and become more eco-friendly. This book looks at how countries with high costs, like Norway, can stay competitive by using smart machines, computer models of production lines, and better ways to involve workers. The authors studied real factories over eight years to see how these changes help businesses grow while being kinder to the planet. They found that combining digital tools with sustainable practices can make manufacturing stronger and more adaptable.

3d-pointcloud-registration-in-the-wild-1.scientist: This study assesses two state-of-the-art (SOTA) pointcloud registration approaches on industrially challenging datasets, focusing on two specific cases. The first case involves the application of Lidar-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) in a tunnel environment, while the second case revolves around aligning RGBD scans from intricately symmetrical cast-iron machine parts within the domain of small-scale industrial production. Our evaluation involves testing state-of-the-art pointcloud registration approaches both with and without fine-tuning, and comparing the results to a classical hand crafted feature extractors. Our experimental findings reveal that existing SOTA models exhibit limited generalization capability when confronted with the more challenging pointcloud data. Moreover, robust generalizable methods beyond training are currently unavailable, highlighting a notable gap in addressing challenges associated with industrial datasets in pointcloud registration.
3d-pointcloud-registration-in-the-wild-1.student: This study tests two leading methods for aligning 3D pointclouds—datasets of points in space captured by sensors like Lidar—on difficult industrial cases. The first case uses Lidar data from a tunnel for mapping and navigation (SLAM), while the second aligns detailed scans of symmetrical cast-iron machine parts. The researchers compared these modern methods, both with and without fine-tuning, against older, manually designed feature-based approaches. Results show that even the best current models struggle to generalize to these challenging datasets. Furthermore, no robust, ready-to-use methods exist that work well without additional training, revealing a gap in handling real-world industrial pointcloud alignment tasks.
3d-pointcloud-registration-in-the-wild-1.layman: Researchers tested two advanced methods for matching 3D scans of objects or spaces, like those from laser sensors, in tough real-world settings. One test involved mapping a tunnel, and another matched scans of complex machine parts. They compared these new methods, with and without adjustments, to older techniques. The findings show that even the best current methods don’t work well on these difficult cases, and no reliable, ready-to-use solution exists yet for such industrial challenges.

automated-3d-burr-detection-in-cast-manu.scientist: For automating deburring of cast parts, this paper proposes a general method for estimating burr height using 3D vision sensor that is robust to missing data in the scans and sensor noise. Specifically, we present a novel data-driven method that learns features that can be used to align clean CAD models from a workpiece database to the noisy and incomplete geometry of a RGBD scan. Using the learned features with Random sample consensus (RANSAC) for CAD to scan registration, learned features improve registration result as compared to traditional approaches by (translation error (± 18.47 mm) and rotation error (± 43°)) and accuracy (35%) respectively. Furthermore, a 3D-vision based automatic burr detection and height estimation technique is presented. The estimated burr heights were verified and compared with measurements from a high resolution industrial CT scanning machine. Together with registration, our burr height estimation approach is able to estimate burr height similar to high resolution CT scans with Z-statistic value (z = 0.279).
automated-3d-burr-detection-in-cast-manu.student: This study addresses the challenge of automating deburring—removing sharp edges (burrs) from cast metal parts—by estimating burr height using a 3D vision sensor. The researchers developed a data-driven method to align clean CAD models (digital designs) with noisy, incomplete 3D scans of workpieces. Their approach uses learned features and a technique called RANSAC to improve alignment accuracy, reducing translation error by ±18.47 mm and rotation error by ±43°, while boosting overall accuracy by 35% compared to traditional methods. They also introduced a 3D-vision-based technique to detect and estimate burr height, which was validated against high-resolution industrial CT scans. The results show their method estimates burr height similarly to CT scans, with a Z-statistic value of 0.279, indicating statistical similarity.
automated-3d-burr-detection-in-cast-manu.layman: The researchers wanted to find a way to automatically detect and measure the sharp edges left on metal parts after casting. They used a 3D camera to scan the parts and created a new method to match these scans with the original digital designs. Their approach improved the alignment accuracy and allowed them to estimate the height of the sharp edges. When compared to a very precise industrial scanner, their method produced similar results.

safesub-safe-and-autonomous-subsea-inter.scientist: The demand for autonomous robotic solutions capable of operating in complex and dangerous environments – such as those found in inspection and maintenance (I&M) operations – is growing. However, the success of autonomous system deployments relies heavily on their actual and human-perceived safety. Current AI-based predictions often lack robust uncertainty handling, which could lead to catastrophic outcomes. In the SAFESUB project, we address this gap by developing a framework for reliable uncertainty estimation and control throughout a sensing, perception, and control pipeline for autonomous uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) interventions. In this paper, we present the overall SAFESUB concept, detail relevant opportunities (use cases) and research challenges for future autonomous UUV intervention in I&M operations, and outline our preliminary results and next steps for the SAFESUB concept components: 1) A novel 3D underwater camera system with built-in uncertainty estimation of sensor data, 2) a basis for perception for 6-DOF pose estimation and corresponding uncertainty, and 3) an uncertainty-aware UUV intervention architecture designed for risk reduction in operations. The components are under development, and details will be shared in subsequent component-specific papers as the purpose of this paper is to give a project-wide overview and promptly share the SAFESUB concept. The paper also explores the state of the art on underwater sensing, perception, and intervention techniques, and provides a categorization of UUV operation concepts.
safesub-safe-and-autonomous-subsea-inter.student: Autonomous robots are increasingly needed for inspection and maintenance in hazardous environments, but their safety—both real and perceived—depends on reliable uncertainty handling in AI predictions. The SAFESUB project tackles this by developing a framework for robust uncertainty estimation across sensing, perception, and control in uncrewed underwater vehicles (UUVs). This paper introduces the SAFESUB concept, outlines use cases and challenges for autonomous UUV interventions, and presents preliminary work on three components: a 3D underwater camera with built-in sensor uncertainty estimation, a perception system for estimating a UUV’s 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) pose (position and orientation) with uncertainty, and an uncertainty-aware control architecture to reduce operational risks. The components are still in development, and this paper provides a high-level overview rather than detailed technical results. It also reviews current underwater sensing, perception, and intervention methods and categorizes UUV operation concepts.
safesub-safe-and-autonomous-subsea-inter.layman: Robots that work underwater without human control are useful for checking and fixing things in dangerous places. But they can make mistakes if they’re not sure about what they’re seeing or doing. This project is working on ways to help these robots better understand and handle their own doubts. The team is building a special underwater camera, a system to track the robot’s exact position, and a control setup that takes uncertainty into account to keep operations safe. The paper explains the overall idea, the challenges, and what’s been done so far, without going into all the technical details.

underwater-marker-based-pose-estimation-.scientist: We propose a system for 6-DoF estimation of Aruco markers with associated uncertainties in the challenging underwater environment. A state-of-the-art object detection framework (EfficientDet) was adapted to predict the corner locations of Aruco markers, while dropout sampling at inference time is used to estimate the predictive 6-DoF pose uncertainty. A dataset of Aruco markers captured in a wide variety of turbidities, with ground truth position of the corner locations, was gathered and used to train the network to robustly predict the 6-DoF pose. We report median translational errors of 2.6cm at low turbidity (8.5m attenuation length) and up to 10.5cm at high turbidities (0.3m attenuation length). The respective uncertainty, reported as interquartile ranges (IQRs), range from 3.2cm up to 27.9cm. The rotational median errors varied from 5.6° to 10.7° with IQRs of 6.4° to 26.2°. We also discuss how the pose uncertainty can be applied to reduce the risk in a subsea intervention operation.
underwater-marker-based-pose-estimation-.student: This study addresses the challenge of estimating the 6-DoF (six degrees of freedom: position and orientation) pose of Aruco markers—square, machine-readable tags—underwater, where visibility is often poor. The researchers adapted EfficientDet, a deep learning model for object detection, to predict the corners of these markers. To account for uncertainty, they used dropout sampling during inference, a technique that estimates how confident the model is in its predictions. They trained the model on a dataset of underwater images with varying turbidity (water clarity), using known marker positions as ground truth. The system achieved median position errors of 2.6 cm in clear water and up to 10.5 cm in murky conditions, with uncertainty ranges (interquartile ranges) from 3.2 cm to 27.9 cm. Rotational errors ranged from 5.6° to 10.7°, with uncertainty spans of 6.4° to 26.2°. The work also explores how these uncertainty estimates could help reduce risks in underwater robotic tasks.
underwater-marker-based-pose-estimation-.layman: The researchers wanted to find the exact position and angle of special square markers underwater, where the water can be very murky. They used a computer program to spot the markers in photos and guess their location, while also figuring out how sure the guess is. They tested this in different water conditions, from clear to very cloudy. In clear water, the guesses were off by about 2.6 cm, but in murky water, the error grew to 10.5 cm. The uncertainty in these guesses also increased with murkier water. They suggest this method could help underwater robots work more safely.

evaluating-clinical-diversity-and-plausi.scientist: Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) is being increasingly used as an alternative imaging modality for complete and non-invasive screening of the gastrointestinal tract. Although this is advantageous in reducing unnecessary hospital admissions, it also demands that a WCE diagnostic protocol be in place so larger populations can be effectively screened. This calls for training and education protocols attuned specifically to this modality. Like training in other modalities such as traditional endoscopy, CT, MRI, etc., a WCE training protocol would require an atlas comprising of a large corpora of images that show vivid descriptions of pathologies, ideally observed over a period of time. Since such comprehensive atlases are presently lacking in WCE, in this work, we propose a deep learning method for utilizing already available studies across different institutions for the creation of a realistic WCE atlas using StyleGAN. We identify clinically relevant attributes in WCE such that synthetic images can be generated with selected attributes on cue. Beyond this, we also simulate several disease progression scenarios. The generated images are evaluated for realism and plausibility through three subjective online experiments with the participation of eight gastroenterology experts from three geographical locations and a variety of years of experience. The results from the experiments indicate that the images are highly realistic and the disease scenarios plausible. The images comprising the atlas are available publicly for use in training applications as well as supplementing real datasets for deep learning.
evaluating-clinical-diversity-and-plausi.student: Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) is a non-invasive way to examine the entire gastrointestinal tract by swallowing a small camera. While it reduces hospital stays, it requires standardized training to interpret the images effectively. Currently, there’s no comprehensive image atlas for WCE, unlike other imaging methods like MRI or CT. This study proposes a deep learning approach using StyleGAN to create a realistic WCE atlas from existing data across institutions. The method generates synthetic images with specific clinical features and simulates disease progression. Eight gastroenterology experts evaluated the images in online experiments, finding them highly realistic and plausible. The atlas is publicly available for training and research.
evaluating-clinical-diversity-and-plausi.layman: Doctors sometimes use a tiny camera you swallow to check your insides without surgery. This method is useful but needs better training tools. Researchers created a way to make realistic fake images of the gut to help train doctors. They asked experts to judge these images, and the experts said they looked real. The images are now free for others to use.

ps-devcem-pathology-sensitive-deep-learn.scientist: We propose a novel pathology-sensitive deep learning model (PS-DeVCEM) for frame-level anomaly detection and multi-label classification of different colon diseases in video capsule endoscopy (VCE) data. Our proposed model is capable of coping with the key challenge of colon apparent heterogeneity caused by several types of diseases. Our model is driven by attention-based deep multiple instance learning and is trained end-to-end on weakly labeled data using video labels instead of detailed frame-by-frame annotation. This makes it a cost-effective approach for the analysis of large capsule video endoscopy repositories. Other advantages of our proposed model include its capability to localize gastrointestinal anomalies in the temporal domain within the video frames, and its generality, in the sense that abnormal frame detection is based on automatically derived image features. The spatial and temporal features are obtained through ResNet50 and residual Long short-term memory (residual LSTM) blocks, respectively. Additionally, the learned temporal attention module provides the importance of each frame to the final label prediction. Moreover, we developed a self-supervision method to maximize the distance between classes of pathologies. We demonstrate through qualitative and quantitative experiments that our proposed weakly supervised learning model gives a superior precision and F1-score reaching 61.6% and 55.1%, as compared to three state-of-the-art video analysis methods respectively. We also show our model’s ability to temporally localize frames with pathologies, without frame annotation information during training. Furthermore, we collected and annotated the first and largest VCE dataset with only video labels. The dataset contains 455 short video segments with 28,304 frames and 14 classes of colorectal diseases and artifacts. Dataset and code supporting this publication will be made available on our home page.
ps-devcem-pathology-sensitive-deep-learn.student: We developed a deep learning model, PS-DeVCEM, to detect and classify colon diseases in video capsule endoscopy (VCE) footage—where a tiny camera travels through the digestive tract. The model addresses the challenge of visual differences caused by various diseases using attention-based deep multiple instance learning, which allows it to learn from video-level labels rather than expensive frame-by-frame annotations. It combines spatial features (from ResNet50) and temporal features (from residual LSTM blocks) to identify anomalies and even localize them within the video. A self-supervision method helps distinguish between disease types. In tests, it outperformed other methods, achieving 61.6% precision and 55.1% F1-score, and could localize issues without frame-level training data. We also created the largest VCE dataset with 455 videos and 14 disease classes, labeled only at the video level.
ps-devcem-pathology-sensitive-deep-learn.layman: Researchers built a computer program to spot and categorize colon problems in videos taken by a swallowed camera. The program learns from whole videos instead of individual images, making it cheaper to use. It can also pinpoint where in the video the issues appear. Tests showed it worked better than other methods, correctly identifying problems about 60% of the time. The team also collected a large set of these videos to help others study the same problem.

this-changes-to-that-combining-causal-an.scientist: Due to the unequivocal need for understanding the decision processes of deep learning networks, both modal-dependent and model-agnostic techniques have become very popular. Although both of these ideas provide transparency for automated decision making, most methodologies focus on either using the modal-gradients (model-dependent) or ignoring the model internal states and reasoning with a model’s behavior/outcome (model-agnostic) to instances. In this work, we propose a unified explanation approach that given an instance combines both model-dependent and agnostic explanations to produce an explanation set. The generated explanations are not only consistent in the neighborhood of a sample but can highlight causal relationships between image content and the outcome. We use Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE) domain to illustrate the effectiveness of our explanations. The saliency maps generated by our approach are comparable or better on the softmax information score.
this-changes-to-that-combining-causal-an.student: Deep learning models, like those used in medical image analysis, often act as 'black boxes,' making it hard to understand how they reach decisions. Current methods for explaining these models either rely on internal data (model-dependent) or focus solely on input-output behavior (model-agnostic). This study introduces a hybrid approach that combines both techniques to generate explanations for a given input. The resulting explanations are consistent for similar inputs and can reveal causal links between image features and the model’s output. The method is tested on Wireless Capsule Endoscopy (WCE), a medical imaging technique, where it produces saliency maps—visual highlights of important image regions—that perform as well as or better than existing methods on a standard evaluation metric.
this-changes-to-that-combining-causal-an.layman: Researchers often struggle to explain how complex computer programs make decisions, especially in medical imaging. This study combines two common explanation methods to create a clearer picture of why a program reaches a certain conclusion. The new approach was tested on images from a tiny camera swallowed to examine the digestive tract. It highlights the most important parts of the images and does so more reliably than older methods.

multi-label-video-classification-for-und.scientist: Today ship hull inspection including the examination of the external coating, detection of defects, and other types of external degradation such as corrosion and marine growth is conducted underwater by means of Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs). The inspection process consists of a manual video analysis which is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. To address this, we propose an automatic video analysis system using deep learning and computer vision to improve upon existing methods that only consider spatial information on individual frames in underwater ship hull video inspection. By exploring the benefits of adding temporal information and analyzing frame-based classifiers, we propose a multi-label video classification model that exploits the self-attention mechanism of transformers to capture spatiotemporal attention in consecutive video frames. Our proposed method has demonstrated promising results and can serve as a benchmark for future research and development in underwater video inspection applications.
multi-label-video-classification-for-und.student: Underwater ship hull inspections, which check for coating damage, corrosion, or marine growth, are currently done using Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs) that record video for manual review—a slow and labor-intensive process. This study proposes an automated system using deep learning and computer vision to analyze these videos more efficiently. Unlike existing methods that only look at individual frames, the new approach incorporates temporal information (changes over time) by using a multi-label video classification model. This model leverages transformers, a type of neural network that uses self-attention to focus on relevant parts of consecutive frames, capturing both spatial and temporal patterns. Early results are promising, suggesting this method could improve underwater inspection efficiency and serve as a benchmark for future work.
multi-label-video-classification-for-und.layman: Inspecting the outside of ships for damage like rust or barnacles is done underwater with cameras on remote-controlled vehicles. Currently, people watch the videos to spot problems, which takes a lot of time. The researchers built a computer system that can watch these videos automatically, learning to recognize issues by studying how things change over time, not just in single pictures. Their method shows early success and could make these inspections faster and more reliable in the future.

data-driven-predictive-control-and-mpc-d.scientist: In this paper, we explore the interplay between Predictive Control and closed-loop optimality, spanning from Model Predictive Control to Data-Driven Predictive Control. Predictive Control in general relies on some form of prediction scheme on the real system trajectories. However, these predictions may not accurately capture the real system dynamics, for e.g., due to stochasticity, resulting in sub-optimal control policies. This lack of optimality is a critical issue in case of problems with economic objectives. We address this by providing sufficient conditions on the underlying prediction scheme such that a Predictive Controller can achieve closed-loop optimality. However, these conditions do not readily extend to Data-Driven Predictive Control. In this context of closed-loop optimality, we conclude that the factor distinguishing the approaches within Data-Driven Predictive Control is if they can be cast as a sequential decision-making process or not, rather than the dichotomy of model-based vs. model-free. Furthermore, we show that the conventional approach of improving the prediction accuracy from data may not guarantee optimality.
data-driven-predictive-control-and-mpc-d.student: This study examines how Predictive Control—an approach where controllers use predictions of system behavior to make decisions—can achieve optimal performance in closed-loop systems (where the controller continuously adjusts based on feedback). Predictive Control often struggles with accuracy due to uncertainties like randomness, leading to suboptimal policies, especially in economically driven problems. The authors derive conditions under which a Predictive Controller can ensure closed-loop optimality, but these conditions don’t directly apply to Data-Driven Predictive Control, which relies on data rather than explicit models. They argue that the key difference in Data-Driven Predictive Control isn’t whether it’s model-based or model-free, but whether it can be framed as a sequential decision-making process. Surprisingly, simply improving prediction accuracy from data doesn’t always guarantee optimality.
data-driven-predictive-control-and-mpc-d.layman: The researchers asked how controllers that predict system behavior can make the best possible decisions in real time. They found that even with good predictions, randomness can lead to poor choices, especially when money is involved. They identified rules to help controllers make optimal decisions, but these rules don’t work the same way for controllers that learn from data. They also discovered that making predictions more accurate doesn’t always mean better decisions. The real difference is whether the controller can make a series of smart choices over time.

addressing-sample-efficiency-and-model-b.scientist: Model-based reinforcement learning promises to be an effective way to bring reinforcement learning to real-world robotic systems by offering a sample efficient learning approach compared to model-free reinforcement learning. However, model-based reinforcement learning approaches at present struggle to match the performance of model-free ones. This work attempts to fill this gap by improving the performance of model-based reinforcement learning while further improving its sample efficiency. To improve the sample efficiency, an exploration strategy is formulated which maximizes the information gain. The asymptotic performance is improved by compensating for the model-bias using a model-free critic. We have evaluated our proposed approach on four reinforcement learning benchmarking tasks in the openAI gym framework.
addressing-sample-efficiency-and-model-b.student: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) uses a learned model of the environment to plan actions, making it more sample-efficient than model-free RL, which learns directly from trial and error. However, model-based methods often underperform model-free ones. This study aims to close that gap by enhancing both sample efficiency and performance. To improve efficiency, the authors designed an exploration strategy that prioritizes actions yielding the most new information. To boost long-term performance, they added a model-free critic—a component that learns from experience—to correct biases in the model. The approach was tested on four standard RL tasks in the OpenAI Gym framework, showing promising results.
addressing-sample-efficiency-and-model-b.layman: Researchers wanted to make robots learn faster and better by using a method that builds a model of their environment. This method is usually slower to learn than another approach that just tries things out. They improved it by making the robot explore in a smarter way and by adding a backup system to fix mistakes. They tested this on four common robot-learning tasks and found it worked well.

optimality-conditions-for-model-predicti.scientist: Optimality is a critical aspect of Model Predictive Control (MPC), especially in economic MPC. However, achieving optimality in MPC presents significant challenges, and may even be impossible, due to inherent inaccuracies in the predictive models. Predictive models often fail to accurately capture the true system dynamics, such as in the presence of stochasticity, leading to suboptimal MPC policies. In this paper, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions on the underlying prediction model for an MPC scheme to achieve closed-loop optimality. Interestingly, these conditions are counterintuitive to the traditional approach of building predictive models that best fit the data. These conditions present a mathematical foundation for constructing models that are directly linked to the performance of the resulting MPC scheme.
optimality-conditions-for-model-predicti.student: Model Predictive Control (MPC) is a method for controlling systems by repeatedly solving an optimization problem over a future time window. In economic MPC, the goal is to optimize economic performance, but this is difficult because predictive models—used to forecast system behavior—are often inaccurate, especially when the system involves randomness. This paper identifies the exact conditions a predictive model must satisfy for MPC to achieve the best possible closed-loop performance. Surprisingly, these conditions differ from the usual goal of making models fit data as closely as possible. Instead, they provide a mathematical basis for designing models that directly improve MPC performance.
optimality-conditions-for-model-predicti.layman: Researchers studied how to best control systems like factories or robots using predictions of future behavior. They found that even the most accurate predictions don’t always lead to the best control. Instead, they discovered specific rules for what makes a prediction useful for control. These rules are different from just making predictions as precise as possible, and they help build better control systems.

reinforcement-learning-for-mpc-fundament.scientist: Recent publications have laid a solid theoretical foundation for the combination of Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control, in view of obtaining high-performance data-driven MPC policies. Early practical results, both in simulation and in experiments, have shown the potential of this combination but have also revealed certain challenges. In addition, the technical complexity of these results makes it difficult for interested readers to gather the fundamental ideas and principles behind this combination. This paper aims to provide a coherent and more accessible picture of these results and to offer significantly deeper and more mature insights into their meaning than has been proposed before. It also aims to identify the current challenges in the field.
reinforcement-learning-for-mpc-fundament.student: Recent work has explored merging Reinforcement Learning (RL), a machine learning method where agents learn by trial and error, with Model Predictive Control (MPC), a control strategy that optimizes actions over a short time horizon. While early simulations and experiments show promise, they also highlight practical difficulties. The technical depth of these studies, however, makes it hard to grasp the core ideas. This paper synthesizes these results into a clearer framework, offering deeper insights into how RL and MPC can work together. It also outlines the key challenges that still need to be addressed in this emerging field.
reinforcement-learning-for-mpc-fundament.layman: Researchers are combining two approaches to improve how machines make decisions: one learns from experience, the other plans ahead. Early tests show this mix can work, but it’s complicated and has problems. This paper explains the main ideas behind the combination in a simpler way and points out what still needs to be solved.

corl-reinforcement-learning-of-milp-poli.scientist: Combinatorial sequential decision-making problems are typically modeled as mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) and solved via branch-and-bound (B&B) algorithms. The inherent difficulty of modeling MILPs that accurately represent stochastic real-world problems leads to suboptimal performance in the real world. Recently, machine-learning methods have been applied to build MILP models for decision quality rather than how accurately they model the real-world problem. However, these approaches typically rely on supervised learning, assume access to true optimal decisions, and use surrogates for the MILP gradients. In this work, we introduce a proof-of-concept CORL framework that end-to-end fine-tunes an MILP scheme using reinforcement learning (RL) on real-world data to maximize its operational performance. We enable this by casting an MILP solved by B&B as a differentiable stochastic policy compatible with RL. We validate the CORL method in a simple illustrative combinatorial sequential decision-making example.
corl-reinforcement-learning-of-milp-poli.student: Sequential decision problems with many possible choices are often tackled using mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), which are mathematical models solved by branch-and-bound algorithms. However, these models struggle to capture real-world uncertainty, leading to poor real-world performance. Recent machine-learning approaches aim to build MILPs for better decision quality rather than perfect real-world representation, but they often rely on supervised learning, assume access to optimal decisions, and use approximations for gradients. Here, we propose a proof-of-concept framework called CORL that fine-tunes an MILP scheme end-to-end using reinforcement learning (RL) on real-world data to improve operational performance. We achieve this by treating the MILP, solved by branch-and-bound, as a differentiable stochastic policy compatible with RL. The method is validated in a simple combinatorial sequential decision-making example.
corl-reinforcement-learning-of-milp-poli.layman: Researchers often use math-based models to solve complex decision problems, but these models can struggle with real-world unpredictability. Newer methods use machine learning to improve decisions, but they have limitations. This study introduces a way to adjust these models using a trial-and-error learning approach on real data to make better decisions. The method was tested on a simple example to show it works.

safe-learning-for-control-using-control-.scientist: Real-world autonomous systems are often controlled using conventional model-based control methods. But if accurate models of a system are not available, these methods may be unsuitable. For many safety-critical systems, such as robotic systems, a model of the system and a control strategy may be learned using data. When applying learning to safety-critical systems, guaranteeing safety during learning as well as testing/deployment is paramount. A variety of different approaches for ensuring safety exists, but the published works are cluttered and there are few reviews that compare the latest approaches. This paper reviews two promising approaches on guaranteeing safety for learning-based robust control of uncertain dynamical systems, which are based on control barrier functions and control Lyapunov functions. While control barrier functions provide an option to incorporate safety in terms of constraint satisfaction, control Lyapunov functions are used to define safety in terms of stability. This review categorises learning-based methods that use control barrier functions and control Lyapunov functions into three groups, namely reinforcement learning, online and offline supervised learning. Finally, the paper presents a discussion of the suitability of the different methods for different applications.
safe-learning-for-control-using-control-.student: Autonomous systems, like robots, often rely on model-based control, which requires precise mathematical models of the system. However, when such models are unavailable, learning-based control methods—where the system and its control strategy are learned from data—become useful, especially for safety-critical applications. Ensuring safety during both learning and deployment is crucial. This paper reviews two key approaches for guaranteeing safety in learning-based control: control barrier functions (which enforce safety by ensuring constraints are met) and control Lyapunov functions (which ensure stability, a form of safety). The review categorises existing methods into three groups: reinforcement learning, online supervised learning, and offline supervised learning. It also discusses which methods suit which applications.
safe-learning-for-control-using-control-.layman: Robots and other self-driving systems usually need exact instructions to work safely. But when those instructions aren’t available, they can learn from experience instead. This paper looks at ways to make sure these learning systems stay safe while they learn and operate. It focuses on two main ideas: one that keeps the system within safe limits, and another that keeps it steady. The paper sorts current methods into three types and explains which ones work best for different tasks.

closing-the-sim2real-performance-gap-in-.scientist: Sim2Real aims at training policies in high-fidelity simulation environments and effectively transferring them to the real world. Despite the developments of accurate simulators and Sim2Real RL approaches, the policies trained purely in simulation often suffer significant performance drops when deployed in real environments. This drop is referred to as the Sim2Real performance gap. Current Sim2Real RL methods optimize the simulator accuracy and variability as proxies for real-world performance. However, these metrics do not necessarily correlate with the real-world performance of the policy as established theoretically and empirically in the literature. We propose a novel framework to address this issue by directly adapting the simulator parameters based on real-world performance. We frame this problem as a bilevel RL framework: the inner-level RL trains a policy purely in simulation, and the outer-level RL adapts the simulation model and in-sim reward parameters to maximize real-world performance of the in-sim policy. We derive and validate in simple examples the mathematical tools needed to develop bi-level RL algorithms that close the Sim2Real performance gap.
closing-the-sim2real-performance-gap-in-.student: Sim2Real is a method for training AI policies in detailed simulations before deploying them in the real world. However, these policies often perform worse in reality than in simulation, a problem called the Sim2Real performance gap. Current approaches try to improve simulators or add variability, but these changes don’t always lead to better real-world results. We introduce a new framework that directly adjusts simulator settings based on real-world performance. It uses a two-level system: the inner level trains the policy in simulation, while the outer level tweaks the simulator and its reward system to improve real-world outcomes. We also develop and test mathematical tools to support this bilevel reinforcement learning approach, showing it can help close the performance gap.
closing-the-sim2real-performance-gap-in-.layman: Researchers train AI in computer simulations to perform tasks in the real world, but the AI often does worse in reality. Current fixes don’t always work. The team created a new method that adjusts the simulation based on how well the AI performs in the real world. They tested this approach with simple examples and showed it can help the AI work better outside the simulation.

predicting-what-matters-training-ai-mode.scientist: Artificial intelligence (AI) models that predict the future behavior of real-world systems and processes (also known as predictive AI models) are central to intelligent decision-making. They are often employed in model-based decision-making frameworks to optimize decisions for real-world tasks based on their predictions. However, decisions optimized using such predictive AI models often result in suboptimal performance when applied in the real world. This is primarily because these models are typically constructed to best fit the behavior of the real-world system, and hence to predict the most likely future rather than to optimize the best possible decisions for a given task. Due to this objective mismatch, their predictions cannot be guaranteed to support optimal decision-making in theory or in practice. In fact, there is increasing empirical evidence and consensus that predictive models must be tailored to decision-making objectives to achieve optimal real-world performance. Supporting this observation, we establish formal (necessary and sufficient) conditions that a predictive model (AI-based or not) must satisfy for a decision-making policy derived using that model to achieve optimal performance in the real world. We then discuss their implications for building predictive AI models for optimal sequential decision-making.
predicting-what-matters-training-ai-mode.student: Predictive AI models, which forecast real-world system behaviors, are widely used in decision-making frameworks to optimize actions. However, these models often lead to suboptimal real-world outcomes because they are designed to predict the most likely future, not to directly support optimal decisions. This mismatch in objectives means their predictions don’t guarantee optimal decision-making. Recent evidence suggests predictive models must align with decision-making goals to perform well. This study formally defines the necessary and sufficient conditions a predictive model (AI or otherwise) must meet for decisions based on it to achieve optimal real-world performance. The findings also explore how these conditions apply to building AI models for sequential decision-making tasks.
predicting-what-matters-training-ai-mode.layman: Researchers often use computer models to predict how things will behave in the future, then make decisions based on those predictions. But these predictions don’t always lead to the best real-world choices because the models are built to guess what will happen, not to help make the best decisions. This study shows what a prediction model must do to ensure the decisions made from it are as good as possible. It also explains how to build better models for making a series of decisions over time.

the-emerging-clinical-relevance-of-artif.scientist: This narrative review introduces key concepts in artificial intelligence (AI), data science, and wearable devices aimed at headache clinicians and researchers. PubMed and IEEEXplore were searched to identify relevant studies, and these were reviewed systematically. We identified six primary research topics. First, the most common application of AI and data science is in the diagnosis of headache disorders, with reported accuracies of up to 90%. Second, AI and data science are used for predicting headache disease trajectories and forecasting attacks. Third, prediction of treatment effects and data-driven individualization of treatment prescription demonstrate promising results, with accuracies ranging from 40% to 83%. Fourth, AI and data science can uncover hidden information within headache datasets, offering clinicians deeper insights. Fifth, wearables, combined with AI and data science, can improve remote monitoring and migraine management. Lastly, user experience studies indicate strong interest from both clinicians and patients in adopting these technologies. The potential applications of AI, data science, and wearable device technologies in headache research are vast. However, many studies are small pilot studies, and models often suffer from poor performance, limited reporting, and lack of external validation, which impede generalizability and clinical implementation.
the-emerging-clinical-relevance-of-artif.student: This review explores how artificial intelligence (AI), data science, and wearable devices are being used in headache research. The authors searched databases like PubMed and IEEE Xplore to gather studies, then organized them into six key areas. AI is most often used to diagnose headache disorders, with some models reaching 90% accuracy. It’s also applied to predict how headaches may progress, forecast attacks, and tailor treatments—though accuracy here varies widely (40-83%). AI can reveal hidden patterns in headache data, while wearables paired with AI improve remote monitoring. Both clinicians and patients show interest in these tools. However, many studies are small, models often perform poorly, lack transparency, or aren’t tested on new data, limiting their real-world use.
the-emerging-clinical-relevance-of-artif.layman: Researchers looked at how computers and smart devices can help with headaches. They found six main uses: diagnosing headaches, predicting when they’ll happen, suggesting treatments, uncovering hidden data patterns, and using wearables to track symptoms. Both doctors and patients like the idea. But many studies are small, and the tools don’t always work well or haven’t been tested enough to be used widely.

an-effective-methodology-for-dynamic-3d-.scientist: The problem of facial expression recognition in dynamic sequences of 3D face scans has received a significant amount of attention in the recent past whereas the problem of retrieval in this type of data has not. A novel retrieval methodology for such data is introduced in this paper. The proposed methodology automatically detects specific facial landmarks and uses them to create a descriptor. This descriptor is the concatenation of three sub-descriptors which capture topological as well as geometric information of the 3D face scans. The motivation behind the proposed hybrid facial expression descriptor is the fact that some facial expressions, like happiness and surprise, are characterized by obvious changes in the mouth topology while others, like anger, fear and sadness, produce geometric but no significant topological changes. The proposed retrieval scheme exploits the Dynamic Time Warping technique in order to compare descriptors corresponding to different 3D facial sequences. A detailed evaluation of the introduced retrieval scheme is presented showing that it outperforms previous state-of-the-art retrieval schemes. Experiments have been conducted using the six prototypical expressions of the standard dataset BU-4DFE and the eight prototypical expressions of the recently available dataset BP4D-Spontaneous. Finally, a majority voting scheme based on the retrieval results is used to achieve unsupervised dynamic 3D facial expression recognition. The achieved classification accuracy is comparable to the state-of-the-art supervised dynamic 3D facial expression recognition techniques.
an-effective-methodology-for-dynamic-3d-.student: This study addresses the less-explored problem of retrieving similar 3D facial expression sequences from a dataset. While recognizing expressions in 3D face scans has been widely studied, finding and matching similar sequences has not. The authors propose a new method that first identifies key facial landmarks (like the corners of the mouth or eyes) and then builds a descriptor—a numerical representation—by combining three sub-descriptors. These capture both the shape (topology) and the spatial arrangement (geometry) of the face. The idea is that some expressions, such as happiness, involve clear changes in mouth shape, while others, like anger, show geometric shifts without major topological changes. To compare sequences, the method uses Dynamic Time Warping, a technique that aligns and compares time-series data even if they vary in speed. Testing on two standard datasets (BU-4DFE and BP4D-Spontaneous), the approach outperforms existing retrieval methods. Additionally, by aggregating retrieval results, the system achieves unsupervised expression recognition with accuracy close to supervised techniques.
an-effective-methodology-for-dynamic-3d-.layman: Researchers tackled a problem: how to find similar facial expressions in sequences of 3D face scans. They created a method that spots key points on the face and uses them to describe each expression, focusing on both the shape and the arrangement of facial features. Some expressions, like smiling, change the mouth’s shape, while others, like frowning, change its position without altering the shape much. They then used a technique to compare these descriptions across different sequences. Testing on two sets of data, their method worked better than older ones. It also helped recognize expressions without prior training, performing nearly as well as methods that do use training.

diagnosing-migraine-from-genome-wide-gen.scientist: Migraine has an assumed polygenic basis, but the genetic risk variants identified in genome-wide association studies only explain a proportion of the heritability. We aimed to develop machine learning models, capturing non-additive and interactive effects, to address the missing heritability. This was a cross-sectional population-based study of participants in the second and third Trøndelag Health Study. Individuals underwent genome-wide genotyping and were phenotyped based on validated modified criteria of the International Classification of Headache Disorders. Four datasets of increasing number of genetic variants were created using different thresholds of linkage disequilibrium and univariate genome-wide associated p-values. A series of machine learning and deep learning methods were optimized and evaluated. The genotype tools PLINK and LDPred2 were used for polygenic risk scoring. Models were trained on a partition of the dataset and tested in a hold-out set. The area under the receiver operating characteristics curve was used as the primary scoring metric. Classification by machine learning was statistically compared to that of polygenic risk scoring. Finally, we explored the biological functions of the variants unique to the machine learning approach. 43,197 individuals (51% women), with a mean age of 54.6 years, were included in the modelling. A light gradient boosting machine performed best for the three smallest datasets (108, 7,771 and 7,840 variants), all with hold-out test set area under curve at 0.63. A multinomial naïve Bayes model performed best in the largest dataset (140,467 variants) with a hold-out test set area under curve of 0.62. The models were statistically significantly superior to polygenic risk scoring (area under curve 0.52 to 0.59) for all the datasets (p<0.001 to p=0.02). Machine learning identified many of the same genes and pathways identified in genome-wide association studies, but also several unique pathways, mainly related to signal transduction and neurological function. Interestingly, pathways related to botulinum toxins, and pathways related to the calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor also emerged. This study suggests that migraine may follow a non-additive and interactive genetic causal structure, potentially best captured by complex machine learning models. Such structure may be concealed where the data dimensionality (high number of genetic variants) is insufficiently supported by the scale of available data, leaving a misleading impression of purely additive effects. Future machine learning models using substantially larger sample sizes could harness both the additive and the interactive effects, enhancing precision and offering deeper understanding of genetic interactions underlying migraine.
diagnosing-migraine-from-genome-wide-gen.student: Migraine is thought to be influenced by many genes, but current genetic studies only explain part of this heritability. This study used machine learning to explore whether non-additive (non-simple) and interactive genetic effects could account for the missing heritability. Using data from 43,197 participants in the Trøndelag Health Study, researchers tested various machine learning and deep learning models on datasets with increasing numbers of genetic variants. The best-performing models (light gradient boosting and multinomial naïve Bayes) achieved an area under the curve (AUC, a measure of model accuracy) of 0.62–0.63, outperforming traditional polygenic risk scoring (AUC 0.52–0.59). The models identified known migraine-related genes and pathways, as well as new ones linked to signal transmission and neurological function. The results suggest migraine may involve complex genetic interactions, which machine learning can better capture than simpler methods, though larger datasets may be needed to fully uncover these patterns.
diagnosing-migraine-from-genome-wide-gen.layman: Migraines are thought to be partly caused by genes, but current research only explains some of this link. Scientists used computer models to see if more complex genetic patterns could help fill the gap. They studied over 43,000 people, testing different models to predict migraines based on their genes. The best models were slightly better than older methods at identifying who might get migraines. They also found new gene pathways that might be involved, including some related to nerve signals. The study suggests migraines may involve complicated genetic interactions that simpler methods miss, and bigger studies could reveal even more.

prediction-of-new-onset-migraine-using-c.scientist: Background Migraine is associated with a range of symptoms and comorbid disorders and has a strong genetic basis, but the currently identified risk loci only explain a small portion of the heritability, often termed the “missing heritability”. We aimed to investigate if machine learning could exploit the combination of genetic data and general clinical features to identify individuals at risk for new-onset migraine. Method This study was a population-based cohort study of adults from the second and third Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT2 and HUNT3). Migraine was captured in a validated questionnaire and based on modified criteria of the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD) and participants underwent genome-wide genotyping. The primary outcome was new-onset migraine defined as a change in disease status from headache-free in HUNT2 to migraine in HUNT3. The migraine risk variants identified in the largest GWAS meta-analysis of migraine were used to identify genetic input features for the models. The general clinical features included demographics, selected comorbidities, medication and stimulant use and non-headache symptoms as predictive factors. Several standard machine learning architectures were constructed, trained, optimized and scored with area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC). The best model during training and validation was used on unseen test sets. Different methods for model explainability were employed. Results A total of 12,995 individuals were included in the predictive modelling (491 new-onset cases). A total of 108 genetic variants and 67 general clinical variables were included in the models. The top performing decision-tree classifier achieved a test set AUC of 0.56 when using only genotypic data, 0.68 when using only clinical data and 0.72 when using both genetic and clinical data. Combining the genotype only and clinical data only models resulted in a lower predictivity with an AUC of 0.67. The most important clinical features were age, marital status and work situation as well as several genetic variants. Conclusion The combination of genotype and routine demographic and non-headache clinical data correctly predict the new onset of migraine in approximately 2 out of 3 cases, supporting that there are important genotypic-phenotypic interactions partaking in the new-onset of migraine.
prediction-of-new-onset-migraine-using-c.student: Migraine has a strong genetic component, but known genetic risk factors explain only part of its heritability. This study used machine learning to see if combining genetic data (108 variants linked to migraine) and clinical features (e.g., age, comorbidities, medication use) could predict new-onset migraine in a large Norwegian cohort (12,995 adults). The best model, a decision-tree classifier, achieved an AUC of 0.72 (where 0.5 is random and 1.0 is perfect) when using both genetic and clinical data, outperforming models using only one type of data. Key predictors included age, marital status, and specific genetic variants. The results suggest that genetic and clinical factors interact to influence migraine onset, though prediction remains modest.
prediction-of-new-onset-migraine-using-c.layman: Researchers wanted to know if they could predict who might develop migraine for the first time by combining genetic information with health and lifestyle details. They studied over 12,000 adults, tracking who developed migraine years later. Using computer models, they found that combining genes and factors like age or work status correctly predicted new migraine cases about 72% of the time. This suggests that both genes and everyday health details play a role in who gets migraine, though the predictions are not perfect.

what-predicts-citation-counts-and-transl.scientist: Background: We aimed to develop the first machine learning models to predict citation counts and the translational impact, defined as inclusion in guidelines or policy documents, of headache research, and assess which factors are most predictive. Methods: Bibliometric data and the titles, abstracts, and keywords from 8600 publications in three headache-oriented journals from their inception to 31 December 2017 were used. A series of machine learning models were implemented to predict three classes of 5-year citation count intervals (0–5, 6–14 and >14 citations); and the translational impact of a publication. Models were evaluated out-of-sample with area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC). Results: The top performing gradient boosting model predicted correct citation count class with an out-of-sample AUC of 0.81. Bibliometric data such as page count, number of references, first and last author citation counts and h-index were among the most important predictors. Prediction of translational impact worked optimally when including both bibliometric data and information from the title, abstract and keywords, reaching an out-of-sample AUC of 0.71 for the top performing random forest model. Conclusion: Citation counts are best predicted by bibliometric data, while models incorporating both bibliometric data and publication content identifies the translational impact of headache research.
what-predicts-citation-counts-and-transl.student: This study built machine learning models to predict how often headache research papers would be cited and whether they would influence medical guidelines or policies. Using data from 8,600 papers—including titles, abstracts, keywords, and bibliometric metrics like page count and author citation counts—the team trained models to classify papers into three citation ranges (0–5, 6–14, or >14 citations) and to predict their translational impact. The best model for citation counts, a gradient boosting algorithm, achieved an out-of-sample AUC of 0.81, with bibliometric data (e.g., references, author h-index) being the strongest predictors. For translational impact, a random forest model combining bibliometric data and text from titles/abstracts performed best, with an AUC of 0.71. The work suggests citation counts rely heavily on bibliometric factors, while broader impact benefits from analyzing the paper’s content.
what-predicts-citation-counts-and-transl.layman: Researchers wanted to predict which headache studies would be cited often or influence medical guidelines. They analyzed 8,600 papers, using details like length, author reputation, and the text of the papers themselves. Their best computer model could guess citation levels with 81% accuracy, mostly by looking at simple paper traits. To predict if a study would shape guidelines, they needed both paper traits and the actual content, achieving 71% accuracy. The study shows that how often a paper is cited depends on basic features, while its real-world impact needs a closer look at what it says.

a-new-user-friendly-visual-environment-f.scientist: In this paper a novel, user friendly visual environment for Breast MRI Data Analysis is presented (BreDAn). Given planar MRI images before and after IV contrast medium injection, BreDAn generates kinematic graphs, color maps of signal increase and decrease and finally detects high risk breast areas. The advantage of BreDAn, which has been validated and tested successfully, is the automation of the radiodiagnostic process in an accurate and reliable manner. It can potentially facilitate radiologists’ workload.
a-new-user-friendly-visual-environment-f.student: This study introduces BreDAn, a new visual tool designed for analyzing breast MRI data. The software takes planar MRI images captured before and after the injection of an intravenous contrast medium—a substance used to enhance visibility of tissues. BreDAn processes these images to produce kinematic graphs (visual representations of motion or change over time), color maps showing areas of signal increase or decrease, and identifies regions at high risk for abnormalities. The tool has been validated and tested, demonstrating its ability to automate parts of the radiodiagnostic process with accuracy and reliability. Its primary benefit is the potential to reduce the workload for radiologists by streamlining analysis.
a-new-user-friendly-visual-environment-f.layman: Researchers created a computer tool to help analyze breast MRI scans. The tool looks at images taken before and after a special dye is injected to highlight areas of concern. It then creates visual maps and graphs to show changes and pinpoint high-risk areas. The tool has been tested and works well, making the process faster and more reliable. This could make the job easier for doctors who read these scans.

cross-time-registration-of-3d-point-clou.scientist: Registration is a ubiquitous operation in visual computing and constitutes an important pre-processing step for operations such as 3D object reconstruction, retrieval and recognition. Particularly in cultural heritage (CH) applications, registration techniques are essential for the digitization and restoration pipelines. Cross-time registration is a special case where the objects to be registered are instances of the same object after undergoing processes such as erosion or restoration. Traditional registration techniques are inadequate to address this problem with the required high accuracy for detecting minute changes; some are extremely slow. A deep learning registration framework for cross-time registration is proposed which uses the DeepGMR network in combination with a novel down-sampling scheme for cross-time registration. A dataset especially designed for cross-time registration is presented (called ECHO) and an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art methods is conducted for the challenging case of cross-time registration.
cross-time-registration-of-3d-point-clou.student: In visual computing, registration aligns multiple scans or images of an object into a single coordinate system, a key step for tasks like 3D reconstruction or object recognition. In cultural heritage, this helps digitize and restore artifacts. Cross-time registration is a specific challenge: it matches versions of the same object at different times, such as before and after erosion or restoration. Traditional methods struggle with the precision needed to detect tiny changes or are too slow. This study proposes a deep learning approach using the DeepGMR network, paired with a new down-sampling technique to improve efficiency. The researchers also introduce ECHO, a dataset designed for cross-time registration, and evaluate existing methods on this task to assess their performance.
cross-time-registration-of-3d-point-clou.layman: Scientists often need to combine multiple scans of an object, like a statue, to create a complete digital model. This is tricky when the object changes over time, such as through wear or repair. Older methods can’t always spot small changes or work quickly enough. The researchers created a new computer system that uses advanced learning techniques to match these scans more accurately. They also built a special collection of test cases to check how well different methods work for this problem.

effective-descriptors-for-human-action-r.scientist: Two novel methods for fully unsupervised human action retrieval using 3D mesh sequences are presented. The first achieves high accuracy but is suitable for sequences consisting of clean meshes, such as artificial sequences or highly post-processed real sequences, while the second one is robust and suitable for noisy meshes, such as those that often result from unprocessed scanning or 3D surface reconstruction errors. The first method uses a spatio-temporal descriptor based on the trajectories of 6 salient points of the human body (i.e. the centroid, the top of the head and the ends of the two upper and two lower limbs) from which a set of kinematic features are extracted. The resulting features are transformed using the wavelet transformation in different scales and a set of statistics are used to obtain the descriptor. An important characteristic of this descriptor is that its length is constant independent of the number of frames in the sequence. The second descriptor consists of two complementary subdescriptors, one based on the trajectory of the centroid of the human body across frames and the other based on the Hybrid static shape descriptor adapted for mesh sequences. The robustness of the second descriptor derives from the robustness involved in extracting the centroid and the Hybrid sub-descriptors. Performance figures on publicly available real and artificial datasets demonstrate our accuracy and robustness claims and in most cases the results outperform the state-of-the-art.
effective-descriptors-for-human-action-r.student: This study introduces two new methods for unsupervised human action retrieval from 3D mesh sequences, which are sequences of 3D models capturing human motion. The first method uses a descriptor based on the movement trajectories of six key body points (e.g., head, limbs, centroid). Kinematic features are extracted from these trajectories, transformed using wavelet analysis at different scales, and summarized with statistics. This method is highly accurate but works best with clean, noise-free meshes. The second method combines two sub-descriptors: one tracking the centroid’s movement and another adapting a shape descriptor for mesh sequences. This approach is robust to noise, such as errors from raw scans or reconstruction. Both methods were tested on public datasets, showing strong performance and often outperforming existing techniques.
effective-descriptors-for-human-action-r.layman: Researchers developed two ways to automatically recognize human actions from 3D motion data without prior training. The first method tracks the movement of six body points, like the head and limbs, and works well with clean data. The second method is tougher, handling messy or incomplete data by focusing on the body’s center and overall shape. Tests on real and artificial data showed both methods work well, often better than older approaches.

action-unit-detection-in-3d-facial-video.scientist: This work introduces a new scheme for action unit detection in 3D facial videos. Sets of features that define action unit activation in a robust manner are proposed. These features are computed based on eight detected facial landmarks on each facial mesh that involve angles, areas and distances. Support vector machine classifiers are then trained using the above features in order to perform action unit detection. The proposed AU detection scheme is used in a dynamic 3D facial expression retrieval and recognition pipeline, highlighting the most important AUs, in terms of providing facial expression information, and at the same time, resulting in better performance than state-of-the-art methodologies.
action-unit-detection-in-3d-facial-video.student: This study presents a new method for detecting action units (AUs)—subtle facial muscle movements that convey expressions—in 3D facial videos. The approach extracts geometric features, such as angles, areas, and distances, from eight key facial landmarks on a 3D mesh. These features are then used to train support vector machine classifiers, a type of machine learning model, to identify active AUs. The method is integrated into a system for retrieving and recognizing 3D facial expressions, where it improves performance compared to existing techniques while emphasizing the most informative AUs for expression analysis.
action-unit-detection-in-3d-facial-video.layman: Researchers developed a way to spot tiny facial movements, called action units, in 3D videos of faces. They measured shapes and distances between key points on the face, then used a computer program to learn which movements show up in different expressions. Their method helps recognize emotions in 3D face videos better than older approaches.

a-comprehensive-model-of-the-psychology-.scientist: To address global environmental challenges it is crucial to understand how humans make decisions about environmentally relevant behaviour, since a shift to alternative behaviours can make a relevant difference. This paper proposes a comprehensive model of determinants of individual environmentally relevant behaviour based on a combination of the most common theories in environmental psychology. The model is tested using a meta-analytical structural equation modelling approach based on a pool of 56 different data sets with a variety of target behaviours. The model is supported by the data. Intentions to act, perceived behavioural control and habits were identified as direct predictors of behaviour. Intentions are predicted by attitudes, personal and social norms, and perceived behavioural control. Personal norms are predicted by social norms, perceived behavioural control, awareness of consequences, ascription of responsibility, an ecological world view and self-transcendence values. Self-enhancement values have a negative impact on personal norms. Based on the model, interventions to change behaviour need not only to include attitude campaigns but also a focus on de-habitualizing behaviour, strengthening the social support and increasing self-efficacy by concrete information about how to act. Value based interventions have only an indirect effect.
a-comprehensive-model-of-the-psychology-.student: To tackle environmental issues, we need to understand what drives people to adopt eco-friendly actions. This study combines major theories in environmental psychology to build a model explaining individual environmentally relevant behaviour. Using meta-analytical structural equation modelling—a statistical method that analyses multiple datasets—the model was tested on 56 datasets covering various behaviours. The results support the model: intentions, perceived control over actions, and habits directly influence behaviour. Intentions themselves are shaped by attitudes, personal and social norms, and perceived control. Personal norms arise from social norms, perceived control, awareness of consequences, responsibility, ecological worldviews, and self-transcendence values, while self-enhancement values weaken them. The findings suggest behaviour change efforts should go beyond attitude campaigns, focusing on breaking habits, boosting social support, and improving self-efficacy through practical guidance. Value-based interventions have only indirect effects.
a-comprehensive-model-of-the-psychology-.layman: Researchers wanted to know what makes people act in eco-friendly ways. They studied many past experiments and found that habits, a sense of control, and plans to act directly shape behaviour. Plans to act are influenced by personal beliefs, social pressure, and feeling capable. Strong personal beliefs come from social pressure, feeling in control, understanding consequences, and caring about nature. Selfish values weaken these beliefs. To encourage greener habits, the study suggests breaking old routines, offering social support, and giving clear instructions on how to act. Changing values alone may not be enough.

beyond-climate-anxiety-development-and-v.scientist: There is a growing research interest in the affective aspects of climate change and their links with pro-climate engagement. Yet, psychometrically valid instruments assessing the wide panorama of emotional responses to climate change are limited. Here, we report on the development and validation of the Inventory of Climate Emotions (ICE), a self-report measure of multiple emotions experienced in relation to climate change. Based on qualitative exploration, literature review, along with expert and target population content validation, we operationally defined a spectrum of emotional responses to climate change which guided the formulation of a large initial item pool. High psychometric quality of the ICE was secured in two quantitative studies conducted in samples from the general population in Poland. In Study 1, based on exploratory factor analysis, we indicate that a broad range of emotional responses to climate change can be viably captured by 8 underlying factors: anger, contempt, enthusiasm, powerlessness, guilt, isolation, anxiety, and sorrow. This structure was corroborated in Study 2 with confirmatory factor analysis on an independent sample. Across studies, we provide evidence for the reliability and validity of the ICE in terms of internal consistency of the subscales and convergent, discriminant and concurrent validity. We also show the functionality of the ICE in the context of pro-climate behaviour. The ICE provides an integrative approach to emotional responses to climate change and it can be used to further the understanding of the complex role of emotions in climate change engagement.
beyond-climate-anxiety-development-and-v.student: Researchers developed a new tool, the Inventory of Climate Emotions (ICE), to measure the range of emotions people feel about climate change. Existing tools often lack psychometric validity—meaning they may not reliably or accurately measure what they claim. The team first identified key emotions through qualitative interviews, literature reviews, and expert input, then created a large set of potential questions.
