In two studies with Polish participants, they tested and refined the ICE. Exploratory factor analysis in Study 1 revealed eight distinct emotional factors: anger, contempt, enthusiasm, powerlessness, guilt, isolation, anxiety, and sorrow. Study 2 confirmed this structure using confirmatory factor analysis. The ICE demonstrated strong reliability and validity, with consistent internal results and alignment with related measures. It also showed utility in predicting pro-climate actions, offering a robust way to study how emotions influence climate engagement.
beyond-climate-anxiety-development-and-v.layman: Scientists created a questionnaire to measure how people feel about climate change. They asked many people what emotions come up for them, then tested the questions to make sure they worked well. They found that feelings like anger, sadness, or hope can be grouped into eight main types. The questionnaire was checked twice with different groups, and it proved reliable. It also helped show how these feelings might connect to actions people take for the climate.

psychological-factors-in-the-diffusion-o.scientist: This paper aims to understand the determinants of the adoption of wood pellet technology for home heating to identify possible strategies against the slow diffusion of wood pellet in Norway. A mail survey of 737 Norwegian households was conducted in 2008, involving wood pellet adopters and non-wood pellet adopters as respondents. An integrated model combining psychological factors (such as intentions, attitudes, perceived behavioral control, habits and norms), perceived wood pellet heating characteristics, and ecological and basic values is applied to predict the installation of a wood pellet stove retrospectively. Results from a path analysis gain empirical support for the proposed integrated model. Wood pellet heating adoption is mainly predicted by a deliberate decision process starting with the evaluation of heating system characteristics, mediated by attitudes and intentions. A lack of perceived behavioral control and behavioral lock-in pose relevant barriers to the adoption process. The influence of norms and values are indirect and only minor in the given market conditions. Therefore, focusing on values or norms should not be of highest priority at the moment, whereas improvement of the subjective evaluation of the functional reliability and the costs related to wood pellet heating should have first priority. The small but significant influence of habitual decision making indicates that presenting alternatives and increase decisional involvement could be other promising strategies to reduce cognitive lock-in in decision-making.
psychological-factors-in-the-diffusion-o.student: This study explores why Norwegian households adopt or avoid wood pellet heating, a renewable energy technology. A 2008 mail survey of 737 households—both adopters and non-adopters—tested an integrated model combining psychological factors (e.g., attitudes, perceived control, habits, and social norms), perceived characteristics of wood pellet systems, and ecological values. Using path analysis, the results support the model: adoption is primarily driven by a deliberate process where households evaluate heating system traits (like reliability and cost), which shape their attitudes and intentions. Barriers include low perceived control over installation and existing habits (behavioral lock-in). Social norms and ecological values play only a minor, indirect role. The findings suggest prioritizing improvements in perceived functionality and cost, while also addressing habitual decision-making to reduce cognitive lock-in.
psychological-factors-in-the-diffusion-o.layman: Researchers wanted to know why some Norwegian homes use wood pellet stoves for heating while others do not. They surveyed 737 households in 2008, asking about their thoughts on the technology. They found that people mostly decide based on practical concerns like cost and reliability, not just personal values or social pressure. Many avoid switching because they feel unsure about making the change or are stuck in old habits. The study suggests making wood pellet heating seem more reliable and affordable could encourage more people to try it.

adoption-and-diffusion-of-heating-system.scientist: Sophisticated modeling techniques can help policy makers examine technology interventions aimed at addressing climate change mitigation and other environmental issues. Since adoption of a new technology is not only based on technical properties, policy makers must also consider human behavior. This paper presents a model for simulating heating system adoption processes from an end-user perspective. A literature review was carried out to identify potential decision-making variables and their relationships. An empirical survey was then conducted to test the variables and their interconnections as well as to derive model parameters. The empirically grounded agent-based model is able to reproduce the general patterns of heating system diffusion observable in Norway. The results suggest that increased adoption of wood-pellet heating is dependent on improved functional reliability and the improvement of fuel stability. Price volatility of both wood-pellets and electricity are important variables. Spatial results indicate that wood-pellet adopters are those closeby wood-pellet suppliers.
adoption-and-diffusion-of-heating-system.student: Policy makers often need to predict how new technologies, like heating systems, will be adopted to address climate change. This study develops a model to simulate how households choose heating systems, focusing on user behavior rather than just technical features. The researchers first reviewed existing literature to identify key factors influencing decisions, such as cost, reliability, and fuel availability. They then conducted a survey to test these factors and gather data for the model. The resulting agent-based model, grounded in real-world data, successfully replicated patterns of heating system adoption in Norway. Findings indicate that wood-pellet heating adoption depends on improved reliability and fuel stability, with price fluctuations in wood-pellets and electricity also playing a role. Spatial analysis showed that households near wood-pellet suppliers were more likely to adopt the technology.
adoption-and-diffusion-of-heating-system.layman: Researchers wanted to understand how people decide to switch to wood-pellet heating systems. They studied what influences these choices, like cost, reliability, and whether fuel is easy to get. They built a computer model based on real survey data to predict adoption patterns. The model showed that people are more likely to use wood-pellet heating if it works well and the fuel is stable. Prices of wood-pellets and electricity also matter. People living near suppliers were more likely to switch.

the-psychology-of-pro-environmental-comm.scientist: This book explores the psychological underpinnings of pro-environmental communication, moving beyond traditional information-based strategies. It examines how communication can effectively promote sustainable behavior by integrating insights from social psychology, decision models, and theories of communication. The work addresses the potential and limitations of environmental communication, the role of media (traditional and new), and innovative approaches such as games, simulations, and large-scale social systems. It also discusses target group segmentation and intervention techniques, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding and improving environmental communication strategies.
the-psychology-of-pro-environmental-comm.student: This book investigates how psychological principles can enhance pro-environmental communication, shifting focus from mere information sharing. It explores how strategies rooted in social psychology, decision-making models, and communication theories can encourage sustainable behavior. The work assesses the strengths and weaknesses of environmental messaging, the influence of both traditional and digital media, and novel methods like interactive games and simulations. It also examines how to tailor messages to specific audiences and applies intervention techniques, offering a structured approach to understanding and refining environmental communication.
the-psychology-of-pro-environmental-comm.layman: This book asks how we can better talk to people to encourage them to act in ways that help the environment. The authors look at what works and what doesn’t in these messages, including how different types of media and new tools like games can play a role. They also explore how to customize messages for different groups of people, aiming to make environmental communication more effective.

balancing-the-norwegian-regulated-power-.scientist: The balancing market for power is designed to account for the difference between predicted supply/demand of electricity and the realised supply/demand. However, increased electrification of society changes the consumption patterns, and increased production from renewable sources leads to larger un-predicted fluctuations in production, both effects potentially leading to increased balancing. We analyse public market data for the balancing market (manual Frequency Restoration Reserve) for Norway from 2016 to 2022 to investigate and document these effects. The data is newer than for similar analyses and the eight years of data is more than double the time span previously covered. The main findings are: (a) The balancing volumes are dominated by hours of zero regulation but for non-zero hours, the balancing volumes are increasing during the eight-year period. (b) The balancing prices are primarily correlated with day-ahead prices and secondarily with balancing volumes. The latter correlation is found to be increasingly non-linear with time. (c) The balancing volumes and the price difference between balancing price and day-ahead price are strongly correlated with the previous hour. (d) The increasing share of wind power has not impacted the frequency of balancing, which has remained stable during the 8 years studied. However, the volumes and share of balancing power compared to overall production have increased, suggesting that the hours which are inherently difficult to predict remain the same. (e) Market data alone cannot predict balancing volumes. If attempting, the auto-correlation becomes the main source of information.
balancing-the-norwegian-regulated-power-.student: The power balancing market adjusts for differences between predicted and actual electricity supply and demand. With more electrification and renewable energy, consumption and production patterns become harder to predict, potentially increasing the need for balancing. This study analyses public data from Norway’s manual Frequency Restoration Reserve (a balancing market mechanism) from 2016 to 2022—newer and more extensive than prior work. Key findings: (a) Most hours require no balancing, but when needed, volumes have risen over time. (b) Balancing prices correlate most with day-ahead prices (prices set a day in advance) and secondarily with balancing volumes, with the latter link growing more non-linear. (c) Balancing volumes and price differences from day-ahead prices are strongly tied to the previous hour’s data. (d) Wind power’s share has grown, but balancing frequency stayed stable; however, balancing volumes and their share of total production have increased. (e) Market data alone cannot predict balancing volumes—past trends (auto-correlation) are the main clue.
balancing-the-norwegian-regulated-power-.layman: Electricity grids must balance supply and demand in real time. As more people use electricity and more power comes from wind and sun, predicting this balance gets harder. Researchers studied eight years of Norwegian data to see how often and how much the grid needed adjustments. They found that while most hours needed no changes, the amount of adjustment grew over time when it was needed. Prices for these adjustments were mostly tied to the next day’s expected prices, and the need for adjustments often depended on what happened the hour before. Wind power didn’t make adjustments more frequent, but the total amount of adjustment did increase. Past data alone couldn’t predict future needs.

topology-of-fracture-networks-be7423.scientist: We propose a mapping from fracture systems consisting of intersecting fracture sheets in three dimensions to an abstract network consisting of nodes and links. This makes it possible to analyze fracture systems with the methods developed within modern network theory. We test the mapping for two-dimensional geological fracture outcrops and find that the equivalent networks are small-world and disassortative. By analyzing the Discrete Fracture Network model, which is used to generate artificial fracture outcrop networks, we also find small world networks. However, the networks turn out to be assortative.
topology-of-fracture-networks-be7423.student: This study addresses how to represent complex geological fracture systems—intersecting cracks in rock—as abstract networks of nodes (junctions) and links (fracture segments). This allows the use of network theory to analyze their structure. The researchers tested this approach on real two-dimensional fracture outcrops and found the resulting networks were *small-world* (nodes are closely connected despite low average connections) and *disassortative* (nodes with many connections tend to link to nodes with few). They also applied the method to a computational model (Discrete Fracture Network) and found small-world properties again, but with *assortative* mixing (nodes with many connections link to similar nodes).
topology-of-fracture-networks-be7423.layman: The researchers wanted to understand how cracks in rocks connect by turning them into simple network maps. They studied real rock surfaces and computer-generated crack patterns. In real rocks, the networks were tightly linked but with a mix of well-connected and poorly connected points. In the computer model, the networks were also tightly linked, but well-connected points tended to link to other well-connected points.

large-scale-offshore-wind-development-an.scientist: Modelling of the energy system in the countries surrounding the North Sea is performed with a focus on Norway and offshore wind farms situated in the North Sea. The geographically heterogeneous consumption and production distribution in Norway warrants a disaggregation of the country into separate regions. The ambitious targets set forth by the Norwegian government to license 30 GW of offshore wind generation capacity by 2040 also make the detailed study of the effects of such a large introduction of intermittent renewable energy relevant. We have selected to adhere to the Norwegian power market price zones in our disaggregation, resulting in five regions in Norway. In addition, a separate offshore zone has been added for offshore wind energy generation. This paper studies the resulting optimal capacity expansion and energy dispatch from the energy system model GENeSYS-MOD as a result of a) the disaggregation of Norway into 5 regions b) the introduction of an offshore region for offshore wind generation connected to NO2. The modeled time frame is from 2018 to 2050. The results show that a large introduction of offshore wind capacity results in less capacity expansion of onshore wind and considerably less solar capacity development.
large-scale-offshore-wind-development-an.student: This study models the energy system of North Sea countries, focusing on Norway and its offshore wind farms. Norway’s uneven energy production and consumption require splitting the country into regions. The Norwegian government aims to license 30 GW of offshore wind by 2040, making it important to study how this intermittent renewable energy affects the system. The model divides Norway into five regions based on its power market price zones and adds a separate offshore zone for wind generation. Using the GENeSYS-MOD energy system model, the paper examines how disaggregating Norway and introducing an offshore wind region (connected to one of Norway’s zones) influence optimal capacity expansion and energy dispatch from 2018 to 2050. Results indicate that adding significant offshore wind capacity reduces the need for onshore wind and solar capacity expansion.
large-scale-offshore-wind-development-an.layman: Researchers studied how adding large amounts of wind power from the North Sea might change Norway’s energy system. They split Norway into five areas to better understand energy use and production. They also created a special zone for offshore wind farms. Using a computer model, they looked at how energy might be produced and used from 2018 to 2050. They found that building more offshore wind farms means less need for wind and solar farms on land.

the-representation-of-hydrogen-in-open-s.scientist: The intermittent nature of wind and solar power has led to a scientific consensus in the international energy research community that a mix of energy sources and carriers is necessary to achieve carbon neutrality. The search for alternatives has sparked renewed interest in Hydrogen (H2) and its derivatives, such as ammonia and methane. It has also motivated researchers to expand their models to study H2 investments in future energy systems. However, despite years of well-motivated research, a single scalable model that captures the unique characteristics of H2 does not yet exist. It is a consequence of the limitations imposed by computational resources and the availability of data. With the above motivation, we review the current literature on relevant aspects for H2. We find that temporal resolution, seasonal storage, spatial resolution and grid representation, uncertainty, and sector-coupling are important to accurately model H2. We then analyze 18 case studies based on 11 open-source Capacity Expansion Models (CEMs) applied to study power or energy systems in developed countries that include H2 and evaluate which models capture these idiosyncrasies best. Although no model covers all aspects simultaneously, some models tend to be more efficient in certain aspects, which ultimately depends on the underlying research questions they aim to address. We also outline potential research directions in this area.
the-representation-of-hydrogen-in-open-s.student: Wind and solar power are intermittent, so energy researchers agree that a mix of sources—like hydrogen (H2) and its derivatives—is needed for carbon neutrality. Yet, no single scalable model fully captures H2’s unique traits due to computational and data limits. This study reviews literature on key aspects for modeling H2: temporal resolution (time detail), seasonal storage, spatial resolution (geographic detail), grid representation, uncertainty, and sector-coupling (linking energy sectors). It then evaluates 18 case studies using 11 open-source Capacity Expansion Models (CEMs)—tools that plan future energy systems—applied in developed countries. While no model covers all aspects, some excel in specific areas depending on their research goals. The work also suggests future research directions.
the-representation-of-hydrogen-in-open-s.layman: Wind and solar power don’t always produce energy, so experts think we need other sources, like hydrogen, to cut carbon emissions. But creating a perfect model for hydrogen is hard because of limited computer power and data. The researchers looked at past studies and found that good models need to account for time, storage, location, and how energy systems connect. They then checked 18 real-world examples using existing planning tools. No model does everything well, but some are better at certain tasks. They also suggest where to focus next.

predictions-of-prices-and-volumes-in-the.scientist: The electricity market is driven by complicated interactions that are hard to model analytically. This is particularly the case for the balancing market, where imbalances between supply and demand after the day-ahead market clearance are balanced. The balancing market bridges the gap between the day-ahead market and the actual power system operations. Being able to predict the necessary balancing volumes and prices some hours in advance of the operational hour will allow power producers to plan their production and trading in a more optimal way. There exist large amounts of open data that could contain predictive information about the balancing market, including day-ahead market data and climatic data. However, the literature on forecasting volume and prices in the balancing market is sparse compared to the rich literature on forecasting for the day-ahead market. Neural networks are powerful functional approximators and well-suited to model the complex relationships in the power market. It may also be used to study the predictability of the balancing volumes and prices forward in time. In this paper, we develop a model based on long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks to predict volumes and prices in the Nordic balancing market based on public accessible data. Results show that the LSTM model performs well when compared to the two baselines selected. However, the performance is not significantly better, which indicates that the market data does not hold significant predictive information.
predictions-of-prices-and-volumes-in-the.student: The electricity market involves complex interactions, especially in the balancing market, which adjusts supply and demand mismatches after the day-ahead market (where electricity is traded for the next day). Predicting balancing volumes and prices hours ahead could help producers optimize production and trading. While open data (e.g., day-ahead market and weather data) exists, forecasting for the balancing market is less studied than for the day-ahead market. Neural networks, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) networks—designed to capture sequential patterns—are well-suited for modeling such complexities. This study uses an LSTM model to predict Nordic balancing market volumes and prices from public data. The model outperforms two baseline methods but not significantly, suggesting the market data may lack strong predictive signals.
predictions-of-prices-and-volumes-in-the.layman: Electricity markets adjust supply and demand in real time to keep the grid stable. This study asked if we can predict these adjustments and their costs hours in advance. Researchers used a type of AI that learns from past data to make these predictions. The AI worked better than simpler methods, but not by much. This suggests that the available data may not hold enough clues to make accurate forecasts.

lessons-for-data-driven-modelling-from-h.scientist: With the advancing integration of fluctuating renewables, a more dynamic demand-side, and a grid running closer to its operational limits, future power system operators require new tools to anticipate unwanted events. Advances in machine learning and availability of data suggest great potential in using data-driven approaches, but these will only ever be as good as the data they are based on. To lay the groundwork for future data-driven modelling, we establish a baseline state by analysing the statistical distribution of voltage measurements from three sites in the Norwegian power grid (22, 66, and 300 kV). Measurements span four years, are line and phase voltages, are cycle-by-cycle, and include all (even and odd) harmonics up to the 96th order. They are based on four years of historical data from three ELSPEC Power Quality Analyzers (corresponding to one trillion samples), which we have extracted, processed, and analyzed. We find that: (i) the distribution of harmonics depends on phase and voltage level; (ii) there is little power beyond the 13th harmonic; (iii) there is temporal clumping of extreme values; and (iv) there is seasonality on different time-scales. For machine learning based modelling these findings suggest that: (i) models should be trained in two steps (first with data from all sites, then adapted to site-level); (ii) including harmonics beyond the 13th is unlikely to increase model performance, and that modelling should include features that (iii) encode the state of the grid, as well as (iv) seasonality.
lessons-for-data-driven-modelling-from-h.student: As power grids incorporate more renewable energy and operate closer to their limits, operators need better tools to predict problems. This study analyzes voltage data from three Norwegian grid sites (22, 66, and 300 kV) over four years, using cycle-by-cycle measurements of line and phase voltages, including all harmonics up to the 96th order. The data, totaling one trillion samples, reveals that harmonic distributions vary by phase and voltage level, with little power beyond the 13th harmonic. Extreme values cluster in time, and seasonal patterns appear at different scales. For machine learning models, these findings imply a two-step training process (general then site-specific), limited benefit from higher harmonics, and the need to account for grid state and seasonality.
lessons-for-data-driven-modelling-from-h.layman: Power grids are getting more complex as they add renewable energy. To help predict issues, researchers studied four years of voltage data from three Norwegian power stations. They found that unusual voltage spikes often happen in groups, and patterns change with the seasons. Most of the useful information comes from the first few voltage fluctuations, with little benefit from looking at higher ones. This suggests future tools should focus on these key details to work better.

the-value-of-multiple-data-sources-in-ma.scientist: We describe a method for assessing the value of additional data sources used in the prediction of unwanted events (voltage dips, earth faults) in the power system. Using this method, machine learning models for event prediction using (combinations of) different data sources are developed. The value of each data source is the improvement in model performance it brings. In addition, feature importance is retrieved using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). The methodology is applied to models that predict faults based on power quality and weather data. We find that models that combine sources outperform models using either in isolation. They predict ground faults and voltage dips with AUCs (Area Under Curve) of 0.74 and 0.80, respectively. Meteorological data appears more valuable than power quality data and the most important features are dew point, month of the year, and the power spectral density at 4.7 Hz.
the-value-of-multiple-data-sources-in-ma.student: This study presents a way to measure how much extra data sources improve predictions of power system faults like voltage dips and earth faults. Researchers built machine learning models using different combinations of power quality data (e.g., voltage measurements) and weather data. The value of each data source was determined by how much it boosted model performance. They also used SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a method to rank feature importance. When applied to real data, models using both power quality and weather data performed better than those using just one. For example, combined models achieved AUC scores of 0.74 for ground faults and 0.80 for voltage dips. Weather data, particularly dew point, month, and a specific frequency in power signals, proved more useful than power quality data alone.
the-value-of-multiple-data-sources-in-ma.layman: The researchers wanted to know if adding weather data helps predict power outages better than just using electrical measurements. They built computer models that used both types of data and found that combining them worked best. The models could predict two kinds of outages with moderate accuracy. Weather information, like humidity and time of year, turned out to be more helpful than the electrical data for making these predictions.

impact-of-seasonal-weather-on-forecastin.scientist: Power supply disruptions, including short-time disturbances, can lead to large direct and indirect financial losses. The ability to predict the risk of these disturbances allows for preventive actions and increases the reliability of the supply. This paper investigates the impact of using seasonal data of combined common weather conditions on the power quality prediction in distribution grids. Our main contribution consists of weather-based predictive models for three types of events that frequently occur in these grids, as well as an analysis of the influence of two training approaches: with either seasonal or all-year data, on their performance. All developed models score higher than arbitrary guessing; in several instances the improvement is considerable. It is demonstrated that in some cases the models improve when the training data is limited to a subset corresponding to a particular meteorological season. Examining variable importance values and distributions of the models’ data, it is shown that this situation takes place particularly when weather conditions correlated with the occurrence of power grid events vary across seasons.
impact-of-seasonal-weather-on-forecastin.student: Power supply disruptions, even brief ones, can cause significant financial damage. This study explores whether using seasonal weather data improves predictions of power quality issues in distribution grids. The researchers built weather-based models to forecast three common types of grid events and tested two training approaches: one using data from a single season and another using year-round data. All models outperformed random guessing, with some showing substantial gains. The results indicate that seasonal training data can enhance model performance, especially when the weather conditions linked to grid events differ between seasons. The analysis also highlights which weather variables most influence the predictions.
impact-of-seasonal-weather-on-forecastin.layman: Power outages, even short ones, can cost a lot of money. This research asked if using weather data from specific seasons could help predict power problems in electrical grids. The team created models that use weather to forecast common grid issues and tested whether training them with seasonal or yearly data worked better. The models did better than random guessing, and in some cases, using only seasonal data improved their accuracy. This happened when the weather patterns causing power issues changed with the seasons.

clustering-and-dimensionality-reduction-.scientist: The power system is changing rapidly, and new tools for predicting unwanted events are needed to keep a high level of security of supply. Large volumes of data from the Norwegian power grid have been collected over several years, and unwanted events such as interruptions, earth faults, voltage dips and rapid voltage changes have been logged. This paper demonstrates the application of clustering and dimensionality-reduction techniques for the purpose of predicting unwanted events. Several techniques have been applied to reduce the dimensionality of the datasets and to cluster events based on analytical features, to separate events containing faults from a normal situation. The paper shows that the developed predictive model has some predictive capability when using balanced datasets containing similar number of fault events and non-fault events. One of the main findings, however, is that this predictive capability is significantly reduced when using unbalanced datasets. Thus, the development of an accurate predictive model based on normal power system conditions, i.e. an unbalanced dataset of events and non-events, is a topic for further research.
clustering-and-dimensionality-reduction-.student: The Norwegian power grid generates large datasets, including records of unwanted events like interruptions, earth faults, and voltage dips. This study applies clustering and dimensionality-reduction techniques—methods that group similar data points and simplify complex datasets—to predict such events. By extracting analytical features from the data, the researchers separated fault events from normal conditions. The predictive model showed some success when tested on balanced datasets (equal numbers of fault and non-fault events). However, its performance dropped significantly with unbalanced datasets, where normal conditions far outnumber faults. This suggests that building an accurate model for real-world, unbalanced data remains an open challenge.
clustering-and-dimensionality-reduction-.layman: Researchers studied years of data from Norway’s power grid to predict problems like outages or voltage drops. They used math tools to sort and simplify the data, finding patterns that signal trouble. Their method worked fairly well when the data had equal numbers of problems and normal cases. But when most of the data was normal, the method struggled. This means predicting real-world issues, where problems are rare, is still difficult.

impact-of-the-temporal-distribution-of-f.scientist: Is it possible to reliably predict voltage anomalies in the power grid minutes in advance using machine learning models trained on large quantities of historical data collected by power quality analysers (PQA)? Very little previous research has been done on this topic. To investigate whether this is possible a machine learning model was developed that attempts to predict voltage anomalies 10 minutes in advance based on the presence of early warning signs in the preceding 50 minutes. The model was trained on voltage data collected from 49 measuring locations in the Norwegian power grid. Although results were inconclusive, it was observed that the time that has passed since the previous fault at the same location is a major factor to consider when estimating the probability that a new fault is imminent. It was observed that the probability that a new fault is imminent is proportional to the logarithm of the time passed since the previous anomaly. This means that the risk of a new anomaly is drastically reduced as more time passes since the previous anomaly. This is important to take into consideration when attempting to develop a model that estimates the probability that a new fault is imminent.
impact-of-the-temporal-distribution-of-f.student: Can machine learning predict voltage anomalies in power grids minutes ahead using historical data from power quality analysers (PQA)? This study explored that question, as prior research is scarce. A model was built to forecast anomalies 10 minutes in advance by detecting early warning signs in the preceding 50 minutes of data. It was trained on voltage measurements from 49 locations in Norway’s grid. While the results were inconclusive, one clear pattern emerged: the time elapsed since the last fault at a given location strongly influences the likelihood of a new one. Specifically, the probability of an imminent fault decreases sharply as more time passes since the last anomaly, following a logarithmic trend. This insight is critical for refining future predictive models.
impact-of-the-temporal-distribution-of-f.layman: Can we predict power grid problems minutes before they happen using past data? Researchers tried this by building a computer model that looks for early warning signs in voltage data from 49 locations in Norway. The results were unclear, but they noticed one thing: the longer it’s been since the last problem at a spot, the less likely a new one is to happen soon. The risk drops quickly at first, then more slowly over time. This could help improve future predictions.

comparative-study-of-event-prediction-in.scientist: There is a growing interest in applying machine learning methods on large amounts of data to solve complex problems, such as prediction of events and disturbances in the power system. This paper is a comparative study of the predictive performance of state-of-the-art supervised machine learning methods. The event prediction models are trained and validated using high-resolution power quality data from measuring instruments in the Norwegian power grid. The recorded event categories in the study were voltage dips, ground faults, rapid voltage changes and interruptions. Out of the tested machine learning methods, the Random Forest models indicated a better prediction performance, with an accuracy of 0.602. The results also indicated that rapid voltage changes (accuracy = 0.710) and voltage dips (accuracy = 0.601) are easiest to predict among the tested power quality events.
comparative-study-of-event-prediction-in.student: Researchers compared how well different machine learning methods predict power system disturbances using real data from Norway’s grid. The disturbances included voltage dips (brief drops in voltage), ground faults (unintended electrical connections to earth), rapid voltage changes, and interruptions. After training models on high-resolution measurements, they found Random Forest—a method that builds multiple decision trees—performed best overall, with an accuracy of about 60%. Rapid voltage changes were the easiest to predict (71% accuracy), followed by voltage dips (60%). The study suggests some disturbances are more predictable than others with current techniques.
comparative-study-of-event-prediction-in.layman: Scientists tested different computer programs to predict problems in Norway’s electricity network, like sudden voltage drops or power cuts. They used real data from the grid and found one program, called Random Forest, worked best, correctly predicting issues about 60% of the time. Some problems, like quick voltage shifts, were easier to foresee than others. The work shows that while predictions are possible, they are not perfect.

fault-detection-and-prediction-in-smart-.scientist: Modern society is to a larger and larger extent dependent on electric energy, and hence the reliance on and utilization of the electric grid is increasing steadily. At the same time the production and consumption patterns are changing from large centralized generation of electric power and pure consumers to distributed generation (DG) and more complex consumers. This transition causes higher stress on an aging infrastructure and major investments are required over the coming years to maintain a reliable supply of electric energy. Better monitoring solutions and predictive methods can increase the possible utilization of the existing grid and reduce the fault frequency. This paper presents some current challenges in the grid and a possible monitoring solution and fault prediction method. This is exemplified with statistics and field-measurements from the Norwegian power grid.
fault-detection-and-prediction-in-smart-.student: As electricity use grows, the power grid faces new pressures. Traditionally, power came from large, centralized plants, but now more energy is produced locally (distributed generation, or DG) and consumers have more complex needs. This shift strains an aging infrastructure, requiring costly upgrades to keep supply reliable. To make better use of the existing grid and reduce outages, improved monitoring and predictive methods are needed. This paper outlines current grid challenges and proposes a monitoring and fault-prediction approach, supported by statistics and field data from Norway’s power grid.
fault-detection-and-prediction-in-smart-.layman: Our electricity system is getting older and more complicated as people both use and produce power in new ways. This can lead to more breakdowns. The researchers looked at the problems facing the grid and tested a way to watch it more closely and predict when things might go wrong. They used real data from Norway to show how this could help keep the lights on.

on-model-predictive-path-following-and-t.scientist: In this article the model predictive path following controller and the model predictive trajectory tracking controller are compared for a robotic manipulator. We consider both the Runge-Kutta and collocation based discretization. We show how path-following can stop at obstructions in a way trajectory tracking cannot. We give simulations for a two-link manipulator, and discuss the real-time viability of our implementations.
on-model-predictive-path-following-and-t.student: This study compares two control methods for robotic arms: path-following and trajectory-tracking. Path-following guides the arm along a predefined path without strict timing, while trajectory-tracking enforces both path and speed. The team tested both using two numerical methods (Runge-Kutta and collocation) to simulate a two-link robotic arm. Results show path-following can pause at obstacles, unlike trajectory-tracking, which cannot. Simulations also assess whether these methods can run in real-time on actual hardware.
on-model-predictive-path-following-and-t.layman: Researchers tested two ways to control a robot arm’s movement. One method lets the arm follow a path at its own pace, stopping if something blocks it. The other forces the arm to follow a set path and speed, which can’t stop for obstacles. Using computer models of a simple robot arm, they showed the first method works better around barriers. They also checked if the system could work in real time.

adaptive-underwater-robotic-sampling-of-.scientist: To get a better understanding of the highly nonlinear processes driving the ocean, efficient and informative sampling is critical. By combining robotic sampling with ocean models we are able to choose informative sampling sites and adaptively change our path based on measurements. We present models exploiting prior information from ocean models as well as real-time information from in situ measurements. The models use compact Gaussian process modeling and objective functions to locate informative sampling sites. Our aim is to get a better understanding of ocean processes and improve real-time monitoring of dispersal dynamics. The case study focuses on a fjord located in Norway containing a seafill for mine tailings. Transportation of the deposited particles are studied, and the sampling method is tested in the area. The results from these sea trials are presented.
adaptive-underwater-robotic-sampling-of-.student: To study the complex, nonlinear processes in the ocean, efficient sampling is essential. This work combines robotic sampling with ocean models to select informative sites and adapt paths based on real-time measurements. The approach uses Gaussian process modeling—a statistical method for predicting spatial patterns—and objective functions to identify key sampling locations. The goal is to improve understanding of ocean dynamics and real-time monitoring of particle dispersal. A case study in a Norwegian fjord, where mine tailings are deposited, tests the method by tracking particle transport. Results from sea trials are presented, demonstrating the approach’s effectiveness in capturing dispersal patterns.
adaptive-underwater-robotic-sampling-of-.layman: Scientists want to better understand how particles move in the ocean, which is complicated and hard to predict. They used underwater robots that collect data and adjust their route based on what they find. The robots rely on computer models to pick the best spots to sample. In a Norwegian fjord, they tested this method to track how mine waste spreads. The results show how well the robots can follow and study the movement of these particles.

sampling-based-3d-aerial-inspection-path.scientist: This article presents a coverage path planning pipeline for inspection of complex structures in 3D using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The approach generates candidate view points through random sampling of an input model and computes an optimal inspection path through a subset of the views using an RRT*-based planner. The planner optimizes coverage and flight time while penalizing hard turns, and ensures a collision-free and safe path by dilation of the mesh model. Software-in-the-loop (SITL) simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the inspection path planning pipeline in producing collision-free, high-coverage inspection paths for complex models that take the camera and gimbal parameters into account.
sampling-based-3d-aerial-inspection-path.student: This study addresses the problem of planning inspection paths for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to examine complex 3D structures. The method first randomly samples an input 3D model to generate potential camera viewpoints. Then, it uses an RRT*-based planner—a pathfinding algorithm that builds a tree of possible routes—to select an optimal subset of these viewpoints. The planner balances coverage, flight time, and smoothness of turns while avoiding collisions by expanding the structure’s mesh model. Simulations show the approach produces safe, collision-free paths with high coverage, accounting for the UAV’s camera and gimbal constraints.
sampling-based-3d-aerial-inspection-path.layman: Researchers developed a way for drones to inspect complicated structures like bridges or buildings. They created a method that picks the best spots for the drone to take pictures and plans a smooth, safe route between them. The drone avoids crashing into the structure while covering as much of it as possible. Tests in a computer simulation showed the method works well, making sure the drone can see everything it needs to without bumping into anything.

estimation-of-future-power-consumption-f.scientist: In drone missions, accurate estimation of remaining flight time is crucial for enhancing mission duration and reducing the risk of losing drones due to power outages. This paper addresses the challenge of predicting future power consumption for a quadcopter UAV, focusing on the energy demands of planned future maneuvers. Existing physics-based energy consumption models assume the drone hovers or moves with constant speed. While orientation and velocity measurements are typically used, acceleration measurements are often ignored, despite being identified as important for power usage prediction in recent machine learning literature. This paper proposes a physics-based, lightweight energy consumption model based on measurements of the quadcopter’s motion, including acceleration. Our model also includes a synthetic wind estimation scheme, enhancing prediction accuracy in outdoor and windy conditions. The model’s predictions for power consumption are compared to real-life flight data, demonstrating the effectiveness of the presented approach despite its relative simplicity.
estimation-of-future-power-consumption-f.student: For drone missions, predicting how much battery remains is key to avoiding crashes and extending flight time. Current physics-based models estimate energy use by assuming drones either hover or move at a steady speed, often ignoring acceleration—even though recent machine learning studies show acceleration affects power consumption. This paper introduces a simple, physics-based model that uses the drone’s motion data, including acceleration, to predict energy use for planned maneuvers. It also estimates wind effects, improving accuracy in outdoor conditions. When tested against real flight data, the model’s predictions matched well, showing that even a straightforward approach can be effective.
estimation-of-future-power-consumption-f.layman: Drones need to know how much battery they have left to avoid running out mid-flight. Most current methods guess energy use by assuming drones either stay still or move at a constant speed, often missing how speeding up or slowing down affects power. This study created a simple model that uses the drone’s movement, including changes in speed, to predict energy use. It also accounts for wind, making it more accurate outdoors. Tests with real drone flights showed the model works well, even though it’s not overly complex.

sensor-guided-motions-for-manipulators-i.scientist: Industrial manipulator arms have traditionally been used for highly repetitive tasks due to their excellent precision, speed and endurance. Today, manufacturing faces higher demands in meeting increased customization, requiring generalization and external sensing. This chapter summarizes efforts on sensor-guided motions within robust and flexible automation in SFI Manufacturing, a cross-disciplinary center for research-based innovation in Norway (2015–2023). It covers applications such as reactive control for assembly, deburring of cast parts, automatic loading and unloading of hanging trolleys, and bin picking of reflective objects. Additionally, it discusses generic methods for planning and control, including nonlinear model predictive control for robot manipulator trajectory tracking and task-priority set-based reactive control. The chapter provides an overview of sensor-guided motions for manipulators in manufacturing and offers recommendations for further research in these areas.
sensor-guided-motions-for-manipulators-i.student: Industrial robot arms excel at repetitive tasks due to their precision and speed, but modern manufacturing demands more adaptability to handle customization. This chapter reviews work from SFI Manufacturing (2015–2023), a Norwegian research center, on using sensors to guide robot movements for flexible automation. Applications include reactive assembly control, smoothing rough cast parts (deburring), loading/unloading hanging trolleys, and picking shiny objects from bins. The text also explores general methods like nonlinear model predictive control—a technique for planning robot paths by predicting and optimizing future states—and task-priority control, which adjusts robot actions based on real-time sensor feedback. The chapter summarizes these advances and suggests directions for future research.
sensor-guided-motions-for-manipulators-i.layman: Factories use robot arms for repetitive jobs because they are fast and precise. But now, factories need to make more varied products, so robots must adapt. Researchers in Norway studied how to use sensors to help robots handle new tasks like assembling parts, smoothing rough edges, or picking up shiny objects. They also developed ways for robots to plan their movements and adjust based on what they sense. The work shows how robots can become more flexible and suggests what to study next.

a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.scientist: Low complexity of a system model is essential for its use in real-time applications. However, sparse identification methods commonly have stringent requirements that exclude them from being applied in an industrial setting. In this article, we introduce a flexible method for the sparse identification of dynamical systems described by ordinary differential equations. Our method relieves many of the requirements imposed by other methods that relate to the structure of the model and the dataset, such as fixed sampling rates, full state measurements, and linearity of the model. The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm is used to solve the identification problem. We show that the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm can be written in a form that enables parallel computing, which greatly diminishes the time required to solve the identification problem. An efficient backward elimination strategy is presented to construct a lean system model.
a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.student: Real-time applications need simple system models, but existing sparse identification methods often impose strict conditions—like fixed sampling rates, full state measurements, or linear models—that make them impractical for industry. This study proposes a flexible approach for identifying dynamical systems described by ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which are equations that model how a system changes over time. Unlike prior methods, it relaxes many constraints on model structure and data. The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm, a numerical technique for solving optimization problems, is adapted here to enable parallel computing, significantly speeding up the identification process. Additionally, a backward elimination strategy is introduced to refine the model, ensuring it remains sparse and efficient.
a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.layman: Researchers wanted to create simple models of complex systems for real-time use, but existing methods often require strict conditions that don’t work in practice. They developed a new, flexible way to build these models using math that describes how systems change over time. They improved a standard problem-solving method to run faster on computers by splitting the work across multiple processors. They also added a step to remove unnecessary parts of the model, making it leaner and more practical.

realizing-lti-models-by-identifying-char.scientist: This paper considers the realization of discrete-time linear time-invariant dynamical systems using input-output data. Starting from a generalized state-space representation that accounts for static offsets, a state-independent system representation is derived using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem and characteristic parameters are introduced to describe the system dynamics in an alternative way. Given input-output data, we present two formulations to address model deviations and to identify characteristic parameters by minimizing considered error terms in a least squares sense. The applicability of the proposed subspace identification method is demonstrated with physical data of the identification database DaISy.
realizing-lti-models-by-identifying-char.student: This study explores how to model discrete-time linear time-invariant systems—systems where the output depends only on the current and past inputs, not on time itself—using only input-output data. The authors start with a generalized state-space model, which includes static offsets, and then simplify it using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem to derive a state-independent representation. They introduce new parameters to describe the system’s behavior differently. Two methods are proposed to handle model errors and estimate these parameters by minimizing error terms via least squares. The approach is tested on real-world data from the DaISy identification database, showing its practical use.
realizing-lti-models-by-identifying-char.layman: The researchers wanted to find a way to predict how a system behaves over time using only its input and output data. They created a new method to describe the system’s behavior without needing its internal details. By adjusting certain values to reduce errors, they could accurately model the system. They tested this method on real data, proving it works in practice.

learning-based-robust-model-predictive-c.scientist: For dynamical systems with uncertainty, robust controllers can be designed by assuming that the uncertainty is bounded. The less we know about the uncertainty in the system, the more conservative the bound must be, which in turn may lead to reduced control performance. If measurements of the uncertain term are available, this data may be used to reduce the uncertainty in order to make bounds as tight as possible. In this paper, we consider a linear system with a sector-bounded uncertainty. We develop a model predictive control algorithm to control the system, and use a weighted Bayesian linear regression model to learn the least conservative sector condition using measurements collected in closed-loop. The resulting robust model predictive control algorithm therefore reduces the conservativeness of the controller, and provides probabilistic guarantees of asymptotic stability and constraint satisfaction. The efficacy of the proposed method is shown in simulation.
learning-based-robust-model-predictive-c.student: In control engineering, robust controllers handle systems with uncertainty by assuming the uncertainty stays within certain bounds. However, if these bounds are too wide, the controller may perform poorly. This study addresses a linear system where the uncertainty is constrained within a sector (a mathematical region defining its behavior). The authors propose a model predictive control (MPC) algorithm, which plans control actions by predicting future system states, combined with a weighted Bayesian linear regression model. This regression model uses real-time measurements to refine the uncertainty bounds, making them as tight as possible. The result is a less conservative MPC controller that still guarantees stability and meets system constraints with high probability. Simulations demonstrate the method’s effectiveness.
learning-based-robust-model-predictive-c.layman: Researchers studied how to better control systems that behave unpredictably. They designed a controller that uses real-time data to reduce guesswork about the system’s behavior. By learning from measurements, the controller becomes more precise without losing reliability. Tests on a computer model showed that this approach works well.

neural-network-based-model-predictive-co.scientist: Learning-based controllers, and especially learning-based model predictive controllers, have been used for a number of different applications with great success. In spite of good performance, a lot of these cases lack stability guarantees. In this paper we consider a scenario where the dynamics of a nonlinear system are unknown, but where input and output data are available. A prediction model is learned from data using a neural network, which in turn is used in a nonlinear model predictive control scheme. The closed-loop system is shown to be input-to-state stable with respect to the prediction error of the learned model. The approach is tested and verified in simulations, by employing the controller to a benchmark system, namely a continuous stirred tank reactor plant. Simulations show that the proposed controller successfully drives the system from random initial conditions, to a reference equilibrium point, even in the presence of noise. The results also verify the theoretical stability result.
neural-network-based-model-predictive-co.student: Learning-based controllers, such as model predictive controllers, often perform well but lack formal stability guarantees. This study addresses a nonlinear system with unknown dynamics but available input-output data. A neural network is trained to predict the system’s behavior from this data, and the resulting model is integrated into a nonlinear model predictive control framework. The closed-loop system is proven to be input-to-state stable relative to the prediction error of the learned model. Simulations on a continuous stirred tank reactor—a common benchmark in control engineering—demonstrate that the controller steers the system from random starting points to a desired equilibrium, even with noise. The results confirm the theoretical stability claim.
neural-network-based-model-predictive-co.layman: Researchers studied how to control a complex system when its inner workings are unknown but past behavior is recorded. They used a computer model trained on this data to predict and guide the system. Their method was tested on a simulated chemical reactor, showing it could reliably steer the system to a target state despite disturbances. The work also proved that the system remains stable under this control.

maritime-object-tracking-from-a-commerci.scientist: The aim of this work was to develop partial maritime situational awareness based on a tracking system using two radars, 12 cameras and common navigational instruments mounted on a commercial vessel operating on the coast of Norway. Objects on the sea surface are tracked based on detections extracted from sensor images which are segmented by convolutional neural networks. The tracker structure consists of a JIPDA filter where marginalized association probabilities are approximated using loopy belief propagation and track initialization is performed using intensities from a PHD filter. The novelties of the proposed tracker are: a) the application to data from a large commercial vessel in operation, b) the use of heterogeneous sensors (multiple radars and optical cameras), and c) the introduction of a visibility state per sensor type enabling the tracker to maintain tracks for objects that are invisible to one of the sensor types. Although no ground truth was available, the results indicate that the implementation efficiently confirms true tracks, discards false tracks, finds and maintains tracks on objects that are (temporarily) invisible to one of the sensor types, and provides increased accuracy compared to a single sensor setup.
maritime-object-tracking-from-a-commerci.student: This study developed a system to monitor maritime activity using sensors on a commercial ship off Norway’s coast. The system combines data from two radars, 12 cameras, and standard navigation tools. Objects on the water are detected by analyzing sensor images with convolutional neural networks, a type of AI that processes visual data. The tracker uses a JIPDA filter (a method for tracking multiple objects with uncertainty) and loopy belief propagation (an algorithm for approximating probabilities) to link detections to objects. It also uses a PHD filter (a tool for estimating the number and states of objects) to start new tracks. The system’s innovations include working on a real, large vessel, using mixed sensor types, and adding a visibility state for each sensor to keep tracking objects even when one sensor can’t see them. Without ground truth data, results suggest the system effectively confirms real objects, ignores false ones, maintains tracks when objects are temporarily hidden from one sensor, and improves accuracy over single-sensor setups.
maritime-object-tracking-from-a-commerci.layman: Researchers built a system to track boats and other objects at sea using sensors on a working ship. They combined data from radars, cameras, and navigation tools, then used computer programs to spot and follow objects. The system can keep track of things even when one sensor loses sight of them. Tests showed it works well at spotting real objects, ignoring false ones, and keeping track better than using just one sensor.

learning-similarity-measures-from-data-0.scientist: Defining similarity measures is a requirement for some machine learning methods. One such method is case-based reasoning (CBR) where the similarity measure is used to retrieve the stored case or a set of cases most similar to the query case. Describing a similarity measure analytically is challenging, even for domain experts working with CBR experts. However, datasets are typically gathered as part of constructing a CBR or machine learning system. These datasets are assumed to contain the features that correctly identify the solution from the problem features; thus, they may also contain the knowledge to construct or learn such a similarity measure. The main motivation for this work is to automate the construction of similarity measures using machine learning. Additionally, we would like to do this while keeping training time as low as possible. Working toward this, our objective is to investigate how to apply machine learning to effectively learn a similarity measure. Such a learned similarity measure could be used for CBR systems, but also for clustering data in semi-supervised learning, or one-shot learning tasks. Recent work has advanced toward this goal which relies on either very long training times or manually modeling parts of the similarity measure. We created a framework to help us analyze the current methods for learning similarity measures. This analysis resulted in two novel similarity measure designs: The first design uses a pre-trained classifier as basis for a similarity measure, and the second design uses as little modeling as possible while learning the similarity measure from data and keeping training time low. Both similarity measures were evaluated on 14 different datasets. The evaluation shows that using a classifier as basis for a similarity measure gives state-of-the-art performance. Finally, the evaluation shows that our fully data-driven similarity measure design outperforms state-of-the-art methods while keeping training time low.
learning-similarity-measures-from-data-0.student: Case-based reasoning (CBR) is a machine learning approach that solves new problems by comparing them to past cases, using a similarity measure to find the closest matches. Defining this measure is difficult, even for experts. This study explores automating its construction using machine learning, aiming for low training time. The researchers developed a framework to analyze existing methods and proposed two new designs: one using a pre-trained classifier to define similarity, and another learning similarity directly from data with minimal modeling. Both were tested on 14 datasets. The classifier-based measure achieved state-of-the-art performance, while the fully data-driven design outperformed existing methods with low training time.
learning-similarity-measures-from-data-0.layman: Researchers wanted to automate how computers judge how similar two things are, which helps them solve problems by comparing them to past examples. They built a system to test different ways of doing this and came up with two new methods. One uses a pre-trained program to decide similarity, and the other learns it directly from data quickly. Both were tested on many examples. The first method worked as well as the best existing ones, and the second worked even better while being fast to train.

divide-and-conquer-for-causal-computatio.scientist: Structural causal models are a powerful framework for causal and counterfactual inference, extending the capabilities of traditional Bayesian networks. These models comprise endogenous and exogenous variables, where the exogenous variables frequently lack clear semantic interpretation. Exogenous variables are typically unobservable, rendering certain counterfactual queries unidentifiable. In such cases, standard inference algorithms for Bayesian networks are insufficient. Recent methods attempt to bound unidentifiable queries through imprecise estimation of exogenous probabilities. However, these methods become computationally infeasible as the cardinality of the exogenous variables increases, thereby constraining the complexity of applicable models. In this paper we study a divide-and-conquer approach that decomposes a general causal model into a set of submodels with low-cardinality exogenous variables, enabling exact calculation of any query within these submodels. By aggregating results from the submodels, efficient approximations of bounds for queries in the original model are obtained. Our proposal is able to handle models with variables of any cardinality assuming that there are no unobserved confounders. We show that the method is theoretically robust, and experimental results demonstrate that it achieves more accurate bounds with lower computational costs compared to existing techniques.
divide-and-conquer-for-causal-computatio.student: Structural causal models (SCMs) extend Bayesian networks to handle cause-and-effect reasoning, including counterfactuals (what-if scenarios). These models include endogenous variables (influenced by others) and exogenous variables (external influences, often unobservable). When exogenous variables are unobservable, some counterfactual questions cannot be answered precisely. Existing methods try to estimate bounds for these answers but become impractical as the number of possible values (cardinality) for exogenous variables grows. This paper proposes a divide-and-conquer approach: it splits a complex SCM into smaller submodels with fewer exogenous values, allowing exact calculations within each. Results from these submodels are then combined to approximate bounds for the original model. The method works for any variable cardinality, assuming no hidden confounders, and is shown to be theoretically sound. Experiments confirm it provides tighter bounds with less computational effort than prior techniques.
divide-and-conquer-for-causal-computatio.layman: Researchers study how to answer 'what-if' questions in complex systems where some causes are hidden. Current methods struggle when there are many possible hidden influences. The team breaks the big problem into smaller, manageable pieces, solves each piece exactly, and combines the results to estimate answers for the whole system. Their approach works for any number of hidden influences, as long as there are no hidden connections between causes. Tests show it gives better estimates faster than older methods.

prediction-intervals-split-normal-mixtur.scientist: Prediction intervals are a machine- and human-interpretable way to represent predictive uncertainty in a regression analysis. In this paper, we present a method for generating prediction intervals along with point estimates from an ensemble of neural networks. We propose a multi-objective loss function fusing quality measures related to prediction intervals and point estimates, and a penalty function, which enforces semantic integrity of the results and stabilizes the training process of the neural networks. The ensembled prediction intervals are aggregated as a split normal mixture accounting for possible multimodality and asymmetricity of the posterior predictive distribution, and resulting in prediction intervals that capture aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Our results show that both our quality-driven loss function and our aggregation method contribute to well-calibrated prediction intervals and point estimates.
prediction-intervals-split-normal-mixtur.student: This study addresses the challenge of representing uncertainty in regression predictions, where the goal is to estimate a continuous output. Prediction intervals provide a range within which the true value is expected to fall with a certain probability. The authors propose a method using an ensemble of neural networks—multiple models combined—to generate both point estimates (single predicted values) and prediction intervals. They introduce a multi-objective loss function, which balances the accuracy of both the intervals and the point estimates, and a penalty term to ensure the results remain meaningful and training is stable. The intervals are combined using a split normal mixture model, which accounts for complex, asymmetric, or multi-peaked uncertainty distributions. The findings suggest that both the loss function and the aggregation method improve the calibration of the prediction intervals and point estimates.
prediction-intervals-split-normal-mixtur.layman: The researchers wanted to improve how computers predict numbers, like future temperatures or house prices, by also showing how uncertain those predictions are. They used a group of AI models working together to create a range where the true answer is likely to be. They designed a new way to train these models so the predictions and their uncertainty ranges are both accurate. They also combined the models’ results in a way that handles messy, uneven uncertainty. The results show this approach makes the predictions and their uncertainty ranges more reliable.

probabilistic-models-with-deep-neural-ne.scientist: Recent advances in statistical inference have significantly expanded the toolbox of probabilistic modeling. Historically, probabilistic modeling has been constrained to very restricted model classes, where exact or approximate probabilistic inference is feasible. However, developments in variational inference, a general form of approximate probabilistic inference that originated in statistical physics, have enabled probabilistic modeling to overcome these limitations: (i) Approximate probabilistic inference is now possible over a broad class of probabilistic models containing a large number of parameters, and (ii) scalable inference methods based on stochastic gradient descent and distributed computing engines allow probabilistic modeling to be applied to massive data sets. One important practical consequence of these advances is the possibility to include deep neural networks within probabilistic models, thereby capturing complex non-linear stochastic relationships between the random variables. These advances, in conjunction with the release of novel probabilistic modeling toolboxes, have greatly expanded the scope of applications of probabilistic models, and allowed the models to take advantage of the recent strides made by the deep learning community. In this paper, we provide an overview of the main concepts, methods, and tools needed to use deep neural networks within a probabilistic modeling framework.
probabilistic-models-with-deep-neural-ne.student: Probabilistic modeling traditionally relied on simple models where exact calculations were possible. Recent progress in variational inference—a method for approximating complex probability distributions—has changed this. Now, researchers can work with large, intricate models, even those with millions of parameters, and apply them to huge datasets using scalable techniques like stochastic gradient descent and distributed computing. A key outcome is the ability to integrate deep neural networks into probabilistic models, letting them capture complex, non-linear relationships between variables. This paper surveys the main ideas, methods, and tools for combining deep neural networks with probabilistic modeling, expanding the range of problems these models can address.
probabilistic-models-with-deep-neural-ne.layman: Scientists used to build simple models to predict uncertain events, but these were limited. New methods now let them create much more complex models and use them on large amounts of data. One big improvement is that these models can now include advanced systems called deep neural networks, which help uncover hidden patterns. This paper explains how to use these new tools together to make better predictions.

bayesian-exploration-in-deep-reinforceme.scientist: Posterior sampling of value functions can give efficient exploration for value-based reinforcement learning algorithms. We introduce BayesianExplore (BE), a posterior sampling-based method for reinforcement learning based on Bayesian function-space variational inference over stochastic processes. This Bayesian formalism allows us to formalize domain knowledge as a prior over the value function. Our approach, therefore, provides an alternative to reward shaping with the added benefit that the algorithm keeps seeking an optimal policy in the original environment instead of the one with altered rewards. We show that BE produces state-of-the-art efficiency in exploration with flat priors, and that it is easy to significantly improve performance by incorporating domain knowledge using simple priors.
bayesian-exploration-in-deep-reinforceme.student: In reinforcement learning, agents learn optimal actions by trial and error, but exploration—trying new actions to discover better strategies—can be inefficient. This study introduces BayesianExplore (BE), a method that uses posterior sampling, a technique where the agent samples possible value functions (estimates of future rewards) from a probability distribution. BE is built on Bayesian variational inference over stochastic processes, allowing it to incorporate prior knowledge about the environment as a starting assumption for the value function. Unlike reward shaping, which modifies the environment’s rewards to guide learning, BE maintains the original reward structure while still improving exploration. The results show that BE achieves state-of-the-art exploration efficiency even with simple, flat priors, and performance can be further enhanced by adding domain-specific knowledge through tailored priors.
bayesian-exploration-in-deep-reinforceme.layman: The researchers asked how a computer program can learn to make good decisions by trying new things without wasting too much time. They created a method called BayesianExplore that lets the program guess possible outcomes based on past experience and a starting assumption about how the world works. Unlike other methods that change the rules of the game to guide learning, this one keeps the original rules but still helps the program explore better. They found it works very well even with simple assumptions, and adding more knowledge about the task makes it even better.

the-multiquadric-kernel-for-moment-match.scientist: Distributional reinforcement learning has gained significant attention in recent years due to its ability to handle uncertainty and variability in the returns an agent will receive for each action it takes. A key challenge in distributional reinforcement learning is finding a measure of the difference between two distributions that is well-suited for use with the distributional Bellman operator, a function that takes in a value distribution and produces a modified distribution based on the agent’s current state and action. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing the multiquadric kernel to moment-matching distributional reinforcement learning. We show that this kernel is both theoretically sound and empirically effective. Our contribution is mainly of a theoretical nature, presenting the first formally sound kernel for moment-matching distributional reinforcement learning with good practical performance. We also provide insights into why the RBF kernel has been shown to provide good practical results despite its theoretical problems. Finally, we evaluate the performance of our kernel on a number of standard benchmarks, obtaining results comparable to the state-of-the-art.
the-multiquadric-kernel-for-moment-match.student: Distributional reinforcement learning (RL) improves how agents learn by modeling the full range of possible rewards, not just their average. A central problem is measuring how different two reward distributions are, especially when using the distributional Bellman operator—a tool that updates these distributions as the agent learns. This paper introduces the multiquadric kernel, a new way to compare distributions in moment-matching RL, which focuses on aligning statistical properties like mean and variance. The authors show this kernel is theoretically valid and works well in practice, offering the first formally sound method of its kind. They also explain why a previously used kernel (RBF) worked despite theoretical flaws. Tests on standard benchmarks show the new kernel performs as well as leading methods.
the-multiquadric-kernel-for-moment-match.layman: Researchers studied how to improve a type of learning system for computers, where the system tries to predict all possible rewards for its actions, not just the average. They created a new way to compare these reward predictions, proving it works both in theory and in tests. They also explained why an older method worked even though it had flaws. The new approach performed as well as the best existing ones in experiments.

asap-attention-based-state-space-abstrac.scientist: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has shown remarkable performance, but end-users do not understand how the system solves tasks due to the black-box nature of neural networks. Many methods from explainable machine learning have been adapted to RL. However, they do not focus on the unique challenges of explaining actions’ short-term and long-term consequences.
