This work introduces a new perspective to understanding RL policies by clustering states into abstract states utilizing attention maps, giving a bird’s-eye view of the policy’s behavior. We learn the attention maps iteratively together with the clustering of states by masking the input features to estimate their importance. In contrast to previous works that have uninterpretable abstract states and/or clustering objectives using state values that are non-human intuitive, we only leverage attention maps in the clustering. The policy only indirectly affects the clustering via attention maps. This allows us to give global explanations from the view of feature attention, a quantity a human can relate to given interpretable features. The experiments demonstrate that our method provides faithful abstractions by capturing state semantics, policy behavior, and feature attention. Furthermore, we show that our attention maps can mask state features without affecting policy performance.
asap-attention-based-state-space-abstrac.student: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) systems, which use neural networks to learn tasks through trial and error, often act as 'black boxes'—their decision-making is hard to interpret. While explainable AI methods exist, they rarely address RL’s unique challenge: explaining both immediate and long-term effects of actions. This study proposes a new approach to interpret RL policies by grouping similar states into abstract categories using attention maps—visual tools that highlight which input features (e.g., sensor readings) the system focuses on. Unlike prior work, which relies on abstract states or clustering based on non-intuitive values, this method clusters states solely using attention maps, making the process more transparent. The policy influences clustering only indirectly, via these maps. Experiments show the method captures meaningful state patterns, policy behavior, and feature importance, while masking irrelevant features without harming performance.
asap-attention-based-state-space-abstrac.layman: Artificial intelligence systems that learn by trial and error often make decisions that are hard to understand. This research aims to explain how these systems work by grouping similar situations together and showing which details they pay attention to. The team created a way to highlight the most important parts of the input data, like a map of what the system focuses on. Tests showed this method helps reveal how the system makes choices and what it considers important, without changing how well it performs.

lecture-notes-in-probabilistic-diffusion.scientist: Diffusion models are loosely modelled based on non-equilibrium thermodynamics, where diffusion refers to particles flowing from high-concentration regions towards low-concentration regions. In statistics, the meaning is quite similar, namely the process of transforming a complex distribution p_complex on R^d to a simple distribution p_prior on the same domain. This constitutes a Markov chain of diffusion steps of slowly adding random noise to data, followed by a reverse diffusion process in which the data is reconstructed from the noise. The diffusion model learns the data manifold to which the original and thus the reconstructed data samples belong, by training on a large number of data points. While the diffusion process pushes a data sample off the data manifold, the reverse process finds a trajectory back to the data manifold. Diffusion models have – unlike variational autoencoder and flow models – latent variables with the same dimensionality as the original data, and they are currently outperforming other approaches – including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) – to modelling the distribution of, e.g., natural images.
lecture-notes-in-probabilistic-diffusion.student: Diffusion models are inspired by physics, where diffusion describes particles spreading from dense to sparse areas. In machine learning, they work similarly: they gradually add noise to data (like images) until it resembles random static, then learn to reverse this process to reconstruct the original. This involves training on many examples to understand the underlying structure, or 'manifold', of the data. Unlike some other methods, diffusion models keep the same number of dimensions as the input data. Currently, they often outperform alternatives like GANs in tasks such as generating realistic images.
lecture-notes-in-probabilistic-diffusion.layman: Researchers studied a way to create new images by first slowly turning them into noise, then learning to reverse the process. They trained a system on many examples to understand how real images are structured. This method, called a diffusion model, often works better than others at making lifelike pictures.

consumer-side-fairness-in-recommender-sy.scientist: In the current landscape of ever-increasing levels of digitalization, we are facing major challenges pertaining to data volume. Recommender systems have become irreplaceable both for helping users navigate the increasing amounts of data and, conversely, aiding providers in marketing products to interested users. Data-driven models are susceptible to data bias, materializing in the bias influencing the models’ decision-making. For recommender systems, such issues are well exemplified by occupation recommendation, where biases in historical data may lead to recommender systems relating one gender to lower wages or to the propagation of stereotypes. In particular, consumer-side fairness, which focuses on mitigating discrimination experienced by users of recommender systems, has seen a vast number of diverse approaches. The approaches are further diversified through differing ideas on what constitutes fair and, conversely, discriminatory recommendations. This survey serves as a systematic overview and discussion of the current research on consumer-side fairness in recommender systems. To that end, a novel taxonomy based on high-level fairness definitions is proposed and used to categorize the research and the proposed fairness evaluation metrics. Finally, we highlight some suggestions for the future direction of the field.
consumer-side-fairness-in-recommender-sy.student: As digital data grows, recommender systems—tools that suggest products or content to users—have become essential for both users and providers. However, these systems can inherit biases from their training data, leading to unfair outcomes, such as associating certain genders with lower-paying jobs or reinforcing stereotypes. This survey focuses on *consumer-side fairness*, which aims to reduce discrimination experienced by users of these systems. The paper reviews existing research on fairness in recommender systems, proposing a new classification system based on broad fairness definitions to organize the work and the metrics used to evaluate fairness. It also offers suggestions for future research directions in this area.
consumer-side-fairness-in-recommender-sy.layman: With so much information online, tools that suggest things to buy or watch are very useful. But these tools can sometimes be unfair, like suggesting lower-paying jobs to one gender or reinforcing old stereotypes. This study looks at how to make these tools fairer for users. It reviews past work, groups the ideas into categories, and suggests ways to improve fairness in the future.

opt-in-transparent-fairness-for-recommen.scientist: Recommender systems serve large, diverse userbases and are subject to fairness concerns. Seminal work on consumer-side fairness in recommender systems tends to focus on mitigating the influence users’ demographic information has on their recommendations. Recent work allows the users to specify which information should be concealed, but these methods are often complex and inadvertently deteriorate the recommendation performance of users who reveal all information. We propose a simple, novel approach that interfaces with trained non-fair models and allows users to opt-in for improved fairness without affecting the recommendations given to others. Unlike previous work, the proposed method includes fairness transparently. Quantitative comparison to the state of the art indicates that the proposed method has a favourable fairness/utility tradeoff.
opt-in-transparent-fairness-for-recommen.student: Recommender systems, which suggest items like movies or products to users, often face fairness issues, as recommendations can be biased by users’ demographic data. Prior research has tried to reduce this bias by hiding demographic information, but these methods can be complex and sometimes worsen recommendations for users who don’t hide their data. We introduce a simple new method that works with existing, non-fair models, letting users choose to improve fairness for themselves without changing others’ recommendations. Unlike earlier approaches, our method makes fairness adjustments clear and transparent. Tests show it balances fairness and recommendation quality better than current leading methods.
opt-in-transparent-fairness-for-recommen.layman: Online services often suggest things you might like, but these suggestions can be unfairly influenced by personal details like age or gender. Researchers have tried to fix this by hiding such details, but this can make the suggestions worse for some people. We created a simple way for users to ask for fairer suggestions without affecting others. It works with existing systems and keeps the process clear. Tests show it does a good job of being fair while still giving useful suggestions.

relu-networks-as-surrogate-models-in-mix.scientist: We consider the embedding of piecewise-linear deep neural networks (ReLU networks) as surrogate models in mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problems. A MILP formulation of ReLU networks has recently been applied by many authors to probe for various model properties subject to input bounds. The formulation is obtained by programming each ReLU operator with a binary variable and applying the big-M method. The efficiency of the formulation hinges on the tightness of the bounds defined by the big-M values. When ReLU networks are embedded in a larger optimization problem, the presence of output bounds can be exploited in bound tightening. To this end, we devise and study several bound tightening procedures that consider both input and output bounds. Our numerical results show that bound tightening may reduce solution times considerably, and that small-sized ReLU networks are suitable as surrogate models in mixed-integer linear programs.
relu-networks-as-surrogate-models-in-mix.student: This study explores how to embed piecewise-linear deep neural networks (ReLU networks, which use the ReLU activation function to introduce non-linearity) into mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problems. MILP is an optimization method that handles both continuous and integer variables. The ReLU networks are represented in MILP by modeling each ReLU operator with a binary variable and using the big-M method, which relies on predefined bounds. The efficiency of this approach depends on how tight these bounds are. The researchers propose and analyze bound-tightening techniques that use both input and output constraints to improve these bounds. Their numerical experiments show that tighter bounds can significantly speed up solving times, and that small ReLU networks work well as surrogate models in MILP problems.
relu-networks-as-surrogate-models-in-mix.layman: The researchers asked if small, simple artificial neural networks can be used to help solve complex optimization problems. They tested ways to make the networks fit better into these problems by adjusting the limits placed on their inputs and outputs. Their experiments showed that these adjustments can make the problems much faster to solve, and that small networks are indeed useful for this purpose.

the-multistage-stochastic-vehicle-routin.scientist: Widespread use of smart phones and cellular networks allow for new solutions to lower the costs of last mile delivery to customers. We consider a setting where a company not only uses its own fleet of vehicles to deliver products from their store, but can also make use of ordinary people who are already on the road. This may include people who visit the store and are willing to take a detour on their way home for a small compensation. The availability of these occasional drivers is naturally highly uncertain, and we assume that some stochastic information is known about them. This leads to a multistage stochastic vehicle routing problem, with dynamic appearance of vehicles. The contributions of this work is to present a formulation of the multistage stochastic programming problem, identifying what type of problem structures that makes this model superior to that of a two-stage formulation, and when a two-stage formulation can be an adequate simplification.
the-multistage-stochastic-vehicle-routin.student: This study explores how companies can reduce delivery costs by using both their own vehicles and occasional drivers—people already on the road, like shoppers willing to take a detour for a fee. Since these drivers appear unpredictably, the problem is modeled as a *multistage stochastic vehicle routing problem*, where decisions (e.g., assigning deliveries) are made in stages as new information (like driver availability) emerges. The work formulates this problem mathematically, identifies when this approach outperforms simpler two-stage models (which assume all uncertainty is resolved at once), and clarifies when a two-stage model might suffice. The key insight is that multistage models better handle dynamic, real-time uncertainty in driver availability.
the-multistage-stochastic-vehicle-routin.layman: The researchers asked if companies could cut delivery costs by using regular people—like shoppers heading home—as extra drivers, alongside their own trucks. Since these drivers show up unpredictably, the team built a math model to plan deliveries in steps, adjusting as new drivers appear. They found that this step-by-step approach works better than simpler methods when driver availability changes often, but simpler methods can work if the changes are rare. The study shows how to decide which method to use.

a-branch-price-and-cut-algorithm-for-the.scientist: In this paper, we propose an exact branch-price-and-cut (BPC) algorithm for the two-echelon vehicle routing problem with time windows. This problem arises in city logistics when high-capacity and low-capacity vehicles are used to transport items from depots to satellites (first echelon) and from satellites to customers (second echelon), respectively. The aim is to determine a set of least-cost first- and second-echelon routes such that the load on the routes respect the capacity of the vehicles, each second-echelon route is supplied by exactly one first-echelon route, and each customer is visited by exactly one second-echelon route within its time window. We model the problem with a route-based formulation where first-echelon routes are enumerated a priori, and second-echelon routes are generated using column generation. The problem is solved using BPC. To generate second-echelon routes, one pricing problem per satellite is solved using a labeling algorithm which keeps track of the first-echelon route associated with each (partial) second-echelon route considered. Furthermore, to speed up the solution process, we introduce effective deep dual-optimal inequalities and apply known valid inequalities. We perform extensive computational experiments on benchmark instances and show that our method outperforms a state-of-the-art algorithm. We also conduct sensitivity analyses on the different components of our algorithm and derive managerial insights related to the structure of the first-echelon routes.
a-branch-price-and-cut-algorithm-for-the.student: This study addresses the two-echelon vehicle routing problem with time windows, a logistics challenge where goods are transported from depots to satellites (first echelon) and then to customers (second echelon) using different vehicle types. The goal is to find the lowest-cost routes while respecting vehicle capacities, time windows, and the requirement that each second-echelon route is supplied by exactly one first-echelon route. The authors propose an exact branch-price-and-cut (BPC) algorithm, a method that combines branching, pricing, and cutting planes to solve complex optimization problems. They use a route-based formulation, pre-defining first-echelon routes and generating second-echelon routes dynamically via column generation. To improve efficiency, they introduce new inequalities and apply existing ones. Computational tests on standard benchmarks show their method outperforms a leading algorithm, and sensitivity analyses provide insights into the structure of first-echelon routes.
a-branch-price-and-cut-algorithm-for-the.layman: The researchers tackled a delivery problem where goods move from warehouses to intermediate points and then to customers, with strict time limits and vehicle capacity constraints. They created a precise mathematical method to find the cheapest routes while ensuring all rules are followed. Their approach involves breaking the problem into parts, solving each part efficiently, and combining the results. Tests on standard problems showed their method works better than existing ones, and they also explored how changes in the setup affect the best routes.

semi-cyclic-rostering-of-ranked-surgeons.scientist: We consider the rostering problem for surgeons in residency at the Clinic of Surgery at St. Olav’s Hospital, Trondheim University Hospital, in Trondheim, Norway. Each surgeon in residency has a rank depending on experience. An exact number of surgeons of each rank must work emergency shifts in a cyclic structure. Each surgeon is affiliated to a section, which has a minimum staffing level. Section shifts can be planned in an acyclic structure, thus establishing a semi-cyclic structure in the full roster. The addition of more typical rostering constraints establishes the novel Semi-Cyclic Ranked Physician Rostering Problem. In manually created rosters, the staffing at sections varies greatly, leading to frequent understaffing. With the addition of absence among staff when rosters are executed, this is problematic for the Clinic of Surgery. We present a two-step matheuristic based on mixed integer linear programming to solve the problem for five real-life instances. Comparing our results with a manually created roster demonstrates superior results in terms of staff availability at sections, greatly improving roster resilience to absence. We also introduce shadow shifts designed to increase the flexibility of rosters to cover for absence at emergency night shifts.
semi-cyclic-rostering-of-ranked-surgeons.student: This study addresses the challenge of scheduling surgeons in training at a Norwegian hospital. Surgeons have different experience levels (ranks) and belong to sections with minimum staffing needs. Emergency shifts follow a repeating cycle, while section shifts do not, creating a mixed (semi-cyclic) structure. Additional rules, like ensuring fair workloads, make this a new type of scheduling problem. Currently, manual schedules often leave sections understaffed, which worsens when staff are absent. The researchers developed a two-part mathematical method (a matheuristic) using optimization techniques to create schedules for five real cases. Their approach improved staffing levels at sections compared to manual schedules, making the system more resilient to absences. They also introduced 'shadow shifts' to add flexibility for covering emergency night shifts.
semi-cyclic-rostering-of-ranked-surgeons.layman: Hospitals need to schedule trainee surgeons for shifts, but current manual plans often leave some areas short-staffed. This causes problems when people are absent. The researchers created a new way to make these schedules using math and computers. They tested it on five real cases and found their method kept more staff available, making the system better at handling absences. They also added extra shifts to help cover emergencies at night.

the-dynamic-electric-carsharing-relocati.scientist: This article addresses a relocation and recharging problem faced by modern carsharing operators who manage a fleet of electric vehicles. As customers utilize the fleet, batteries are depleted and vehicles are possibly left in low-demand locations. Consequently, carsharing operators need to arrange the charging of depleted batteries and the relocation of poorly positioned vehicles in order to better meet the demand of the customers. Most of these activities require the intervention of dedicated staff. This article provides a framework for planning recharging and relocation activities based on periodically routing and scheduling a number of dedicated staff as a result of updated system information. The periodic planning problem is formulated as a Mixed Integer Linear Program and solved in a rolling-horizon fashion. For the solution of the problem a fast Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search heuristic is proposed. Tests based on data for the city of Oslo show that the heuristic can deliver, in reasonable computational time, high quality solutions for instances compatible with real-life planning problems.
the-dynamic-electric-carsharing-relocati.student: This study tackles a challenge for electric carsharing services: keeping vehicles charged and in the right places. As users drive the cars, batteries drain and vehicles may end up in areas with little demand. Operators must then recharge batteries and move cars to high-demand spots, often using staff. The research proposes a planning framework that schedules these tasks by routing staff periodically, using updated system data. The problem is modeled as a Mixed Integer Linear Program—a mathematical method for optimization—and solved incrementally over time. To speed up solutions, an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search heuristic (a problem-solving shortcut) is used. Tests with Oslo’s data show this approach quickly finds practical, high-quality solutions for real-world scenarios.
the-dynamic-electric-carsharing-relocati.layman: The researchers asked how carsharing companies can keep their electric cars charged and in the right places for customers. They created a system to plan when and where staff should move and recharge the cars based on current demand. Using real data from Oslo, they tested a method that finds good solutions quickly, showing it works well for everyday use.

a-branch-and-cut-embedded-matheuristic-f.scientist: This paper presents an improved version of the solution method that won the inventory routing problem track of the 12th DIMACS Implementation Challenge. The solution method is a branch-and-cut embedded matheuristic where a matheuristic is called every time a new primal solution is found in a branch-and-cut method. The matheuristic consists of a construction heuristic and an improvement heuristic. The construction heuristic uses a giant tour method and a shifting assignments method to generate a set of promising routes which, in turn, are combined into a feasible solution to the problem by solving a route-based mathematical program. The improvement heuristic then solves a series of extended route-based mathematical programs where clusters of customers may be inserted and/or removed from the routes of the initial feasible solution. We have, to the best of our knowledge, gathered all detailed results from previously published methods for the inventory routing problem and made this overview available online. Compared with these results, the proposed method found the best-known solution for 741 out of 878 multi-vehicle inventory routing instances, where 247 of them are strictly better than the previously best-known solutions. Furthermore, we prove optimality for 458 of these solutions. The proposed method is also able to find the best-known solution for 116 out of 226 benchmark instances for the split delivery vehicle routing problem, and improve three best-known solutions from the CVRPlib for the capacitated vehicle routing problem.
a-branch-and-cut-embedded-matheuristic-f.student: This study improves a winning method for solving the inventory routing problem, a logistics challenge where delivery routes and stock levels must be optimised simultaneously. The approach combines branch-and-cut (a method that systematically explores possible solutions while discarding unpromising ones) with a matheuristic—a hybrid of mathematical optimisation and heuristic techniques. The matheuristic first constructs initial routes using a giant tour and shifting assignments, then refines them by solving route-based mathematical programs. It further improves solutions by adjusting customer clusters in the routes. The authors compiled all known results for this problem and compared their method against them. Their approach found the best-known solutions for 741 of 878 multi-vehicle cases, improving 247 of these, and proved optimality for 458. It also matched or improved best-known solutions for related vehicle routing problems.
a-branch-and-cut-embedded-matheuristic-f.layman: The researchers tackled a problem where companies must plan delivery routes while managing stock levels efficiently. They built on a previous winning method, mixing math-based problem-solving with practical shortcuts to find better routes. Their approach first creates rough delivery plans, then refines them by adjusting which customers are served together. They tested it against all known results for this problem and found it outperformed most, improving many existing solutions and proving some were the best possible. It also worked well for similar delivery planning problems.

a-framework-for-integrated-resource-plan.scientist: The problem under study is based on the challenges faced by the Orthopaedic Clinic at St. Olav’s Hospital in Trondheim, Norway. Variations in demand and supply cause fluctuating waiting lists, and it is challenging to level the activities between the clinic’s two units, the outpatient clinic and the operating theater, to obtain short waiting times for all activities. Based on these challenges, we describe and present a planning problem referred to as the Long-term Master Scheduling Problem (LMSP), where the objective is to construct an integrated Long-term Master Schedule (LMS) that facilitates short waiting times in both units. The LMS can be separated into two schedules, one cyclic high-level schedule, and one non-cyclic low-level schedule. The demand for outpatient clinic consultations and surgeries is stochastic, as are the waiting lists. To account for this, we propose a planning framework consisting of an optimization model to solve the LMSP, and a two-level planning procedure. In the planning procedure, we first solve the LMSP to construct the LMS for the upcoming planning horizon. Then, to adjust to the fluctuating waiting lists, we periodically refine the low-level schedule by solving a constrained LMSP. We also develop a simulation-based evaluation procedure to evaluate the planning framework in a real-life setting and use this to investigate different planning strategies. We find that imposing flexible, dynamic and agile planning strategies improve waiting time outcomes and patient throughput. Furthermore, combining the strategies yields additive improvements.
a-framework-for-integrated-resource-plan.student: The Orthopaedic Clinic at St. Olav’s Hospital faces uneven demand for outpatient consultations and surgeries, leading to long and fluctuating waiting lists. To address this, the study introduces the Long-term Master Scheduling Problem (LMSP), which aims to create an integrated schedule for both the outpatient clinic and operating theater to minimize waiting times. The schedule has two parts: a repeating high-level plan and a detailed, non-repeating low-level plan. Since demand and waiting lists are unpredictable, the researchers developed a planning framework with an optimization model and a two-step procedure. First, they generate a long-term schedule, then periodically adjust the detailed plan to adapt to changes. A simulation tested this approach in a real-world setting, showing that flexible, dynamic, and agile planning strategies reduce waiting times and improve patient flow. Combining these strategies further enhances results.
a-framework-for-integrated-resource-plan.layman: A hospital clinic struggles with long and changing wait times for appointments and surgeries. The researchers created a scheduling system to balance these services and keep waits short. They designed a two-part plan: a general repeating schedule and a detailed, adjustable one. Since patient needs change often, they also built a way to update the schedule regularly. Testing this system showed that flexible and adaptable planning helps patients get care faster. Using multiple strategies together works even better.

fomosim-an-open-source-simulator-for-rig.scientist: Existing simulation models for micromobility systems often face significant limitations: they are typically custom-built for specific contexts, lack generalizability, are not open-source, and undergo limited testing, which again question their reliability and applicability in broader settings. To address these challenges, this paper presents FOMOsim, an open-source simulator developed to analyze micromobility systems. The simulator’s modular design allows for better scalability and usability, facilitating detailed and realistic simulations of shared transport operations. New benchmark instances, utilizing data from bike-sharing systems (BSSs) in major American and Norwegian cities, are created and embedded within the simulator. Additionally, we introduce a new greedy heuristic for the dynamic bike rebalancing problem, integrated within FOMOsim. Rigorous testing demonstrates that the proposed heuristic, when combined with FOMOsim, outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly improving BSS performance by reducing bike shortages and surpluses. Furthermore, a comprehensive experimental study is designed to assess the impact of key strategic and operational decisions on BSS performance. The findings underscore the simulator’s adaptability in addressing various planning challenges and its potential to improve BSS management through informed decision-making. Consequently, FOMOsim provides the research community with a robust platform for replicating experiments, generating new instances, and exploring innovative solutions in BSS management, thereby substantially enriching the field’s body of knowledge.
fomosim-an-open-source-simulator-for-rig.student: Current simulation tools for micromobility systems, like bike-sharing, are often tailored to specific cases, not open-source, and poorly tested, limiting their broader use. This paper introduces FOMOsim, an open-source simulator with a modular design that improves scalability and usability for realistic shared transport simulations. The tool includes new benchmark datasets from bike-sharing systems in U.S. and Norwegian cities. The authors also propose a greedy heuristic—a step-by-step problem-solving approach—for dynamically rebalancing bikes (moving them to meet demand). Testing shows this heuristic, combined with FOMOsim, outperforms existing methods, reducing bike shortages and surpluses. A detailed experimental study further explores how strategic and operational decisions affect system performance, highlighting FOMOsim’s adaptability for various planning challenges.
fomosim-an-open-source-simulator-for-rig.layman: Bike-sharing systems often struggle with uneven bike distribution, leaving some areas with too many bikes and others with none. Researchers built a new, freely available computer tool called FOMOsim to simulate these systems more realistically. They also created a simple but effective method to move bikes around as needed. Tests using real data from cities in the U.S. and Norway show this approach works better than older methods, helping keep the right number of bikes in the right places. The tool can also help study how different decisions affect the system’s success.

integrated-resource-scheduling-for-patie.scientist: Managing the time that patients wait for their next appointment is a well-known challenge in hospitals. Scarce resources must be efficiently planned and coordinated to create schedules that allow departments of a hospital to keep these waiting times below set targets. The problem studied in this work is based on the situation in the Orthopedic Department at St.Olav’s hospital in Norway. Here, patients undergo an initial assessment by surgeons during a consultation appointment in the outpatient clinic (OC), and if they are diagnosed with the need for surgeries, times in operating rooms (OR) for the surgeries are assigned. After surgery, patients visit the surgeons at the OC for follow-up consultations. To perform these activities, in addition to surgeons, patients need resources, including OC rooms, ORs, and beds in wards. We have developed a new model for the Integrated Multi-Appointment Blueprint Scheduling Problem reflecting the planning problem at the department. The model combines a detailed representation of the queues of patients waiting for consultations and surgeries with integrated scheduling of the OC and ORs. The model creates tactical blueprints that assign activities to surgeons and rooms over a planning horizon. The model manages the waiting times of patients and targets set on individual queues while minimizing the total number of patients in all queues at the end of the planning horizon. To evaluate the proposed optimization model on the OC and OR performance, we create four cases of different size. Additionally, we study two aspects of cyclicity, cyclic or non-cyclic availability of surgeons and cyclic or non-cyclic room schedules. Finally, we compare the solutions of the proposed model with another model in a simulation experiment. The computational results show that our model improves the blueprints in terms of patient waiting time and waiting lists and is capable of handling the trade-off between waiting time targets and end queues more efficiently.
integrated-resource-scheduling-for-patie.student: Hospitals struggle to manage patient waiting times due to limited resources like rooms, operating theatres, and staff. This study focuses on the Orthopedic Department at St.Olav’s Hospital in Norway, where patients first see a surgeon in an outpatient clinic (OC), then may need surgery in an operating room (OR), followed by follow-up visits. The researchers developed a new scheduling model, called the Integrated Multi-Appointment Blueprint Scheduling Problem, which combines patient queues for consultations and surgeries with the scheduling of OC and OR resources. The model creates plans that assign tasks to surgeons and rooms over time, aiming to keep patient waiting times below targets while reducing the number of patients still waiting at the end of the planning period. They tested the model on four different scenarios and compared it to another model. Results show their approach better manages waiting times and patient queues, balancing these goals more effectively.
integrated-resource-scheduling-for-patie.layman: Hospitals often have long waits for appointments because resources like rooms and doctors are limited. This study looked at an orthopedic department where patients see a doctor, may need surgery, and then return for check-ups. The researchers created a new way to schedule these visits and surgeries to reduce waiting times. They tested it in different situations and found their method helps patients wait less and keeps the number of people waiting at the end lower than before.

manywells-simulation-of-multiphase-flow-.scientist: A multiphase flow simulator and curated datasets are shared with the community to facilitate research on machine learning and other data-driven methodologies. The simulator is based on a drift-flux model and provides low-fidelity, one-dimensional, steady-state solutions that capture the main characteristics of multiphase flow in vertical wells. A sampling strategy for the model parameters is proposed which results in a diverse set of oil and gas wells with different geometric, fluid, and thermal properties. Sampling strategies are also devised to simulate stationary and non-stationary boundary conditions and different operating modes. The method is used to generate three large datasets, each with one million data points from 2000 wells. The simulated data is compared to real production data from more than 300 wells in a comprehensive data analysis. The simulator implementation is validated by demonstrating accurate predictions of pressures and flow rates for a real well. Finally, the generated datasets are applied in a couple of machine learning examples.
manywells-simulation-of-multiphase-flow-.student: Researchers developed a simulator for multiphase flow—where multiple fluids (like oil, gas, and water) move together in a pipe—in vertical wells. The tool uses a drift-flux model, a simplified approach that assumes steady, one-dimensional flow to approximate real-world behavior. They created a method to sample diverse well parameters (e.g., geometry, fluid properties) and boundary conditions, generating three large datasets (1M data points each from 2000 simulated wells). The simulator’s accuracy was checked against real production data from over 300 wells, confirming it reliably predicts pressures and flow rates. The datasets were also tested in machine learning tasks, showing their potential for data-driven research in this field.
manywells-simulation-of-multiphase-flow-.layman: Scientists built a computer tool to simulate how oil, gas, and water flow together in a well. They used it to create large sets of fake but realistic well data, testing different conditions. They checked that the tool’s predictions matched real-world data from hundreds of wells. The fake data was then used to test machine learning methods, showing it could help improve how we study and predict well behavior.

novel-bayesian-framework-for-calibration.scientist: This study presents a novel Bayesian framework for statistical calibration of spatially distributed physical-based landslide prediction models. The calibration process is formulated in a statistical setting with the model parameters simulated as spatially variable with random fields and the model calibration defined within the Bayesian framework. The implementation of such calibration process is challenging due to large numbers of calibration parameters and high-dimensional likelihood functions, which are central in establishing a relation between observations and the corresponding model predictions. The former challenge was resolved by reformulating the Bayesian updating problem as an equivalent reliability problem and solving it with efficient reliability methods. The latter challenge was resolved by developing novel lower-dimensional approximate likelihood formulations, suitable for the interpretation of landslide initiation zones, based on the Approximate Bayesian Computation method. The novelties of the proposed approach stem from describing landslide model parameters as spatially variable, development of a statistical framework to calibrate landslide prediction models, and introduction of approximate likelihood formulations.
novel-bayesian-framework-for-calibration.student: This study tackles the challenge of calibrating landslide prediction models, which simulate where landslides might start. The researchers used a Bayesian framework—a statistical method that updates predictions as new data comes in—to treat model parameters as varying across space. Calibration is difficult because it involves many parameters and complex likelihood functions, which link observations to model outputs. To simplify, they reframed the Bayesian problem as a reliability problem, using efficient methods to handle the large number of parameters. They also created a lower-dimensional approximate likelihood, based on Approximate Bayesian Computation, to better interpret landslide initiation zones. The work introduces a new way to model spatial variability in landslide parameters and a statistical framework for calibration.
novel-bayesian-framework-for-calibration.layman: Researchers wanted to improve how we predict where landslides might start. They used a math-based method to adjust their models, treating the factors that influence landslides as changing from place to place. The process was tricky because it involved many variables and complex comparisons between real data and model predictions. To simplify, they used a different approach to handle the large amount of data and created a simpler way to compare predictions with reality. Their method offers a new way to make landslide predictions more accurate.

hyperspheric-integral-reliability-method.scientist: This paper introduces the Hyperspheric Integral Reliability Method (HINT) for efficient reliability analysis of geotechnical ultimate limit states. The method is motivated by the mechanism of the Shear Strength Reduction Method (SSRM), which is often employed to calculate the factor of safety for geotechnical ultimate limit states. HINT exploits the observation that a factor of safety, computed by the SSRM, is not only a pointwise estimate of safety, but also a measure of distance to the failure limit along a radial direction in the space of the shear strength parameters. This observation is utilized to transform the reliability integral in the hyperspheric coordinate system and develop an efficient estimator of failure probability for geotechnical ultimate limit states. HINT was examined on several benchmarking problems, demonstrating stable and highly efficient performance on low to medium dimensional reliability problems. HINT can be also applied to general reliability problems if a radial search mechanism is implemented as in the SSRM. Given that the SSRM is already available in most commercial geotechnical software packages, HINT is perfectly suited to advance geotechnical reliability analyses and make them accessible to a wider set of use-cases.
hyperspheric-integral-reliability-method.student: This study presents a new method, called HINT (Hyperspheric Integral Reliability Method), for assessing the reliability of geotechnical structures under extreme conditions. Geotechnical engineers often use the Shear Strength Reduction Method (SSRM) to calculate a factor of safety, which indicates how close a structure is to failure. The authors observed that this factor also measures the distance to failure in a multi-dimensional space of shear strength parameters. By transforming the reliability calculation into a hyperspheric coordinate system, HINT efficiently estimates the probability of failure. The method was tested on standard problems and performed well for low to medium complexity cases. Since SSRM is widely available in commercial software, HINT can be easily integrated to improve reliability analyses in geotechnical engineering.
hyperspheric-integral-reliability-method.layman: Researchers developed a new way to predict how likely a slope or foundation is to fail. They noticed that a common safety check in engineering also shows how far a structure is from breaking. Using this insight, they created a method to calculate failure risk more efficiently. They tested it on several examples and found it works well for simpler cases. Because the method builds on existing tools, it could be widely used to make safety checks more reliable.

application-of-machine-learning-to-the-i.scientist: Geotechnical classification is vital for site characterization and geotechnical design. Field tests such as the cone penetration test with pore water pressure measurement (CPTu) are widespread because they represent a faster and cheaper alternative for sample recovery and testing. However, classification schemes based on CPTu measurements are fairly generic because they represent a wide variety of soil conditions and, occasionally, they may fail when used in special soil types like sensitive or quick clays. Quick and highly sensitive clay soils in Norway have unique conditions that make them difficult to be identified through general classification charts. Therefore, new approaches to address this task are required. The following study applies machine learning methods such as logistic regression, Naive Bayes, and hidden Markov models to classify quick and highly sensitive clays at two sites in Norway based on normalized CPTu measurements. Results showed a considerable increase in the classification accuracy despite limited training sets.
application-of-machine-learning-to-the-i.student: Geotechnical classification helps assess soil properties for construction and design. The cone penetration test with pore water pressure measurement (CPTu) is a common field test that quickly and affordably gathers soil data. However, standard classification methods based on CPTu results are often too broad, struggling with special soils like sensitive or quick clays—soils prone to sudden collapse. In Norway, these clays have unique traits that make them hard to identify using general charts. This study used machine learning techniques, including logistic regression, Naive Bayes, and hidden Markov models, to classify quick and highly sensitive clays at two Norwegian sites using normalized CPTu data. The results showed improved classification accuracy, even with limited training data.
application-of-machine-learning-to-the-i.layman: Engineers often test soil to plan safe construction. One common test uses a cone pushed into the ground to measure soil strength. But this method struggles with rare, unstable clays in Norway that can suddenly turn to liquid. Researchers tried using computer programs that learn from data to better spot these risky clays. Even with little training data, the programs improved the ability to identify these soils.

application-of-physics-informed-neural-n.scientist: This paper investigates the application of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to inverse problems in unsaturated groundwater flow. PINNs are applied to the types of unsaturated groundwater flow problems modelled with the Richards partial differential equation and the van Genuchten constitutive model. The inverse problem is formulated here as a problem with known or measured values of the solution to the Richards equation at several spatio-temporal instances, and unknown values of solution at the rest of the problem domain and unknown parameters of the van Genuchten model. PINNs solve inverse problems by reformulating the loss function of a deep neural network such that it simultaneously aims to satisfy the measured values and the unknown values at a set of collocation points distributed across the problem domain. The novelty of the paper originates from the development of PINN formulations for the Richards equation that requires training of a single neural network. The results demonstrate that PINNs are capable of efficiently solving the inverse problem with relatively accurate approximation of the solution to the Richards equation and estimates of the van Genuchten model parameters.
application-of-physics-informed-neural-n.student: This study explores using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to solve inverse problems in unsaturated groundwater flow, where the flow is described by the Richards equation and the van Genuchten model (a mathematical model for soil water retention). The inverse problem involves known measurements of water flow at certain points in space and time, with unknown flow values elsewhere and unknown soil parameters. PINNs tackle this by training a neural network to minimize a loss function that accounts for both the known measurements and the governing equations at other points. The paper introduces a new PINN formulation for the Richards equation, requiring only one neural network. Results show PINNs can efficiently approximate the flow solution and estimate soil parameters with reasonable accuracy.
application-of-physics-informed-neural-n.layman: Researchers tested a new method to figure out how water moves through soil when some parts are dry and others are wet. They used a type of computer program that learns from data and also follows the rules of physics. By feeding it some measurements of water flow, the program could guess the missing details and soil properties. The method worked well, giving a good picture of the water movement and the soil’s behavior.

generation-of-erosion-hotspot-zones-alon.scientist: An erosion-induced quick clay landslide (QCL) is a geological hazard that poses a severe risk to human life and property. The recent disaster in Norway at Gjerdrum in 2020 caused loss of 11 lives and destroyed many infrastructures overnight. One of the reasons for the Gjerdrum landslide was continuous erosion that led to deterioration of the slope’s stability. However, not many researchers have worked on identifying and mapping this erosion along the streams. Hence, the present study attempts to identify precise erosion hotspots zones of a study area close to Gjerdrum incorporating significant erosion causing factors and deep learning model. To achieve this, first, erosion and non-erosion data were extracted using 1 m resolution lidar data and incorporating change detection technique. Second, twenty erosion-causing factors were correlated with 70% of the data using a Deep Neural Network (DNN) model, and the accuracy of the model was evaluated using the remaining 30%. Lastly, the trained model was used to generate erosion susceptibility map highlighting the hotspots erosion zones along the streams. The results show that about 21% of the study area comes under very high susceptibility erosion hotspot zones. Also, these hotspots can extend up to 300 m from one side of the streams while on the other side they may not exist. The DNN model accomplished an accuracy of 0.88 utilizing fourteen significant factors. The study concludes that the erosion hotspot zones require more in-depth site-specific investigation along with numerical slope stability analysis considering erosion under cutting the slope.
generation-of-erosion-hotspot-zones-alon.student: Quick clay landslides, triggered by erosion, are sudden and destructive, as seen in Norway’s 2020 Gjerdrum disaster. This study focuses on mapping erosion hotspots near streams, a less-explored factor in slope instability. Using high-resolution lidar data (1 m), researchers detected erosion and non-erosion areas via change detection. A deep neural network (DNN) model then linked 20 potential erosion-causing factors to 70% of the data, with the remaining 30% used for validation. The model, achieving 88% accuracy with 14 key factors, produced a susceptibility map showing 21% of the study area as high-risk erosion zones, extending up to 300 m from streams. The findings suggest these hotspots need further site-specific investigation, including slope stability analysis, to assess erosion’s role in undermining slopes.
generation-of-erosion-hotspot-zones-alon.layman: In 2020, a sudden landslide in Norway destroyed homes and took lives, partly because water slowly wore away the ground. Scientists studied a nearby area to find where this erosion happens most. They used detailed scans of the land and a computer program to spot risky spots. The program, trained on past data, found that about one-fifth of the area is highly vulnerable, with some risks stretching 300 meters from streams. The results show where to look closer to prevent future disasters.

optimizing-number-locations-and-types-of.scientist: This study examines the application of Value of Information (VOI) analysis to identify the optimal number, types, and locations of ground investigations for slope safety assessment. VOI analysis integrates a probabilistic slope stability model with uncertain shear strength of clay, a detailed ground investigation model, and a utility function to assess the benefits of reducing uncertainties in soil properties by conducting ground investigations. This study extends earlier VOI approaches for optimising ground investigations by examining not only the optimal number and locations, but also the types of ground investigations. The optimal ground investigations are determined among several common ground investigation methods for estimating undrained shear strength of clay including cone penetration, triaxial, uniaxial compression, and vane shear tests. A comprehensive ground investigation model is implemented to realistically evaluate the costs for each of the investigation methods. This was complemented by a detailed assessment of the quality of the investigation methods by accounting for the measurement and transformation errors. The optimal number, locations and types of ground investigations were examined for a range of parameters that can affect outcomes of VOI analyses including the level of prior knowledge on uncertain soil properties, spatial similarity of soil properties, and consequences of slope failures.
optimizing-number-locations-and-types-of.student: This study explores how Value of Information (VOI) analysis can determine the best number, types, and locations of ground investigations to assess slope safety. VOI combines a probabilistic model of slope stability—where the shear strength of clay is uncertain—with a ground investigation model and a utility function to weigh the benefits of reducing uncertainty in soil properties. Unlike prior work, this research also considers the types of investigations, such as cone penetration, triaxial, uniaxial compression, and vane shear tests. A realistic cost model for each method is used, alongside an evaluation of their accuracy, including measurement and transformation errors. The study examines how factors like prior knowledge of soil properties, spatial similarity of soil, and the consequences of slope failure influence the optimal investigation strategy.
optimizing-number-locations-and-types-of.layman: Researchers wanted to find the best way to test the ground to predict if a slope might collapse. They used a method that balances the cost of testing against the value of the information gained. They compared different types of soil tests and where to do them, considering how much we already know about the soil and how serious a collapse would be. The study found which tests and locations give the most useful information for the least cost.

quantification-of-climate-change-impact-.scientist: Climate change impact on rainfall-induced landslide susceptibility of a certain region is often implied based on expected changes in rainfall patterns and rarely explicitly quantified. This study aims to address this gap by implementing coupled landslide and climate modelling chains to explicitly assess the effects of changing rainfall patterns on rainfall-induced landslide susceptibility. The effects of climate change are integrated into the landslide modelling chain via Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves for the present and future climate conditions for a landslide-prone study area located in central Norway. The effects of climate change on landslide susceptibility are examined by using a physical-based landslide prediction model with rainfall events of varying duration and intensity that are simulated based on the climate-dependent IDF curves. The novelty of this study is the proposition of a novel probabilistic framework to assess the climate change impact on landslide susceptibility for rainfall events with a given duration. The proposed framework accounts for both the uncertainties of rainfall events through probabilistic interpretation of IDF curves and the uncertainties in the landslide model with the Monte Carlo method. Compared to results based on only intense rainfall events, the proposed framework leads to a lower increase in the probability of landslide initiation and landslide-susceptible extents due to climate change.
quantification-of-climate-change-impact-.student: Most studies assume climate change will increase landslide risk because heavier rainfall is expected, but few quantify this link. This work fills that gap by combining climate and landslide models for a region in central Norway. Researchers used Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves—graphs showing how often rain of a given strength and duration occurs—to project future rainfall under climate change. They then fed these projections into a physics-based landslide model to test how different rain events affect slope stability. A new probabilistic method was introduced to handle uncertainties in both rainfall predictions and the landslide model, using Monte Carlo simulations. The results show that, when accounting for a range of possible rainfall events rather than just extreme ones, the expected rise in landslide probability and affected area due to climate change is smaller than previously thought.
quantification-of-climate-change-impact-.layman: Scientists often say that climate change will cause more landslides because rain will get heavier, but they rarely test this idea with numbers. In this study, researchers looked at a landslide-prone area in Norway. They predicted future rainfall patterns and used a computer model to see how these changes might trigger landslides. They also created a new way to include the uncertainty in their predictions. Their findings suggest that, when considering all kinds of rain—not just the heaviest—the increase in landslide risk from climate change may be less than expected.

exploring-occupant-detection-model-gener.scientist: This study explores two modeling approaches for occupancy detection at room level for residential buildings in Denmark. The aim is to assess the performance and generalizability of occupant detection models using XGBoost method trained on a rich dataset comprising indoor environmental quality (IEQ) variables and occupancy ground truth. A global approach (all rooms) and a room-specific approach are considered. After a thorough feature selection and importance analysis process, the occupancy detection models (ODMs) are trained and tested in a nested cross-validation schema. The time of the day, indoor CO2 concentration, and feature transforms related to short-term IEQ dynamics were found to be the most important features of the ODMs. Both the global and room-specific models show good occupancy prediction performance, especially for bedrooms. When tested for generalizability with an unseen dataset from a different residential building, the ODMs maintain very good performance for the bedroom but not for the office room. This discrepancy could be explained by significant differences in occupancy and ventilation patterns, and large air infiltration from adjacent rooms. Although currently limited in terms of generalizability, XGBoost-based ODMs using IEQ data have the potential to provide robust and scalable occupancy detection for occupant-centric control and occupant-aware building performance assessments. The IEQ dataset with occupancy ground truth collected for this study is made available in open access.
exploring-occupant-detection-model-gener.student: This study compares two ways to predict whether a room in a Danish home is occupied: one model trained on data from all rooms (global) and another trained per room (room-specific). Both use XGBoost, a machine learning method, and rely on indoor environmental quality (IEQ) data—like CO2 levels and temperature—paired with known occupancy records. After selecting the most relevant features (e.g., time of day, CO2, and short-term IEQ changes), the models were trained and tested using nested cross-validation. Both approaches performed well, especially for bedrooms, but struggled with offices when tested on data from a different building. This drop in performance may stem from differences in how offices are used or ventilated, or air leaking from nearby rooms. While not yet fully generalizable, these models show promise for detecting occupancy using IEQ data, and the dataset is publicly available.
exploring-occupant-detection-model-gener.layman: Researchers wanted to see if they could tell when a room in a home is occupied by looking at things like air quality and temperature. They tried two methods: one that learns from all rooms together and one that learns from each room separately. Both worked well for bedrooms, but not as well for offices when tested in a different house. This might be because offices are used differently or have more air flowing in from other rooms. The results suggest this approach could work, but it needs improvement to be reliable in all cases.

barriers-and-drivers-for-implementation-.scientist: This study aimed to assess the current status of Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) implementation in building Automated Fault Detection and Diagnosis and Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems in the building industry. Semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted with 29 experts from different HVAC company types in the building industry. In addition, a literature review was performed to investigate academic research on FDD implementation. The study identified barriers and drivers to implementing FDD systems, these included; technological and technical, economic and business, users, social and societal, and regulatory. An Automatic Fault Detection and Diagnosis (AFDD) implementation matrix was developed to evaluate FDD implementation in building systems, and all interviewed companies were classified based on their FDD knowledge, services, and type. Results show that expert-rule systems are still prevalent in the industry. The literature review revealed a scarcity of FDD implementation studies in academic research due to challenges in testing and validating results in actual building operation conditions. Lastly, this study discusses the key findings: 1) FDD does not sell, 2) Lack of actively engaging and promoting FDD services, 3) FDD seems to be an academic definition, 4) The bottlenecks: The fault handling process and user’s mindset towards FDD, and 5) Governmental regulations and legislatives drive the implementation focus.
barriers-and-drivers-for-implementation-.student: This study examined how Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD)—a process for identifying and diagnosing issues in building systems like HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning)—is currently used in the industry. Researchers conducted interviews with 29 HVAC experts and reviewed academic literature. They found that barriers to FDD adoption include technical, economic, user-related, social, and regulatory factors. An implementation matrix was created to classify companies based on their FDD knowledge and services. The study revealed that expert-rule systems (a type of FDD relying on predefined rules) remain common, and academic research on FDD implementation is limited due to challenges in real-world testing. Key findings include low market demand for FDD, insufficient promotion of FDD services, and the role of government regulations in driving adoption.
barriers-and-drivers-for-implementation-.layman: Researchers wanted to know how often and why building systems use automated checks to find and fix problems. They talked to 29 experts and read past studies. They found that these checks are not widely used because of cost, lack of interest, and other hurdles. Most companies still rely on simple, rule-based methods. There are few studies on this topic because testing in real buildings is hard. The main issues are that people don’t see the value, companies don’t promote it, and rules from the government push its use.

fault-detection-in-ahu-a-walkthrough-for.scientist: The implementation of fault detection in research articles is relatively sparse, yet it holds significant potential to contribute to the decarbonization of our building stock. This study proposes a Fault Detection (FD) methodology that can be split into three stages. 1) FD algorithm development, testing, and validation on known datasets. 2) platform creation, data collection and curation, and method implementation. 3) FD algorithm testing on an operational system running under normal conditions with no artificially induced faults. The results showed that for step 1, using suitable evaluation metrics for realistic datasets is highly important, as otherwise wrong conclusions can be drawn. It was further found that the proposed FD methodology, as intended, led to choosing an algorithm that did not cause many false alarms, as the emphasis was on avoiding these, but also that changing the weighting of the included terms could shift the focus to prioritize other issues.
fault-detection-in-ahu-a-walkthrough-for.student: Fault detection (FD) in building systems—identifying when equipment like HVAC isn’t working properly—is underused but could help reduce carbon emissions from buildings. This study outlines a three-step FD approach: first, developing and testing algorithms on known datasets; second, building a platform to collect and process real-world data; and third, testing the algorithm on a live system without artificial faults. The results showed that choosing the right evaluation metrics for realistic datasets is critical to avoid misleading conclusions. The proposed method successfully prioritized minimizing false alarms, but adjusting the weights of different terms in the algorithm could shift the focus to other priorities, like detecting more faults.
fault-detection-in-ahu-a-walkthrough-for.layman: Buildings waste energy when their systems break down. This study tested a way to automatically spot these problems. The team first created and checked their method using existing data, then tried it on a real building. They found that picking the right way to measure success matters a lot. Their approach worked to avoid false alarms, but they could tweak it to focus on other goals if needed.

further-development-and-validation-of-th.scientist: Long-term forecasts of the aggregate energy load profiles are crucial for energy system planning. Previous work has developed a load profile model named PROFet to forecast aggregated weather-dependent load profiles with an hourly resolution for buildings based on energy measurements from buildings connected to district heating. In this study, further development of the PROFet model is presented, including the extension of measurements in the database, the separation of building categories into three efficiency levels, and the separation of energy load profiles for electric loads, space heating, and domestic hot water heating. Load profiles created with PROFet for apartments have been validated against out-of-sample data (load measurements from buildings with hourly resolutions). This study shows that the out-of-sample datasets are in good agreement with the PROFet prediction. Also, the validation results are satisfactory as they are below the threshold values for the statistical indicators. A lasting contribution is a tool for creating aggregated load forecasts, which provides crucial information in grid planning and modelling. The results also provide typical load profiles that can be used as reference values when evaluating a neighbourhood/area's energy flexibility.
further-development-and-validation-of-th.student: Energy system planning relies on accurate long-term forecasts of total energy demand, especially for buildings connected to district heating. The PROFet model, previously developed to predict hourly, weather-dependent load profiles, has been enhanced in this study. Improvements include expanding the measurement database, categorizing buildings by efficiency (low, medium, high), and separating energy loads into electric use, space heating, and domestic hot water. The updated model was tested on new, unseen data from apartments, and the predictions matched the actual measurements well, with statistical errors below predefined thresholds. The study provides a tool for generating aggregated load forecasts, useful for grid planning, and offers typical load profiles as reference values for assessing energy flexibility in neighborhoods.
further-development-and-validation-of-th.layman: Researchers wanted to predict how much energy buildings will use in the future, which helps plan power systems. They improved a computer model that estimates hourly energy use for heating and electricity in homes. The model now groups buildings by how energy-efficient they are and separates different types of energy use. When tested on real data, the predictions were accurate. The result is a tool that helps plan energy grids and provides standard energy-use patterns for neighborhoods.

towards-automated-fault-detection-and-di.scientist: This study aims to develop a framework for automated fault detection and diagnosis (AFDD) in district heating (DH) substations by comprehensively understanding typical faults. AFDD is presently dependent on manual detection and diagnosis, leading to limitations. To address this issue, the study utilized data from 158 fault reports and smart heat meter data from residential buildings in Denmark to investigate common faults and conduct a fault impact assessment. The study suggests additional indicators for use by DH utility companies to detect anomalies in the future. The findings indicate that greater attention to fault detection and diagnosis can decrease energy usage and return temperatures, demonstrating the significance of AFDD implementation.
towards-automated-fault-detection-and-di.student: This research addresses the challenge of automating fault detection and diagnosis (AFDD) in district heating (DH) substations, which currently rely on manual processes. District heating systems distribute hot water for space heating, and substations manage this flow. The study analyzed 158 fault reports and smart heat meter data from Danish residential buildings to identify common faults and assess their impact. It proposes new indicators for DH companies to detect anomalies more effectively. The results suggest that improved fault detection could reduce energy consumption and lower return water temperatures, highlighting the potential benefits of AFDD systems.
towards-automated-fault-detection-and-di.layman: The researchers wanted to find a better way to automatically spot and fix problems in heating systems that deliver hot water to homes. Right now, people have to check these systems by hand, which is slow. They looked at records of past problems and data from smart meters in Danish homes. They found that catching these issues earlier could save energy and make the systems work better. They also suggested new ways for heating companies to notice when something is wrong.

impact-of-typical-faults-occurring-in-de.scientist: This study evaluates typical faults occurring in demand-controlled ventilation (DCV) system and the impact on three output results: energy use, thermal comfort, and indoor air quality. The methodologies used in this study were qualitative interviews of selected Norwegian Heating Ventilation Air Condition (HVAC) system experts and numerical modeling using the building performance simulation tool IDA ICE. The faults deduced from the qualitative interviews were modeled as the fault's different consequences to account for a large variety of faults. With a Norwegian school classroom as a case study, a local approach applying a one-at-a-time (OAT) simulation was used to perform an analysis of the extreme fault conditions that can occur. The results from the fault modeling demonstrated that greater attention is needed to avoid faults in the HVAC systems due to its impact on the indoor environment quality and energy efficiency of buildings.
impact-of-typical-faults-occurring-in-de.student: This study examined common faults in demand-controlled ventilation (DCV) systems—systems that adjust airflow based on occupancy—and their effects on energy use, thermal comfort, and indoor air quality. Researchers conducted qualitative interviews with Norwegian HVAC experts to identify typical faults, then used the building simulation tool IDA ICE to model these faults in a school classroom. A one-at-a-time (OAT) approach was applied to test extreme fault scenarios. The findings suggest that such faults can significantly degrade indoor environmental quality and energy efficiency, highlighting the need for better fault prevention in HVAC systems.
impact-of-typical-faults-occurring-in-de.layman: Researchers wanted to see what happens when ventilation systems in buildings don’t work properly. They asked experts about common problems and then used computer models to test how these issues affect energy use, comfort, and air quality in a classroom. The results show that even small faults can make the air worse and waste energy, so it’s important to keep these systems in good shape.

fault-detection-and-diagnosis-encycloped.scientist: This review aims to provide an up-to-date, comprehensive, and systematic summary of fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) in building systems. The latter was performed through a defined systematic methodology with the final selection of 221 studies. This review provides insights into four topics: (1) glossary framework of the FDD processes; (2) a classification scheme using energy system terminologies as the starting point; (3) the data, code, and performance evaluation metrics used in the reviewed literature; and (4) future research outlooks. FDD is a known and well-developed field in the aerospace, energy, and automotive sector. Nevertheless, this study found that FDD for building systems is still at an early stage worldwide. This was evident through the ongoing development of algorithms for detecting and diagnosing faults in building systems and the inconsistent use of the terminologies and definitions. In addition, there was an apparent lack of data statements in the reviewed articles, which compromised the reproducibility, and thus the practical development in this field. Furthermore, as data drove the research activity, the found dataset repositories and open code are also presented in this review. Finally, all data and documentation presented in this review are open and available in a GitHub repository.
fault-detection-and-diagnosis-encycloped.student: This review systematically summarizes the state of fault detection and diagnosis (FDD)—methods to identify and analyze problems—in building systems. The authors analyzed 221 studies, organizing findings into four areas: (1) a framework defining FDD processes, (2) a classification system based on energy terminology, (3) the data, code, and performance metrics used in research, and (4) future directions. While FDD is mature in fields like aerospace and automotive, the review finds it remains early-stage for buildings, with inconsistent terminology, evolving algorithms, and limited data sharing. Many studies lacked clear data statements, hindering reproducibility. The review also compiles available datasets and open-source code, all accessible via a GitHub repository.
fault-detection-and-diagnosis-encycloped.layman: Researchers reviewed 221 studies to understand how problems are spotted and fixed in building systems, like heating or cooling. They found that while this process is well-developed in other industries, it’s still new for buildings. Many studies used unclear terms or didn’t share their data, making it hard to repeat or build on their work. The review lists available data and tools, all shared publicly, to help others move the field forward.

preparing-buildings-for-data-driven-oper.scientist: This report elaborates on how to prepare buildings for data-driven operation, with a spotlight on the solutions implemented in the ZEB Lab. As buildings evolve into dynamic, data-centric entities, the ability to harness measurement data for improved operations becomes paramount. The report begins by emphasizing the critical role of building automation systems (BAS) in the contemporary operation of energy-flexible buildings. It elaborates on how BAS integrates different systems such as HVAC, lighting, and energy management into a cohesive framework, optimizing energy usage and occupant comfort. The heart of this report lies in the innovative solutions deployed within the ZEB Lab. Established in 2021, the ZEB Lab has invested significant effort and resources regarding its building automation for energy-flexible operations. The report showcases the instrumentation and data flow of the ZEB Lab, linking the measurement data to a time-series database (InfluxDB). This setup facilitates real-time data collection, storage, and visualization, empowering the ZEB Lab to leverage data for algorithm-based decision-making. The report dives into the practical applications of this approach, showcasing how data is used to enhance energy efficiency and how the heating system can be operated in a more predictive manner. As digitalization transforms buildings, the report stresses the inevitability of data-driven applications. It sheds light on the role of Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) in enabling continuous data-driven operations. Furthermore, it outlines API requirements and provides examples of energy-related data-driven applications under development in the ZEB Lab. This report underscores the significance of building automation, delves into challenges, and demonstrates how cutting-edge solutions can improve building operations, facilitating efficiency and demand side flexibility.
preparing-buildings-for-data-driven-oper.student: This report explores how modern buildings can be prepared for data-driven operation, focusing on the ZEB Lab as a case study. As buildings become more complex and energy-conscious, building automation systems (BAS)—which integrate HVAC, lighting, and energy management—are key to optimizing performance. The ZEB Lab, established in 2021, uses BAS to collect real-time data from sensors, storing it in a time-series database (InfluxDB) for analysis. This setup enables algorithm-based decisions, such as predictive heating control, to improve energy efficiency. The report also highlights the role of APIs (interfaces that allow software to communicate) in enabling continuous data-driven operations, detailing their requirements and showcasing energy-related applications under development. Challenges and solutions for implementing these systems are discussed, emphasizing their role in enhancing building efficiency and flexibility.
preparing-buildings-for-data-driven-oper.layman: This study looks at how buildings can use data to work smarter. Researchers set up a test building, the ZEB Lab, with sensors and systems that track energy use in real time. They store this data and use it to make decisions, like adjusting heating before it’s needed. The team also explains how different software can share this data to keep things running smoothly. The goal is to show how buildings can save energy and adapt to changing needs by using information more effectively.

rfid-technology-in-the-manufacture-of-cu.scientist: While Radio Frequency Identification (or RFId) technology has gained significant traction in the downstream operations and industries like retail, adoption upstream of the value-chain has been much slower.
