Few reported cases of implementations in job-shops exists today for several reasons, key among which is the relative cost of the technology and uncertainties regarding the expected results. In this paper, we present the insights from the evaluation and pre-implementation stage of a project to implement RFId technology in the customized products’ department of a large process manufacturing company in Europe. The case company is an innovation leader in the European pipe and drainage systems’ manufacturing industry. Preliminary findings indicate the need to align RFId implementation with strategic goals to minimize the risk associated with the implementation and increase the chance of success.
rfid-technology-in-the-manufacture-of-cu.student: Radio Frequency Identification (RFId) uses radio waves to track objects and is widely used in retail, but its adoption in earlier stages of production, like job-shops, has been limited. This is partly due to high costs and uncertainty about benefits. This study examines the evaluation and pre-implementation phase of an RFId project in a European company that manufactures customized pipe and drainage systems. The company is a leader in its industry. Early results suggest that aligning RFId implementation with the company’s strategic goals can reduce risks and improve the likelihood of success.
rfid-technology-in-the-manufacture-of-cu.layman: A tracking technology called RFId is common in stores but rarely used in factories. A European pipe-making company tested whether it could help. They found that planning carefully and matching the technology to the company’s long-term goals makes it more likely to work well.

logistics-4-0-and-emerging-sustainable-b.scientist: The drive towards Logistics 4.0 as an element of Industry 4.0 gives possibilities for new business models. Instant information exchange, automated solutions and real-time big data analysis are among the features of Logistics 4.0 paving the way for new business models. The role and importance of information are changing as we can see today. The demand for sustainability of business creates on the other hand new requirements to the operations of manufacturing and logistics. This paper addresses these challenges, illustrates current trends, and offers a model to understand and relate the different elements of business operations.
logistics-4-0-and-emerging-sustainable-b.student: The shift toward Logistics 4.0, part of the broader Industry 4.0 movement, introduces new business opportunities through instant data sharing, automation, and real-time analysis of large datasets. This evolution changes how information is valued and used in supply chains. At the same time, growing sustainability demands are reshaping manufacturing and logistics operations. This study examines these challenges, outlines emerging trends, and proposes a framework to help understand and connect the various components of business operations in this changing landscape.
logistics-4-0-and-emerging-sustainable-b.layman: Businesses are changing how they move and manage goods, using new technology to share information instantly and make decisions automatically. At the same time, there’s a push to make these processes more environmentally friendly. This research looks at these changes, explains what’s happening now, and suggests a way to see how all the different parts of a business fit together.

the-fit-of-industry-4-0-applications-in-.scientist: The fourth industrial revolution, Industry 4.0, is expected to cause disruptive changes in industrial production. It is driven by rapid technological developments and the need for manufacturing companies to make themselves independent of high labor costs. Industry 4.0 concerns several aspects of industrial production, including manufacturing logistics, business models and products and services. The applications of Industry 4.0 have been vastly outlined. However, the fit of Industry 4.0 applications in different production environments is not clear. The purpose of this paper is to identify and investigate the Industry 4.0 technologies that are applicable to manufacturing logistics, and how the production environment influences the applicability of these technologies. This is done through a multiple case study of four Norwegian manufacturing companies. The findings from the study indicate that the applicability of Industry 4.0 in manufacturing logistics is dependent on the production environment. Companies with a low degree of production repetitiveness see less potential in applying Industry 4.0 technologies in manufacturing logistics, while companies with a highly repetitive production see a higher potential.
the-fit-of-industry-4-0-applications-in-.student: Industry 4.0, the fourth industrial revolution, aims to transform manufacturing through advanced technologies like automation and data exchange. While its potential is widely discussed, it remains unclear which of its applications suit different production settings. This study explores which Industry 4.0 technologies are viable for manufacturing logistics and how the production environment affects their use. Using a multiple case study of four Norwegian manufacturing companies, the research finds that the suitability of Industry 4.0 in logistics depends on the production environment. Companies with less repetitive production processes see fewer benefits, whereas those with highly repetitive production find greater potential for applying these technologies.
the-fit-of-industry-4-0-applications-in-.layman: Researchers wanted to know if new factory technologies, part of a trend called Industry 4.0, work well in all types of manufacturing. They studied four Norwegian companies and found that these technologies are more useful in factories that make the same products over and over. Factories that produce a wider variety of items see less benefit from the new tools.

operationalizing-lean-principles-for-lea.scientist: The engineer-to-order (ETO) manufacturing approach is used in companies developing and producing highly customized products. ETO operations include some characteristic business processes such as the sales and tendering process, engineering and design and project management. The characteristics of the ETO environment creates high complexity in these processes, resulting in considerable amounts of waste. The potential for lead time reduction is therefore high also in these processes, not only in the production and assembly processes. Building on lean manufacturing this paper seeks to operationalize lean principles in ETO operations. Through an in-depth case study of an ETO company this paper investigates the challenges, problems and improvement opportunities in the business processes of an ETO company by applying an adapted value stream mapping (VSM) approach. The study served to identify main sources of waste which negatively affect lead time in ETO operations. The paper further presents specific guidelines that operationalizes lean principles in order to reduce waste and improve lead time in ETO operations.
operationalizing-lean-principles-for-lea.student: Engineer-to-order (ETO) manufacturing involves creating highly customized products, leading to complex processes like sales, engineering, and project management. These complexities often result in inefficiencies, or 'waste,' which can delay production. This study explores how lean manufacturing principles—traditionally used to streamline production—can be applied to ETO operations. Using a detailed case study of an ETO company, the researchers adapted value stream mapping (VSM), a tool for identifying inefficiencies, to pinpoint sources of waste in business processes. The findings highlight key areas where waste occurs, negatively impacting lead times. The paper also provides practical guidelines for applying lean principles to reduce waste and improve efficiency in ETO settings.
operationalizing-lean-principles-for-lea.layman: Some companies make one-of-a-kind products, which can slow things down because every step is unique. This study looked at one such company to see where delays happen in their planning and design work, not just in building the product. They used a method to track how work flows and found places where time is wasted. The researchers then suggested ways to cut out these delays and speed up the process.

digitalized-manufacturing-logistics-in-e.scientist: The high complexity in Engineer-To-Order (ETO) operations causes major challenges for manufacturing logistics, especially in complex ETO, i.e. one-of-a-kind production. Increased digitalization of manufacturing logistics processes and activities can facilitate more efficient coordination of the material and information flows for manufacturing operations in general. However, it is not clear how to do this in the ETO environment, where products are highly customized and production is non-repetitive. This paper aims to investigate the challenges related to manufacturing logistics in ETO and how digital technologies can be applied to address them. Through a case study of a Norwegian shipyard, four main challenges related to manufacturing logistics are identified. Further, by reviewing recent literature on ETO and digitalization, the paper identifies specific applications of digital technologies in ETO manufacturing. Finally, by linking manufacturing logistics challenges to digitalization, the paper suggests four main features of digitalized manufacturing logistics in ETO: (i) seamless, digitalized information flow, (ii) identification and interconnectivity, (iii) digitalized operator support, and (iv) automated and autonomous material flow. Thus, the paper provides valuable insights into how ETO companies can move towards digitalized manufacturing logistics.
digitalized-manufacturing-logistics-in-e.student: Engineer-To-Order (ETO) manufacturing, where products are custom-built to unique specifications, creates complex logistics challenges due to non-repetitive production and high customization. This study explores how digital technologies can improve coordination of materials and information in such environments. Using a case study of a Norwegian shipyard and a literature review, the research identifies four key logistics challenges in ETO. It then links these challenges to digital solutions, proposing four features for digitalized manufacturing logistics: seamless digital information flow, identification and interconnectivity of components, digital support for operators, and automated material handling. The findings suggest practical ways ETO companies might adopt digital tools to streamline operations.
digitalized-manufacturing-logistics-in-e.layman: Factories that build one-of-a-kind products, like custom ships, face messy coordination problems because every item is different. Researchers studied a shipyard and reviewed existing work to see how digital tools could help. They found four main issues in such factories and matched each with a digital solution, like better tracking of parts or automated movement of materials. The work shows how these businesses might use technology to work more smoothly.

factors-affecting-shipyard-operations-an.scientist: Shipyards around the world have several differences that affect the logistics processes at each yard. The purpose of this paper is to develop a framework for mapping the key factors affecting shipyard logistics. We test and validate the framework by applying it to three case shipyards: one Norwegian and two South Korean. To develop the framework, we first identify key factors affecting shipyard logistics, based on a review of the existing literature. The framework is then applied using data from the three cases. Through a comparative analysis of the collected data, we identify and outline the main logistics differences and the key factors’ main implications for the shipyards. The findings from the analysis indicate that there are important differences between the shipyards, and these have implications for their scope of planning and execution of shipyard activities, their primary focus of coordination, and their primary flows, among others. Through the framework development and comparative analysis, the paper contributes to an enhanced understanding of shipyard logistics, as well as how it is affected by internal and external yard characteristics.
factors-affecting-shipyard-operations-an.student: Shipyards differ in how they manage logistics—the movement and coordination of materials, parts, and information. This study creates a framework to identify and map the key factors influencing these processes. First, we reviewed existing research to pinpoint these factors. Then, we tested the framework on three shipyards: one in Norway and two in South Korea. By comparing data from these cases, we found clear differences in how each yard plans, executes, and coordinates activities, as well as in their primary material and information flows. The framework helps explain how internal and external characteristics, like yard size or local regulations, shape logistics. The results show that these differences significantly impact how shipyards operate.
factors-affecting-shipyard-operations-an.layman: Shipyards around the world work differently, which affects how they move and manage parts and information. Researchers created a method to identify what influences these processes. They studied three shipyards—one in Norway and two in South Korea—and compared how each one operates. They found that each shipyard plans, organizes, and moves materials in its own way, often because of differences like size or local rules. The method helps explain why these differences matter and how they shape daily work.

sustainability-challenges-and-how-indust.scientist: The shipbuilding industry is under significant economic pressure and in need of more efficient solutions to secure economically sustainable operations. It is also challenged by social issues and the need for a greener maritime industry is critical. Accordingly, the shipbuilding industry is pressured across all three dimensions of sustainability. This paper aims to identify the sustainability challenges in shipbuilding supply chains and explore how Industry 4.0 technologies can impact the sustainability of shipbuilding. This is achieved through a case study of a shipbuilding supply chain, which results in the identification of its primary sustainability challenges. Further, this work proposes a set of nine digital solutions to support sustainable operations in shipbuilding as the paper’s primary contribution. This lays the foundation for further empirical research on sustainability and digitalization in shipbuilding, while for practice the paper provides enhanced insight into how Industry 4.0 technologies can be adopted in shipbuilding supply chains.
sustainability-challenges-and-how-indust.student: The shipbuilding industry faces economic, social, and environmental pressures, as it must balance cost efficiency with sustainability and social responsibility. This study examines the sustainability challenges in shipbuilding supply chains and explores how Industry 4.0 technologies—advanced digital tools like automation, data analytics, and the Internet of Things—could address them. Using a case study of a shipbuilding supply chain, the research identifies key sustainability issues and proposes nine digital solutions to improve operations. The findings suggest that these technologies may help the industry meet its sustainability goals, though further empirical research is needed to confirm their effectiveness. The work also offers practical insights for integrating Industry 4.0 into shipbuilding supply chains.
sustainability-challenges-and-how-indust.layman: Shipbuilders struggle with high costs, social concerns, and the need to be more eco-friendly. Researchers studied a shipbuilding supply chain to find its biggest sustainability problems. They then suggested nine digital tools, like smart sensors and data analysis, that might help make shipbuilding more sustainable. The study shows these tools could be useful, but more testing is needed. It also gives ideas on how shipbuilders might start using these new technologies.

towards-a-concept-for-digitalized-yard-l.scientist: Yards are industrial sites for production and servicing of ships and offshore maritime installations, such as oil and gas platforms and modules, offshore windmills, and fish farms—all essential products in the maritime industry. Although many yards are performing highly complex and technically advanced production, there is still a need to bring the internal logistics of yards to a corresponding level of advancement. Industry 4.0 technologies may answer this need, and this paper presents a concept for digitalized yard logistics. The concept is developed through a concept development activity inspired by design science research, based on a multiple case study of 8 Norwegian yards, including shipyards and offshore construction yards. By mapping these yards, in particular their current level of digitalization, we propose a concept grounded in practice. The concept is built upon four main features of digitalized yard logistics: i) seamless, digitalized information flow, ii) identification and interconnectivity of objects, iii) digitalized operator support, and iv) automated and autonomous material flow. The paper describes and visualizes how currently available digital technologies can be applied in the yard logistics context, to achieve those four main features. The concept may be used as inspiration for moving towards the next generation of yard logistics. The paper also addresses qualitatively the potential effects of digitalized yard logistics on yard logistics performance. In this way, the paper may serve as a starting point for more advanced and specific developments, as well as possible realizations, of digitalized yard logistics systems.
towards-a-concept-for-digitalized-yard-l.student: Shipyards and offshore construction sites, called yards, build and service complex maritime structures like oil platforms and wind turbines. While their production is advanced, their internal logistics—how materials and information move—often lag behind. This study proposes a digitalized logistics concept for yards, developed through a design science approach and a case study of eight Norwegian yards. The concept aims to modernize logistics with four key features: seamless digital information flow, object identification and interconnectivity (e.g., tracking parts with sensors), digital support for operators, and automated material handling. The paper shows how existing digital technologies can enable these features and discusses potential performance improvements. It serves as a foundation for future, more detailed developments in yard logistics.
towards-a-concept-for-digitalized-yard-l.layman: Shipyards build and repair ships and offshore structures like oil rigs. Their work is high-tech, but the way they move materials and information around is often outdated. Researchers studied eight Norwegian yards to design a better system using digital tools. Their idea includes tracking parts with sensors, giving workers digital help, and automating material transport. They show how current technology can make this happen and suggest it could improve efficiency. The work is a starting point for making yard operations more modern.

yard-logistics-framework-and-classificat.scientist: For shipyards and offshore construction yards delivering highly customized and complex products via an engineer-to-order (ETO) manufacturing approach, the importance of logistics performance is increasing. This is occurring because of lower profit margins and more challenging market environments, especially in the Norwegian yard industry. However, yard logistics has not yet received adequate academic attention, and there is a lack of knowledge on how to address the current need for more cost-efficient logistics at yards. Therefore, this paper aims to develop and structure knowledge on yard logistics. Via a multiple case study of eight Norwegian yards, this paper builds on empirical evidence to establish a definition and description of yards as logistics systems in ETO manufacturing. Specifically, the paper outlines the constituents and main activities of yard logistics and describes the key characteristics of yard logistics. Furthermore, a classification model is developed to differentiate between the logistics requirements of three main types of yards: fabrication yards, outfitting yards, and service yards. This classification helps in understanding the specific logistics needs and challenges faced by different types of yards, contributing to the academic literature and providing practical insights for practitioners to enhance yard logistics performance.
yard-logistics-framework-and-classificat.student: In highly customized shipbuilding and offshore construction, where products are engineered to order (ETO), logistics performance is becoming critical due to shrinking profit margins and tougher market conditions, particularly in Norway. Yet, academic research on yard logistics remains limited, leaving gaps in how to improve cost efficiency. This study addresses this by examining eight Norwegian yards through a multiple case study. It defines yard logistics as a system within ETO manufacturing, identifying its key components, activities, and characteristics. The paper also introduces a classification model distinguishing three yard types—fabrication, outfitting, and service—each with unique logistics demands. This framework helps clarify the specific challenges and needs of different yards, offering both academic insights and practical guidance for industry professionals.
yard-logistics-framework-and-classificat.layman: Shipyards that build custom ships and offshore structures face growing pressure to cut costs and work more efficiently. However, little research has explored how to improve their logistics—the movement and management of materials and parts. This study looked at eight Norwegian shipyards to understand how logistics works in this industry. It describes the main tasks and features of shipyard logistics and groups shipyards into three types, each with different needs. The findings help explain what makes logistics in these places unique and how they can work better.

analyzing-the-factors-affecting-storage-.scientist: Offshore construction yards are under pressure to improve cost-efficiency and productivity, as they transition from oil and gas projects to new renewable energy markets such as offshore wind. These emerging markets are characterized by tighter margins, increased risk, and higher volumes of equipment, which in turn place greater demands on internal logistics and material handling. A key challenge is the management of on-site storage, where high inventory levels can lead to congestion, inefficiencies, and delays. This paper investigates the underlying factors that affect storage space management through elevating storage needs or limiting storage capacity at offshore construction yards. Using a qualitative single-case study approach, we analyze data from a Norwegian offshore construction yard collected through interviews and a validation workshop. The findings identify eight main factors, spanning supplier collaboration, planning practices, project execution, and internal coordination. The study proposes targeted strategies to reduce on-site storage, including revised planning parameters, improved supplier interfaces, project differentiation, and enhanced cross-functional coordination. A conceptual model is developed to visualize the relationships between these factors, their consequences, and proposed interventions. The paper contributes to a better understanding of logistics challenges in complex engineer-to-order environments and offers recommendations for offshore yards seeking to improve material flow and reduce inventory-related constraints.
analyzing-the-factors-affecting-storage-.student: Offshore construction yards, traditionally focused on oil and gas, are shifting to renewable energy projects like offshore wind, where tighter budgets, higher risks, and larger equipment volumes strain logistics. A major issue is on-site storage: excess inventory causes congestion and delays. This study explores factors that increase storage needs or limit capacity at a Norwegian yard. Using interviews and a workshop, it identifies eight key factors—such as supplier collaboration, planning, and project execution—that influence storage. The research suggests strategies like better planning, supplier coordination, and cross-functional teamwork to reduce storage. A conceptual model maps these factors, their effects, and solutions, offering insights for improving material flow in complex, custom-engineered environments.
analyzing-the-factors-affecting-storage-.layman: Construction sites that build offshore structures are moving from oil and gas to wind energy, where costs are tighter and projects are bigger. Storing too much material on-site causes delays and clutter. Researchers studied one Norwegian site to find out why storage becomes a problem. They talked to workers and found eight main reasons, like poor planning or weak teamwork. They suggest better coordination and planning to keep storage under control. The study helps these sites work more smoothly.

comparison-of-two-different-types-of-red.scientist: Computerized solutions for field management optimization often require reduced-order models to be computationally tractable. The purpose of this paper is to compare two different graph-based approaches for building such models. The first approach represents the reservoir as a graph of 1D numerical flow models that each connects an injector to a producer. One thus builds a network in which the topology is primarily determined by ‘well nodes’ to which ‘non-well nodes’ can be connected if need be. The second approach aims at building richer models so that the connectivity graph mimics the intercell connections in a conventional, coarse 3D grid model. One thus builds a network with topology defined by a mesh-like placement of ‘non-well nodes’, to which wells can be subsequently connected. The two approaches thus can be seen as graph-based analogues of traditional streamline and finite-volume simulation models. Both model types can be trained to match well responses obtained from underlying fine-scale simulations using standard misfit minimization methods; herein we rely on adjoint-based gradient optimization. Our comparisons show that graph models having a connectivity graph that mimics the intercell connectivity in coarse 3D models can represent a wider range of fluid connections and are generally more robust and easier to train than graph models built upon 1D subgridded interwell connections between injectors and producers only.
comparison-of-two-different-types-of-red.student: Optimizing field management in subsurface reservoirs often relies on simplified, or reduced-order, models to keep computations feasible. This study compares two graph-based methods for constructing such models. The first method treats the reservoir as a network of 1D flow paths, each linking an injection well to a production well, with additional nodes added as needed. The second method builds a mesh-like graph where non-well nodes are arranged to mimic the connections in a coarse 3D grid, to which wells are then attached. These approaches parallel traditional streamline and finite-volume simulations. Both model types are trained to match well responses from fine-scale simulations using adjoint-based gradient optimization. Results indicate that the mesh-like graph models, which replicate 3D connectivity, capture a broader range of fluid pathways and are generally more robust and easier to train than the 1D interwell models.
comparison-of-two-different-types-of-red.layman: Researchers wanted to find the best way to simplify complex underground fluid flow models for practical use. They tested two methods: one that connects injection and production wells with simple lines, and another that uses a grid-like network to better represent the underground structure. Both were adjusted to match detailed simulations. The grid-like method proved more reliable and easier to adjust, as it better captured how fluids move through the underground space.

agentic-scientific-simulation-execution-.scientist: We ask whether an LLM agent can serve as a genuine scientific assistant for physics-based simulation: given a natural-language description of a model, can it produce an executable, physically valid simulation configuration that faithfully represents the user’s intent, navigating API contracts, unit conventions, and global constraints in the way a knowledgeable research assistant would? The challenge is not merely generating code that runs or even satisfies physical consistency tests. Natural-language descriptions of simulation models are inherently underspecified, and different admissible resolutions of implicit choices produce physically valid but scientifically distinct configurations. Without explicit detection and resolution of these ambiguities, neither the correctness of the result nor its reproducibility from the original description can be assured. This paper investigates agentic scientific simulation, where model construction is organized as an execution-grounded interpret–act–validate loop, and the simulator serves as the authoritative arbiter of physical validity rather than merely a runtime. We present JutulGPT, a reference implementation built on the fully differentiable Julia-based reservoir simulator JutulDarcy. The agent combines structured retrieval of documentation and examples with code synthesis, static analysis, code execution, and systematic interpretation of solver diagnostics. Underspecified modelling choices are detected explicitly and resolved either autonomously (with logged assumptions) or through targeted user queries. The results demonstrate that agent-mediated model construction can be grounded in simulator validation while also revealing a structural limitation: choices resolved tacitly through simulator defaults are invisible to the assumption log and therefore to any downstream representation. A secondary experiment, autonomous reconstruction of a reference model from progressively abstract textual descriptions, shows that reconstruction variability exposes latent degrees of freedom in simulation descriptions and provides a practical methodology for auditing reproducibility. All code, prompts, and agent logs are publicly available.
agentic-scientific-simulation-execution-.student: This study explores whether a large language model (LLM) can act as a reliable assistant for creating physics-based simulations. The challenge is to turn a natural-language description of a model into a working, physically valid simulation setup that matches the user’s intent, handling technical details like API rules, unit systems, and global constraints. The issue is that such descriptions are often incomplete, leaving room for different but equally valid interpretations. Without addressing these ambiguities, the simulation’s correctness and reproducibility are at risk. The paper introduces JutulGPT, an LLM-based agent that uses a loop of interpretation, action, and validation, with the simulator itself checking for physical validity. The agent retrieves documentation, writes code, analyses it, runs it, and interprets solver outputs. It detects and resolves underspecified choices, either on its own (with logged assumptions) or by asking the user. Results show this approach grounds model construction in simulator validation but also reveals a limitation: simulator defaults can hide assumptions. A secondary test shows that reconstructing a model from abstract descriptions highlights hidden flexibility in simulation setups, offering a way to audit reproducibility. All code and logs are public.
agentic-scientific-simulation-execution-.layman: Can a smart computer program help scientists create accurate simulations of physical systems just from a written description? The problem is that these descriptions often leave out details, leading to different but valid interpretations. The researchers built a system that turns the description into a working simulation, checks it for physical accuracy, and asks the user to clarify any missing details. They found that while this works, some hidden choices in the simulation software can go unnoticed. They also showed that trying to rebuild a model from vague descriptions reveals how much flexibility exists in such setups, which helps check if the results can be repeated. All their work is available for others to see.

data-driven-modelling-with-coarse-grid-n.scientist: We propose to use a conventional simulator, formulated on the topology of a coarse volumetric 3D grid, as a data-driven network model that seeks to reproduce observed and predict future well responses. The conceptual difference from standard history matching is that the tunable network parameters are calibrated freely without regard to the physical interpretation of their calibrated values. The simplest version uses a minimal rectilinear mesh covering the assumed map outline and base/top surface of the reservoir. The resulting CGNet models fit immediately in any standard simulator and are very fast to evaluate because of the low cell count. We show that surprisingly accurate network models can be developed using grids with a few tens or hundreds of cells. Compared with similar interwell network models (e.g., Ren et al., 2019, 10.2118/193855-MS), a typical CGNet model has fewer computational cells but a richer connection graph and more tunable parameters. In our experience, CGNet models therefore calibrate better and are simpler to set up to reflect known fluid contacts, etc. For cases with poor vertical connection or internal fluid contacts, it is advantageous if the model has several horizontal layers in the network topology. We also show that starting with a good ballpark estimate of the reservoir volume is a precursor to a good calibration.
data-driven-modelling-with-coarse-grid-n.student: This study explores using a standard reservoir simulator, based on a coarse 3D grid, as a data-driven model to replicate past and predict future well responses. Unlike traditional history matching, the model’s adjustable parameters are tuned freely, without requiring physical meaning. The simplest version uses a basic rectangular grid covering the reservoir’s outline and depth. These models, called CGNet, integrate easily into existing simulators and run quickly due to their low cell count. Surprisingly, grids with only tens or hundreds of cells can produce accurate results. Compared to similar interwell network models, CGNet uses fewer cells but has a more complex connection structure and more tunable parameters, leading to better calibration and easier setup. For reservoirs with poor vertical flow or internal fluid barriers, adding horizontal layers improves performance. A rough estimate of reservoir volume also helps achieve better calibration.
data-driven-modelling-with-coarse-grid-n.layman: Researchers tested a simple computer model to predict how fluids move in underground reservoirs, like those holding oil or water. Instead of building a detailed, physically accurate model, they used a basic grid and adjusted its settings freely to match real-world data. Even with very few grid points, the model worked well. It was faster and more flexible than older methods, especially when the reservoir had layers or barriers. A rough guess of the reservoir’s size also helped the model work better.

the-application-of-flow-diagnostics-for-.scientist: Flow diagnostics, as referred to herein, are computational tools derived from controlled numerical flow experiments that yield quantitative information regarding the flow behavior of a reservoir model in settings much simpler than would be encountered in the actual field. In contrast to output from traditional reservoir simulators, flow-diagnostic measures can be obtained within seconds. The methodology can be used to evaluate, rank, and/or compare realizations or strategies, and the computational speed makes it ideal for interactive visualization output. We also consider application of flow diagnostics as proxies in optimization of reservoir-management work flows. In particular, by use of finite-volume discretizations for pressure, time of flight (TOF), and stationary tracers, we efficiently compute general Lorenz coefficients (and variants) that are shown to correlate well with simulated recovery. For efficient optimization, we develop an adjoint code for gradient computations of the considered flow-diagnostic measures. We present several numerical examples, including optimization of rates, well placements, and drilling sequences for two- and three-phase synthetic and real field models. Overall, optimizing the diagnostic measures implies substantial improvement in simulation-based objectives.
the-application-of-flow-diagnostics-for-.student: This study introduces flow diagnostics—fast computational tools that analyze simplified reservoir models to quantify flow behavior, unlike slower traditional simulators. These tools, derived from controlled numerical experiments, can evaluate, rank, or compare reservoir models or strategies in seconds, making them useful for real-time visualization. The researchers use finite-volume methods to compute metrics like Lorenz coefficients (measures of flow heterogeneity) and time of flight (TOF), which correlate well with oil recovery. They also develop an adjoint code to efficiently calculate gradients for optimization. Examples include optimizing production rates, well placements, and drilling sequences in synthetic and real reservoir models. The results show that improving these diagnostic measures leads to better performance in full simulations.
the-application-of-flow-diagnostics-for-.layman: The researchers asked how to quickly predict and improve oil recovery from underground reservoirs. They created fast computer tools that analyze simplified models of how fluids move through rock. These tools can compare different strategies in seconds, unlike slower traditional methods. By measuring how unevenly fluids flow, they found these quick checks match well with actual recovery results. They also built a way to fine-tune these checks for better decisions. Tests showed that using these tools to guide choices like where to drill or how much to pump can lead to better oil recovery.

a-novel-hybrid-physics-data-driven-model.scientist: Fractured reservoir simulation plays a crucial role in understanding various subsurface geo-energy recovery and storage processes, including shale gas/oil extraction, enhanced geothermal systems, and CO2 sequestration in basaltic rocks. However, such simulations often entail significant computational expenses due to the high contrast in permeability and pore volume between matrix and fractures. To address this challenge, we introduce a reduced-order model (ROM) tailored for fractured reservoir simulation that offers flexible fracture representations by generating coarse matrix nodes based on reservoir outlines and adding extra diagonal connections between unconnected matrix nodes, whose corresponding volumes are intersected by fractures. This approach avoids the need for additional fracture nodes, effectively reducing computational costs. Dimensionality reduction methods, such as principal component analysis (PCA), are used to give quality priors for sampling matrix transmissibility and PV arrays. Tuning to well observation data, such as flow rates and bottomhole pressures (BHPs), is achieved through a gradient-based optimization method within a general automatic-differentiable simulator framework. Our results demonstrate robust calibration using synthetic well observation data from a fine-scale reference simulation model. Incorporating dominant flow physics, such as water breakthrough, from observation data improves history-matching (HM) convergence and prediction accuracy. Additionally, PCA for parameterization enhances the convergence rate of model calibration compared with random initialization. Calibrated transmissibilities align with high-connectivity regions from the fine-scale reference model, rendering the model interpretable in terms of reservoir connectivity or geology. This feature enables our method to be used effectively for reservoir HM and optimization using field observation data.
a-novel-hybrid-physics-data-driven-model.student: Fractured reservoirs—subsurface rock formations with cracks that store fluids like oil, gas, or CO2—are hard to simulate because fractures and the surrounding rock (matrix) have very different flow properties. This study proposes a reduced-order model (ROM) that simplifies the simulation by grouping matrix cells and adding connections where fractures intersect them, avoiding extra fracture nodes. To improve accuracy, the model uses dimensionality reduction (like PCA) to guide the sampling of flow properties (transmissibility and pore volume). It then adjusts these properties to match real-world data (e.g., flow rates, pressures) using optimization. Tests on synthetic data show the model calibrates well, captures key flow behaviors (like water breakthrough), and speeds up convergence compared to random starts. The calibrated results also reflect the reservoir’s true connectivity, making the model both efficient and interpretable for real-world applications.
a-novel-hybrid-physics-data-driven-model.layman: Researchers studied how fluids move through cracked underground rock, which is important for extracting oil, storing CO2, or using geothermal energy. Simulating this is usually slow and complex. They created a simpler model that groups parts of the rock and adds connections where cracks pass through, making calculations faster. They also used a method to improve the model’s starting guesses and adjusted it to match real data, like fluid flow rates. The model worked well in tests, captured key behaviors, and matched the rock’s true structure, making it useful for real-world predictions.

calculating-bayesian-model-evidence-for-.scientist: We consider calculation of the Bayesian model evidence, which is an essential component in realistic uncertainty quantification. The main motivation is large-scale porous-media-flow problems, where plain Monte-Carlo (MC) integration is computationally infeasible. We propose a simplistic multilevel (ML) estimator and argue why this estimator is expected to perform well within a certain problem class, and point out that many important problems, including many porous-media-flow problems, belong to this class. Four test cases are utilized to assess the performance of the proposed ML estimator. Test cases I and II contain two strongly linked toy models, but only Test case II belongs to the problem class where the proposed ML estimator is expected to perform well. Test cases III and IV are concerned with single-phase and two-phase porous-media flows, respectively. The results show that the ML estimator clearly and consistently outperforms MC integration in Test cases II, III, and IV, while this is not the case for Test case I.
calculating-bayesian-model-evidence-for-.student: This study addresses the challenge of computing Bayesian model evidence—a key part of quantifying uncertainty in predictions. The focus is on large-scale porous-media-flow problems, where standard Monte-Carlo (MC) methods are too slow. The authors propose a multilevel (ML) estimator, a simplified approach expected to work well for a specific class of problems, which includes many porous-media-flow cases. They test this estimator on four scenarios: two linked toy models (only one fits the expected class), and two real-world porous-media flows (single-phase and two-phase). Results show the ML estimator outperforms MC in three cases (II, III, IV) but not in the first, confirming its effectiveness depends on the problem type.
calculating-bayesian-model-evidence-for-.layman: Researchers wanted to improve how they measure uncertainty in predictions for fluid flow through porous materials, like water through soil. Standard methods are too slow for large problems, so they tried a new, simpler approach. They tested it on four examples, including two realistic fluid-flow cases. The new method worked better than the old one in three tests but not the first, showing it helps in some situations but not all.

verification-of-a-real-time-ensemble-bas.scientist: The complexity of geomodelling workflows is a limiting factor for quantifying and updating uncertainty in real-time during drilling. We propose Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for parametrization and generation of geomodels, combined with Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (EnRML) for rapid updating of subsurface uncertainty. This real-time ensemble method is known to be approximate for non-linear forward models and might therefore produce inaccurate and/or biased posterior solutions when combined with a highly non-linear model arising from the neural-network modeling sequences. This paper illustrates the predictive ability of EnRML on several examples where we assimilate local extra-deep electromagnetic logs. Statistical verification with MCMC confirms that the proposed workflow can produce reliable results required for geosteering wells.
verification-of-a-real-time-ensemble-bas.student: Geomodelling workflows are complex, making it hard to update subsurface uncertainty in real-time during drilling. This study explores using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)—a type of machine learning model that generates synthetic data—to create geomodels, paired with Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (EnRML), a method for rapid uncertainty updates. Since EnRML is approximate for non-linear models, combining it with neural networks (which are highly non-linear) may introduce inaccuracies. The paper tests this approach on examples using extra-deep electromagnetic logs, showing EnRML’s predictive ability. Statistical checks with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) confirm the workflow can produce reliable results for guiding well drilling (geosteering).
verification-of-a-real-time-ensemble-bas.layman: Drilling for oil or gas requires constant updates about what lies underground, but current methods are slow and complex. Researchers tested a new approach using AI to create underground models and a fast method to update predictions as new data comes in. They checked if this combo works well by comparing it to a trusted but slower method. The results suggest the new approach can reliably guide drilling decisions in real time.

deep-learning-for-prediction-of-complex-.scientist: During a geosteering operation the well path is intentionally adjusted in response to the new data acquired while drilling. To achieve consistent high-quality decisions, especially when drilling in complex environments, decision support systems can help cope with high volumes of data and interpretation complexities. They can assimilate the realtime measurements into a probabilistic earth model and use the updated model for decision recommendations. Recently, machine learning (ML) techniques have enabled a wide range of methods that redistribute computational cost from on-line to offline calculations. In this paper, we introduce two ML techniques into the geosteering decision support framework. Firstly, a complex earth model representation is generated using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). Secondly, a commercial extra-deep electromagnetic simulator is represented using a Forward Deep Neural Network (FDNN). The numerical experiments demonstrate that the combination of the GAN and the FDNN in an ensemble randomized maximum likelihood data assimilation scheme provides real-time estimates of complex geological uncertainty. This yields reduction of geological uncertainty ahead of the drill-bit from the measurements gathered behind and around the well bore.
deep-learning-for-prediction-of-complex-.student: Geosteering adjusts a well’s path in real time using data collected while drilling. In complex environments, decision support systems help manage large data volumes and interpretation challenges by updating a probabilistic earth model with real-time measurements to guide decisions. This study integrates two machine learning (ML) methods into such a system. First, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)—a type of ML model that generates synthetic data—creates a detailed earth model. Second, a Forward Deep Neural Network (FDNN) replaces a computationally expensive electromagnetic simulator. Numerical tests show that combining the GAN and FDNN within a data assimilation framework improves real-time estimates of geological uncertainty, reducing uncertainty ahead of the drill bit using measurements from behind and around the wellbore.
deep-learning-for-prediction-of-complex-.layman: When drilling a well, workers adjust its path based on data collected as they go. This can be tricky in complex underground areas. Researchers built a system that uses computer programs to process this data and predict what lies ahead. They tested two new methods: one creates realistic underground models, and the other speeds up a slow but accurate simulation. Together, these methods help the system make better predictions in real time, reducing guesswork about what’s ahead of the drill.

distinguish-workflow-a-new-paradigm-of-d.scientist: The real-time process of directional changes while drilling, known as geosteering, is crucial for hydrocarbon extraction and emerging directional drilling applications such as geothermal energy, civil infrastructure, and CO2 storage. The geo-energy industry seeks an automatic geosteering workflow that continually updates the subsurface uncertainties and captures the latest geological understanding given the most recent observations in real-time. We propose “DISTINGUISH”: a real-time, AI-driven workflow designed to transform geosteering by integrating Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for geological parameterization, ensemble methods for model updating, and global discrete dynamic programming (DDP) optimization for complex decision-making during directional drilling operations. The DISTINGUISH framework relies on offline training of a GAN model to reproduce relevant geology realizations and a Forward Neural Network (FNN) to model Logging-While-Drilling (LWD) tools’ response for a given geomodel. This paper introduces a first-of-its-kind workflow that progressively reduces GAN-geomodel uncertainty around and ahead of the drilling bit and adjusts the well plan accordingly. The workflow automatically integrates real-time LWD data with a DDP-based decision support system, enhancing predictive models of geology ahead of drilling and leading to better steering decisions. We present a simple yet representative benchmark case and document the performance target achieved by the DISTINGUISH workflow prototype. This benchmark will be a foundation for future methodological advancements and workflow refinements.
distinguish-workflow-a-new-paradigm-of-d.student: Geosteering, the real-time adjustment of a drill’s direction, is vital for oil and gas extraction and other applications like geothermal energy or CO2 storage. The industry needs an automated system that updates geological models as new data arrives. We propose DISTINGUISH, an AI-driven workflow that uses Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)—a type of machine learning—to create realistic geological models, ensemble methods to refine these models with incoming data, and dynamic programming to optimize drilling decisions. The system trains a GAN offline to simulate subsurface conditions and a neural network to predict sensor responses. During drilling, it continuously updates the geological model and adjusts the well path using real-time sensor data. A benchmark case demonstrates the prototype’s performance, serving as a basis for future improvements.
distinguish-workflow-a-new-paradigm-of-d.layman: Drilling for resources like oil or geothermal energy requires constant adjustments to stay on course. Researchers created an AI system called DISTINGUISH to help drillers make better decisions in real time. The system uses machine learning to predict what lies underground and updates its predictions as new data comes in. It then suggests the best path for the drill. A test case shows the system works, and it will be improved further.

ensemble-history-matching-workflow-using.scientist: Ensemble history matching adjusts multiple geomodels used for reservoir simulation, conditioning them to historical data. It reduces and quantifies the uncertainty in the unknown model parameters to increase the models’ reliability for decision support. In this study, we adapt the latest generation of generative artificial intelligence algorithms, SPADE-GANs. In geosciences, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) learn to simulate complex geological patterns. SPADE (SPatially Adaptive DEnormalisation) layers in the GAN generator learn conditioning to the coarse geological structure provided as coarse-scale maps, enabling explainable output, stable training, and higher variability of resulting outputs. Our statistical method, an iterative ensemble smoother, assimilates data into an ensemble of these maps, interpreted as the channel proportions. This Bayesian data assimilation conditions the ensemble of GAN-geomodels to a combination of well data and flow data, thus extending the usability of pretrained SPADE-GANs in subsurface applications. Our numerical experiments convincingly demonstrate the method’s capacity to replicate previously unseen geological configurations beyond GAN’s training data. This proficiency is particularly valuable in data-scarce scenarios typical for renewable geo-energy, where the GAN captures realistic geology, but its output geomodels must be adjusted to match observed data. Furthermore, our fully open-source developments lay the foundation for future multi-scale enhancements of history matching workflows.
ensemble-history-matching-workflow-using.student: This study improves reservoir simulation by adjusting multiple geological models to match real-world data, reducing uncertainty in predictions. The approach uses SPADE-GANs, a type of generative AI that learns to create complex geological patterns. SPADE layers allow the AI to adapt to coarse geological structures, producing varied and explainable outputs. The researchers combined this with an iterative ensemble smoother, a statistical method that integrates well and flow data into the AI-generated models. This Bayesian data assimilation ensures the models align with observed data, even for geological configurations not seen during training. The method is particularly useful in renewable geo-energy, where data is scarce. Numerical experiments show it can replicate unseen geological setups, and the open-source tools support future multi-scale improvements.
ensemble-history-matching-workflow-using.layman: Researchers wanted to improve predictions about underground rock layers, which are hard to study directly. They used a type of AI that creates realistic rock patterns and adjusted these patterns to match real measurements from wells and fluid flow. Their method works even when there’s little data and can handle new, unseen rock formations. This helps make better decisions in areas like renewable energy, where understanding the underground is key.

uncertainty-aware-well-placement-simulat.scientist: Geosteering, the art of navigating wells to maximize the reservoir resources, is fraught with challenges of geological uncertainty and the relentless pace of real-time operations. In this paper, we present a novel framework that integrates Particle Filters (PF) for probabilistic subsurface interpretation with a Dual-Network Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) model for adaptive decision-making in geosteering operations. The PF component quantifies subsurface uncertainties, providing a probabilistic interpretation of geological boundaries, while the DRL model leverages this information to generate optimal steering decisions. This synergy ensures robust trajectory planning that dynamically adapts to real-time geological changes. The framework incorporates key features, such as target-line alignment to maintain wellbore proximity to reservoir zones and dog-leg severity constraints to ensure operational feasibility. Extensive verification in an industry-standard environment accessed via an API demonstrates the model’s ability to accurately track reservoir boundaries, predict gamma-ray values, and optimize well trajectories. The results highlight significant improvements over traditional geosteering approaches and standard DRL-based methods in terms of reservoir contact, decision-making efficiency, and trajectory accuracy, even in low-data scenarios. The proposed framework provides a scalable and robust solution for quantifying uncertainties in real-time geosteering, paving the way for informed operational decisions improving value-creation and drilling efficiency.
uncertainty-aware-well-placement-simulat.student: Geosteering involves steering a drill bit through underground rock layers to hit the best parts of a reservoir. This study tackles the problem of geological uncertainty and the need for quick, real-time decisions. The researchers built a system that combines Particle Filters (a method for estimating uncertain subsurface conditions) with a Dual-Network Deep Reinforcement Learning model (a type of AI that learns optimal actions through trial and error). The Particle Filter maps likely geological boundaries, while the AI uses this data to decide the best drilling path. The system also ensures the drill stays close to the target layer and avoids sharp turns that could damage equipment. Tests in a standard industry simulator showed the method outperforms older geosteering techniques and basic AI approaches, especially when data is scarce. It better tracks reservoir edges, predicts rock properties, and plans efficient paths, offering a reliable way to handle uncertainty in real-time drilling.
uncertainty-aware-well-placement-simulat.layman: Drilling for oil or gas requires steering a drill bit through underground rock to find the best spots. This is hard because the rock layers are uncertain and decisions must be made fast. The researchers created a system that uses a type of AI to make smart, real-time choices about where to drill. It combines a method to guess the rock layers with another to pick the best path. Tests showed it works better than older methods, even with little data. This could make drilling more precise and efficient.

an-adaptive-large-neighborhood-search-he.scientist: This paper considers a generalized version of the planar storage location problem arising in the stowage planning for Roll-on/Roll-off ships. A ship is set to sail along a predefined voyage where given cargoes are to be transported between different port pairs along the voyage. We aim at determining the optimal stowage plan for the vehicles stored on a deck of the ship so that the time spent moving vehicles to enable loading or unloading of other vehicles (shifting), is minimized. We propose a novel mixed integer programming model for the problem, considering both the stowage and shifting aspect of the problem. An adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) heuristic with several new destroy and repair operators is developed. We further show how the shifting cost can be effectively evaluated using Dijkstra’s algorithm by transforming the stowage plan into a network graph. The computational results show that the ALNS heuristic provides high quality solutions to realistic test instances.
an-adaptive-large-neighborhood-search-he.student: This study tackles an extended version of the planar storage location problem, specifically for stowage planning on Roll-on/Roll-off (Ro-Ro) ships. These ships transport vehicles between ports, and the goal is to arrange vehicles on the deck to minimize the time spent moving them (shifting) to load or unload others. The researchers created a mixed integer programming model to address both stowage and shifting. They also developed an adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) heuristic, a method that iteratively improves solutions by destroying and repairing parts of them, with new operators tailored to this problem. To efficiently calculate shifting costs, they used Dijkstra’s algorithm by converting the stowage plan into a network graph. Tests on realistic scenarios show the ALNS heuristic produces strong solutions.
an-adaptive-large-neighborhood-search-he.layman: The researchers studied how to best arrange vehicles on a ship to reduce the time spent moving them when loading or unloading. They designed a mathematical model and a computer method to find good solutions. They also used a well-known path-finding technique to calculate the effort needed to move vehicles. Their approach worked well on realistic examples.

evaluating-passing-ability-in-associatio.scientist: In this paper, the passing ability of football players is determined by building three generalized additive mixed models that each explains a different aspect of a pass’ success: difficulty, risk and potential. The models are built on data from the 2014–2016 seasons of the Norwegian top division Eliteserien, and their predictive power is tested on the 2017 season. The results provide insight into the factors affecting the success of a pass in Eliteserien. These include the location of the pass, the relationship to previous passes and to situations such as throw-ins, corners, free kicks or tackles, as well as conditions specific to the Eliteserien, such as the time of season and the ground surface type. Finally, the key pass makers in the league are identified.
evaluating-passing-ability-in-associatio.student: This study assesses how well football players pass the ball by creating three statistical models—generalized additive mixed models—that predict different aspects of pass success: difficulty, risk, and potential. Using data from the 2014–2016 Norwegian Eliteserien seasons, the models were trained and then tested on the 2017 season to evaluate their accuracy. The findings reveal that pass success depends on factors like the pass’s location on the field, its relation to prior passes or game situations (e.g., throw-ins, corners), and league-specific conditions such as the time of year or the type of ground surface. The study also identifies the top pass makers in the league.
evaluating-passing-ability-in-associatio.layman: Researchers wanted to find out what makes a good pass in professional football. They studied data from Norwegian league games over several years, building models to predict how difficult, risky, or useful a pass might be. They found that where the pass is made, what happened just before it, and even the time of year or the type of field all affect whether it succeeds. They also picked out the best passers in the league.

maritime-fleet-composition-under-future-.scientist: This paper studies the maritime fleet composition problem with uncertain future fuel and carbon prices under the restriction of complying with future greenhouse gas (GHG) emission restrictions. We propose a two-stage stochastic programming model that can be adapted to two different variants of this problem. The first variant considers the Maritime Fleet Renewal Problem where there is an existing initial fleet to be renewed through scrapping and acquisitions, as well as retrofitting of ships in the current fleet. The second variant considers the Maritime Fleet Size and Mix Problem, where also the initial fleet must be determined. When applying the model to a fleet of Supramax bulk carriers as a case study, we find that LNG- and methanol-based power systems are favorable initial choices. Two different scenario sets, with 50% and 90% reduction restrictions by 2045, are investigated. Depending on the ambition level, retrofits towards ammonia can be cost-effective.
maritime-fleet-composition-under-future-.student: This study addresses the challenge of planning a maritime fleet under uncertain future fuel and carbon prices while meeting greenhouse gas (GHG) emission limits. The authors develop a two-stage stochastic programming model—a method that accounts for uncertainty by considering multiple possible future scenarios. The model is applied to two versions of the problem: one where an existing fleet is renewed through scrapping, acquisitions, or retrofitting ships, and another where the initial fleet size and composition must also be determined. In a case study of Supramax bulk carriers, LNG- and methanol-based power systems emerge as strong initial choices. The analysis also explores two emission reduction targets (50% and 90% by 2045), finding that retrofits to ammonia may become cost-effective depending on the stringency of the target.
maritime-fleet-composition-under-future-.layman: Researchers looked at how shipping companies can plan their fleets when future fuel costs and carbon prices are uncertain, while still meeting strict pollution limits. They created a model to test different options, like buying new ships, scrapping old ones, or upgrading existing vessels. For a type of cargo ship, they found that using liquefied natural gas or methanol as fuel is a good starting point. If pollution rules get very strict, switching some ships to ammonia could save money.

combining-hybrid-genetic-search-with-rui.scientist: The Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) has been subject to intense research efforts for more than sixty years. Yet, significant algorithmic improvements are still being made. The most competitive heuristic solution algorithms of today utilize, and often combine, strategies and elements from evolutionary algorithms, local search, and ruin-and-recreate based large neighborhood search. In this paper we propose a new hybrid metaheuristic for the CVRP, where the education phase of the hybrid genetic search (HGS) algorithm proposed by Vidal (Hybrid Genetic Search for the CVRP: Open-Source Implementation and SWAP* Neighborhood 2020) is extended by applying large neighborhood search (LNS). By performing a series of computational experiments, we attempt to answer the following research questions: 1) Is it possible to gain performance by adding LNS as a component in the education phase of HGS? 2) How does the addition of LNS change the relative importance of the local search neighborhoods of HGS? 3) What is the effect of devoting computational efforts to the creation of an elite solution in the initial population of HGS? Through a set of computational experiments we answer these research questions, while at the same time obtaining a good configuration of global parameter settings for the proposed heuristic. Testing the heuristic on benchmark instances from the literature with limited computing time, it outperforms existing algorithms, both in terms of the final gap and the primal integral.
combining-hybrid-genetic-search-with-rui.student: The Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) involves optimising delivery routes for a fleet of vehicles with limited capacity. Current top-performing algorithms combine strategies like evolutionary methods, local search, and large neighborhood search (LNS), which explores solutions by partially destroying and rebuilding them. This study introduces a new hybrid approach by integrating LNS into the education phase of the Hybrid Genetic Search (HGS) algorithm. The researchers tested whether adding LNS improves performance, how it affects the importance of HGS’s local search components, and the impact of starting with a high-quality initial solution. Through computational experiments, they found that the hybrid method outperforms existing algorithms on standard test cases, both in solution quality and efficiency, while also identifying optimal parameter settings.
combining-hybrid-genetic-search-with-rui.layman: Researchers studied how to plan the best delivery routes for trucks with limited space. They tested a new method that combines existing techniques, including one that rebuilds parts of a route to find better options. By running experiments, they checked if this new approach works better, how it changes the way the system searches for solutions, and if starting with a good initial plan helps. The results show their method finds better routes faster than older methods when tested on standard problems.

an-improved-formulation-for-the-inventor.scientist: The Inventory Routing Problem (IRP) is a broad class of complex routing problems where the quantities of delivered products must also be determined. In this paper, we consider the classic IRP where a single supplier must determine when to visit its customers, how much to deliver and how to combine the customer visits in each period into routes. We propose a branch-and-cut algorithm based on a new mathematical formulation for the IRP, improving the average lower bound obtained from algorithms based on the branch-and-cut methodology. The new formulation substitutes parts of the original formulation with a convex combination of extreme points. We call these extreme points customer schedules and for each customer they contain information about delivery periods and corresponding delivered quantities. We show that this algorithm outperforms a state-of-the-art branch-and-cut algorithm on instances with time-varying demands. The customer schedule-based algorithm obtains better lower bounds, which improves the average optimality gap by 29% and 15% on two new sets of instances with time-varying demands.
an-improved-formulation-for-the-inventor.student: The Inventory Routing Problem (IRP) involves planning delivery routes and quantities for a supplier serving multiple customers over time. This study tackles the classic IRP, where the supplier must decide visit times, delivery amounts, and route combinations for each period. The authors introduce a new mathematical model that replaces parts of the original problem with a mix of extreme points—called customer schedules—which detail delivery periods and quantities for each customer. Using a branch-and-cut algorithm (a method for solving complex optimization problems by dividing them into smaller subproblems and cutting off non-optimal solutions), they improve the lower bounds (the best possible solution value that cannot be exceeded) compared to existing approaches. On test cases with changing demand over time, their method outperforms a leading algorithm, reducing the average gap to the optimal solution by 29% and 15% on two new datasets.
an-improved-formulation-for-the-inventor.layman: This research looks at how a supplier can best plan deliveries to customers, deciding when to visit, how much to deliver, and the best routes to take. The team created a new way to model the problem, using a mix of possible delivery plans for each customer. They then used a computer method to solve it more effectively than before. When tested on scenarios where customer demand changes over time, their approach found better solutions, closing the gap to the ideal plan by 29% and 15% in two different sets of examples.

new-benchmark-instances-for-the-inventor.scientist: The existing sets of benchmark instances for the inventory routing problem (IRP) have been beneficial for investigating and illustrating the properties of the problem. However, they possess certain features and design choices that are not necessarily representative of all real-world IRPs. Therefore, we propose a new collection of 270 real-world-like instances ranging from 10 to 200 customers. These instances vary in terms of the number of vehicles and their capacity, the length of the planning horizon, the demand structure, and the geographical distribution of customers. Transportation and inventory holding costs resemble costs found in practice. We present an instance space analysis showing that the new instances nicely complement the original instances. To derive lower and upper bounds for each instance, we present computational experiments with two high-quality solution methods: a matheuristic and an exact branch-and-cut method. The results confirm that the new set of instances is hard to solve with the proposed methods, and they demonstrate the need for developing new solution methods.
new-benchmark-instances-for-the-inventor.student: The inventory routing problem (IRP) combines delivery scheduling with stock management to minimize costs. Current benchmark datasets help study IRP but don’t fully reflect real-world conditions. We created 270 new, realistic instances with 10–200 customers, varying vehicle numbers, capacities, planning periods, demand patterns, and customer locations. Costs for transport and storage mirror practical scenarios. An analysis shows these instances complement existing ones. Using a matheuristic (a hybrid of mathematical and heuristic methods) and an exact branch-and-cut method (a precise optimization approach), we tested solvability. Results indicate these instances are challenging for current methods, suggesting a need for improved solutions.
new-benchmark-instances-for-the-inventor.layman: Researchers study how to best deliver goods while keeping storage costs low. Current test cases for this problem don’t always match real-life situations. So, they made 270 new, realistic examples with different numbers of customers, vehicles, and delivery needs. They checked if these new examples are harder to solve than old ones. The answer is yes, meaning better methods are needed to tackle real-world delivery and storage challenges.

vendor-managed-inventory-in-tramp-shippi.scientist: This paper introduces a new problem to the OR community that combines traditional tramp shipping with a vendor managed inventory (VMI) service. Such a service may replace the more traditional contract of affreightment (COA) which for decades has been the standard agreement between a tramp shipping company and a charterer. We present a mathematical formulation describing the routing and scheduling problem faced by a tramp shipping company that offers a VMI service to its customers. The problem is formulated as an arc-flow model, and is then reformulated as a path-flow model which is solved using a hybrid approach that combines branch-and-price with a priori path-generation. To solve larger, and more realistic, instances we present a heuristic path-generation algorithm. Computational experiments show that the heuristic approach is much faster than the exact method, with insignificant reductions in solution quality. Further, we investigate the economic impact of introducing a VMI service, by comparing the results obtained with the new model with results obtained by solving the traditional routing and scheduling problem faced by tramp shipping companies using COA. The computational results show that it is possible to substantially increase supply chain profit and efficiency by replacing the traditional COAs with VMI services.
vendor-managed-inventory-in-tramp-shippi.student: This study addresses a new challenge in operations research: integrating tramp shipping (where ships carry bulk cargo like grain or coal without fixed routes) with vendor managed inventory (VMI), a service where the supplier manages stock levels for the buyer. Traditionally, tramp shipping uses contracts of affreightment (COA), fixed agreements for transporting goods. The authors develop a mathematical model to optimize routing and scheduling for a shipping company offering VMI. They first use an arc-flow model, then reformulate it as a path-flow model, solved via a hybrid method combining branch-and-price (a technique for solving complex optimization problems) with pre-generated paths. For larger problems, a heuristic (approximate) path-generation algorithm is introduced. Tests show this heuristic is much faster than the exact method, with only minor quality trade-offs. The study also compares VMI to COA, finding that VMI can significantly improve supply chain profit and efficiency.
vendor-managed-inventory-in-tramp-shippi.layman: Researchers looked at how shipping companies that transport bulk goods like coal or grain could better manage their routes and deliveries. Normally, these companies use fixed contracts to move goods. The team created a new system where the shipping company also manages the customer’s inventory. They built a detailed plan to test this idea and found a faster, simpler way to solve the problem for real-world cases. When they compared the new system to the old one, it made the supply chain more profitable and efficient.

optimizing-vessel-fleet-size-and-mix-to-.scientist: This paper considers the problem of determining the optimal vessel fleet to support maintenance operations at an offshore wind farm. We propose a two-stage stochastic programming (SP) model of the problem where the first stage decisions are what vessels to charter. The second stage decisions are how to support maintenance tasks using the chartered vessels from the first stage, given uncertainty in weather conditions and the occurrence of failures. To solve the resulting SP model we perform an ad-hoc Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition where, unlike standard decomposition approaches for SP models, parts of the second stage problem remain in the master problem. The decomposed model is then solved as a matheuristic by apriori generating a subset of the possible extreme points from the Dantzig–Wolfe subproblems. A computational study in three parts is presented. First, we verify the underlying mathematical model by comparing results to leading work from the literature. Then, results from in-sample and out-of-sample stability tests are presented to verify that the matheuristic gives stable results. Finally, we exemplify how the model can help offshore wind farm operators and vessel developers improve their decision making processes.
optimizing-vessel-fleet-size-and-mix-to-.student: This study tackles the challenge of selecting the best set of vessels to maintain an offshore wind farm. The authors use a two-stage stochastic programming model: first, they decide which vessels to charter, and then, under uncertain weather and failure conditions, they determine how to use those vessels for maintenance tasks. To solve this complex model, they apply a modified Dantzig–Wolfe decomposition, keeping parts of the second stage in the main problem and solving it as a matheuristic (a hybrid of mathematical and heuristic methods). The approach is tested in three ways: comparing results to existing research, checking stability through in-sample and out-of-sample tests, and demonstrating its practical use for wind farm operators and vessel developers.
optimizing-vessel-fleet-size-and-mix-to-.layman: The researchers asked how to choose the best boats to keep an offshore wind farm running smoothly. They built a model that first picks the boats and then plans how to use them, even when weather or breakdowns are unpredictable. They solved this tricky problem with a special math-based method and tested it to ensure it works well. The model can help wind farm managers and boat designers make better decisions.
