a-dual-level-stochastic-fleet-size-and-m.scientist: This paper studies the strategic problem of finding a cost optimal fleet of vessels to support maintenance operations at offshore wind farms. A dual-level stochastic model is formulated, taking into account both long-term strategic uncertainty and short-term operational uncertainty in a single optimization model. The model supports wind farm owners in making strategic decisions regarding the number, placement, charter length, and types of vessels to charter, to meet maintenance demands throughout the lifetime of a wind farm. To evaluate the quality of strategic fleet size and mix decisions, the model also considers the operational decisions of how to utilize the fleet to support maintenance operations. The model accounts for strategic uncertainties that have not been considered in previously developed optimization models for offshore wind, such as uncertainty related to long-term trends in electricity prices and subsidy levels, the stepwise development of wind farms, and technology development in the vessel industry. To solve the proposed stochastic programming model we have developed an ad hoc integer L-shaped method, with customized optimality cuts. The computational experiments show that the proposed method outperforms solving the deterministic equivalent using a commercial MIP solver.
a-dual-level-stochastic-fleet-size-and-m.student: This study addresses the challenge of cost-effectively selecting a fleet of vessels to maintain offshore wind farms. The researchers built a two-level stochastic model that combines long-term uncertainties (like electricity price trends, subsidy changes, and vessel technology advances) with short-term operational uncertainties (like daily maintenance needs). The model helps wind farm owners decide how many vessels to charter, their types, locations, and contract lengths to meet maintenance demands over the farm’s lifetime. It also evaluates how well these strategic choices work by simulating day-to-day fleet use. To solve the complex model, the team developed a specialized algorithm (an integer L-shaped method with custom optimality cuts) that proved more efficient than standard commercial solvers for this type of problem.
a-dual-level-stochastic-fleet-size-and-m.layman: The researchers asked how to choose the best mix of boats to keep offshore wind farms running at the lowest cost. They created a computer model that considers both long-term changes, like future energy prices or new boat designs, and daily needs, like repairs. The model helps decide how many boats to rent, what kinds, and where to place them. To make the model work, they designed a new method that solves the problem faster than older tools. The results show their method works better for this task.

a-multi-start-route-improving-matheurist.scientist: This paper considers the multi-vehicle production routeing problem with a maximum-level replenishment policy. This is a well-established problem within vendor managed inventory where production, inventory and routeing decisions are made simultaneously. We present a novel method to solve the problem that outperforms existing methods both in terms of solution gaps and the number of best-known solutions. The proposed matheuristic is tested on three different sets of benchmark instances consisting of 1218 instances and finds or improves the best-known solution for 632 of them. For the remaining instances, the matheuristic is less than 2.5% from the best-known solutions. The method is particularly proficient on large instances and is also efficient for the inventory routeing problem. The success of the method is largely due to its improvement phase where a novel path-flow-inspired mathematical model is introduced. Here, a route set obtained from the current solution is used and retailers can be simultaneously inserted and removed from a route, making the method flexible even when a small route set is used. In addition, we introduce a new production sub-problem that approximates the costs of using a vehicle instead of approximating the costs of visiting a retailer, making it very fast to solve.
a-multi-start-route-improving-matheurist.student: This study tackles the multi-vehicle production routing problem under a maximum-level replenishment policy, a common scenario in vendor-managed inventory where production, inventory, and routing decisions are made together. The authors propose a new solution method, a matheuristic (a hybrid of mathematical programming and heuristics), which outperforms existing approaches in both solution quality and the number of best-known solutions found. Tested on 1,218 benchmark instances, it finds or improves the best-known solution for 632 cases and stays within 2.5% of the best for the rest. The method excels on large instances and is also effective for the inventory routing problem. Its strength lies in an improvement phase using a novel path-flow-inspired model, allowing flexible route adjustments, and a fast-to-solve production sub-problem that approximates vehicle costs rather than retailer visit costs.
a-multi-start-route-improving-matheurist.layman: The researchers studied how to best plan delivery routes and production schedules for multiple vehicles under a system where stock is refilled to a set maximum level. They created a new method that works better than current ones, finding the best or improved solutions for over half of the 1,218 test cases and staying close to the best for the rest. Their approach is especially good for large, complex problems and can quickly adjust routes and production plans.

guidelines-for-standardised-classificati.scientist: This document provides guidance on how to report and classify failure and maintenance data for safety equipment, as a basis for improved follow-up and future automation. Standardised equipment grouping, equipment properties and simplified failure taxonomies are suggested. Focus is on safety instrumented systems (SIS) but selected non-instrumented safety critical equipment types are also covered. As part of future digitalisation, establishing a standardised information model for functional safety and safety instrumented function (SIF) follow-up will be an important prerequisite. A main objective with this guideline is to contribute towards such a model, by identifying standardised equipment properties and associated property values. The suggested taxonomies and properties have therefore been compared and mapped against recognised standards and relevant electronic equipment libraries.
guidelines-for-standardised-classificati.student: This work addresses the challenge of reporting and classifying failures and maintenance data for safety equipment, aiming to improve follow-up and enable future automation. It proposes standardised ways to group equipment, define their properties, and categorise failures using simplified taxonomies. While the focus is on safety instrumented systems (SIS)—automated systems designed to prevent hazardous events—it also includes some non-instrumented safety-critical equipment. The study compares its suggested taxonomies and properties with existing standards and electronic equipment libraries to ensure alignment. The goal is to contribute to a standardised information model for functional safety, which would support better tracking and management of safety instrumented functions (SIFs).
guidelines-for-standardised-classificati.layman: The researchers looked at how to better record and sort problems with safety equipment, so they can be fixed and prevented in the future. They suggest a clear way to group equipment, describe its features, and classify issues. Mostly, they focus on automated safety systems but also include some manual ones. They checked their ideas against existing rules and databases to make sure they fit. The aim is to create a shared system for tracking safety equipment, making it easier to manage and improve.

potential-for-automated-follow-up-of-saf.scientist: On petroleum facilities, safety equipment is installed to obtain risk reduction. To ensure that the desired risk reduction is achieved during the operational phase, follow-up of the reliability of such equipment is important. Essential means to follow up safety-critical equipment are the reporting, classification and analysis of failure data. However, experience shows that considerable manual effort is needed to attain high-quality data, and therefore, this report investigates possibilities for automated failure reporting and failure class determination. The proposed approaches involve the potential to guide the user with pre-defined help-texts for improved failure reporting, the possibility to utilize relevant information from systems such as the safety and automation system etc. for automatic determination of failure mode and detection method, the potential to automate failure class determination based on standardized failure mode and detection method hierarchies, as well as the use of technical language processing (TLP) methods to extract key information for improved and efficient failure class determination.
potential-for-automated-follow-up-of-saf.student: Petroleum facilities use safety equipment to reduce risk, but ensuring this equipment remains reliable over time requires tracking failures. Currently, collecting and classifying failure data is labor-intensive. This study explores ways to automate parts of this process. The proposed methods include guiding users with predefined help-texts to improve failure reports, pulling relevant data from existing systems (like safety and automation systems) to automatically identify failure modes and detection methods, and using standardized hierarchies to automate failure classification. Additionally, technical language processing (TLP) methods could extract key details to streamline and enhance failure class determination. The goal is to reduce manual effort while maintaining data quality.
potential-for-automated-follow-up-of-saf.layman: Oil and gas plants use safety gear to prevent accidents, but keeping this gear working well means tracking when it fails. Right now, this tracking is done by hand, which takes a lot of time. The researchers looked for ways to do some of this work automatically. They suggest using pre-written guides to help workers report failures better, pulling useful information from existing systems to spot problems faster, and using computer methods to sort failures into categories. The aim is to make the process quicker and more reliable without losing accuracy.

extremum-seeking-control-for-nonlinear-s.scientist: Extremum-seeking control is a powerful adaptive technique to optimize system performance. To this date, extremum-seeking control has mainly been used to optimize plants with constant steady-state outputs, whereas the non-equilibrium case, in which the steady-state outputs are time varying, has received relatively little attention compared to the equilibrium case. In this paper, we propose an extremum-seeking scheme for the optimization of nonlinear plants with periodic steady-state outputs. Extremum-seeking control in this non-equilibrium setting is relevant in, for example, the scope of tracking and disturbance rejection problems. Using the concept of semi-global practical asymptotic stability, we show that under certain assumptions the proposed extremum-seeking controller design guarantees that for an arbitrarily large set of initial conditions the steady-state performance of the plant converges arbitrarily close to its optimal value.
extremum-seeking-control-for-nonlinear-s.student: Extremum-seeking control is a method that automatically adjusts a system to find its best performance. Most work so far has focused on systems that settle to a fixed output, but this study looks at systems where the output changes over time in a repeating pattern. The authors design a new extremum-seeking controller for such nonlinear systems with periodic steady states. This is useful in problems like tracking moving targets or rejecting disturbances. Using the idea of semi-global practical asymptotic stability—a way to describe how a system’s performance gets close to the best possible value over time—they show that, under certain conditions, their controller can make the system’s performance approach its optimal value, no matter how large the initial conditions are.
extremum-seeking-control-for-nonlinear-s.layman: Researchers studied how to automatically tune a system to work at its best when its output changes in a repeating pattern over time. They created a new method to do this for systems that don’t settle to a fixed state. Their approach ensures the system gets very close to its best possible performance, even if it starts far from that point.

asymptotic-stability-of-perturbation-bas.scientist: We introduce a perturbation-based extremum-seeking controller for general nonlinear dynamical plants with an arbitrary number of tunable plant parameters. The controller ensures asymptotic convergence of the plant parameters to their performance-optimizing values for any initial plant condition under the assumptions in this work. The key to this result is that the amplitude and the frequencies of the perturbations, as well as other tuning parameters of the controller, are time varying. Remarkably, the time-varying tuning parameters can be chosen such that asymptotic convergence is achieved for all plants that satisfy the assumptions, thereby guaranteeing stability of the resulting closed-loop system of plant and controller regardless of tuning.
asymptotic-stability-of-perturbation-bas.student: This study presents a new control method, called perturbation-based extremum-seeking, designed for nonlinear systems with any number of adjustable parameters. The goal is to automatically tune these parameters to their optimal values, ensuring the system performs at its best. The controller works by introducing small, time-varying disturbances (perturbations) and adjusting their amplitude and frequency over time. Under certain assumptions, this approach guarantees that the system parameters will converge to their optimal settings, no matter the starting conditions. Importantly, the controller remains stable for all systems meeting these assumptions, without requiring manual tuning of its own parameters.
asymptotic-stability-of-perturbation-bas.layman: Researchers developed a way to automatically adjust settings in complex systems to make them work as well as possible. They did this by adding small, changing disturbances to the system and observing how it responds. Over time, the system learns the best settings on its own. The method works reliably for many types of systems, as long as they meet certain basic conditions.

a-dither-free-extremum-seeking-control-a.scientist: In this paper, we present a novel type of extremum-seeking controller, which continuously uses past data of the performance map to estimate the gradient of this performance map by means of a 1st-order least squares fit. The approach is intuitive by nature and avoids the need of dither in the extremum-seeking loop. The avoidance of dither allows for an asymptotic stability result (opposed to practical stability in dither-based schemes) and, hence, for exact convergence to the performance optimal parameter. Additionally, the absence of dither eliminates one of the time-scales of classical extremum-seeking schemes, allowing for a possibly faster convergence. A stability proof is presented for the static-map setting which relies on a Lyapunov-Razumikhin type of proof for time-delay systems. Simulations illustrate the effectiveness of the approach also for the dynamic setting.
a-dither-free-extremum-seeking-control-a.student: This study introduces a new extremum-seeking controller, a method used to find the best settings for a system by continuously optimizing its performance. Unlike traditional methods that use a small, deliberate disturbance (called dither) to estimate improvements, this approach uses past performance data to estimate the slope (gradient) of the performance map via a simple linear fit. This removes the need for dither, leading to a more stable system that can precisely reach the optimal settings. The absence of dither also simplifies the system, potentially speeding up convergence. The researchers provide a stability proof for a fixed performance map using a Lyapunov-Razumikhin argument, a technique for analyzing time-delay systems. Simulations show the method also works well for changing performance maps.
a-dither-free-extremum-seeking-control-a.layman: The researchers developed a new way to automatically find the best settings for a system, like tuning a machine for peak efficiency. Instead of using a small, intentional shake to test improvements, their method uses past data to predict the best direction. This makes the system more stable and accurate. They proved it works for steady conditions and tested it in changing ones. The approach may also be faster because it removes a step from older methods.

a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.scientist: Low complexity of a system model is essential for its use in real-time applications. However, sparse identification methods commonly have stringent requirements that exclude them from being applied in an industrial setting. In this article, we introduce a flexible method for the sparse identification of dynamical systems described by ordinary differential equations. Our method relieves many of the requirements imposed by other methods that relate to the structure of the model and the dataset, such as fixed sampling rates, full state measurements, and linearity of the model. The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm is used to solve the identification problem. We show that the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm can be written in a form that enables parallel computing, which greatly diminishes the time required to solve the identification problem. An efficient backward elimination strategy is presented to construct a lean system model.
a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.student: Real-time applications need simple system models, but existing sparse identification methods often impose strict conditions—like fixed sampling rates, full state measurements, or linear models—that make them impractical for industry. This paper proposes a flexible approach for identifying dynamical systems described by ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which are equations that model how a system changes over time. Unlike prior methods, it relaxes many constraints on model structure and data. The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm, a numerical technique for solving optimization problems, is adapted here to enable parallel computing, significantly speeding up the identification process. Additionally, a backward elimination strategy is introduced to refine the model, ensuring it remains sparse and efficient.
a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.layman: Researchers wanted to create simple models of complex systems for real-time use, but existing methods had strict rules that made them hard to apply in practice. They developed a new, flexible way to build these models from data, removing many of the old restrictions. They also improved a mathematical tool to run faster by using multiple processors at once. Finally, they added a step to trim unnecessary parts from the model, making it as simple as possible.

extremum-seeking-control-for-harmonic-mi.scientist: This paper focuses on the minimization of the harmonic distortion in multibus electrical grids of marine vessels using a single active power filter. An active power filter is commonly used for local harmonic mitigation. However, local filtering may lead to a “whack-a-mole” effect, where the reduction of harmonic distortion at the point of installation is coupled to an increase of distortion in other grid nodes. The few existing filtering methods that consider system-wide mitigation are based on an accurate model of the power grid, which may not be available if the complexity and the scale of the grid are large. In this work, we investigate the use of an extremum-seeking control method to optimize the injection current of an active power filter for system-wide harmonic mitigation. Because the extremum-seeking control method is model-free, it can be used without knowledge of the electrical grid. Moreover, the method can be implemented on top of the existing approaches to combine the fast transient response of conventional harmonic-mitigation methods with the optimizing capabilities of extremum-seeking control.
extremum-seeking-control-for-harmonic-mi.student: This study addresses harmonic distortion—unwanted voltage or current fluctuations—in the electrical grids of marine vessels, which can damage equipment. While active power filters (devices that inject compensating currents to reduce distortion) are often used locally, they can inadvertently shift the problem to other parts of the grid, a phenomenon known as the 'whack-a-mole' effect. Most system-wide solutions rely on detailed grid models, which are impractical for large, complex systems. Here, the authors propose using extremum-seeking control, a model-free optimization technique, to adjust the filter’s injection current for system-wide harmonic reduction. This approach works without prior knowledge of the grid and can be added to existing methods to improve performance.
extremum-seeking-control-for-harmonic-mi.layman: The researchers studied how to reduce electrical noise in ship power systems, which can harm equipment. Current fixes often solve the problem in one spot but cause it elsewhere. Most wide-scale solutions need detailed maps of the system, which are hard to make. The team tested a new method that adjusts the filter’s output without needing a map. It can also work alongside existing fixes to make them more effective.

estimation-of-future-power-consumption-f.scientist: In drone missions, accurate estimation of remaining flight time is crucial for enhancing mission duration and reducing the risk of losing drones due to power outages. This paper addresses the challenge of predicting future power consumption for a quadcopter UAV, focusing on the energy demands of planned future maneuvers. Existing physics-based energy consumption models assume the drone hovers or moves with constant speed. While orientation and velocity measurements are typically used, acceleration measurements are often ignored, despite being identified as important for power usage prediction in recent machine learning literature. This paper proposes a physics-based, lightweight energy consumption model based on measurements of the quadcopter’s motion, including acceleration. Our model also includes a synthetic wind estimation scheme, enhancing prediction accuracy in outdoor and windy conditions. The model’s predictions for power consumption are compared to real-life flight data, demonstrating the effectiveness of the presented approach despite its relative simplicity.
estimation-of-future-power-consumption-f.student: For drone missions, predicting how much power a quadcopter will use is key to avoiding crashes from running out of battery. Most current models assume the drone either hovers or moves at a steady speed, relying on its orientation and velocity but ignoring acceleration—even though recent machine learning studies show acceleration matters. This paper introduces a simple, physics-based model that uses the drone’s motion data, including acceleration, to estimate future power needs. It also adds a method to estimate wind effects, improving accuracy in outdoor conditions. When tested against real flight data, the model’s predictions matched well, showing it works despite its simplicity.
estimation-of-future-power-consumption-f.layman: Drones can run out of battery mid-flight, which is dangerous. This study looks at how to better predict how much power a drone will use during its trip. Most current methods ignore how quickly the drone speeds up or slows down, even though this affects power use. The researchers created a simple model that includes these changes in speed, as well as wind effects, to make better predictions. Tests with real drone flights showed the model works well.

realizing-lti-models-by-identifying-char.scientist: This paper considers the realization of discrete-time linear time-invariant dynamical systems using input-output data. Starting from a generalized state-space representation that accounts for static offsets, a state-independent system representation is derived using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem and characteristic parameters are introduced to describe the system dynamics in an alternative way. Given input-output data, we present two formulations to address model deviations and to identify characteristic parameters by minimizing considered error terms in a least squares sense. The applicability of the proposed subspace identification method is demonstrated with physical data of the identification database DaISy.
realizing-lti-models-by-identifying-char.student: This study explores how to model discrete-time linear time-invariant systems—systems where the output depends only on the current and past inputs, not on time itself—using only input and output data. The authors start with a generalized state-space model, which includes static offsets, and simplify it using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem to derive a state-independent representation. They then introduce characteristic parameters to describe the system’s behavior differently. Two methods are proposed to handle model errors and estimate these parameters by minimizing error terms via least squares. The approach is tested on real-world data from the DaISy identification database, showing its practical use.
realizing-lti-models-by-identifying-char.layman: The researchers wanted to find a way to predict how a system behaves over time using only its input and output data. They created a simplified model that ignores internal details but still captures the system’s behavior. They then developed two methods to adjust this model to fit real data as closely as possible. Finally, they tested their approach on actual data from a known database, showing it works in practice.

nondisturbing-extremum-seeking-control-f.scientist: Industrial applications of extremum seeking control (ESC) can be a hit and miss affair. Although a gain in performance can be achieved, the dither applied to excite the system causes unwanted fluctuations in the performance of the system. The fluctuations in systems with a single extremum seeking loop are generally small. However, for systems with many extremum seeking loops, the fluctuations in each loop may add up to an intolerable amount of fluctuation in the total performance. In this article, we propose a method to cancel the dither-induced fluctuations in the overall system performance to a large extent by smartly constructing the dither signals in each extremum seeking loop using a centralized coordinator. The novelty of our method lies in the direct calculation of the dither signals that avoids the heavy computations required by other methods. Moreover, we provide a solvability analysis for the problem of cancelling dither-induced fluctuations in the total performance of the system. Furthermore, a complete stability analysis of the overall ESC scheme with dither coordination is given.
nondisturbing-extremum-seeking-control-f.student: Extremum seeking control (ESC) is a method used in engineering to automatically tune a system to its best performance by continuously searching for an optimal operating point. However, the small, deliberate disturbances (called dither) used to probe the system can cause unwanted fluctuations in performance. In systems with multiple ESC loops, these fluctuations can accumulate, leading to significant instability. This study presents a new approach to reduce these fluctuations by coordinating the dither signals across all loops using a central controller. The method directly calculates the dither signals, avoiding complex computations, and includes a mathematical analysis to confirm that the fluctuations can be effectively canceled. Additionally, the stability of the entire system under this coordinated approach is rigorously examined.
nondisturbing-extremum-seeking-control-f.layman: Engineers often use a method to automatically find the best settings for a system, but this can cause small, unwanted wobbles in performance. When many such systems work together, these wobbles can add up and cause big problems. This research proposes a way to reduce these wobbles by carefully adjusting the signals that create them. The method is simpler than others and includes checks to ensure it works and that the system remains stable.

on-the-stability-bounds-of-kalman-filter.scientist: In this article, we prove input-to-state stability of the estimation error of the discrete-time Kalman filter under suitable assumptions. Input-to-state stability is an important prerequisite for the use of many contemporary analysis tools for cascaded and interconnected systems. In this way, this article provides a missing link for the rigorous analysis of systems, of which the Kalman filter is a subsystem, using these tools.
on-the-stability-bounds-of-kalman-filter.student: This study addresses the stability of the estimation error in the discrete-time Kalman filter, a widely used algorithm for estimating the state of a dynamic system from noisy measurements. The authors prove that the error remains bounded (input-to-state stability) under certain conditions. Input-to-state stability is a key property for analyzing interconnected systems, where the Kalman filter might be one component. By establishing this property, the work enables the use of modern analysis tools for systems that include the Kalman filter as a subsystem.
on-the-stability-bounds-of-kalman-filter.layman: The researchers studied how well a common prediction tool, the Kalman filter, keeps its mistakes under control when tracking changing systems. They showed that, under the right conditions, the errors stay manageable. This is useful because it means the tool can be safely used as part of larger, more complex systems without causing problems.

learning-based-robust-model-predictive-c.scientist: For dynamical systems with uncertainty, robust controllers can be designed by assuming that the uncertainty is bounded. The less we know about the uncertainty in the system, the more conservative the bound must be, which in turn may lead to reduced control performance. If measurements of the uncertain term are available, this data may be used to reduce the uncertainty in order to make bounds as tight as possible. In this paper, we consider a linear system with a sector-bounded uncertainty. We develop a model predictive control algorithm to control the system, and use a weighted Bayesian linear regression model to learn the least conservative sector condition using measurements collected in closed-loop. The resulting robust model predictive control algorithm therefore reduces the conservativeness of the controller, and provides probabilistic guarantees of asymptotic stability and constraint satisfaction. The efficacy of the proposed method is shown in simulation.
learning-based-robust-model-predictive-c.student: In control engineering, robust controllers handle systems with uncertainty by assuming the uncertainty stays within certain bounds. The less we know about the uncertainty, the wider these bounds must be, often leading to poorer performance. This study addresses a linear system where the uncertainty is constrained within a sector (a mathematical region). The authors propose a model predictive control (MPC) algorithm, which plans control actions by predicting future system behavior, and combine it with a weighted Bayesian linear regression model. This regression model uses real-time measurements to tighten the uncertainty bounds, making the controller less conservative. The result is a robust MPC that improves performance while still guaranteeing stability and constraint satisfaction with probabilistic certainty. Simulations demonstrate the method’s effectiveness.
learning-based-robust-model-predictive-c.layman: Researchers studied how to better control systems that have unpredictable parts. Normally, controllers assume the worst to stay safe, but this can make them less effective. Here, they used real-time data to reduce the guesswork, making the controller more precise. They tested this approach in computer simulations and found it worked well while still keeping the system stable and within safe limits.

agentic-scientific-simulation-execution-.scientist: We ask whether an LLM agent can serve as a genuine scientific assistant for physics-based simulation: given a natural-language description of a model, can it produce an executable, physically valid simulation configuration that faithfully represents the user’s intent, navigating API contracts, unit conventions, and global constraints in the way a knowledgeable research assistant would? The challenge is not merely generating code that runs or even satisfies physical consistency tests. Natural-language descriptions of simulation models are inherently underspecified, and different admissible resolutions of implicit choices produce physically valid but scientifically distinct configurations. Without explicit detection and resolution of these ambiguities, neither the correctness of the result nor its reproducibility from the original description can be assured. This paper investigates agentic scientific simulation, where model construction is organized as an execution-grounded interpret–act–validate loop, and the simulator serves as the authoritative arbiter of physical validity rather than merely a runtime. We present JutulGPT, a reference implementation built on the fully differentiable Julia-based reservoir simulator JutulDarcy. The agent combines structured retrieval of documentation and examples with code synthesis, static analysis, code execution, and systematic interpretation of solver diagnostics. Underspecified modelling choices are detected explicitly and resolved either autonomously (with logged assumptions) or through targeted user queries. The results demonstrate that agent-mediated model construction can be grounded in simulator validation while also revealing a structural limitation: choices resolved tacitly through simulator defaults are invisible to the assumption log and therefore to any downstream representation. A secondary experiment, autonomous reconstruction of a reference model from progressively abstract textual descriptions, shows that reconstruction variability exposes latent degrees of freedom in simulation descriptions and provides a practical methodology for auditing reproducibility. All code, prompts, and agent logs are publicly available.
agentic-scientific-simulation-execution-.student: This study explores whether a large language model (LLM) can act as a reliable assistant for creating physics-based simulations. The challenge is to turn a natural-language description of a model into an executable, physically valid simulation that matches the user’s intent, handling technical details like API rules, unit systems, and global constraints. The issue is that such descriptions are often incomplete, leaving room for multiple valid but scientifically different interpretations. Without addressing these ambiguities, the simulation’s correctness and reproducibility are at risk. The paper introduces JutulGPT, an agent built on the Julia-based simulator JutulDarcy, which uses a loop of interpretation, action, and validation, with the simulator ensuring physical validity. The agent detects and resolves underspecified choices, either autonomously (with logged assumptions) or by asking the user. Results show that this approach grounds model construction in validation but also reveals a limitation: simulator defaults can hide assumptions. A secondary test reconstructs a reference model from abstract descriptions, highlighting variability and offering a way to audit reproducibility. Code and logs are publicly available.
agentic-scientific-simulation-execution-.layman: Can an AI assistant create a working physics simulation from a simple description? Researchers tested this by having an AI turn vague instructions into a valid, executable model, ensuring it follows the rules of physics and the user’s intent. The problem is that unclear instructions can lead to different but equally valid results, making it hard to guarantee accuracy or repeatability. The team built an AI system that checks its work against a physics simulator, asks for clarification when needed, and logs its assumptions. They found it works but has a blind spot: some choices are made automatically without being recorded. Another test showed that rebuilding a model from different descriptions reveals hidden flexibility in how simulations are defined. All their work is open for others to review.

jutuldarcy-jl-a-fully-differentiable-hig.scientist: Reservoir simulators are highly complex computer programs and are often treated as “black boxes” that act on standardized input formats. In part, this is due to the closed-source nature of commercial offerings commonly used in industry, but even when the source-code is available, modification of a fully featured simulator can be a daunting task: A reservoir simulation problem, when fully specified, can have a great number of parameters and functional relationships that are tightly coupled together in most implementations. This is an obstacle to workflows that go beyond forecasting and into optimization, parameter fitting and sensitivity analysis where the solution quantity of interest should be paired with gradients taken with respect to forces and parameters. The monolithic design of typical reservoir simulation codes cannot be separated from the technical and mathematical choices made when discretizing the governing equations: The implicitness required to handle pressure changes and strong coupling between different solution variables means that the Jacobian of the governing equations must be implemented with respect to the primary variables: An error-prone process when done manually, and highly time-consuming when considering coupled systems. Automatic differentiation (AD) is a common cure to this problem that can generate Jacobians, but often comes at a severe cost in runtime performance. A more practical issue is that high computational performance for simulation problems relevant to modern geoenergy operations necessitates implementation in a compiled language while optimization and history matching workflows that integrate many data sources are most naturally expressed in high-level scripting languages. We describe the design of JutulDarcy, an open-source porous media simulator written in the Julia language. JutulDarcy is designed from the ground up with extensibility and computation of sensitivities in mind, starting from the assumption that high-performance automatic differentiation enables us to radically rethink the way simulators are designed. Highlights of this design include arbitrary execution graphs for the equation terms, in which dependence relationships can be re-configured on the fly, easy coupling of models, computation of sensitivities with respect to all model parameters through an adjoint method with a parameter declaration system, and an assembly process with performance that can exceed that of compiled simulators with hand-coded Jacobians. We validate the simulator on a number of standard test cases (immiscible, black-oil, CO2 and compositional flow) and demonstrate MPI parallel performance on multimillion cell models. In addition, we offer a frank assessment of the relative strengths and weaknesses of the Julia programming language for scientific computing.
jutuldarcy-jl-a-fully-differentiable-hig.student: Reservoir simulators are complex programs used to model fluid flow in underground reservoirs, often seen as 'black boxes' due to their closed-source nature or intricate code. These simulators involve many tightly coupled parameters, making modifications difficult, especially for tasks like optimization or sensitivity analysis, which require gradients of outputs with respect to inputs. Traditional simulators use implicit methods to handle pressure changes, requiring manual Jacobian (a matrix of partial derivatives) implementation—a time-consuming and error-prone process. Automatic differentiation (AD) can generate Jacobians but often slows performance. Additionally, high-performance simulations need compiled languages, while optimization workflows are easier in scripting languages. JutulDarcy is an open-source simulator written in Julia, designed for extensibility and sensitivity computation. It uses high-performance AD to enable flexible equation term graphs, easy model coupling, and efficient sensitivity calculations via adjoint methods. The simulator is validated on standard test cases and shows strong parallel performance. The paper also evaluates Julia’s strengths and weaknesses for scientific computing.
jutuldarcy-jl-a-fully-differentiable-hig.layman: Researchers built a new computer tool to model how fluids move underground, like oil or water in rock layers. Older tools are hard to change or combine with other data because they are complex and closed off. This new tool, called JutulDarcy, is open and designed to be flexible, allowing users to easily adjust it for different tasks, like testing how small changes affect the results. It also runs quickly and can handle very large, detailed models. The team tested it on common problems and found it works well, while also noting the pros and cons of the programming language they used.

learned-multiphysics-inversion-with-diff.scientist: We present the Seismic Laboratory for Imaging and Modeling/Monitoring open-source software framework for computational geophysics and, more generally, inverse problems involving the wave equation (e.g., seismic and medical ultrasound), regularization with learned priors, and learned neural surrogates for multiphase flow simulations. By integrating multiple layers of abstraction, the software is designed to be both readable and scalable, allowing researchers to easily formulate problems in an abstract fashion while exploiting the latest developments in high-performance computing. The design principles and their benefits are illustrated and demonstrated by means of building a scalable prototype for permeability inversion from time-lapse crosswell seismic data, which, aside from coupling of wave physics and multiphase flow, involves machine learning.
learned-multiphysics-inversion-with-diff.student: This work introduces an open-source software framework, SLIM, designed for computational geophysics and related inverse problems—such as seismic imaging or medical ultrasound—where the wave equation plays a key role. The framework also supports regularization using learned priors (data-driven constraints) and neural network surrogates for multiphase flow simulations. By combining high-level abstraction with high-performance computing, SLIM lets researchers define problems intuitively while scaling efficiently. The authors demonstrate its capabilities by building a prototype for permeability inversion (estimating subsurface rock properties) from time-lapse crosswell seismic data, integrating wave physics, multiphase flow, and machine learning.
learned-multiphysics-inversion-with-diff.layman: Researchers created a free, open tool to help solve complex problems like imaging underground rock layers or medical scans. The tool uses advanced computing to handle large amounts of data and can incorporate machine learning to improve accuracy. They tested it by estimating how fluids move through rock using sound waves, showing it works well for real-world applications.

thinking-responsibly-about-responsible-a.scientist: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been argued to offer a myriad of improvements in how we work and live. The notion of AI comprises a wide-ranging set of technologies that allow individuals and organizations to integrate and analyze data and use that insight to improve or automate decision-making. While most attention has been placed on the positive aspects companies realize by the adoption and use of AI, there is a growing concern around the negative and unintended consequences of such technologies. In this special issue we have made a call for research papers that help us explore the dark side of AI use. By adopting a dark side lens, we aimed to expand our understanding of how AI should be implemented in practice, and how to minimize or avoid negative outcomes. In this editorial, we build on the notion of responsible AI, to highlight the different ways in which AI can potentially produce unintended consequences, as well as to suggest alternative paths future IS research can follow to improve our knowledge about how to mitigate such occurrences. We further expand on dark side theorizing in order to uncover hidden assumptions of current literature as well as to propose other prominent themes that can guide future IS research on AI adoption and use.
thinking-responsibly-about-responsible-a.student: Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to technologies that process data to support or automate decisions. While AI is often praised for its benefits, this special issue examines its potential downsides. The editors invited research on the 'dark side' of AI—unintended negative effects like bias, privacy risks, or job displacement. The editorial builds on the idea of responsible AI, discussing how AI can lead to unforeseen problems and suggesting ways to reduce these risks. It also critiques current assumptions in AI research and proposes new themes for future studies, aiming to guide more balanced and cautious AI adoption in practice.
thinking-responsibly-about-responsible-a.layman: AI is often seen as a tool for progress, but it can also cause unexpected harm. This collection of papers looks at the less-discussed problems AI might create, like unfair decisions or privacy issues. The editors explain how these problems can happen and suggest ways to prevent them. They also point out gaps in how we currently think about AI and offer new ideas for studying its risks. The goal is to help us use AI more carefully and responsibly.

responsible-artificial-intelligence-gove.scientist: The widespread and rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into all types of organizational activities necessitates the ethical and responsible deployment of these technologies. Various national and international policies, regulations, and guidelines aim to address this issue, and several organizations have developed frameworks detailing the principles of responsible AI. Nevertheless, the understanding of how such principles can be operationalized in designing, executing, monitoring, and evaluating AI applications is limited. The literature is disparate and lacks cohesion, clarity, and, in some cases, depth. Subsequently, this scoping review aims to synthesize and critically reflect on the research on responsible AI. Based on this synthesis, we developed a conceptual framework for responsible AI governance (defined through structural, relational, and procedural practices), its antecedents, and its effects. The framework serves as the foundation for developing an agenda for future research and critically reflects on the notion of responsible AI governance.
responsible-artificial-intelligence-gove.student: As AI spreads quickly across organizations, ensuring its ethical and responsible use has become urgent. While policies and guidelines exist, it remains unclear how to put responsible AI principles into practice during design, implementation, and evaluation. This scoping review examines existing research to address this gap, synthesizing fragmented literature into a clearer picture. The authors propose a conceptual framework that defines responsible AI governance through structural (e.g., policies), relational (e.g., stakeholder interactions), and procedural (e.g., decision-making processes) practices, along with their causes and effects. The framework also outlines future research directions and critically assesses the idea of responsible AI governance itself.
responsible-artificial-intelligence-gove.layman: AI is being used more and more in workplaces, raising questions about how to use it ethically. Many guidelines exist, but it’s unclear how to apply them in real situations. Researchers reviewed existing studies to understand this better. They created a model that explains how organizations can govern AI responsibly, including rules, relationships, and processes. This model also suggests what to study next and questions what responsible AI really means.

artificial-intelligence-and-business-val.scientist: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a wide-ranging set of technologies that promise several advantages for organizations in terms of added business value. Over the past few years, organizations are increasingly turning to AI in order to gain business value following a deluge of data and a strong increase in computational capacity. Nevertheless, organizations are still struggling to adopt and leverage AI in their operations. The lack of a coherent understanding of how AI technologies create business value, and what type of business value is expected, therefore necessitates a holistic understanding. This study provides a systematic literature review that attempts to explain how organizations can leverage AI technologies in their operations and elucidate the value-generating mechanisms. Our analysis synthesizes the current literature and highlights: (1) the key enablers and inhibitors of AI adoption and use; (2) the typologies of AI use in the organizational setting; and (3) the first- and second-order effects of AI. The paper concludes with an identification of the gaps in the literature and develops a research agenda that identifies areas that need to be addressed by future studies.
artificial-intelligence-and-business-val.student: Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers potential business benefits, but many organizations struggle to adopt it effectively. This study reviews existing research to understand how AI creates value for businesses. The authors analyzed prior work to identify what helps or hinders AI adoption, how companies use AI, and the direct and indirect effects of AI on operations. They also pinpointed gaps in current knowledge and suggested areas for future research. The review synthesizes findings without overstating certainty, focusing on patterns in how AI is implemented and the types of value it may generate.
artificial-intelligence-and-business-val.layman: Businesses see potential in using AI to improve their work, but many find it hard to use effectively. Researchers reviewed past studies to understand how AI helps companies and what stands in the way. They looked at how AI is used, what benefits it brings, and what problems it might cause. The study also points out what we still don’t know and where more research is needed.

examining-the-interplay-between-big-data.scientist: The potential of big data analytics in enabling improvements in business processes has urged researchers and practitioners to understand if, and under what combination of conditions, such novel technologies can support the enactment and management of business processes. While there is much discussion around how big data analytics can impact a firm’s incremental and radical process innovation capabilities, we still know very little about what big data analytics resources firms must invest in to drive such outcomes. To explore this topic, we ground this study on a theory-driven conceptualisation of big data analytics based on the resource-based view (RBV) of the firm. Based on this conceptualisation, we examine the fit between the big data analytics resources that underpin the notion, and their interplay with organisational contextual factors in driving a firm’s incremental and radical process innovation capabilities. Survey data from 202 chief information officers and IT managers working in Norwegian firms are analysed by means of fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results show that under different combinations of contextual factors the significance of big data analytics resources varies, with specific configurations leading to high levels of incremental and radical process innovation capabilities.
examining-the-interplay-between-big-data.student: Researchers investigated how big data analytics—using large, complex datasets to uncover patterns—can improve business processes, specifically incremental (small, gradual changes) and radical (major, transformative changes) innovation. While the potential is widely discussed, little is known about what specific resources firms need to invest in to achieve these outcomes. Using the resource-based view (RBV), which sees firms as bundles of unique resources, the study examined how big data analytics resources interact with organisational factors (like culture or structure) to drive innovation. Survey data from 202 Norwegian IT leaders was analysed using fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), a method for identifying combinations of conditions leading to outcomes. Findings suggest that the importance of big data resources varies depending on the mix of contextual factors, with certain configurations strongly linked to high innovation capabilities.
examining-the-interplay-between-big-data.layman: The study asked how companies can use large amounts of data to improve their business processes, both in small steps and big leaps. Researchers surveyed IT leaders in Norway to see what tools and conditions help. They found that the right mix of data resources and company traits—like culture or structure—can lead to better innovation, but the best combination depends on the situation.

building-dynamic-capabilities-by-leverag.scientist: Although big data analytics have been claimed to revolutionize the way firms operate and do business, there is a striking lack of knowledge about how organizations should adopt and routinize such technologies to support their strategic objectives. The aim of this research is to explore how different inertial forces during deployments of big data analytics hinder the emergence of dynamic capabilities. To do so, we follow a multiple-case study design approach of 27 European firms and examine the different forms of inertia that materialize during big data analytics diffusion. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on how big data analytics can be leveraged effectively to enable and strengthen a firm’s dynamic capabilities. By disaggregating dynamic capabilities into the underlying capabilities of sensing, seizing and transforming, findings indicate that different combinations of organizational inertia including economic, political, socio-cognitive, negative psychology, and socio-technical hamper the formation of each type of capability.
building-dynamic-capabilities-by-leverag.student: While big data analytics are said to transform business operations, little is known about how firms should adopt and integrate these technologies to meet strategic goals. This study explores how various inertial forces—resistances to change—during big data deployments hinder the development of dynamic capabilities, which are a firm’s abilities to adapt, innovate, and respond to market shifts. Using a multiple-case study of 27 European firms, the research identifies different forms of inertia, such as economic, political, socio-cognitive, negative psychological, and socio-technical barriers. The findings suggest that these inertial forces, in different combinations, impede the formation of the three underlying dynamic capabilities: sensing (identifying opportunities), seizing (exploiting them), and transforming (reconfiguring resources).
building-dynamic-capabilities-by-leverag.layman: Big data tools are supposed to change how companies work, but we don’t fully understand how businesses should use them effectively. This study looked at 27 European companies to see what kinds of resistance slow down the adoption of these tools. It found that different types of resistance—like financial costs, office politics, or outdated ways of thinking—can block a company’s ability to spot new opportunities, take advantage of them, or adjust its operations. The research helps explain why some firms struggle to benefit from big data.

explainable-artificial-intelligence-xai-.scientist: The rapid growth and use of artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems have raised concerns regarding explainability. Recent studies have discussed the emerging demand for explainable AI (XAI); however, a systematic review of explainable artificial intelligence from an end user’s perspective can provide a comprehensive understanding of the current situation and help close the research gap. The purpose of this study was to perform a systematic literature review of explainable AI from the end user’s perspective and to synthesize the findings. To be precise, the objectives were to 1) identify the dimensions of end users’ explanation needs; 2) investigate the effect of explanation on end user’s perceptions, and 3) identify the research gaps and propose future research agendas for XAI, particularly from end users’ perspectives based on current knowledge. The final search query for the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted on July 2022. Initially, we extracted 1707 journal and conference articles from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. Inclusion and exclusion criteria were then applied, and 58 articles were selected for the SLR. The findings show four dimensions that shape the AI explanation, which are format (explanation representation format), completeness (explanation should contain all required information, including the supplementary information), accuracy (information regarding the accuracy of the explanation), and currency (explanation should contain recent information). Moreover, along with the automatic representation of the explanation, the users can request additional information if needed. We have also described five dimensions of XAI effects: trust, transparency, understandability, usability, and fairness. We investigated current knowledge from selected articles to problematize future research agendas as research questions along with possible research paths. Consequently, a comprehensive framework of XAI and its possible effects on user behavior has been developed.
explainable-artificial-intelligence-xai-.student: As AI systems become more widespread, concerns about their explainability—how well users can understand their decisions—have grown. This study conducted a systematic literature review to examine explainable AI (XAI) from the end user’s perspective, aiming to identify what users need from explanations, how explanations affect their perceptions, and where research gaps exist. From 1,707 initial articles, 58 were selected for analysis. The findings reveal four key dimensions of AI explanations: format (how explanations are presented), completeness (whether all necessary information is included), accuracy (the correctness of the explanation), and currency (whether the information is up-to-date). Additionally, explanations can influence users in five ways: trust, transparency, understandability, usability, and fairness. The study proposes a framework for XAI and suggests future research directions based on these insights.
explainable-artificial-intelligence-xai-.layman: Researchers wanted to understand how people can better grasp decisions made by AI systems. They reviewed many studies to see what users need from explanations, how these explanations affect their views, and what’s missing in current research. They found that good explanations should be clear, complete, accurate, and up-to-date. These explanations can also shape how much users trust, understand, or find the AI fair and useful. The study suggests ways to improve AI explanations and guide future work.

enabling-ai-capabilities-in-government-a.scientist: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is gradually becoming an integral part of the digital strategy of organizations. Yet, the use of AI in public organizations is still lagging significantly compared to private organizations. Prior literature looking into aspects that facilitate adoption and use of AI has concentrated on challenges concerning technical aspects of AI technologies, providing little insight regarding the organizational deployment of AI, particularly in public organizations. Building on this gap, this study seeks to examine what aspects enable public organizations to develop AI capabilities. To answer this question, we built an integrated and extended model from the Technology-Organization-Environment framework (TOE) and asked high-level technology managers from municipalities in Europe about factors that influence their development of AI capabilities. We collected data from 91 municipalities from three European countries (i.e., Germany, Norway, and Finland) and analyzed responses by means of structural equation modeling. Our findings indicate that five factors i.e. perceived financial costs, organizational innovativeness, perceived governmental pressure, government incentives, regulatory support – have an impact on the development of AI capabilities. We also find that perceived citizen pressure and perceived value of AI solutions are not important determinants of AI capability formation. Our findings bear the potential to stimulate a more reflected adoption of AI supporting managers in public organizations to develop AI capabilities.
enabling-ai-capabilities-in-government-a.student: While AI is increasingly adopted in private companies, public organizations lag behind. Most research focuses on technical challenges, leaving organizational factors underexplored. This study investigates what enables public organizations to develop AI capabilities. Using the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework—an approach that examines how technological, organizational, and environmental factors influence adoption—we surveyed 91 European municipalities (in Germany, Norway, and Finland). High-level technology managers reported on factors affecting AI development. Through structural equation modeling, we found that financial costs, organizational innovativeness, governmental pressure, government incentives, and regulatory support significantly influence AI capability development. However, citizen pressure and the perceived value of AI solutions did not play a major role. The results highlight key drivers for public sector AI adoption.
enabling-ai-capabilities-in-government-a.layman: Public agencies use AI less than private companies. To understand why, researchers asked officials from 91 European cities what helps their organizations adopt AI. They found that money, a culture of trying new things, government pressure, support, and clear rules matter most. Surprisingly, public demand or the expected benefits of AI did not. This shows what public agencies should focus on to use AI more effectively.

artificial-intelligence-capabilities-for.scientist: This study explores the interlink between AI capabilities and circular business models (CBMs) through a literature review. Extant literature reveals that AI can act as efficiency catalyst, empowering firms to implement CBM. However, the journey to harness AI for CBM is fraught with challenges as firms grapple with the lack of sophisticated processes and routines to tap into AI’s potential. The fragmented literature leaves a void in understanding the barriers and development pathways for AI capabilities in CBM contexts. Bridging this gap, adopting a capabilities perspective, this review intricately brings together four pivotal capabilities: integrated intelligence capability, process automation and augmentation capability, AI infrastructure and platform capability, and ecosystem orchestration capability as drivers of AI-enabled CBM. These capabilities are vital to navigating the multi-level barriers to utilizing AI for CBM. The key contribution of the study is the synthesis of an AI-enabled CBM framework, which not only summarizes the results but also sets the stage for future explorations in this dynamic field.
artificial-intelligence-capabilities-for.student: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can support circular business models (CBMs)—approaches where companies reuse, repair, or recycle materials to reduce waste. Through a review of existing research, the authors find that AI can improve efficiency and help firms adopt CBMs, but many struggle due to a lack of advanced processes to leverage AI effectively. The literature is scattered, leaving gaps in understanding the obstacles and pathways for developing AI capabilities in CBM contexts. To address this, the review identifies four key capabilities: integrating AI-driven insights, automating and enhancing processes, building AI infrastructure, and managing partnerships within business ecosystems. These capabilities help overcome barriers to using AI in CBMs. The study’s main contribution is a framework that synthesizes these findings and guides future research.
artificial-intelligence-capabilities-for.layman: This research looks at how artificial intelligence can help companies reduce waste by reusing or recycling materials. The team reviewed past studies and found that AI can make these efforts more efficient, but many businesses lack the right systems to use AI well. The existing research is incomplete, so the authors identified four key skills companies need to use AI effectively in this area. They created a framework to explain how these skills can help overcome challenges and improve waste reduction efforts.

toward-ai-governance-identifying-best-pr.scientist: In recent years artificial intelligence (AI) has been seen as a technology with tremendous potential for enabling companies to gain an operational and competitive advantage. However, despite the use of AI, businesses continue to face challenges and are unable to immediately realize performance gains. Furthermore, firms need to introduce robust AI systems and mitigate AI risks, which emphasizes the importance of creating suitable AI governance practices. This study explores how AI governance is applied to promote the development of robust AI applications that do not introduce negative effects, based on a comparative case analysis of three firms in the energy sector. The study illustrates which practices are placed to produce knowledge that assists with decision making while at the same time overcoming barriers with recommended actions leading to desired outcomes. The study contributes by exploring the main dimensions relevant to AI’s governance in organizations and by uncovering the practices that underpin them.
toward-ai-governance-identifying-best-pr.student: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly adopted by companies to improve operations and competitiveness, yet many still struggle to see immediate benefits. Additionally, firms must ensure AI systems are reliable and address risks, highlighting the need for effective AI governance. This study examines how AI governance—frameworks and processes to manage AI development and deployment—supports the creation of robust AI applications without unintended negative effects. Through a comparative case study of three energy sector firms, the research identifies practices that help generate actionable insights for decision-making while addressing obstacles. The findings outline key dimensions of AI governance and the specific practices that support them, offering insights into how organizations can structure their AI initiatives.
toward-ai-governance-identifying-best-pr.layman: Companies use artificial intelligence to work better, but often don’t see quick results. They also need to make sure AI is safe and doesn’t cause problems, which means having good rules for how it’s used. This study looked at three energy companies to see how they set up these rules. It found which steps help them make good decisions and solve problems. The work shows what parts of these rules matter most and how companies can put them into practice.

an-efficient-screening-technique-for-acc.scientist: Workload assessment is required for human factors validation of control rooms. The NASA Task Load Index (TLX) is a popular measure for this purpose. However, acceptability of workload is difficult to interpret based on the scores, and the measure is time consuming for use in test scenario breaks. This paper reports the identification and evaluation of a one-item subjective rating for the acceptability of mental workload. Study 1 found that one item, mental demand, highly represented the multidimensional TLX and that operators rated this item to be distinct from performance and situation awareness. Study 2 investigated the acceptance scale’s sensitivity to control room modification, and the study found that operators’ rating of level of mental demand and rating of acceptability of mental demand were moderately related. The rating of acceptability, compared with the original scale, was more sensitive to control room modernisation and was more strongly related to subjective performance. Operators’ rating of acceptable workload was significantly related to observers’ assessment of team performance, while the rating of level was not. Both acceptable and non-acceptable workload were related to high levels of the original TLX scales, indicating that operators’ perception of acceptable workload was not fixated on a particular level of the original TLX scale. The results supported that efficient assessment can be achieved by applying only the TLX mental demand item and by supplementing or replacing the original rating scale with an acceptability rating scale. The approach presented applies to establishing ‘redlines’ for human performance constructs beyond mental workload. Relevance to industry: High-consequence industries are required to perform human factors validation for new and substantially modified design. While numerous human factors measures are available, approaches for establishing cut-off scores or ‘redlines’ are lacking. This paper investigates acceptability rating to address this challenge.
an-efficient-screening-technique-for-acc.student: Assessing mental workload is critical in control room design, often using the NASA Task Load Index (TLX), a multi-item questionnaire. However, TLX is time-consuming and its scores are hard to interpret for acceptability. This study explored a simpler approach: a single-item rating for workload acceptability. In Study 1, the TLX’s *mental demand* item (a measure of perceived cognitive effort) was found to strongly represent the full TLX, and operators distinguished it from performance and situation awareness (their understanding of the environment). Study 2 tested this item’s sensitivity to control room changes. Results showed that operators’ ratings of mental demand *level* and its *acceptability* were moderately linked. The acceptability rating was more sensitive to modernisation and better predicted subjective performance than the original TLX. It also correlated with observers’ assessments of team performance, unlike the level rating. Both acceptable and non-acceptable workloads corresponded to high TLX scores, suggesting acceptability isn’t tied to a fixed workload level. The findings support using just the mental demand item with an acceptability scale for efficient assessment, a method that could extend to other human performance metrics.
an-efficient-screening-technique-for-acc.layman: Researchers wanted to know if a simple question could replace a long survey used to measure how mentally demanding a control room job is. They found that asking workers to rate just one thing—how much mental effort a task requires—captured most of what the longer survey did. They also tested whether workers could judge if that mental effort was acceptable. The results showed that this single question, combined with an acceptability rating, worked better than the old method. It was more sensitive to changes in the workplace and better matched how well teams performed. This could make it easier to check if a job’s mental demands are reasonable.

comparing-control-room-operators-and-exp.scientist: Operators’ self-assessment has received limited interest within process control or human-system evaluation. Research on self-assessment has been criticised for poor assessment methodology, and consequently, its status is unclear. This study hypothesised that, given adequate assessment methods (such as task-specific assessment items and scenario replay), we could observe relatively accurate self-assessment results. Eighteen licensed operators and two experts assessed team performance in six nuclear control room scenarios. The results reveal an overall agreement between operators and experts, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient, ranging from 0.60 to 0.70, which lies close to the intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.75 for the experts. This demonstrates potential for achievement of relatively accurate operator self-assessment for complex work. The agreement varied in a similar manner for both expert agreement and operator-expert agreement across eight performance dimensions. In addition, the operators’ self-assessment provided additional information beyond observer assessment in identifying non-acceptable performance items.
comparing-control-room-operators-and-exp.student: Researchers examined whether operators in complex environments, like nuclear control rooms, can accurately assess their own team performance. Prior studies on self-assessment were criticized for weak methods, leaving its reliability unclear. Here, 18 licensed operators and two experts evaluated team performance across six scenarios using task-specific questions and scenario replays. The study found strong agreement between operators’ and experts’ assessments, with statistical measures (intraclass correlation coefficients) ranging from 0.60 to 0.70—close to the experts’ own consistency of 0.75. This suggests operators can self-assess effectively under the right conditions. Agreement patterns were similar across eight performance dimensions, and operators’ self-assessments also highlighted performance issues not caught by observers.
comparing-control-room-operators-and-exp.layman: Can workers in high-stakes jobs, like nuclear plant operators, judge their own team’s performance accurately? Past research was unsure due to flawed methods. In this study, 18 operators and two experts rated teamwork in six simulated scenarios. The operators’ ratings matched the experts’ closely, showing they can assess themselves well when given the right tools. Their judgments also spotted problems that outside observers missed.

measuring-cognitive-workload-in-the-nucl.scientist: Despite the substantial literature and human factors guidance, evaluators report challenges in selecting cognitive workload measures for the evaluation of complex human–technology systems. A review of 32 articles found that self-report measures and secondary tasks were systematically sensitive to human–system interface conditions and correlated with physiological measures. Therefore, including a self-report measure of cognitive workload is recommended when evaluating human–system interfaces. Physiological measures were mainly used in method studies, and future research must demonstrate the utility of these measures for human–system evaluation in complex work settings. However, indexes of physiological measures showed promise for cognitive workload assessment. The review revealed a limited focus on the measurement of excessive cognitive workload, although this is a key topic in nuclear process control. To support human–system evaluation of adequate cognitive workload, future research on behavioural measures may be useful in the identification and analysis of underload and overload.
measuring-cognitive-workload-in-the-nucl.student: Evaluators often struggle to choose the right cognitive workload measures for assessing complex human–technology systems, despite existing guidelines. A review of 32 studies found that self-report measures (where participants rate their own mental effort) and secondary tasks (additional tasks performed alongside the main one) were consistently sensitive to differences in human–system interfaces and aligned with physiological measures like heart rate or brain activity. The review recommends including self-reports in interface evaluations. Physiological measures were mostly used in method-focused studies, and their practical use in real-world, complex work environments remains to be demonstrated, though they show potential. The review also noted little attention to excessive cognitive workload, a critical issue in fields like nuclear process control. Future work on behavioural measures may help identify both underload and overload in human–system evaluations.
measuring-cognitive-workload-in-the-nucl.layman: Researchers wanted to know the best ways to measure how hard people are thinking when using complex systems, like control panels in power plants. They looked at 32 studies and found that asking people how mentally tired they feel and giving them extra tasks to do were good ways to spot differences in system designs. These methods also matched up with body signals like heart rate. They suggest always asking people about their mental effort when testing systems. Body signals might be useful too, but more work is needed to see if they help in real jobs. The studies didn’t focus much on when people are overworked, even though that’s important in some fields. Future research could look at how people act to spot when they’re not thinking enough or thinking too much.

an-investigation-of-speech-features-plan.scientist: Objective: To investigate speech features, human–machine alarms, and operator–system interaction for the estimation of cognitive workload in full-scale realistic simulated scenarios. Background: Theories and models of cognitive workload are critical for the design and evaluation of human–machine systems. Unfortunately, there are very few nonintrusive cognitive workload measures available for realistic dynamic human–machine interaction. Method: The study was conducted in a full-scope control room research simulator of an advanced nuclear reactor. Six crews, each consisting of three operators, participated in 12 scenarios. The operators rated their workload every second minute. Machine learning algorithms were trained to estimate operators’ workload based on crew communication, operator–system interaction, and system alarms. Results: Random Forest (RF) utilizing speech and system features achieved an accuracy of 67% on test data. Utilizing speech features only, the accuracy achieved was 63%. The most important speech features were pitch, amplitude, and articulation rate. A 61% accuracy was achieved when alarms and operator–system interaction features were used. The most important features were the number of alarms and amount of operator–system interaction. Accuracy for algorithms trained for each operator ranged from 39% to 98%, with an average of 72%. For a majority of analyses performed, RF and extreme gradient boosting (XGB) outperformed other algorithms.
