We demonstrate our framework on the inverted pendulum control task, reducing the total computation time of the control system by 36% while also improving the control performance by 18.4%.
optimization-of-the-model-predictive-con.student: Model predictive control (MPC) is a control strategy that plans actions by solving an optimization problem at each step, but it can be computationally expensive and requires careful tuning of its parameters. This paper addresses these challenges by using reinforcement learning (RL) to automatically adjust MPC’s meta-parameters—settings that influence the controller’s behavior but are not directly optimized in the MPC solution. The method introduces a multivariate RL approach to optimize these parameters based on system data, improving closed-loop performance. The control algorithm combines event-triggered MPC (which decides when to recompute control actions) with a dual-mode strategy (switching between MPC and a simpler linear feedback law). The RL policy uses a mixture distribution to handle non-differentiable parameters, and joint optimization of these parameters yields better results than tuning them individually. The approach is tested on an inverted pendulum, reducing computation time by 36% and improving control performance by 18.4%.
optimization-of-the-model-predictive-con.layman: Researchers wanted to improve a control method used in fast-moving systems, which is slow and hard to adjust. They used a learning-based approach to automatically fine-tune the system’s settings. Their method decides when to recalculate actions and switches between complex and simple control strategies. By testing it on a balancing task, they showed it works faster and better than before, cutting processing time by over a third and improving performance by nearly a fifth.

mpc-approaches-for-modulating-air-to-wat.scientist: A modulating heat pump and water tank result in a nonlinear model due to the load dependency of the heat pump performance, and variable water flows. Nonlinear model predictive control is an effective way to deal with many physical constraints and nonlinear formulations. Alternatively, linear time-varying MPC can be used, based on successive linearizations around a reference trajectory. The goal of the paper is to analyze the advantages and disadvantages of those MPC techniques for temperature control in radiant-floor buildings. The results show that nonlinear on-line optimization is real-time feasible for the application considered here, as the slow dynamics allows for a fairly long sampling time. Alternatively, the linear time-varying MPC approach shows a significantly better performance compared to the Standard MPC scheme if a feasible reference trajectory is provided. Nonlinear MPC can save up to 6% energy and improve the comfort by 4% with respect to Standard MPC for the given application, while its difference with LTV-MPC is negligible. Moreover, a robustness analysis has been conducted, showing the impact of the heat pump efficiency on the control performance.
mpc-approaches-for-modulating-air-to-wat.student: This study compares two control methods for managing temperature in buildings with radiant floors, where heat pumps and water tanks create a nonlinear system due to changing loads and flows. The first method, nonlinear model predictive control (MPC), handles physical constraints and nonlinearities directly. The second, linear time-varying MPC, simplifies the problem by linearizing around a reference path. The research finds that nonlinear MPC is feasible in real time for this slow-dynamics application, as the long sampling time allows for on-line optimization. Linear time-varying MPC performs better than standard MPC when a good reference trajectory is used. Nonlinear MPC saves up to 6% energy and improves comfort by 4% over standard MPC, with little difference compared to linear time-varying MPC. A robustness test also shows how heat pump efficiency affects control performance.
mpc-approaches-for-modulating-air-to-wat.layman: Researchers tested two ways to control the temperature in buildings with heated floors. One method uses a complex approach to handle changing conditions, while the other simplifies the problem. They found both methods work well, with the complex one saving a little energy and improving comfort slightly. The simpler method also performed better than the usual way of doing things. They also checked how changes in the heating system’s efficiency affect the results.

personalized-dynamic-pricing-policy-for-.scientist: With the increasing number of fast-electric vehicle charging stations (fast-EVCSs) and the popularization of information technology, electricity price competition between fast-EVCSs is highly expected, in which the utilization of public and/or privacy-preserved information will play a crucial role. Self-interest electric vehicle (EV) users, on the other hand, try to select a fast-EVCS for charging in a way to maximize their utilities based on electricity price, estimated waiting time, and their state of charge. While existing studies have largely focused on finding equilibrium prices, this study proposes a personalized dynamic pricing policy (PeDP) for a fast-EVCS to maximize revenue using a reinforcement learning (RL) approach. We first propose a multiple fast-EVCSs competing simulation environment to model the selfish behavior of EV users using a game-based charging station selection model with a monetary utility function. In the environment, we propose a Q-learning-based PeDP to maximize fast-EVCS’ revenue. Through numerical simulations based on the environment: (1) we identify the importance of waiting time in the EV charging market by comparing the classic Bertrand competition model with the proposed PeDP for fast-EVCSs (from the system perspective); (2) we evaluate the performance of the proposed PeDP and analyze the effects of the information on the policy (from the service provider perspective), and the robustness of the proposed approach; and (3) it can be seen that privacy-preserved information sharing can be misused by artificial intelligence-based PeDP in a certain situation in the EV charging market (from the customer perspective).
personalized-dynamic-pricing-policy-for-.student: As fast electric vehicle charging stations (fast-EVCSs) grow in number, competition over electricity prices is expected, with public or private data playing a key role. EV users, acting in their own interest, choose stations to maximize their benefit based on price, waiting time, and battery level. While past work focused on equilibrium prices, this study introduces a personalized dynamic pricing policy (PeDP) for fast-EVCSs to boost revenue using reinforcement learning (RL). The researchers built a simulation with multiple competing stations, modeling user choices via a game-theoretic approach with a monetary utility function. They then applied a Q-learning-based PeDP to maximize station revenue. Simulations showed: (1) waiting time significantly impacts the EV charging market when comparing PeDP to classic Bertrand competition; (2) PeDP performs well, and its effectiveness depends on available information; and (3) in some cases, privacy-preserved data can be exploited by AI-driven pricing policies.
personalized-dynamic-pricing-policy-for-.layman: As more fast electric car charging stations open, they will compete on price, and drivers will pick stations based on cost, wait time, and battery level. This study created a computer model where stations use a smart pricing system to earn more money. Tests showed that wait times matter a lot in this market. The new pricing system works well, but it can sometimes misuse shared data to its advantage.

data-driven-economic-nmpc-using-reinforc.scientist: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful tool to perform data-driven optimal control without relying on a model of the system. However, RL struggles to provide hard guarantees on the behavior of the resulting control scheme. In contrast, Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Economic NMPC (ENMPC) are standard tools for the closed-loop optimal control of complex systems with constraints and limitations, and benefit from a rich theory to assess their closed-loop behavior. Unfortunately, the performance of (E)NMPC hinges on the quality of the model underlying the control scheme. In this paper, we show that an (E)NMPC scheme can be tuned to deliver the optimal policy of the real system even when using a wrong model. This result also holds for real systems having stochastic dynamics. This entails that ENMPC can be used as a new type of function approximator within RL. Furthermore, we investigate our results in the context of ENMPC and formally connect them to the concept of dissipativity, which is central for the ENMPC stability. Finally, we detail how these results can be used to deploy classic RL tools for tuning (E)NMPC schemes. We apply these tools on both a classical linear MPC setting and a standard nonlinear example from the ENMPC literature.
data-driven-economic-nmpc-using-reinforc.student: Reinforcement Learning (RL) learns optimal control policies from data without needing a system model, but it lacks strong guarantees on performance. Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Economic NMPC (ENMPC) are model-based methods for controlling complex systems with constraints, offering robust theoretical guarantees. However, their performance depends on the accuracy of the model. This study demonstrates that even with an incorrect model, an (E)NMPC scheme can be adjusted to achieve the optimal policy for the real system, including systems with random (stochastic) behavior. This means ENMPC can act as a function approximator in RL. The work also links these findings to *dissipativity*—a key property for ENMPC stability—and shows how RL tools can be used to tune (E)NMPC. Results are tested on a linear MPC example and a nonlinear ENMPC case.
data-driven-economic-nmpc-using-reinforc.layman: Researchers asked if a control method that relies on a model of a system can still work well even if the model is wrong. They found that, with careful adjustments, it can still produce the best possible actions for the real system, even when the system behaves unpredictably. This means the method can be used in a different way, like a tool for learning from experience. They also showed how this connects to a property that keeps the system stable and how to use learning techniques to improve the method. They tested their ideas on two examples.

safe-reinforcement-learning-using-robust.scientist: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has recently impressed the world with stunning results in various applications. While the potential of RL is now well-established, many critical aspects still need to be tackled, including safety and stability issues. These issues, while secondary for the RL community, are central to the control community which has been widely investigating them. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is one of the most successful control techniques because, among others, of its ability to provide such guarantees even for uncertain constrained systems. Since MPC is an optimization-based technique, optimality has also often been claimed. Unfortunately, the performance of MPC is highly dependent on the accuracy of the model used for predictions. In this paper, we propose to combine RL and MPC in order to exploit the advantages of both and, therefore, obtain a controller which is optimal and safe. We illustrate the results with two numerical examples in simulations.
safe-reinforcement-learning-using-robust.student: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in complex tasks, but its safety and stability—key concerns in control engineering—remain underdeveloped. Model Predictive Control (MPC), a widely used control method, addresses these by using optimization to ensure stability and constraint satisfaction, even with uncertainty. However, MPC’s performance relies heavily on the accuracy of its predictive model. This paper proposes merging RL and MPC to create a controller that leverages RL’s adaptability and MPC’s safety guarantees. The approach is tested in two simulated scenarios, demonstrating its potential to balance optimality and reliability.
safe-reinforcement-learning-using-robust.layman: Researchers combined two methods for controlling systems: one that learns from experience and one that plans carefully to avoid mistakes. The first method is powerful but can be unsafe, while the second is reliable but depends on accurate predictions. By blending them, the team created a system that aims to be both smart and safe. They tested it in two computer simulations to show it works.

safe-reinforcement-learning-via-projecti.scientist: For all its successes, Reinforcement Learning (RL) still struggles to deliver formal guarantees on the closed-loop behavior of the learned policy. Among other things, guaranteeing the safety of RL with respect to safety-critical systems is a very active research topic. Some recent contributions propose to rely on projections of the inputs delivered by the learned policy into a safe set, ensuring that the system safety is never jeopardized. Unfortunately, it is unclear whether this operation can be performed without disrupting the learning process. This paper addresses this issue. The problem is analysed in the context of Q-learning and policy gradient techniques. We show that the projection approach is generally disruptive in the context of Q learning though a simple alternative solves the issue, while simple corrections can be used in the context of policy gradient methods in order to ensure that the policy gradients are unbiased. The proposed results extend to safe projections based on robust MPC techniques.
safe-reinforcement-learning-via-projecti.student: Reinforcement Learning (RL) trains agents to make decisions, but it often lacks guarantees that the agent’s actions will keep a system safe, especially in critical applications. One approach is to project the agent’s outputs into a predefined safe set, ensuring safety but risking interference with learning. This study examines whether such projections disrupt learning in two common RL methods: Q-learning and policy gradients. For Q-learning, projections are generally disruptive, but a straightforward adjustment resolves the issue. For policy gradients, small corrections can keep the learning process unbiased. The findings also apply to safe projections using robust Model Predictive Control (MPC), a technique for controlling dynamic systems under constraints.
safe-reinforcement-learning-via-projecti.layman: Researchers are working on ways to make AI systems that learn by trial and error safer, especially when mistakes could cause harm. One idea is to adjust the AI’s actions to always stay within safe limits. This study tested whether this adjustment interferes with the learning process. They found that for one learning method, it does interfere, but a simple fix works. For another method, small tweaks prevent the problem. The results also apply to more advanced safety checks.

reinforcement-learning-for-mixed-integer.scientist: Model Predictive Control has been recently proposed as policy approximation for Reinforcement Learning, offering a path towards safe and explainable Reinforcement Learning. This approach has been investigated for Q-learning and actor-critic methods, both in the context of nominal Economic MPC and Robust (N)MPC, showing very promising results. In that context, actor-critic methods seem to be the most reliable approach. Many applications include a mixture of continuous and integer inputs, for which the classical actor-critic methods need to be adapted. In this paper, we present a policy approximation based on mixed-integer MPC schemes, and propose a computationally inexpensive technique to generate exploration in the mixed-integer input space that ensures a satisfaction of the constraints. We then propose a simple compatible advantage function approximation for the proposed policy, that allows one to build the gradient of the mixed-integer MPC-based policy.
reinforcement-learning-for-mixed-integer.student: Reinforcement Learning (RL) trains agents to make decisions by trial and error, but its policies can be hard to interpret or guarantee safety. Model Predictive Control (MPC), a control method that optimizes actions over a short horizon, has been used to approximate RL policies, offering better explainability and safety. Prior work applied MPC to Q-learning and actor-critic methods—RL approaches where an agent learns a value function or a policy directly—using both standard and robust MPC, with actor-critic showing the most promise. However, many real-world problems involve mixed continuous and integer inputs (e.g., switching between discrete modes and adjusting continuous variables), which standard actor-critic methods struggle with. This paper introduces a policy approximation using mixed-integer MPC, which handles such inputs. It also proposes a low-cost exploration method to satisfy constraints and a compatible advantage function to compute the policy gradient, enabling learning in these complex settings.
reinforcement-learning-for-mixed-integer.layman: Researchers are working on ways to make AI systems that learn by trial and error safer and easier to understand. One approach uses a method called Model Predictive Control, which plans actions step by step. This has worked well for some AI learning techniques, but many real problems involve a mix of smooth adjustments and on/off choices. The study presents a new way to handle these mixed choices using the same planning method. It also includes a simple way to explore options while staying within rules and a method to improve the AI’s learning. The result is a more reliable way to train AI for complex tasks.

combining-system-identification-with-rei.scientist: In this paper we propose and compare methods for combining system identification (SYSID) and reinforcement learning (RL) in the context of data-driven model predictive control (MPC). Assuming a known model structure of the controlled system, and considering a parametric MPC, the proposed approach simultaneously: a) Learns the parameters of the MPC using RL in order to optimize performance, and b) fits the observed model behaviour using SYSID. Six methods that avoid conflicts between the two optimization objectives are proposed and evaluated using a simple linear system. Based on the simulation results, hierarchical, parallel projection, nullspace projection, and singular value projection achieved the best performance.
combining-system-identification-with-rei.student: This study explores ways to merge system identification (SYSID, which estimates a system’s behavior from data) and reinforcement learning (RL, a trial-and-error method for optimizing decisions) within data-driven model predictive control (MPC, a control strategy that uses a model to predict and optimize future actions). The approach assumes a known structure for the system and a parametric MPC, then simultaneously: (a) uses RL to tune the MPC’s parameters for better performance, and (b) refines the system model using SYSID. Six methods were tested to balance these two goals on a simple linear system. Results suggest that hierarchical, parallel projection, nullspace projection, and singular value projection methods performed best in simulations.
combining-system-identification-with-rei.layman: The researchers asked how to combine two ways of improving a control system: one that learns from data how the system behaves, and another that learns by trial and error how to make better decisions. They tested six methods on a simple system. The best-performing methods were those that carefully balanced the two learning goals, showing promise for making control systems more effective.

learning-for-mpc-with-stability-safety-g.scientist: The combination of learning methods with Model Predictive Control (MPC) has attracted a significant amount of attention in the recent literature. The hope of this combination is to reduce the reliance of MPC schemes on accurate models, and to tap into the fast developing machine learning and reinforcement learning tools to exploit the growing amount of data available for many systems. In particular, the combination of reinforcement learning and MPC has been proposed as a viable and theoretically justified approach to introduce explainable, safe and stable policies in reinforcement learning. However, a formal theory detailing how the safety and stability of an MPC-based policy can be maintained through the parameter updates delivered by the learning tools is still lacking. This paper addresses this gap. The theory is developed for the generic Robust MPC case, and applied in simulation in the robust tube-based linear MPC case, where the theory is fairly easy to deploy in practice. The paper focuses on Reinforcement Learning as a learning tool, but it applies to any learning method that updates the MPC parameters online.
learning-for-mpc-with-stability-safety-g.student: Researchers are exploring how to combine Model Predictive Control (MPC), a control method that uses a model of a system to predict and optimize its behavior, with machine learning to reduce reliance on perfect models and leverage large datasets. A promising approach is integrating reinforcement learning (RL) with MPC to create policies that are explainable, safe, and stable. However, there’s no formal theory yet on how to ensure safety and stability when MPC parameters are updated via learning. This paper fills that gap by developing a theory for Robust MPC, a version of MPC that accounts for uncertainties, and tests it in simulations using a linear MPC setup. The work focuses on RL but applies to any online learning method updating MPC parameters.
learning-for-mpc-with-stability-safety-g.layman: Scientists are studying how to mix a control method called Model Predictive Control with machine learning to make systems work better without needing perfect models. They want to use learning to improve safety and reliability, but there’s no clear rule yet on how to keep things safe when the system learns. This paper creates such a rule for a type of control that handles uncertainties and tests it in a simple computer simulation. The idea works for any learning method, not just the one they focused on.

reinforcement-learning-of-the-prediction.scientist: Model predictive control (MPC) is a powerful trajectory optimization control technique capable of controlling complex nonlinear systems while respecting system constraints and ensuring safe operation. The MPC’s capabilities come at the cost of a high online computational complexity, the requirement of an accurate model of the system dynamics, and the necessity of tuning its parameters to the specific control application. The main tunable parameter affecting the computational complexity is the prediction horizon length, controlling how far into the future the MPC predicts the system response and thus evaluates the optimality of its computed trajectory. A longer horizon generally increases the control performance, but requires an increasingly powerful computing platform, excluding certain control applications. The performance sensitivity to the prediction horizon length varies over the state space, and this motivated the adaptive horizon model predictive control (AHMPC), which adapts the prediction horizon according to some criteria. In this paper we propose to learn the optimal prediction horizon as a function of the state using reinforcement learning (RL). We show how the RL learning problem can be formulated and test our method on two control tasks — showing clear improvements over the fixed horizon MPC scheme — while requiring only minutes of learning.
reinforcement-learning-of-the-prediction.student: Model predictive control (MPC) is a method for controlling complex systems by repeatedly solving an optimization problem to find the best future trajectory while respecting system limits. However, MPC requires heavy computation, an accurate system model, and careful tuning of parameters like the prediction horizon—the time window over which future behavior is predicted. Longer horizons improve control but demand more computing power, making them impractical for some applications. Since the ideal horizon length varies depending on the system’s current state, researchers developed adaptive horizon MPC (AHMPC), which adjusts the horizon dynamically. This paper proposes using reinforcement learning (RL), a machine learning approach, to learn the optimal horizon as a function of the system’s state. The RL problem is formulated, and the method is tested on two control tasks, showing better performance than fixed-horizon MPC after only minutes of training.
reinforcement-learning-of-the-prediction.layman: Researchers studied a way to improve a control method that helps machines make smart decisions by predicting future actions. The method works well but is slow and needs fine-tuning. One key setting, how far ahead it predicts, affects both performance and speed. The team used a learning approach to automatically adjust this setting based on the machine’s current state. They tested it on two tasks and found it worked better than the old method, with quick learning time.

reinforcement-learning-based-on-mpc-mhe-.scientist: This paper proposes an observer-based framework for solving Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) when an accurate model is not available. We first propose to use a Moving Horizon Estimation-Model Predictive Control (MHE-MPC) scheme in order to provide a policy for the POMDP problem, where the full state of the real process is not measured and necessarily known. We propose to parameterize both MPC and MHE formulations, where certain adjustable parameters are regarded for tuning the policy. In this paper, for the sake of tackling the unmodeled and partially observable dynamics, we leverage the Reinforcement Learning (RL) to tune the parameters of MPC and MHE schemes jointly, with the closed-loop performance of the policy as a goal rather than model fitting or the MHE performance. Illustrations show that the proposed approach can effectively increase the performance of close-loop control of systems formulated as POMDPs.
reinforcement-learning-based-on-mpc-mhe-.student: This study addresses control problems where the system’s full state is hidden and no precise model exists, a scenario known as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). The authors combine Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE), which estimates unmeasured states, with Model Predictive Control (MPC), which plans actions based on those estimates. Both MHE and MPC are parameterized, meaning their behavior can be adjusted via tunable settings. Instead of relying on a known model, the researchers use reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize these parameters, focusing on the overall control performance rather than just estimation accuracy. Simulations demonstrate that this approach improves closed-loop control for POMDP systems.
reinforcement-learning-based-on-mpc-mhe-.layman: The researchers tackled a problem where a system’s full state is hidden and no perfect model exists. They combined two methods: one to guess the missing information and another to decide the best actions based on those guesses. Instead of relying on a fixed model, they used a learning approach to fine-tune the system’s settings, aiming for better overall performance. Tests showed this method works well for controlling such uncertain systems.

mpc-based-reinforcement-learning-for-eco.scientist: In this paper, we are interested in optimal control problems with purely economic costs, which often yield optimal policies having a (nearly) bang-bang structure. We focus on policy approximations based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) and the use of the deterministic policy gradient method to optimize the MPC closed-loop performance in the presence of unmodelled stochasticity or model error. When the policy has a (nearly) bang-bang structure, we observe that the policy gradient method can struggle to produce meaningful steps in the policy parameters. To tackle this issue, we propose a homotopy strategy based on the interior-point method, providing a relaxation of the policy during the learning. We investigate a specific well-known battery storage problem, and show that the proposed method delivers a homogeneous and faster learning than a classical policy gradient approach.
mpc-based-reinforcement-learning-for-eco.student: This study examines optimal control problems where costs are purely economic, often leading to policies that switch abruptly between extreme actions (a 'bang-bang' structure). The authors use Model Predictive Control (MPC), a method that repeatedly solves short-term optimization problems to guide long-term decisions, and apply the deterministic policy gradient method to improve MPC performance under uncertainty or model errors. However, when policies are nearly bang-bang, the gradient method struggles to adjust parameters effectively. To address this, they introduce a homotopy strategy—gradually relaxing the policy constraints using an interior-point method—during learning. Tested on a battery storage problem, their approach achieves smoother and faster learning compared to standard policy gradient methods.
mpc-based-reinforcement-learning-for-eco.layman: The researchers studied how to best control systems like battery storage when costs are purely financial. They found that the best strategies often involve sudden switches between extreme actions. To improve these strategies under uncertainty, they used a method that adjusts decisions step by step. However, this method struggles when strategies involve abrupt changes. So, they created a new approach that gradually eases the constraints during learning. When tested on a battery storage problem, their new method learned faster and more smoothly than the old one.

data-driven-predictive-control-and-mpc-d.scientist: In this paper, we explore the interplay between Predictive Control and closed-loop optimality, spanning from Model Predictive Control to Data-Driven Predictive Control. Predictive Control in general relies on some form of prediction scheme on the real system trajectories. However, these predictions may not accurately capture the real system dynamics, for e.g., due to stochasticity, resulting in sub-optimal control policies. This lack of optimality is a critical issue in case of problems with economic objectives. We address this by providing sufficient conditions on the underlying prediction scheme such that a Predictive Controller can achieve closed-loop optimality. However, these conditions do not readily extend to Data-Driven Predictive Control. In this context of closed-loop optimality, we conclude that the factor distinguishing the approaches within Data-Driven Predictive Control is if they can be cast as a sequential decision-making process or not, rather than the dichotomy of model-based vs. model-free. Furthermore, we show that the conventional approach of improving the prediction accuracy from data may not guarantee optimality.
data-driven-predictive-control-and-mpc-d.student: This study examines how Predictive Control—an approach where controllers use predictions of system behavior to make decisions—can achieve optimal performance in closed-loop systems. Predictive Control, including Model Predictive Control and Data-Driven Predictive Control, often suffers from inaccuracies in predictions (e.g., due to randomness), leading to suboptimal control, especially in economically sensitive problems. The authors derive conditions under which a Predictive Controller can ensure closed-loop optimality, but these conditions don’t directly apply to Data-Driven Predictive Control. Instead, they find that the key difference among Data-Driven methods lies in whether they can be framed as sequential decision-making processes, not just whether they use models. They also show that simply improving prediction accuracy from data doesn’t necessarily lead to optimal control.
data-driven-predictive-control-and-mpc-d.layman: The researchers studied how control systems that predict future behavior can be made to work perfectly. They found that even with good predictions, these systems can still make mistakes, especially when money is involved. They figured out some rules to help these systems work better, but these rules don’t apply to systems that learn from data. Instead, the real difference is in how these systems make decisions step by step. They also discovered that making predictions more accurate doesn’t always mean the system will work perfectly.

all-ai-models-are-wrong-but-some-are-opt.scientist: AI models that predict the future behavior of a system (a.k.a. predictive AI models) are central to intelligent decision-making. However, decision-making using predictive AI models often results in suboptimal performance. This is primarily because AI models are typically constructed to best fit the data, and hence to predict the most likely future rather than to enable high-performance decision-making. The hope that such prediction enables high-performance decisions is neither guaranteed in theory nor established in practice. In fact, there is increasing empirical evidence that predictive models must be tailored to decision-making objectives for performance. In this paper, we establish formal (necessary and sufficient) conditions that a predictive model (AI-based or not) must satisfy for a decision-making policy established using that model to be optimal. We then discuss their implications for building predictive AI models for sequential decision-making.
all-ai-models-are-wrong-but-some-are-opt.student: Predictive AI models, which forecast future system behavior, are widely used in decision-making but often lead to suboptimal outcomes. This happens because these models are usually designed to predict the most likely future (i.e., best fit the data) rather than to support high-performance decisions. Theory and practice show that prediction alone does not guarantee good decisions. Recent evidence suggests models must be tailored to decision-making goals. This paper provides formal conditions—both necessary and sufficient—that any predictive model (AI or otherwise) must meet for a decision policy based on it to be optimal. The work also explores how these conditions affect the design of AI models for sequential decision-making.
all-ai-models-are-wrong-but-some-are-opt.layman: AI systems that predict the future are often used to make decisions, but these decisions can be poor. The problem is that these systems are built to guess what will happen next, not to help make the best choices. Research shows that to make good decisions, the predictions need to be adjusted for that purpose. This study explains the exact rules a prediction system must follow to ensure the best possible decisions. It also discusses how to build such systems for making a series of decisions over time.

synthesis-of-model-predictive-control-an.scientist: The fields of model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning (RL) consider two successful control techniques for Markov decision processes. Both approaches are derived from similar fundamental principles, and both are widely used in practical applications, including robotics, process control, energy systems, and autonomous driving. Despite their similarities, MPC and RL follow distinct paradigms that emerged from diverse communities and different requirements. Various technical discrepancies, particularly the role of an environment model as part of the algorithm, lead to methodologies with nearly complementary advantages. Due to their orthogonal benefits, research interest in combination methods has recently increased significantly, leading to a large and growing set of complex ideas leveraging MPC and RL. This work illuminates the differences, similarities, and fundamentals that allow for different combination algorithms and categorizes existing work accordingly. Particularly, we focus on the versatile actor-critic RL approach as a basis for our categorization and examine how the online optimization approach of MPC can be used to improve the overall closed-loop performance of a policy.
synthesis-of-model-predictive-control-an.student: Model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning (RL) are two widely used methods for controlling systems that evolve over time, like robots or energy grids. Both rely on similar mathematical foundations but were developed separately, leading to different strengths: MPC uses a known model of the system to plan actions, while RL learns from trial and error. This paper explores how these methods differ and where they overlap, focusing on their core principles. It then categorizes recent efforts to combine them, particularly using the actor-critic RL framework—a method where one part (the actor) selects actions and another (the critic) evaluates them. The work shows how MPC’s real-time optimization can enhance the performance of RL-based policies, offering a structured way to merge the two approaches.
synthesis-of-model-predictive-control-an.layman: Researchers compared two ways to control machines like robots or self-driving cars. One method plans actions using a model of how the system works, while the other learns by testing different actions. Both have strengths, so scientists are now trying to combine them. This study explains how they differ, where they are similar, and how they can be merged. It looks at one popular learning method and shows how adding planning can make the system work better.

data-driven-distributionally-robust-cont.scientist: In this paper, we propose a distributionally robust control synthesis for an agent with stochastic dynamics that interacts with other agents under uncertainties and constraints expressed by signal temporal logic (STL). We formulate the control synthesis as a chance-constrained program (CCP) with STL specifications that must be satisfied with high probability under all uncertainty tubes induced by the other agents. To tackle the CCP, we propose two methods based on concentration of measure (CoM) theory and conditional value at risk (CVaR) and compare the required assumptions and resulting optimizations. These approaches convert the CCP into an expectation-constrained program (ECP), which is simpler to solve than the original CCP. To estimate the expectation using a finite set of observed data, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) approach. The underlying DRO can be approximated as a robust data-driven optimization that provides a probabilistic under-approximation to the original ECP, where the probability depends on the number of samples. Therefore, under feasibility, the original STL constraints are satisfied with two layers of designed confidence: the confidence of the chance constraint and the confidence of the approximated data-driven optimization, which depends on the number of samples. We then provide details on solving the resulting robust data-driven optimization numerically. Finally, we compare the two proposed approaches through case studies.
data-driven-distributionally-robust-cont.student: This study addresses the problem of designing a controller for an agent with random (stochastic) behavior that must interact with other agents while satisfying strict logical rules (signal temporal logic, or STL) under uncertainty. The goal is to ensure these rules are met with high probability despite unpredictable actions from other agents. The authors frame this as a chance-constrained program (CCP), a type of optimization problem where constraints must hold with a certain probability. To solve it, they propose two methods: one using concentration of measure (CoM) theory, which bounds how much a random variable can deviate from its mean, and another using conditional value at risk (CVaR), a risk measure that focuses on the worst-case outcomes. Both methods transform the CCP into a simpler expectation-constrained program (ECP). To handle real-world data, they use distributionally robust optimization (DRO), which accounts for uncertainty in the data distribution. The result is a data-driven optimization problem that guarantees the original STL constraints are satisfied with two layers of confidence: one from the chance constraint and another from the data approximation. The paper concludes with numerical solutions and case studies comparing the two approaches.
data-driven-distributionally-robust-cont.layman: The researchers wanted to create a reliable way for a system, like a robot, to follow strict rules while dealing with unpredictable situations and other moving parts. They turned this into a math problem where the rules must hold most of the time, even with uncertainty. They came up with two methods to solve it, each turning the problem into a simpler version. They also used a way to handle real-world data that isn’t perfect. In the end, they showed that the rules are likely to be followed, with two layers of certainty, and tested their methods with examples.

differentiable-nonlinear-model-predictiv.scientist: The efficient computation of parametric solution sensitivities is a key challenge in the integration of learning-enhanced methods with nonlinear model predictive control (MPC), as their availability is crucial for many learning algorithms. While approaches presented in the machine learning community are limited to convex or unconstrained formulations, this paper discusses the computation of solution sensitivities of general nonlinear programs (NLPs) using the implicit function theorem (IFT) and smoothed optimality conditions treated in interior-point methods (IPM). We detail sensitivity computation within a sequential quadratic programming (SQP) method which employs an IPM for the quadratic subproblems. The publication is accompanied by an efficient open-source implementation within the acados framework, providing both forward and adjoint sensitivities for general optimal control problems, achieving speedups exceeding 3x over the state-of-the-art solver mpc.pytorch.
differentiable-nonlinear-model-predictiv.student: This study addresses the challenge of efficiently computing how solutions to optimization problems change with parameters, which is important for combining machine learning with nonlinear model predictive control (MPC). While existing machine learning methods often assume simple, convex problems, this work extends sensitivity analysis to general nonlinear programs (NLPs) using the implicit function theorem and interior-point methods (IPM). The authors implement this within a sequential quadratic programming (SQP) framework, where IPM solves quadratic subproblems. They provide an open-source tool in the acados framework that computes both forward and adjoint sensitivities for optimal control problems, outperforming the current state-of-the-art solver mpc.pytorch by over three times.
differentiable-nonlinear-model-predictiv.layman: The researchers wanted to find a faster way to see how small changes in a problem’s setup affect the best possible solution, especially for complex systems like self-driving cars or robots. They developed a new method that works even when the problem isn’t simple, and they built a free tool to do this quickly. Their approach is more than three times faster than the best existing method.

offline-guarded-safe-reinforcement-learn.scientist: When applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) in healthcare scenarios, the out-of-distribution (OOD) issues pose significant risks, as inappropriate generalization beyond clinical expertise can result in potentially harmful recommendations. While existing methods like conservative Q-learning (CQL) attempt to address the OOD issue, their effectiveness is limited by only constraining action selection by suppressing uncertain actions. This action-only regularization imitates clinician actions that prioritize short-term rewards, but it fails to regulate downstream state trajectories, thereby limiting the discovery of improved long-term treatment strategies. To safely improve policy beyond clinician recommendations while ensuring that state-action trajectories remain in-distribution, we propose Offline Guarded Safe Reinforcement Learning (OGSRL), a theoretically grounded model-based offline RL framework. OGSRL introduces a novel dual constraint mechanism for improving policy with reliability and safety. First, the OOD guardian is established to specify clinically validated regions for safe policy exploration. By constraining optimization within these regions, it enables the reliable exploration of treatment strategies that outperform clinician behavior by leveraging the full patient state history, without drifting into unsupported state-action trajectories. Second, we introduce a safety cost constraint that encodes medical knowledge about physiological safety boundaries, providing domain-specific safeguards even in areas where training data might contain potentially unsafe interventions. Notably, we provide theoretical guarantees on safety and near-optimality: policies that satisfy these constraints remain in safe and reliable regions and achieve performance close to the best possible policy supported by the data. When evaluated on the MIMIC-III sepsis treatment dataset, OGSRL demonstrated significantly better OOD handling than baselines. OGSRL achieved a 78% reduction in mortality estimates and a 51% increase in reward compared to clinician decisions.
offline-guarded-safe-reinforcement-learn.student: In healthcare, offline reinforcement learning (RL) uses past patient data to suggest treatments, but risks arise when the system generalizes beyond known clinical cases—called out-of-distribution (OOD) issues—leading to unsafe recommendations. Current methods like conservative Q-learning (CQL) only limit actions, not the full patient state trajectories, so they miss better long-term strategies. We propose Offline Guarded Safe Reinforcement Learning (OGSRL), a model-based framework that adds two safeguards: an OOD guardian to keep exploration within clinically validated regions, and a safety cost constraint to enforce physiological boundaries. This ensures policies stay reliable and safe while improving on clinician decisions. On a sepsis dataset (MIMIC-III), OGSRL outperformed baselines, reducing estimated mortality by 78% and increasing reward by 51% compared to clinician choices.
offline-guarded-safe-reinforcement-learn.layman: Researchers studied how to use past patient records to suggest better treatments without risking unsafe advice. Current methods only limit the actions taken, not the full patient journey, so they miss better long-term care. The team created a new system that keeps suggestions within safe, known medical limits while still improving on doctor decisions. Tested on real patient data, it cut estimated death rates by 78% and improved outcomes by 51% compared to what doctors chose.

computationally-efficient-gauss-newton-r.scientist: Model predictive control (MPC) is widely used in process control due to its interpretability and ability to handle constraints. As a parametric policy in reinforcement learning (RL), MPC offers strong initial performance and low data requirements compared to black-box policies like neural networks. However, most RL methods rely on first-order updates, which scale well to large parameter spaces but converge at most linearly, making them inefficient when each policy update requires solving an optimal control problem, as is the case with MPC. While MPC policies are typically sparsely parameterized and thus amenable to second-order approaches, existing second-order methods demand second-order policy derivatives, which can be computationally and memory-wise intractable. This work introduces a Gauss-Newton approximation of the deterministic policy Hessian that eliminates the need for second-order policy derivatives, enabling superlinear convergence with minimal computational overhead. To further improve robustness, we propose a momentum-based Hessian averaging scheme for stable training under noisy estimates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on a nonlinear continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR), showing faster convergence and improved data efficiency over state-of-the-art first-order methods.
computationally-efficient-gauss-newton-r.student: Model predictive control (MPC) is a popular method in process control because it is easy to understand and can handle system limits. In reinforcement learning (RL), MPC acts as a rule-based policy that performs well initially and needs less data than black-box methods like neural networks. However, most RL approaches use first-order updates, which work for large systems but improve slowly when each update requires solving an optimal control problem, as with MPC. While MPC’s simple structure suits second-order methods, these usually need complex second-order derivatives, which are hard to compute. This study presents a Gauss-Newton approximation of the policy Hessian (a matrix measuring curvature) that avoids these derivatives, allowing faster-than-linear improvement with little extra computation. A momentum-based averaging method is also introduced to stabilise training with noisy data. The approach is tested on a nonlinear chemical reactor, showing quicker convergence and better data efficiency than first-order methods.
computationally-efficient-gauss-newton-r.layman: Researchers wanted to improve a control method used in chemical plants and robotics, which is easy to understand but slow to learn. They developed a new way to speed up its learning process without heavy calculations. The method avoids complex math that usually slows things down and adds a trick to handle messy data. When tested on a chemical reactor, it learned faster and needed less data than older methods.

safe-reinforcement-learning-using-action.scientist: Projection-based safety filters, which modify unsafe actions by mapping them to the closest safe alternative, are widely used to enforce safety constraints in reinforcement learning (RL). Two integration strategies are commonly considered: Safe environment RL (SE-RL), where the safeguard is treated as part of the environment, and safe policy RL (SP-RL), where it is embedded within the policy through differentiable optimization layers. Despite their practical relevance in safety-critical settings, a formal understanding of their differences is lacking. In this work, we present a theoretical comparison of SE-RL and SP-RL. We identify a key distinction in how each approach is affected by action aliasing, a phenomenon in which multiple unsafe actions are projected to the same safe action, causing information loss in the policy gradients. In SE-RL, this effect is implicitly approximated by the critic, while in SP-RL, it manifests directly as rank-deficient Jacobians during backpropagation through the safeguard. Our contributions are threefold: (i) a unified formalization of SE-RL and SP-RL in the context of actor-critic algorithms, (ii) a theoretical analysis of their respective policy gradient estimates, highlighting the role of action aliasing, and (iii) a comparative study of mitigation strategies, including a novel penalty-based improvement for SP-RL that aligns with established SE-RL practices. Empirical results support our theoretical predictions, showing that action aliasing is more detrimental for SP-RL than for SE-RL. However, with appropriate improvement strategies, SP-RL can match or outperform improved SE-RL across a range of environments. These findings provide actionable insights for choosing and refining projection-based safe RL methods based on task characteristics.
safe-reinforcement-learning-using-action.student: Reinforcement learning (RL) often uses projection-based safety filters to adjust unsafe actions to the nearest safe ones. Two common approaches are Safe Environment RL (SE-RL), where the filter is part of the environment, and Safe Policy RL (SP-RL), where it’s built into the policy via differentiable layers. This study compares them theoretically, focusing on *action aliasing*—when multiple unsafe actions map to the same safe one, losing information in policy updates. In SE-RL, the critic approximates this effect, while in SP-RL, it causes issues during backpropagation. The work formalizes both methods, analyzes their policy gradients, and tests fixes, including a new penalty for SP-RL. Experiments show action aliasing hurts SP-RL more, but with tweaks, SP-RL can match or beat SE-RL. The results guide choosing or improving safe RL methods based on the task.
safe-reinforcement-learning-using-action.layman: Researchers studied two ways to keep AI systems safe while they learn from trial and error. One method treats safety as part of the learning environment, the other builds it directly into the AI’s decision-making. They found that when many unsafe choices get forced into the same safe choice, the second method struggles more. But with adjustments, it can work as well as or better than the first. The study helps pick the best safety approach for different tasks.

day-ahead-scheduling-and-real-time-econo.scientist: This paper presents a model for day-ahead scheduling of the combined heat and electric energy production for a residential microgrid taking into account the economic factors in a liberalized electricity market, the technical factors in the safety/quality of supply, and the consumer preferences. This day-ahead scheduling model is complemented with a real-time economic model predictive control (MPC) model for a subsequent control with respect to the outcomes of the day-ahead scheduling. This combined scheduling and economic MPC provides a general set-up capable of overcoming several major difficulties encountered with a typical scheduling + tracking MPC set-up, e.g., the problems of connecting the economic objectives with different temporal resolution and different requirements in terms of delivery.
day-ahead-scheduling-and-real-time-econo.student: This study addresses the challenge of planning daily heat and electricity production for a small, local energy network (a residential microgrid) that must balance costs, technical safety, and user preferences. The researchers developed a day-ahead scheduling model to optimize production while considering market prices, supply reliability, and consumer needs. They then paired this with a real-time control method called economic model predictive control (MPC), which adjusts operations based on the initial plan. Together, these models solve common issues in energy systems, such as aligning short-term and long-term economic goals and ensuring consistent energy delivery.
day-ahead-scheduling-and-real-time-econo.layman: The researchers wanted to find the best way to plan and manage heat and electricity for a small community energy system. They created a daily plan that considers costs, safety, and what users want. Then, they added a real-time system to fine-tune the plan as things change. This approach helps balance immediate needs with long-term goals, making the energy supply more reliable and efficient.

a-game-approach-for-charging-station-pla.scientist: The placement of electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs), which encourages the rapid development of electric vehicles (EVs), should be considered from not only operational perspective such as minimizing installation costs, but also user perspective so that their strategic and competitive charging behaviors can be reflected. This paper proposes a methodological framework to consider crowdedness and individual preferences of electric vehicle users (EVUs) in the selection of locations for fast-charging stations. The electric vehicle charging station placement problem (EVCSPP) is solved via a decentralized game theoretical decision-making algorithm and k-means clustering algorithm. The proposed algorithm, referred to as k-GRAPE, determines the locations of charging stations to maximize the sum of utilities of EVUs. In particular, we analytically present that 50% of suboptimality of the solution can be at least guaranteed, which is about 17% better than the existing game theoretical based framework. We show a few variants to describe the utility functions that may capture the difference in preferences of EVUs. Finally, we demonstrate the viability of the decision framework via three real-world data-based experiments. The results of the experiments, including a comparison with a baseline method are then discussed.
a-game-approach-for-charging-station-pla.student: Placing electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs) requires balancing cost efficiency with user needs, as drivers may choose stations based on crowding and personal preferences. This study introduces a framework to model these user behaviors in selecting fast-charging locations. The problem, called the electric vehicle charging station placement problem (EVCSPP), is addressed using a decentralized game-theoretic algorithm (where decisions are made by individual agents) combined with k-means clustering (a method to group similar data points). The resulting algorithm, k-GRAPE, aims to maximize the total benefit, or utility, for EV users. The solution guarantees at least 50% of the optimal outcome, improving on prior game-theoretic approaches by about 17%. The paper also explores different utility functions to reflect varied user preferences and validates the framework with real-world data experiments, comparing it to a baseline method.
a-game-approach-for-charging-station-pla.layman: Researchers studied where to place electric car charging stations so that drivers can easily find one that suits their needs, not just to save money. They created a method that considers how crowded stations get and what drivers prefer. Using math and data, they designed a system that picks locations to benefit as many drivers as possible. Their approach is about 17% better than older methods at finding good spots. They tested it with real data and showed it works well compared to a simpler way of choosing locations.

a-learning-based-model-predictive-contro.scientist: This paper presents a model predictive control (MPC)-based reinforcement learning (RL) approach for a home energy management system (HEMS). The house consists of an air-to-water heat pump connected to a hot water tank that supplies thermal energy to a water-based floor heating system. Additionally, it includes a photovoltaic (PV) array and a battery storage system. The HEMS is supposed to exploit the house thermal inertia and battery storage to shift demand from peak hours to off-peak periods and earn benefits by selling excess energy to the utility grid during periods of high electricity prices. However, designing such a HEMS is challenging because the discrepancies due to model mismatch make erroneous predictions of the system dynamics, leading to a non-optimal decision making. Besides, uncertainties in the house thermodynamics, misprediction in the forecasting of PV generation, outdoor temperature, and user load demand make the problem more challenging. We solve this issue by approximating the optimal policy by a parameterized MPC scheme and updating the parameters via a compatible delayed deterministic actor-critic (with gradient Q-learning critic, i.e., CDDAC-GQ) algorithm. Simulation results show that the proposed MPC-based RL HEMS can effectively deliver a policy that satisfies both indoor thermal comfort and economic costs even in the case of inaccurate model and system uncertainties. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough comparison between the CDDAC-GQ algorithm and the conventional twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) algorithm, the results of which affirm the efficacy of our proposed method in addressing complex HEMS problems.
a-learning-based-model-predictive-contro.student: This study tackles the challenge of managing home energy efficiently using a combination of model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning (RL). The system includes a heat pump, hot water tank, floor heating, solar panels, and a battery. The goal is to shift energy use away from peak hours and sell excess power when prices are high, but this is difficult due to uncertainties like weather, user demand, and model inaccuracies. The researchers use a parameterized MPC scheme and update it with a delayed deterministic actor-critic algorithm (CDDAC-GQ) to handle these uncertainties. Simulations show the approach maintains indoor comfort and reduces costs, even with imperfect models. It also outperforms a standard RL method (TD3) in managing complex home energy systems.
a-learning-based-model-predictive-contro.layman: Researchers wanted to find a better way to manage energy use in a home with solar panels, a battery, and heating systems. The goal was to use less energy during expensive peak times and sell extra power when prices are high. They created a smart system that learns from experience to make good decisions, even when weather or user habits change. Tests showed it keeps the home comfortable and saves money, working better than older methods.

can-ai-abuse-personal-information-in-an-.scientist: In order to alleviate the range anxiety of electric vehicle users (EVUs), several researches focus on facilitating the efficiency of fast-electric vehicle charging stations (fast-EVCSs) using artificial intelligence (AI). This paper first proposes a fast-EVCS revenue maximization pricing policy using an AI approach, and we argue that the AI algorithm can learn to abuse EVUs information for maximizing its revenue. In order to investigate the hypothesis, firstly, a simulation environment is developed using vehicle performance models and an EVU’s charging station selection game. Then, we formulate the charging station revenue maximization problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) and propose a personalized dynamic pricing policy using a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm. From numerical simulation results, it is found that if the RL approach focuses solely on increasing revenue of the fast-EVCSs, it can learn to misuse personal information without any human intervention. To prevent such abuse, we suggest intuitive guidelines for policymakers and urban planners via numerical experiments.
can-ai-abuse-personal-information-in-an-.student: To help electric vehicle users (EVUs) worried about running out of charge, this study explores how fast-charging stations can use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve efficiency. The researchers propose an AI-based pricing strategy to maximize station revenue but note that the AI might exploit user data to do so. They built a simulation using vehicle models and a game where EVUs choose stations, then framed the revenue problem as a Markov decision process (a mathematical model for decision-making under uncertainty). Using reinforcement learning (an AI method that learns by trial and error), they designed a dynamic pricing policy. Simulations showed that if the AI focuses only on revenue, it can misuse personal data without human input. The study concludes with policy guidelines to prevent such abuse.
can-ai-abuse-personal-information-in-an-.layman: The researchers asked if fast-charging stations for electric cars could use smart computer programs to set prices that make more money. They found that these programs might use personal information about drivers in unfair ways to increase profits. To test this, they created a computer model of how drivers pick charging stations and how the stations set prices. The results showed that the programs could indeed misuse data if left unchecked. The team then suggested simple rules to stop this from happening.

convex-neural-network-based-cost-modific.scientist: Developing model predictive control (MPC) schemes can be challenging for systems where an accurate model is not available, or too costly to develop. With the increasing availability of data and tools to treat them, learning-based MPC has of late attracted wide attention. It has recently been shown that adapting not only the MPC model, but also its cost function is conducive to achieving optimal closed-loop performance when an accurate model cannot be provided. In the learning context, this modification can be performed via parametrizing the MPC cost and adjusting the parameters via, e.g., reinforcement learning (RL). In this framework, simple cost parametrizations can be effective, but the underlying theory suggests that rich parametrizations in principle can be useful. In this paper, we propose such a cost parametrization using a class of neural networks (NNs) that preserves convexity. This choice avoids creating difficulties when solving the MPC problem via sensitivity-based solvers. In addition, this choice of cost parametrization ensures nominal stability of the resulting MPC scheme. Moreover, we detail how this choice can be applied to economic MPC problems where the cost function is generic and therefore does not necessarily fulfill any specific property.
convex-neural-network-based-cost-modific.student: Model predictive control (MPC) is a method for controlling systems by repeatedly solving an optimization problem to find the best input. However, MPC can be hard to apply when an accurate system model is unavailable or expensive to build. Recent work shows that, in such cases, learning-based MPC can improve performance by adapting not just the model but also the cost function—the part of MPC that defines what ‘good’ control looks like. This adaptation can be done by parametrizing the cost (i.e., expressing it with adjustable parameters) and tuning those parameters using reinforcement learning. While simple parametrizations work, theory suggests richer ones could be better. Here, we propose a cost parametrization using neural networks that keeps the cost function convex, which helps solvers find solutions efficiently and ensures the resulting MPC remains stable. We also show how this approach can be used for economic MPC, where the cost function is arbitrary and may lack special properties.
convex-neural-network-based-cost-modific.layman: Researchers often use a method called model predictive control to guide systems like robots or factories, but it needs a precise description of how the system works. When that’s missing, they can use data to improve the method. This study explores a way to adjust not just the system description but also the goals the method tries to achieve. They use a type of computer model called a neural network to make these goals flexible yet reliable. The approach keeps the system stable and works even when the goals are complex or unclear.

entropic-risk-based-predictive-control-f.scientist: Energy systems with a significant share of renewable energy production require control strategies that can handle the effects of uncertainty to ensure stable and reliable operation. Simultaneously, liberalized energy markets balance supply and demand on a large scale. In an effort towards renewable energy integration, this paper proposes a stochastic model predictive control framework to handle the energy management of an offshore wind energy system while trading on the day-ahead spot and intraday markets. Furthermore, the framework is extended with the entropic risk measure (ERM) to handle risk-sensitive decision-making. The uncertainty is modeled in discrete scenarios, which propagate uncertainty through a nonlinear model. The proposed framework is validated in simulation with historical data. Results show that the proposed method balances demand and supply while minimizing operational costs through market participation. Furthermore, the framework is compared to itself with different degrees of risk aversion to illustrate the effects of risk sensitivity on the system.
entropic-risk-based-predictive-control-f.student: Renewable energy systems, like offshore wind farms, face uncertainty in power generation, making grid stability and cost management challenging. This study addresses this by proposing a stochastic model predictive control (MPC) framework—a method that uses probabilistic models to optimize decisions under uncertainty. The framework manages energy from an offshore wind system while trading in day-ahead and intraday electricity markets. It also incorporates the entropic risk measure (ERM), a tool to adjust decision-making based on risk tolerance. Uncertainty is modeled using discrete scenarios, which are then processed through a nonlinear system model. Simulations with historical data validate the approach, showing it effectively balances supply and demand while reducing operational costs via market participation. The study also compares different risk aversion levels to demonstrate how risk sensitivity impacts system performance.
entropic-risk-based-predictive-control-f.layman: Wind farms produce unpredictable amounts of energy, making it hard to keep the power grid stable and affordable. Researchers created a computer system to manage an offshore wind farm’s energy while buying and selling electricity in markets. The system uses past data to predict and plan for uncertainty, and it can adjust how cautious it is with decisions. Tests showed it keeps supply and demand balanced and cuts costs. The team also showed how being more or less cautious changes the results.

reinforcement-learning-based-on-mpc-and-.scientist: In this paper, we present a methodology to implement the stochastic policy gradient method using actor-critic techniques, when the policy is approximated using an MPC scheme. The paper proposes a computationally inexpensive approach to build a stochastic policy generating samples that are guaranteed to be feasible for the MPC constraints. For a continuous input space, imposing hard constraints on the policy poses technical difficulties in the computation of the score function of the policy, required in the policy gradient computation. We propose an approach that solves this issue, and detail how the score function can be computed based on parametric Nonlinear Programming and primal-dual interior point. The approach is illustrated on a simple example.
reinforcement-learning-based-on-mpc-and-.student: This study addresses the challenge of applying stochastic policy gradient methods—where a policy is adjusted based on random samples—to systems controlled by Model Predictive Control (MPC), a strategy that optimizes actions over a future horizon. The key difficulty is ensuring that the randomly generated actions (samples) satisfy MPC’s strict constraints, which is computationally demanding. The authors propose a low-cost method to generate feasible samples and compute the policy’s score function (a measure of how changes in policy parameters affect performance), which is essential for policy gradient updates. Their solution leverages parametric Nonlinear Programming and primal-dual interior point methods to handle constraints efficiently. The approach is demonstrated on a simple example.
reinforcement-learning-based-on-mpc-and-.layman: The researchers tackled a problem in controlling systems where decisions must follow strict rules. They developed a way to test random decision-making strategies while ensuring those decisions still obey the rules. Normally, this is hard and slow, but their method makes it faster and more practical. They showed it works with a simple test case.

reinforcement-learning-for-mpc-fundament.scientist: Recent publications have laid a solid theoretical foundation for the combination of Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control, in view of obtaining high-performance data-driven MPC policies. Early practical results, both in simulation and in experiments, have shown the potential of this combination but have also revealed certain challenges. In addition, the technical complexity of these results makes it difficult for interested readers to gather the fundamental ideas and principles behind this combination. This paper aims to provide a coherent and more accessible picture of these results and to offer significantly deeper and more mature insights into their meaning than has been proposed before. It also aims to identify the current challenges in the field.
reinforcement-learning-for-mpc-fundament.student: Recent work has explored merging Reinforcement Learning (RL), a machine learning method where agents learn by trial and error, with Model Predictive Control (MPC), a control strategy that optimizes actions over a short time horizon. While early studies in simulations and experiments show promise for creating high-performance, data-driven MPC policies, they also highlight technical hurdles. The complexity of these results, however, makes it hard to grasp the core ideas. This paper synthesizes these findings into a clearer, more accessible framework, offering deeper insights into their implications and identifying key challenges that remain in combining RL and MPC effectively.
reinforcement-learning-for-mpc-fundament.layman: Researchers are trying to combine two approaches for making smart decisions in systems like robots or factories. One method learns from experience, while the other plans ahead using predictions. Early tests show this mix can work well, but it’s complicated and has some problems. This paper explains the main ideas behind this combination in a simpler way, points out what’s still unclear, and helps others understand how to use it better.

integration-of-energy-communities-via-mu.scientist: Energy Communities (ECs) are groups of prosumers engaging in local energy trading, typically within the shared infrastructure (e.g., behind the same transformer). Local energy markets have emerged as a solution to balance energy demand and production, assuming ECs are price-takers on the main grid. These markets empower prosumers to set local prices and provide scalable pathways for small prosumers to participate in energy systems. As ECs become more prominent, they may transition from price-takers to active market participants, interacting with broader energy markets. This paper investigates interconnected ECs, each operating local energy markets while trading energy through limited transmission infrastructure, and proposes an integrated two-level market optimization framework: local markets set energy prices, while a system-wide market manages transmission capacity and energy exchanges between ECs, maximizing societal welfare. The approach differs from traditional day-ahead markets by optimizing local prices in a time-coupled manner, considering short-term flexibility resources such as batteries and flexible demand. Using a rolling-horizon Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme, the framework integrates day-ahead and real-time balancing market, reducing planning errors and improving market efficiency. Additionally, we present a Second-Order Optimization Method that rapidly clears prices at both local and system levels, accounting for time coupling. This framework supports dynamic and efficient energy trading, paving the way for ECs to participate in larger energy markets while maintaining operational efficiency.
integration-of-energy-communities-via-mu.student: Energy Communities (ECs) are groups of energy producers and consumers (prosumers) trading energy locally, often within shared infrastructure like a transformer. Local energy markets allow ECs to set their own prices, helping small prosumers join larger energy systems. This study explores interconnected ECs, each running local markets while trading energy through limited transmission lines. The researchers propose a two-level optimization framework: local markets set prices, and a system-wide market manages energy exchanges between ECs to maximize overall benefit. Unlike traditional markets, this approach optimizes prices over time, considering flexible resources like batteries. Using a rolling-horizon Model Predictive Control (MPC) method, it combines day-ahead and real-time markets to reduce errors and improve efficiency. A Second-Order Optimization Method is also introduced to quickly determine prices at both levels, accounting for time dependencies. The framework aims to enable dynamic and efficient energy trading for ECs in broader markets.
integration-of-energy-communities-via-mu.layman: Researchers studied groups of people who both produce and use energy, called Energy Communities, and how they trade energy locally. They wanted to see how these groups could work together even when their connections are limited. The team created a system where each group sets its own energy prices, while a larger system manages how energy moves between them to benefit everyone. This system plans ahead but also adjusts in real time, using tools like batteries to stay flexible. The goal is to help these communities trade energy more efficiently and join bigger energy markets.

mpc4rl-a-software-package-for-reinforcem.scientist: In this paper, we present an early software integrating Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Model Predictive Control (MPC). Our aim is to make recent theoretical contributions from the literature more accessible to both the RL and MPC communities. We combine standard software tools developed by the RL community, such as Gymnasium, stable-baselines3, or CleanRL with the acados toolbox, a widely-used software package for efficient MPC algorithms. Our core contribution is MPC4RL, an open-source Python package that supports learning-enhanced MPC schemes for existing acados implementations. The package is designed to be modular, extensible, and user-friendly, facilitating the tuning of MPC algorithms for a broad range of control problems. It is available on GitHub.
mpc4rl-a-software-package-for-reinforcem.student: This work introduces MPC4RL, an open-source Python package that bridges Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Model Predictive Control (MPC), two approaches for designing controllers in dynamic systems. RL learns optimal actions through trial and error, while MPC solves control problems by repeatedly optimizing over a finite time horizon. The package integrates popular RL tools (e.g., Gymnasium, stable-baselines3) with acados, a widely used MPC toolbox. It enables users to enhance MPC schemes with learning-based methods, offering a modular and extensible framework for tuning MPC algorithms across various control problems. The software is publicly available on GitHub.
mpc4rl-a-software-package-for-reinforcem.layman: The researchers created a free, easy-to-use tool that combines two methods for controlling systems like robots or vehicles. One method learns by trial and error, while the other plans ahead step by step. Their tool lets users mix these approaches to improve control. It’s designed to be simple and adaptable, and anyone can download and use it.

multi-agent-battery-storage-management-u.scientist: In this paper, we present the use of Model Predictive Control (MPC) based on Reinforcement Learning (RL) to find the optimal policy for a multi-agent battery storage system. A time-varying prediction of the power price and production-demand uncertainty are considered. We focus on optimizing an economic objective cost while avoiding very low or very high state of charge, which can damage the battery. We consider the bounded power provided by the main grid and the constraints on the power input and state of each agent.
