A parametrized MPC-scheme is used as a function approximator for the deterministic policy gradient method and RL optimizes the closed-loop performance by updating the parameters. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method is able to tackle the constraints and deliver the optimal policy.
multi-agent-battery-storage-management-u.student: This study explores how to optimally manage a group of battery storage units using a control method called Model Predictive Control (MPC), enhanced by Reinforcement Learning (RL). MPC is a strategy that predicts future actions to optimize a system, while RL is a machine learning approach where an agent learns by interacting with its environment. The goal is to minimize economic costs for energy storage while avoiding battery damage from extreme charge levels. The system also accounts for fluctuating power prices, uncertain energy demand, and physical limits on grid power and battery operations. By using MPC as a function approximator within RL, the method learns to improve performance over time. Simulations show it effectively handles constraints and finds an optimal control policy.
multi-agent-battery-storage-management-u.layman: Researchers wanted to find the best way to manage a group of batteries that store energy, considering changing electricity prices and unpredictable energy needs. They used a smart control method that learns from experience to make better decisions over time. The system aims to save money while keeping the batteries from being overcharged or drained. Tests showed that this approach works well and meets all the required limits.

flipping-based-policy-for-chance-constra.scientist: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising approach for many real-world decision-making problems where ensuring safety is a critical necessity. In safe RL research, while expected cumulative safety constraints (ECSCs) are typically the first choices, chance constraints are often more pragmatic for incorporating safety under uncertainties. This paper proposes a flipping-based policy for Chance-Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CCMDPs). The flipping-based policy selects the next action by tossing a potentially distorted coin between two action candidates. The probability of the flip and the two action candidates vary depending on the state. We establish a Bellman equation for CCMDPs and further prove the existence of a flipping-based policy within the optimal solution sets. Since solving the problem with joint chance constraints is challenging in practice, we then prove that joint chance constraints can be approximated into Expected Cumulative Safety Constraints (ECSCs) and that there exists a flipping-based policy in the optimal solution sets for constrained MDPs with ECSCs. As a specific instance of practical implementations, we present a framework for adapting constrained policy optimization to train a flipping-based policy. This framework can be applied to other safe RL algorithms. We demonstrate that the flipping-based policy can improve the performance of the existing safe RL algorithms under the same limits of safety constraints on Safety Gym benchmarks.
flipping-based-policy-for-chance-constra.student: Reinforcement learning (RL) helps agents learn optimal actions in environments, but safety is crucial in real-world applications. This study focuses on Chance-Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CCMDPs), where safety is enforced probabilistically (e.g., 'the agent must avoid failure with at least 95% certainty'). The authors propose a *flipping-based policy*: at each step, the agent randomly chooses between two actions, with probabilities that depend on the current state. They derive a Bellman equation (a recursive formula for optimal decision-making) for CCMDPs and prove that such flipping policies can be optimal. Since solving CCMDPs directly is hard, they show that joint chance constraints can be approximated using simpler expected safety constraints. They also provide a framework to train flipping-based policies using existing safe RL methods and demonstrate improved performance on Safety Gym benchmarks while respecting safety limits.
flipping-based-policy-for-chance-constra.layman: Researchers studied how to make AI systems safer when learning to make decisions. They created a method where the AI randomly picks between two actions, with the odds changing based on the situation. They proved this approach can work well and showed it can be simplified for practical use. Tests on standard problems confirmed it performs better while still meeting safety rules.

optimal-power-management-of-multi-energy.scientist: This paper proposes a market mechanism that enables the advanced distribution management system (ADMS) for energy trading in the local energy market. Two primary functions of the ADMS are discussed: reducing operational costs and coordinating the energy community (EC). The integration of these two functionalities considers all the constraints for maintaining distribution system reliability. Two energy transaction actions are allowed for the ECs: 1) each prosumer in the EC trades energy locally to maximize the global social welfare and pay network usage fees to the distributed system operator (DSO); 2) the EC trades energy with the DSO to sell their excess energy or purchase energy to meet their load demand. The payment among the ECs is subject to a clearing price. In the market, the Newton distributed algorithm has been used to achieve the equilibrium point, and the ADMS actively optimizes voltage, and reactive power (Volt-VAR) via controlling distributed energy resources (DER) and managing the iterative process. To confirm the functionality of the model, 33-bus networks have been used to model the ECs.
optimal-power-management-of-multi-energy.student: This study presents a market mechanism for energy trading in local energy markets, managed by an advanced distribution management system (ADMS). The ADMS aims to lower operational costs and coordinate energy communities (ECs), which are groups of energy producers and consumers (prosumers). The system ensures grid reliability by respecting all technical constraints. ECs can trade energy locally to maximize collective benefit, paying network fees to the grid operator (DSO), or trade with the DSO to buy or sell excess energy. Prices are set by a clearing mechanism, and the Newton distributed algorithm helps find market equilibrium. The ADMS also optimizes voltage and reactive power (Volt-VAR) by controlling distributed energy resources (DERs) and managing the trading process. The model was tested on a 33-bus network to validate its performance.
optimal-power-management-of-multi-energy.layman: Researchers designed a system to help local groups trade energy more efficiently. These groups, made up of people who both produce and use energy, can buy and sell power among themselves or with the main grid. The system keeps costs low, ensures the grid stays stable, and sets fair prices. It also balances the flow of electricity to prevent problems. The idea was tested on a simulated network to see if it works as intended.

optimisation-based-coordination-of-conne.scientist: In this paper, we analyse the performance of a model predictive controller for coordination of connected, automated vehicles at intersections. The problem has combinatorial complexity, and we propose to solve it approximately by using a two stage procedure where (1) the vehicle crossing order in which the vehicles cross the intersection is found by solving a mixed integer quadratic program and (2) the control commands are subsequently found by solving a nonlinear program. We show that the controller is persistently safe and compare its performance against traffic lights and two simpler optimisation-based coordination schemes. The results show that our approach outperforms the considered alternatives in terms of both energy consumption and travel-time delay, especially for medium to high traffic loads.
optimisation-based-coordination-of-conne.student: This study examines how a model predictive controller can coordinate connected, automated vehicles at intersections. The challenge is complex due to the many possible vehicle interactions. The researchers use a two-step method: first, they determine the order in which vehicles cross the intersection by solving a mixed integer quadratic program (a type of optimisation problem with both integer and continuous variables). Second, they calculate the control commands (like acceleration or braking) using a nonlinear program. The controller is proven to maintain safety consistently. When compared to traffic lights and two simpler optimisation-based methods, this approach reduces energy use and travel delays, particularly in medium to high traffic conditions.
optimisation-based-coordination-of-conne.layman: The researchers asked how self-driving cars could safely and efficiently cross busy intersections. They designed a system that first decides the order in which cars should go, then calculates the best speed and timing for each. They tested it against traffic lights and simpler systems. Their method proved safer and cut both fuel use and waiting times, especially when traffic was heavy.

optimal-coordination-of-automated-vehicl.scientist: In this paper, we present a bilevel, model predictive controller for coordination of automated vehicles at intersections. The bilevel controller consists of a coordination level, where intersection occupancy timeslots are allocated, and a vehicle level, where the control commands for the vehicles are computed. We establish persistent feasibility and stability of the bilevel controller under some mild assumptions and derive conditions under which closed-loop collision avoidance can be ensured with bounded position uncertainty. We thereafter detail an implementation of the coordination controller on a three-vehicle test bed, where the intersection-level optimization problem is solved using a distributed Sequential Quadratic Programming method. We present and discuss results from an extensive experimental campaign, where the proposed controller was validated. The experimental results indicate the practical applicability of the bilevel controller and show that safety can be ensured for large positioning uncertainties.
optimal-coordination-of-automated-vehicl.student: This study designs a two-layer control system for automated vehicles at intersections. The upper layer assigns time slots for each vehicle to pass through the intersection, while the lower layer calculates the precise movements for each vehicle. The authors prove that, under reasonable conditions, the system remains stable and avoids collisions even when vehicle positions are not perfectly known. They then test the system on three vehicles, using a distributed optimization method to solve the intersection-level problem. Experiments show the controller works in practice and maintains safety despite significant uncertainty in vehicle positions.
optimal-coordination-of-automated-vehicl.layman: Researchers created a system to help self-driving cars safely cross intersections. The system has two parts: one decides when each car can enter the intersection, and the other controls how each car moves. They proved it can prevent crashes even if the cars’ exact positions are unclear. Tests with three cars showed the system works well and keeps everyone safe, even with some uncertainty about where the cars are.

assessment-of-tso-dso-coordination-to-en.scientist: The growing penetration of renewable energy sources (RES) and distributed energy resources (DERs) has introduced new challenges in power system stability, voltage regulation, and congestion management. Therefore, effective TSO-DSO coordination is crucial for addressing these operational complexities and ensuring a reliable and flexible grid. This paper examines critical coordination domains, including voltage control, congestion management, frequency control, operational planning, system restoration, and ancillary services. We evaluate three principal coordination models—TSO-managed, DSO-managed, and hybrid TSO-DSO approaches—alongside six market schemes that define flexibility service procurement processes. Through analysis of centralized, distributed, and hierarchical technical solutions, we identify structural, regulatory, and technical gaps limiting effective coordination. Our examination of existing initiatives reveals that many projects treat balancing and congestion management as separate processes rather than integrated functions, overlooking potential synergies. Integrating these functions could enhance market efficiency, reduce system costs, and improve grid reliability, particularly within Nordic balancing market frameworks. The paper concludes by recommending innovative technologies, market designs, and operational strategies to enhance grid resilience, optimize DER integration, and promote efficient flexibility markets across transmission and distribution networks, contributing to the development of sustainable, reliable power systems.
assessment-of-tso-dso-coordination-to-en.student: As renewable energy sources like wind and solar grow, power grids face new stability and voltage control challenges. This study explores how transmission system operators (TSOs, managing high-voltage grids) and distribution system operators (DSOs, handling local networks) can coordinate better. We analyzed key areas such as voltage control, congestion management, and frequency regulation, comparing three coordination models (TSO-led, DSO-led, and hybrid) and six market schemes for procuring flexibility services. The research found that current projects often separate balancing and congestion management, missing opportunities to combine them for greater efficiency. Integrating these functions could lower costs and improve reliability, especially in Nordic markets. The paper suggests new technologies, market designs, and strategies to strengthen grid resilience and support renewable energy integration.
assessment-of-tso-dso-coordination-to-en.layman: As more wind and solar power join the grid, keeping electricity flowing smoothly becomes harder. This study looks at how the companies running big power lines and local networks can work together better. They tested different ways to coordinate and found that treating problems separately wastes chances to save money and improve reliability. Combining these efforts could make the system more efficient, especially in places like the Nordic countries. The researchers suggest new tools and rules to help the grid handle more clean energy while staying stable.

safe-reinforcement-learning-using-wasser.scientist: In this paper, we address the chance-constrained safe Reinforcement Learning (RL) problem using the function approximators based on Stochastic Model Predictive Control (SMPC) and Distributionally Robust Model Predictive Control (DRMPC). We use Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) to measure the probability of constraint violation and safety. In order to provide a safe policy by construction, we first propose using parameterized nonlinear DRMPC at each time step. DRMPC optimizes a finite-horizon cost function subject to the worst-case constraint violation in an ambiguity set. We use a statistical ball around the empirical distribution with a radius measured by the Wasserstein metric as the ambiguity set. Unlike the sample average approximation SMPC, DRMPC provides a probabilistic guarantee of the out-of-sample risk and requires lower samples from the disturbance. Then the Q-learning method is used to optimize the parameters in the DRMPC to achieve the best closed-loop performance. Wheeled Mobile Robot (WMR) path planning with obstacle avoidance will be considered to illustrate the efficiency of the proposed method.
safe-reinforcement-learning-using-wasser.student: This study tackles a safe reinforcement learning problem, where an agent must learn a policy while ensuring safety constraints are met with high probability. The approach uses Distributionally Robust Model Predictive Control (DRMPC), a method that optimizes future actions while accounting for worst-case uncertainties in the environment. Here, uncertainty is modeled using a statistical 'ball' around observed data, measured by the Wasserstein metric, which ensures robustness to distribution shifts. Unlike traditional methods that rely on average samples, DRMPC provides stronger safety guarantees with fewer samples. The parameters of DRMPC are then fine-tuned using Q-learning, a reinforcement learning technique, to improve performance. The method is tested on a wheeled mobile robot navigating obstacles, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining safety while learning.
safe-reinforcement-learning-using-wasser.layman: Researchers developed a way for robots to learn safe paths while avoiding obstacles. They used a method that plans ahead but also prepares for unexpected changes, like a driver accounting for possible bad weather. Instead of relying only on past data, they added a buffer to handle surprises. This approach needs less data and gives stronger safety promises. They then adjusted the system to work better over time. The robot was tested in a task where it had to move around obstacles, showing the method works well.

simultaneous-constraints-on-the-number-a.scientist: Recent indications from both particle physics and cosmology suggest the existence of more than three neutrino species. In cosmological analyses the effects of neutrino mass and number of species can in principle be disentangled for fixed cosmological parameters. However, since we do not have perfect measurements of the standard Λ Cold Dark Matter model parameters some correlation remains between the neutrino mass and number of species, and both parameters should be included in the analysis. Combining the newest observations of several cosmological probes (cosmic microwave background, large scale structure, expansion rate) we obtain N_eff = 3.58 +0.16 −0.15 (68% CL) +0.53 −0.55 (95% CL) and Σm_ν < 0.60 eV (95% CL), which are currently the strongest constraints on N_eff and Σm_ν from an analysis including both parameters. The preference for N_eff > 3 is now at a 2σ level.
simultaneous-constraints-on-the-number-a.student: Evidence from particle physics and cosmology hints that there may be more than the three known types of neutrinos. Neutrinos are tiny, neutral particles that barely interact with matter. In cosmology, their mass and the number of species can affect the universe's evolution, but these effects are hard to separate because we don’t know all the parameters of the standard cosmological model perfectly. By combining the latest data from the cosmic microwave background (the afterglow of the Big Bang), the large-scale structure of the universe, and its expansion rate, researchers estimated the effective number of neutrino species (N_eff) as 3.58 with a small uncertainty, and the total neutrino mass (Σm_ν) as less than 0.60 electronvolts. These are the tightest constraints yet when both parameters are considered together, and the data slightly favor more than three neutrino species at a 2σ confidence level.
simultaneous-constraints-on-the-number-a.layman: Scientists have long known about three kinds of tiny, ghostly particles called neutrinos. Recent clues suggest there might be more. To check, researchers studied the early universe’s light, the way galaxies clump together, and how fast space is expanding. They found that the number of neutrino types is likely a bit more than three, and their total mass is very small. The results are the most precise so far, and they hint that extra neutrinos might exist, though the evidence is still not strong enough to be sure.

constraints-on-the-presence-of-a-3-5-kev.scientist: Context. Recent findings of line emission at 3.5 keV in both individual and stacked X-ray spectra of galaxy clusters have been speculated to have dark matter origin. Aims. If the origin is indeed dark matter, the emission line is expected to be detectable from the Milky Way dark matter halo. Methods. We perform a line search in public Chandra X-ray observations of the region near Sgr A*. We derive upper limits on the line emission flux for the 2.0 − 9.0 keV energy interval and discuss their potential physical interpretations including various scenarios of decaying and annihilating dark matter. Results. While we find no clear evidence for its presence, the upper flux limits are not inconsistent with the recent detections for conservative mass profiles of the Milky Way. Conclusions. The results depend mildly on the spectral modelling and strongly on the choice of dark matter profile.
constraints-on-the-presence-of-a-3-5-kev.student: A recent study reported an unexplained X-ray emission line at 3.5 keV in galaxy clusters, possibly linked to dark matter. This work tests whether the same signal appears in our own galaxy’s dark matter halo. Using public X-ray data from the Chandra telescope targeting the region near the Milky Way’s center (Sgr A*), the authors searched for the line across energies from 2.0 to 9.0 keV. No clear signal was detected, but the upper limits on its strength do not rule out the earlier findings if the Milky Way’s dark matter is distributed in a conservative (less dense) way. The results vary slightly with spectral models and strongly with assumptions about the dark matter’s spatial distribution.
constraints-on-the-presence-of-a-3-5-kev.layman: Scientists have spotted a faint X-ray glow in distant galaxy clusters that might come from dark matter, the invisible stuff thought to hold galaxies together. To check if the same glow exists in our own galaxy, they studied X-ray images of its center. They found no clear sign of the glow, but the absence doesn’t disprove the idea—it could still be there, just too weak to see with current data. The answer depends on how dark matter is spread through the Milky Way.

deep-reinforcement-learning-for-long-ter.scientist: We explore the use of deep reinforcement learning to provide strategies for long term scheduling of hydropower production. We consider a use-case where the aim is to optimise the yearly revenue given week-by-week inflows to the reservoir and electricity prices. The challenge is to decide between immediate water release at the spot price of electricity and storing the water for later power production at an unknown price, given constraints on the system. We successfully train a soft actor-critic algorithm on a simplified scenario with historical data from the Nordic power market. The presented model is not ready to substitute traditional optimisation tools but demonstrates the complementary potential of reinforcement learning in the data-rich field of hydropower scheduling.
deep-reinforcement-learning-for-long-ter.student: This study applies deep reinforcement learning—a machine learning approach where an agent learns optimal actions through trial and error—to long-term hydropower scheduling. The goal is to maximise yearly revenue by deciding whether to release water immediately to generate electricity at current prices or store it for future use, given uncertain future prices and reservoir constraints. Using historical data from the Nordic power market, the researchers trained a soft actor-critic algorithm, a method for continuous control tasks, on a simplified scenario. The model shows promise as a complementary tool to traditional optimisation methods but is not yet ready to replace them in real-world hydropower operations.
deep-reinforcement-learning-for-long-ter.layman: The researchers asked if a computer could learn to manage a dam’s water to make the most money over a year. They taught it to decide whether to use water now to generate electricity or save it for later, based on past prices and water levels. The computer did well in a simple test but isn’t ready to take over from current methods. It shows that this kind of learning could one day help with such decisions.

inferring-feature-importance-with-uncert.scientist: Estimating feature importance is a significant aspect of explaining data-based models. Besides explaining the model itself, an equally relevant question is which features are important in the underlying data generating process. We present a Shapley value based framework for inferring the importance of individual features, including uncertainty in the estimator. We build upon the recently published feature importance measure of SAGE (Shapley additive global importance) and introduce sub-SAGE which can be estimated without resampling for tree-based models. We argue that the uncertainties can be estimated from bootstrapping and demonstrate the approach for tree ensemble methods. The framework is exemplified on synthetic data as well as high-dimensional genomics data.
inferring-feature-importance-with-uncert.student: Explaining machine learning models often involves identifying which input features (variables) drive predictions. A related but distinct question is which features matter in the true data-generating process. We propose a framework using Shapley values—a concept from cooperative game theory that fairly distributes contributions among features—to estimate feature importance while accounting for uncertainty. Building on SAGE (a global Shapley-based importance measure), we introduce sub-SAGE, a computationally efficient variant for tree-based models that avoids resampling. Uncertainty is estimated via bootstrapping, and we demonstrate the method on synthetic data and high-dimensional genomics datasets, showing its practicality for real-world applications.
inferring-feature-importance-with-uncert.layman: Researchers wanted to know which pieces of information most influence a computer’s decisions and which truly matter in the real world. They created a method to measure this, using a fair way to split credit among the pieces. They also made it faster for certain types of models and added a way to show how sure they are of the results. They tested it on made-up data and real genetic data to show it works.

a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.scientist: Low complexity of a system model is essential for its use in real-time applications. However, sparse identification methods commonly have stringent requirements that exclude them from being applied in an industrial setting. In this paper, we introduce a flexible method for the sparse identification of dynamical systems described by ordinary differential equations. Our method relieves many of the requirements imposed by other methods that relate to the structure of the model and the data set, such as fixed sampling rates, full state measurements, and linearity of the model. The Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm is used to solve the identification problem. We show that the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm can be written in a form that enables parallel computing, which greatly diminishes the time required to solve the identification problem. An efficient backward elimination strategy is presented to construct a lean system model.
a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.student: Real-time applications need simple system models, but existing sparse identification methods often impose strict conditions—like fixed sampling rates, full state measurements, or linear models—that make them impractical for industry. This paper proposes a flexible approach to identify dynamical systems (systems that change over time, described by differential equations) without these constraints. The method uses the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, a numerical technique for solving optimization problems, which we adapt for parallel computing to speed up calculations. We also introduce an efficient backward elimination strategy to refine the model, ensuring it remains simple and practical for real-world use.
a-levenberg-marquardt-algorithm-for-spar.layman: Researchers wanted to create simple models of changing systems for real-time use, but existing methods had strict rules that made them hard to apply in industry. They developed a new, flexible way to build these models without those rules. They used a math-based problem-solving tool and made it work faster by splitting the work across multiple computers. They also added a step to trim the model down to its essential parts, making it easier to use in practice.

mutual-information-estimation-for-graph-.scientist: Measuring model performance is a key issue for deep learning practitioners. However, we often lack the ability to explain why a specific architecture attains superior predictive accuracy for a given data set. Often, validation accuracy is used as a performance heuristic quantifying how well a network generalizes to unseen data, but it does not capture anything about the information flow in the model. Mutual information can be used as a measure of the quality of internal representations in deep learning models, and the information plane may provide insights into whether the model exploits the available information in the data. The information plane has previously been explored for fully connected neural networks and convolutional architectures. We present an architecture-agnostic method for tracking a network’s internal representations during training, which are then used to create the mutual information plane. The method is exemplified for graph-based neural networks fitted on citation data. We compare how the inductive bias introduced in graph-based architectures changes the mutual information plane relative to a fully connected neural network.
mutual-information-estimation-for-graph-.student: Deep learning models often perform well, but it’s unclear why certain designs work better for specific datasets. Validation accuracy tells us how well a model generalizes to new data but doesn’t explain how information moves through the network. Mutual information, a measure of how much one variable tells us about another, can assess the quality of a model’s internal representations. The information plane visualizes this, showing how information is processed. Previous work has used this for standard neural networks, but we developed a method to track internal representations in any architecture, creating a mutual information plane. We tested this on graph-based neural networks (which process data structured as networks, like citations) and compared their information flow to fully connected networks, showing how their built-in assumptions (inductive bias) affect the plane.
mutual-information-estimation-for-graph-.layman: Researchers often don’t know why some AI models work better than others. A common test checks how well a model handles new data, but this doesn’t explain how the model uses information. We created a way to track how information moves inside any AI model during training. This helps us see if the model is making good use of the data. We tested it on models designed for network-like data, such as citation networks, and compared them to simpler models to see how their design choices change the way they process information.

pseudo-hamiltonian-neural-networks-with-.scientist: Hybrid machine learning based on Hamiltonian formulations has recently been successfully demonstrated for simple mechanical systems, both energy conserving and not energy conserving. We introduce a pseudo-Hamiltonian formulation that is a generalization of the Hamiltonian formulation via the port-Hamiltonian formulation, and show that pseudo-Hamiltonian neural network models can be used to learn external forces acting on a system. We argue that this property is particularly useful when the external forces are state dependent, in which case it is the pseudo-Hamiltonian structure that facilitates the separation of internal and external forces. Numerical results are provided for a forced and damped mass-spring system and a tank system of higher complexity, and a symmetric fourth-order integration scheme is introduced for improved training on sparse and noisy data.
pseudo-hamiltonian-neural-networks-with-.student: Researchers have extended Hamiltonian mechanics—a framework for modeling physical systems using energy—to create a new method called pseudo-Hamiltonian learning. Hamiltonian systems conserve energy, but real-world systems often lose energy (e.g., due to friction). The pseudo-Hamiltonian approach, derived from port-Hamiltonian theory, allows machine learning models to distinguish between internal system dynamics and external forces, even when those forces depend on the system’s state. The team tested this on a damped mass-spring system and a more complex tank system, showing the model can learn external forces effectively. They also introduced a numerical integration method to improve training with limited or noisy data.
pseudo-hamiltonian-neural-networks-with-.layman: Scientists often use math to predict how things like springs or tanks behave. But real systems lose energy, making predictions harder. The researchers created a new way to teach computers to separate the system’s own behavior from outside pushes or pulls. They tested this on a spring and a tank, and it worked well even with messy data. This could help computers better understand and predict how real-world systems move and change.

neural-operator-learning-for-long-time-i.scientist: Deep neural networks are an attractive alternative for simulating complex dynamical systems, as in comparison to traditional scientific computing methods, they offer reduced computational costs during inference and can be trained directly from observational data. Existing methods, however, cannot extrapolate accurately and are prone to error accumulation in long-time integration. Herein, we address this issue by combining neural operators with recurrent neural networks, learning the operator mapping, while offering a recurrent structure to capture temporal dependencies. The integrated framework is shown to stabilize the solution and reduce error accumulation for both interpolation and extrapolation of the Korteweg-de Vries equation.
neural-operator-learning-for-long-time-i.student: Deep neural networks can efficiently simulate complex systems, like fluid flows, by learning from data rather than solving equations step-by-step. However, they often struggle with long-term predictions, as errors build up over time. This study tackles that problem by merging two approaches: neural operators, which learn the underlying mathematical rules of a system, and recurrent neural networks, which track how the system changes over time. The combined method was tested on the Korteweg-de Vries equation, a model for wave motion. Results show it improves stability and reduces error buildup, both for predicting within known data ranges and beyond them.
neural-operator-learning-for-long-time-i.layman: Scientists often use computers to predict how things like waves or weather will change over time. A newer method, using AI, can do this faster but sometimes makes mistakes that grow worse the longer it runs. This research combines two AI techniques to fix that. They tested it on a math problem that describes waves. The new method made more accurate predictions, even for longer periods, without the usual errors piling up.

pseudo-hamiltonian-system-identification.scientist: Identifying the underlying dynamics of physical systems can be challenging when only provided with observational data. In this work, we consider systems that can be modelled as first-order ordinary differential equations. By assuming a certain pseudo-Hamiltonian formulation, we are able to learn the analytic terms of internal dynamics even if the model is trained on data where the system is affected by unknown damping and external disturbances. In cases where it is difficult to find analytic terms for the disturbances, a hybrid model that uses a neural network to learn these can still accurately identify the dynamics of the system as if under ideal conditions. This makes the models applicable in some situations where other system identification models fail. Furthermore, we propose to use a fourth-order symmetric integration scheme in the loss function and avoid actual integration in the training, and demonstrate on varied examples how this leads to increased performance on noisy data.
pseudo-hamiltonian-system-identification.student: Understanding the hidden rules governing physical systems from raw observations is difficult. Here, we focus on systems described by first-order differential equations, which model how quantities change over time. By assuming a pseudo-Hamiltonian structure—a framework that captures energy-like relationships—we can uncover the exact mathematical terms driving the system, even when the data includes unknown damping or external noise. If the disturbances are too complex to describe analytically, we combine this approach with a neural network to learn them, still recovering the true dynamics. We also introduce a fourth-order integration method in the training process, avoiding direct integration, which improves accuracy on noisy data. The method works in cases where traditional approaches fail.
pseudo-hamiltonian-system-identification.layman: Scientists often struggle to figure out the hidden rules that govern how things move or change over time, especially when their data is messy. This study shows a way to uncover those rules even when outside forces are interfering. The researchers used a mix of math and computer learning to separate the true behavior of a system from the noise. They also found a smarter way to process the data, making their method more reliable when the information is unclear. The approach works in situations where older methods do not.

don-lstm-multi-resolution-learning-with-.scientist: Deep operator networks (DeepONets, DONs) offer a distinct advantage over traditional neural networks in their ability to be trained on multi-resolution data. This property becomes especially relevant in real-world scenarios where high-resolution measurements are difficult to obtain, while low-resolution data is more readily available. Nevertheless, DeepONets alone often struggle to capture and maintain dependencies over long sequences compared to other state-of-the-art algorithms. We propose a novel architecture, named DON-LSTM, which extends the DeepONet with a long short-term memory network (LSTM). Combining these two architectures, we equip the network with explicit mechanisms to leverage multi-resolution data, as well as capture temporal dependencies in long sequences. We test our method on long-time-evolution modeling of multiple non-linear systems and show that the proposed multi-resolution DON-LSTM achieves significantly lower generalization error and requires fewer high-resolution samples compared to its vanilla counterparts.
don-lstm-multi-resolution-learning-with-.student: Deep operator networks (DeepONets) are a type of neural network that can learn from data at different resolutions, which is useful when high-resolution data is scarce. However, they often struggle to model long-term dependencies in sequences. We introduce DON-LSTM, a new architecture that combines DeepONets with long short-term memory networks (LSTMs), a type of neural network designed to handle sequential data. This hybrid model retains the ability to use multi-resolution data while improving its capacity to capture long-term patterns. We tested DON-LSTM on several non-linear systems and found it outperformed standard DeepONets, achieving lower errors and requiring fewer high-resolution samples.
don-lstm-multi-resolution-learning-with-.layman: Researchers created a new tool to predict how complex systems change over time. The tool combines two types of computer models: one that works well with limited data and another that remembers past information to make better predictions. They tested it on different systems and found it made more accurate predictions than older tools, even when given less detailed data.

balancing-the-norwegian-regulated-power-.scientist: The balancing market for power is designed to account for the difference between predicted supply/demand of electricity and the realised supply/demand. However, increased electrification of society changes the consumption patterns, and increased production from renewable sources leads to larger un-predicted fluctuations in production, both effects potentially leading to increased balancing. We analyse public market data for the balancing market (manual Frequency Restoration Reserve) for Norway from 2016 to 2022 to investigate and document these effects. The data is newer than for similar analyses and the eight years of data is more than double the time span previously covered. The main findings are: a) The balancing volumes are dominated by hours of zero regulation but for non-zero hours, the balancing volumes are increasing during the eight-year period. b) The balancing prices are primarily correlated with day-ahead prices and secondary with balancing volumes. The latter correlation is found to be increasingly non-linear with time. c) The balancing volumes and the price difference between balancing price and day-ahead price are strongly correlated with the previous hour. d) The increasing share of wind power has not impacted the frequency of balancing, which has remained stable during the 8 years studied. However, the volumes and share of balancing power compared to overall production have increased, suggesting that the hours which are inherently difficult to predict remain the same. e) Market data alone cannot predict balancing volumes. If attempting, the auto-correlation becomes the main source of information.
balancing-the-norwegian-regulated-power-.student: The power balancing market adjusts for differences between predicted and actual electricity supply and demand. With more electrification and renewable energy, consumption and production patterns become harder to predict, potentially increasing the need for balancing. This study analyses public data from Norway’s manual Frequency Restoration Reserve (a balancing market mechanism) from 2016 to 2022—newer and more extensive than prior work. Key findings: (a) Most hours require no balancing, but when needed, volumes have risen over time. (b) Balancing prices correlate mainly with day-ahead prices (prices set the day before delivery) and secondarily with balancing volumes, with the latter link growing more non-linear. (c) Balancing volumes and price differences between balancing and day-ahead prices are strongly tied to the previous hour’s data. (d) Wind power’s share has grown, but balancing frequency stayed stable; however, balancing volumes and their share of total production have increased. (e) Market data alone cannot predict balancing volumes, with past trends (auto-correlation) being the only useful signal.
balancing-the-norwegian-regulated-power-.layman: Electricity grids must constantly balance supply and demand. As more people use electricity and more power comes from wind and sun, predicting this balance gets harder. Researchers studied eight years of Norwegian data to see how often and how much the grid needed adjustments. They found that while most hours needed no changes, the amount of adjustment grew over time when it was needed. Prices for these adjustments were mostly tied to the next day’s expected prices, and the need for adjustments often depended on the previous hour. Wind power did not make adjustments more frequent, but the total amount of adjustment did increase. Past data alone could not reliably predict future needs.

road-graph-generator-mapping-roads-at-co.scientist: We propose a new method for inferring roads from GPS trajectories to map construction sites. This task presents a unique challenge due to the erratic and nonstandard movement patterns of construction machinery, which significantly diverge from typical vehicular traffic on established roads. Our proposed method first identifies intersections in the road network that serve as critical decision points, and then connects them with edges to produce a graph, which can subsequently be used for planning and task allocation. The method includes several physically meaningful parameters that can be tuned to adapt it to different scenarios. We demonstrate the approach by mapping roads at a real-life construction site in Norway. The method is validated on four increasingly complex segments of the map. In our tests, the method achieved perfect precision and recall in detecting intersections and inferring roads in data with no or low noise, while its performance was reduced in areas with significant noise and consistently missing GPS updates.
road-graph-generator-mapping-roads-at-co.student: This study addresses the challenge of mapping roads at construction sites using GPS data from machinery, which moves unpredictably unlike regular vehicles. The proposed method detects key intersections—points where paths split or merge—and connects them to form a network graph, useful for planning and task allocation. The approach uses adjustable parameters to fit different scenarios. Tested on a Norwegian construction site, it perfectly identified intersections and roads in clean GPS data but struggled with noisy or incomplete data. The work shows how GPS trajectories can be turned into usable road maps under varying conditions.
road-graph-generator-mapping-roads-at-co.layman: Researchers wanted to map the temporary roads at a construction site using GPS signals from the machines working there. They created a method that finds where paths cross or split and then draws lines between these points to make a map. It worked perfectly when the GPS data was clear, but had trouble when the signals were messy or missing. This shows how GPS can help track roads even in chaotic places like construction sites.

recency-weighted-temporally-segmented-en.scientist: Time-series modeling in process industries faces the challenge of dealing with complex, multifaceted, and evolving data characteristics. Conventional single model approaches often struggle to capture the interplay of diverse dynamics, resulting in suboptimal forecasts. Addressing this, we introduce the Recency-Weighted Temporally-Segmented (ReWTS, pronounced ‘roots’) ensemble model, a novel chunk-based approach for multi-step forecasting. The key characteristics of the ReWTS model are twofold: 1) It facilitates specialization of models into different dynamics by segmenting the training data into ‘chunks’ of data and training one model per chunk. 2) During inference, an optimization procedure assesses each model on the recent past and selects the active models, such that the appropriate mixture of previously learned dynamics can be recalled to forecast the future. This method not only captures the nuances of each period, but also adapts more effectively to changes over time compared to conventional ‘global’ models trained on all data in one go. We present a comparative analysis, utilizing two years of data from a wastewater treatment plant and a drinking water treatment plant in Norway, demonstrating the ReWTS ensemble’s superiority. It consistently outperforms the global model in terms of mean squared forecasting error across various model architectures by 10-70% on both datasets, notably exhibiting greater resilience to outliers. This approach shows promise in developing automatic, adaptable forecasting models for decision-making and control systems in process industries and other complex systems.
recency-weighted-temporally-segmented-en.student: Forecasting in process industries, like water treatment, is hard because the data changes over time and has many interacting parts. Traditional models, trained on all data at once, often miss these shifting patterns. We propose ReWTS, an ensemble model that splits the data into smaller segments or 'chunks' and trains a separate model on each. During prediction, it picks the best models based on recent data, blending their outputs to forecast future trends. Tested on two years of data from Norwegian water plants, ReWTS outperformed single global models by 10-70% in accuracy, handling outliers better. This suggests it could improve automated forecasting for complex, evolving systems.
recency-weighted-temporally-segmented-en.layman: Predicting how systems like water treatment plants will behave is tricky because conditions keep changing. The researchers created a new method that breaks past data into smaller pieces and uses many small models instead of one big one. When making predictions, it checks which small models work best with recent data and combines their results. Tested on real plant data, this approach made better predictions than older methods, especially when unusual events occurred. It could help industries make more reliable forecasts.

testing-topological-data-analysis-for-co.scientist: We present an investigation of how topological data analysis (TDA) can be applied to condition-based monitoring (CBM) of wind turbines for energy generation. TDA is a branch of data analysis focusing on extracting meaningful information from complex datasets by analyzing their structure in state space and computing their underlying topological features. By representing data in a high-dimensional state space, TDA enables the identification of patterns, anomalies, and trends in the data that may not be apparent through traditional signal processing methods. For this study, wind turbine data was acquired from a wind park in Norway via standard vibration sensors at different locations of the turbine’s gearbox. Both the vibration acceleration data and its frequency spectra were recorded at infrequent intervals for a few seconds at high frequency and failure events were labelled as either gear-tooth or ball-bearing failures. The data processing and analysis are based on a pipeline where the time series data is first split into intervals and then transformed into multi-dimensional point clouds via a time-delay embedding. The shape of the point cloud is analyzed with topological methods such as persistent homology to generate topology-based key health indicators based on Betti numbers, information entropy and signal persistence. Such indicators are tested for CBM and diagnosis (fault detection) to identify faults in wind turbines and classify them accordingly. Topological indicators are shown to be an interesting alternative for failure identification and diagnosis of operational failures in wind turbines.
testing-topological-data-analysis-for-co.student: This study explores how topological data analysis (TDA), a method for extracting structural patterns from complex datasets, can improve condition-based monitoring (CBM) of wind turbines. TDA examines the shape of data in high-dimensional space to detect anomalies or trends that traditional signal processing might miss. Researchers collected vibration data from a Norwegian wind park, capturing short, high-frequency recordings from gearbox sensors, with failures labeled as gear-tooth or ball-bearing issues. The data was split into intervals, transformed into multi-dimensional point clouds using time-delay embedding, and analyzed with topological tools like persistent homology. This produced health indicators (e.g., Betti numbers, entropy) to detect and classify faults. The results suggest topological indicators are a promising alternative for identifying operational failures in wind turbines.
testing-topological-data-analysis-for-co.layman: Researchers wanted to see if a new way of analyzing data could help spot problems in wind turbines before they get worse. They collected vibration readings from a wind farm in Norway, focusing on parts like the gearbox. Using math to study the shape of the data, they created warning signs that could flag issues like worn gears or bearings. The method worked well at picking up these problems, offering a fresh way to keep turbines running smoothly.

accounting-for-optimal-control-in-the-si.scientist: Decarbonization of isolated or off-grid energy systems through phase-in of large shares of intermittent solar or wind generation requires co-installation of energy storage or continued use of existing fossil dispatchable power sources to balance supply and demand. The effective CO2 emission reduction depends on the relative capacity of the energy storage and renewable sources, the stochasticity of the renewable generation, and the optimal control or dispatch of the isolated energy system. While the operations of the energy storage and dispatchable sources may impact the optimal sizing of the system, it is challenging to account for the effect of finite horizon, optimal control at the stage of system sizing. Here, we present a flexible and computationally efficient sizing framework for energy storage and renewable capacity in isolated energy systems, accounting for uncertainty in the renewable generation and the optimal feedback control. To this end, we implement an imitation learning approach to stochastic neural model predictive control (MPC) which allows us to relate the battery storage and wind peak capacities to the emissions reduction and investment costs while accounting for finite horizon, optimal control. Through this approach, decision makers can evaluate the effective emission reduction and costs of different storage and wind capacities at any price point while accounting for uncertainty in the renewable generation with limited foresight. We evaluate the proposed sizing framework on a case study of an offshore energy system with a gas turbine, a wind farm and a battery energy storage system (BESS). In this case, we find a nonlinear, nontrivial relationship between the investment costs and reduction in gas usage relative to the wind and BESS capacities, emphasizing the complexity and importance of accounting for optimal control in the design of isolated energy systems.
accounting-for-optimal-control-in-the-si.student: For isolated energy systems like remote islands, replacing fossil fuels with wind or solar power requires storage (e.g., batteries) to balance supply and demand, since renewables are intermittent. The actual CO₂ reduction depends on how much storage and renewable capacity is installed, the unpredictability of renewable output, and how the system is optimally controlled. Designing such systems is tricky because the way storage and fossil generators are operated affects the ideal size of the system, and this must account for limited future knowledge. We developed a flexible, efficient method to size storage and renewable capacity, using machine learning to mimic optimal control under uncertainty. This lets decision-makers assess emissions cuts and costs for different storage and wind sizes, even with imperfect forecasts. In a case study with a gas turbine, wind farm, and battery, we found a complex, nonlinear link between investment costs and reduced gas use, showing why optimal control must be considered in system design.
accounting-for-optimal-control-in-the-si.layman: How can remote places like islands switch from fossil fuels to wind or solar power without running out of electricity? Researchers built a tool to help plan the right mix of wind turbines, batteries, and backup generators. They tested it on an island with a gas generator, a wind farm, and a battery. The tool shows how much pollution and cost can be cut for different setups, even when wind power is unpredictable. The results reveal that the best choices aren’t always obvious, as costs and savings don’t change in a simple way when you add more wind or batteries.

on-a-time-frequency-blurring-operator-wi.scientist: Inspired by the success of recent data augmentation methods for signals which act on time-frequency representations, we introduce an operator which convolves the short-time Fourier transform of a signal with a specified kernel. Analytical properties including boundedness, compactness and positivity are investigated from the perspective of time-frequency analysis. A convolutional neural network and a vision transformer are trained to classify audio signals using spectrograms with different augmentation setups, including the above mentioned time-frequency blurring operator, with results indicating that the operator can significantly improve test performance, especially in the data-starved regime.
on-a-time-frequency-blurring-operator-wi.student: Recent work has shown that modifying time-frequency representations (like spectrograms, which show how a signal’s frequency content changes over time) can improve machine learning models for audio tasks. Here, we propose a new operator that applies a convolution—a mathematical operation that blends a signal with a kernel—to the short-time Fourier transform (a way to represent signals in time and frequency). We analyze its mathematical properties, such as boundedness and compactness, to understand its behavior. Then, we train two deep learning models (a convolutional neural network and a vision transformer) on audio classification using spectrograms, some of which are augmented with our operator. The results suggest this method can notably boost performance, particularly when training data is limited.
on-a-time-frequency-blurring-operator-wi.layman: Researchers wanted to see if blurring parts of sound data in a specific way could help computers recognize sounds better. They created a new method to do this and tested it on two types of computer programs. The results showed that this blurring can help the programs perform better, especially when there isn’t much training data available.

a-column-generation-heuristic-for-the-dy.scientist: Public bicycle sharing systems are becoming an essential part of the future urban mobility system. Real-time monitoring of the system state through sensors on bicycles and/or stations gives possibilities for advanced coordination of the system. In this paper, we consider the dynamic bicycle rebalancing problem, where bicycles are re-positioned by service vehicles to prevent stations from becoming completely full or empty, and so satisfying the demand for bicycles or locks. We solve the problem in a rolling horizon fashion with dynamic deterministic bicycle rebalancing subproblems (DDBRS) at the decision epochs. To solve the DDBRS within a few seconds in real-time, we propose a novel column generation heuristic (CGH). The CGH is tested within a simulation framework based on real data from the bicycle sharing system in Oslo. We show that the CGH is able to solve large real-life instances with computational times that are suitable for actual operation and that it provides significantly improved solutions compared with current planning practice. We also perform a number of tests to analyze the effect of changing the number of bicycles and locks in the system, as well as adding extra service vehicles. The case company is now making preparations to implement an optimization-based decision support system based on the CGH proposed in this paper.
a-column-generation-heuristic-for-the-dy.student: Public bike-sharing systems rely on stations where users pick up and return bicycles. A common issue is imbalance: some stations run out of bikes while others overflow, leaving users without options. This study tackles the dynamic bicycle rebalancing problem, where service vehicles redistribute bikes to keep stations functional. The authors use a rolling horizon approach, solving smaller, deterministic subproblems (DDBRS) at each decision point. To speed up real-time calculations, they develop a column generation heuristic (CGH), a method that efficiently breaks down complex problems. Tested on real data from Oslo’s bike-sharing system, the CGH solves large-scale instances quickly and outperforms current planning methods. Additional tests explore how changing bike/lock numbers or adding service vehicles affects performance. The case company is now preparing to adopt this optimization-based system.
a-column-generation-heuristic-for-the-dy.layman: Bike-sharing programs often have too many bikes at some stations and none at others. This study looks at how to move bikes around using service trucks to keep stations stocked. The researchers created a fast, smart method to plan these moves in real time. They tested it using data from Oslo’s bike system and found it works better than current methods. They also checked how adding more bikes, locks, or trucks changes the results. The company running the system is now planning to use this new approach.

vehicle-routing-with-endogenous-learning.scientist: When a particular service is performed many times, the duration of the service might reduce due to the effect of learning from similar tasks that have been performed before. In this article, we present an approach to account for such learning effects that arise in the context of vehicle routing operations. Our approach enables the consideration of endogenous learning, where the service times are dependent on the experience that is to be gained in the same routing horizon. We apply our approach to the problem of planning an offshore plug and abandonment campaign, where different vessels are being used to perform plugging operations on offshore oil and gas wells. We extend existing instances for this problem with observed learning data and investigate the effects of learning and cooperation. Results show that the inclusion of an endogenous learning effect leads to different and significantly better solutions compared to those that are found when the learning effect is neglected.
vehicle-routing-with-endogenous-learning.student: In operations like vehicle routing, repeated tasks can become faster as workers learn from experience. This study introduces a method to model this learning effect, where service times improve as more tasks are completed within the same planning period. The approach is applied to offshore plug and abandonment campaigns, where vessels plug old oil and gas wells. The researchers added real-world learning data to existing problem instances and examined how learning and teamwork between vessels affect outcomes. The findings show that accounting for this learning effect produces noticeably better and different solutions than ignoring it.
vehicle-routing-with-endogenous-learning.layman: When people do the same task over and over, they often get faster at it. This study looks at how that learning can be included in planning work schedules, like for ships plugging old oil wells. The researchers tested their idea using real data and found that planning with this learning in mind leads to better and different results than planning without it.

a-look-ahead-policy-for-dynamic-bike-reb.scientist: Bike-sharing systems (BSSs) offer a flexible and eco-friendly transportation option in urban areas, but often encounter challenges due to imbalances in spatial and temporal demand. These imbalances can make it difficult for users to rent or return bikes. To restore efficiency within the system, rebalancing operations are crucial. Most bike rebalancing models assume that demand is dynamic and independent at station level, neglecting the interactions between neighborhoods. This phenomenon, known as roaming or spillover effects, occurs when users find a station unavailable and redirect to nearby alternatives. Ignoring these interactions distorts the representation of demand and results in suboptimal rebalancing strategies. This paper presents the Dynamic Bike Rebalancing Problem with Neighborhood Interactions (DBRP-NI), which explicitly models these spillover effects. To address the DBRP-NI, we have developed a heuristic framework based on a rolling horizon approach that incorporates look-ahead decision-making. We evaluated our solution method within a discrete-event simulation framework using real-world data from BSSs in Norway and the United States. The computational results demonstrate that our proposed method consistently outperforms benchmark policies, especially in large and imbalanced systems. It reduces long-distance roaming and enhances vehicle utilization while maintaining computational efficiency. Additional findings highlight the operational benefits of integrating neighborhood interactions and look-ahead strategies into rebalancing decisions for modern BSSs.
a-look-ahead-policy-for-dynamic-bike-reb.student: Bike-sharing systems help people move around cities but often face uneven demand across locations and times, making it hard to find or return bikes. Most rebalancing models treat each station’s demand as independent, ignoring how users redirect to nearby stations when one is full or empty—a phenomenon called spillover. This paper introduces the Dynamic Bike Rebalancing Problem with Neighborhood Interactions (DBRP-NI), which accounts for these spillover effects. The authors propose a heuristic method using a rolling horizon approach, which makes decisions while anticipating future demand. Tested with real data from Norway and the U.S., their method outperforms existing strategies, especially in large, imbalanced systems, by reducing long-distance user detours and improving bike usage without sacrificing computational speed.
a-look-ahead-policy-for-dynamic-bike-reb.layman: Bike-sharing programs let people rent and return bikes at stations around a city, but sometimes stations run out of bikes or space. When this happens, users go to the next closest station, which can cause problems elsewhere. Most solutions ignore this chain reaction. The researchers created a new way to manage bike distribution that accounts for these knock-on effects. They tested it with real data and found it works better than older methods, especially in busy cities, by cutting down on long walks to find a bike and making better use of the available bikes.

stram-a-strategic-network-design-model-f.scientist: National freight transport models are valuable tools for assessing the impact of various policies and investments on achieving decarbonization targets under different future scenarios. However, these models struggle to address several critical elements necessary for strategic planning, such as the development and adoption of new fuel technologies over time, inertia in transport fleets, and uncertainty surrounding future transport costs. In this paper, we develop a strategic network design model, named STraM, that explicitly incorporates these key factors. STraM, being a two-stage stochastic program, effectively handles long-term uncertainty by considering different future scenarios in its decision-making process. It provides a network design plan that includes infrastructure investments and fuel technology decisions, aiming to achieve cost-effective decarbonization of the freight transport system. The model output can be used as input for higher-resolution national freight transport models to yield results with greater operational detail. We demonstrate the application of STraM through a case study of Norway, offering valuable insights into the strategic planning of decarbonizing freight transport.
stram-a-strategic-network-design-model-f.student: Freight transport models help evaluate how policies and investments can meet decarbonization goals under different future conditions. However, existing models often overlook key factors like the gradual adoption of new fuels, the slow turnover of vehicle fleets, and uncertainty in future transport costs. This study introduces STraM, a strategic network design model that addresses these gaps. STraM is a two-stage stochastic program, meaning it accounts for long-term uncertainty by considering multiple future scenarios in its planning. It produces a network design that includes infrastructure investments and fuel technology choices to cost-effectively decarbonize freight transport. The model’s output can also feed into more detailed national freight models for finer operational insights. A case study of Norway demonstrates its practical application.
stram-a-strategic-network-design-model-f.layman: Planning how to reduce pollution from shipping goods is hard because the future is uncertain. Current tools miss important details, like how new fuels take time to catch on or how old trucks stay on the road for years. This research created a new planning tool that includes these missing pieces. It helps decide where to build new roads or fuel stations and which cleaner fuels to use, while keeping costs down. The tool was tested using Norway as an example, showing how it can guide long-term decisions for cleaner shipping.

temporal-granularity-and-charging-strate.scientist: This study addresses the Time-Dependent Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Partial Recharging (TDEVRP-PR), an extension of the classical EVRP that accounts for segmented time-dependent travel times and partial battery replenishment. We further extend this problem by incorporating vehicle heterogeneity and nonlinear, load-dependent energy consumption. Traditional formulations often assume static traffic and full recharging, limiting their methodological and practical relevance in contexts with congestion patterns and constrained charging infrastructure. We develop a mixed-integer linear programming formulation for the TDEVRP-PR, incorporating a discretized time-dependent speed function derived from high-resolution floating car data and a nonlinear energy consumption model in which recharging time is modeled as a function of the state of charge. To solve large-scale instances, we employ a customized Genetic Algorithm with random-key encoding and Taguchi-based parameter calibration. Computational experiments on 15 synthetic and empirical instances show that solutions derived from low-resolution speed profiles, while sometimes achieving the lowest nominal costs, often perform poorly under realistic traffic conditions. This effect is particularly pronounced in large-scale instances, where infeasibility rates can be very high. Accuracy and operational feasibility improve substantially as temporal resolution increases, with diminishing gains beyond a certain point. Notably, the required temporal resolution should scale with instance size, as larger instances benefit from finer discretization to better capture congestion patterns and fully leverage the advantages of partial recharging. In addition, partial recharging strategies increase the frequency of charging events without systematically extending route durations per vehicle, indicating that they provide operational flexibility without compromising efficiency, even in larger and more complex instances. Sensitivity analyses further confirm that the advantages of partial recharging and time-dependent routing persist across increases in battery capacity. Our framework provides a scalable, data-driven approach to energy-aware electric vehicle routing in urban environments, highlighting the importance of modeling time-dependency with sufficient granularity to achieve realistic and operationally viable routing plans.
temporal-granularity-and-charging-strate.student: This study tackles the Time-Dependent Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Partial Recharging (TDEVRP-PR), which plans routes for electric vehicles considering time-varying traffic and partial battery top-ups. Unlike simpler models, it accounts for different vehicle types and energy use that changes with load. The researchers built a mathematical model using real traffic data to capture speed changes over time and a nonlinear energy model where recharging time depends on battery level. To handle large problems, they used a Genetic Algorithm, a method inspired by natural selection, with fine-tuned parameters. Tests on 15 cases showed that low-resolution traffic data often leads to unrealistic or infeasible routes, especially for large problems. Higher temporal resolution improves accuracy, though gains level off. Partial recharging adds flexibility without increasing route times, and its benefits hold even with larger batteries. The work suggests that detailed time modeling is key for practical electric vehicle routing.
temporal-granularity-and-charging-strate.layman: Researchers studied how to plan the best routes for electric delivery vehicles in cities where traffic changes throughout the day. They built a system that uses real traffic data and allows vehicles to charge their batteries partially, not just fully. They found that using rough traffic estimates often leads to bad or impossible routes, especially for big jobs. More detailed traffic data makes the plans more reliable. Charging a little at a time also helps without making trips longer. The results show that careful planning with good data can make electric vehicle deliveries work better in real-world conditions.

addressing-long-term-uncertainty-in-ener.scientist: Assumptions play a central role in developing long-term energy system models, yet many are highly uncertain and may critically affect results. Most studies rely on deterministic approaches, while stochastic programming remains underutilized due to its computational complexity. Deterministic models fail to account for uncertainty, whereas stochastic programming provides a more robust framework by optimizing decisions across multiple probabilistic future scenarios. However, large-scale implementation is often computationally intractable, highlighting the need for effective and scalable scenario generation and reduction methods. In this study, we introduce a cost-driven scenario reduction approach with a novel sparse cost-opportunity matrix, which improves computational performance by avoiding redundant calculations while preserving decision-relevant information. To our knowledge, this is the first application of a cost-driven reduction technique in long-term energy system optimization models. The approach is tested on the Norwegian energy system using a refined TIMES model. Results show that our method reduces computation time by up to 70%, while delivering first-stage investment decisions nearly identical to the full stochastic problem, and it can be further accelerated through parallelization. In the Norwegian case study, the methodology highlights robust wait-and-see strategies for electricity generation, where delaying investments increases resilience to uncertain developments. This work demonstrates that cost-driven reduction can make stochastic energy system modeling both tractable and practically relevant, providing a scalable tool for planners and researchers under long-term uncertainty.
addressing-long-term-uncertainty-in-ener.student: Long-term energy system models rely on assumptions that are often uncertain, yet most use deterministic methods—single, fixed projections—ignoring variability. Stochastic programming, which optimizes decisions across many possible future scenarios, is more robust but computationally expensive. This study proposes a cost-driven scenario reduction method using a sparse cost-opportunity matrix to cut redundant calculations while keeping key decision-making information. Applied to Norway’s energy system via a TIMES model, the approach reduced computation time by up to 70% and produced investment decisions nearly identical to the full stochastic model. It also revealed that delaying electricity generation investments can improve resilience under uncertainty. The work shows that cost-driven reduction can make stochastic modeling feasible for large-scale, long-term energy planning.
addressing-long-term-uncertainty-in-ener.layman: Energy planners often make decisions based on fixed predictions, but the future is uncertain. A better method considers many possible futures, but this is usually too slow for large systems. The researchers created a way to simplify these futures without losing important details. Tested on Norway’s energy system, their method worked much faster and gave similar results to the full approach. It also suggested that waiting to invest in power plants can be a safer strategy. This could help planners make better long-term decisions under uncertainty.

scheduling-and-routing-of-automated-guid.scientist: Automation in container terminals has become increasingly critical in response to the surging global trade volumes and the demand for enhanced operational efficiency. This work focuses on the applications of AGVs in container terminals, as they represent a promising transport technology with significant economic, technical, and ecological advantages. This paper studies the problem of conflict-free AGV scheduling and routing (CF-ASR) in container terminals. It finds applications in environments where a homogeneous fleet of AGVs is employed to fulfill container pickup and delivery requests between specified pairs of nodes within given time windows. The primary challenge is to ensure that the AGVs operate without interference, which is difficult to anticipate without scheduling and controlling detailed movements of vehicles. The main contributions of this paper are: (1) a time-space network (TSN) model with conflict-free routing constraints and valid inequalities, (2) a novel matheuristic adapting the Restrict-and-Fix heuristic to the AGV scheduling and routing problem, and (3) a computational study based on real case port operations.
scheduling-and-routing-of-automated-guid.student: Container terminals handle vast numbers of shipping containers, and automation—like using Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs)—can improve efficiency. This study tackles the problem of scheduling and routing AGVs without conflicts, ensuring they don’t collide or block each other while moving containers between locations within set time windows. The researchers developed a time-space network model to represent AGV movements and constraints, added mathematical rules to prevent conflicts, and created a new optimization method (a matheuristic) that combines mathematical programming with heuristic strategies. They tested their approach using real-world port data, showing how it can manage AGV fleets effectively in complex, dynamic environments.
scheduling-and-routing-of-automated-guid.layman: Shipping ports move thousands of containers daily, and robots called AGVs help transport them. The challenge is to plan their routes so they don’t crash or get in each other’s way. The researchers designed a system to map out safe paths and times for these robots, using math to avoid conflicts. They also created a new method to solve this problem efficiently and tested it with real port data. The work helps ports use robots more smoothly and safely.

fomosim-an-open-source-simulator-for-rig.scientist: Existing simulation models for micromobility systems often face significant limitations: they are typically custom-built for specific contexts, lack generalizability, are not open-source, and undergo limited testing, which again question their reliability and applicability in broader settings. To address these challenges, this paper presents FOMOsim, an open-source simulator developed to analyze micromobility systems. The simulator’s modular design allows for better scalability and usability, facilitating detailed and realistic simulations of shared transport operations. New benchmark instances, utilizing data from bike-sharing systems (BSSs) in major American and Norwegian cities, are created and embedded within the simulator. Additionally, we introduce a new greedy heuristic for the dynamic bike rebalancing problem, integrated within FOMOsim. Rigorous testing demonstrates that the proposed heuristic, when combined with FOMOsim, outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly improving BSS performance by reducing bike shortages and surpluses.
