We tested it on two different computer programs and it worked, showing the method is practical and easy to use.

model-fusion-with-physics-guided-machine.scientist: The unprecedented amount of data generated from experiments, field observations, and large-scale numerical simulations at a wide range of spatiotemporal scales has enabled the rapid advancement of data-driven and especially deep learning models in the field of fluid mechanics. Although these methods are proven successful for many applications, there is a grand challenge of improving their generalizability. This is particularly essential when data-driven models are employed within outer-loop applications like optimization. In this work, we put forth a physics-guided machine learning (PGML) framework that leverages the interpretable physics-based model with a deep learning model. Leveraging a concatenated neural network design from multi-modal data sources, the PGML framework is capable of enhancing the generalizability of data-driven models and effectively protects against or inform about the inaccurate predictions resulting from extrapolation. We apply the PGML framework as a novel model fusion approach combining the physics-based Galerkin projection model and long- to short-term memory (LSTM) network for parametric model order reduction of fluid flows. We demonstrate the improved generalizability of the PGML framework against a purely data-driven approach through the injection of physics features into intermediate LSTM layers. Our quantitative analysis shows that the overall model uncertainty can be reduced through the PGML approach, especially for test data coming from a distribution different than the training data. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach can be used as an inverse diagnostic tool providing a confidence score associated with models and observations. The proposed framework also allows for multi-fidelity computing by making use of low-fidelity models in the online deployment of quantified data-driven models.
model-fusion-with-physics-guided-machine.student: Fluid mechanics increasingly relies on deep learning to analyze vast datasets from experiments and simulations. However, these models often struggle with generalizability—performing poorly when applied to new, unseen conditions, especially in tasks like optimization. This study introduces a physics-guided machine learning (PGML) framework that combines interpretable physics-based models (like the Galerkin projection) with deep learning (e.g., LSTM networks) to improve robustness. By integrating physics-based features into the neural network, the framework enhances accuracy and reduces uncertainty, particularly for data outside the training distribution. It also provides a confidence score for predictions and supports multi-fidelity computing, using simpler models to refine complex ones. The approach is tested on fluid flow simulations, showing better performance than purely data-driven methods.
model-fusion-with-physics-guided-machine.layman: Scientists use computers to study how fluids move, but these programs sometimes give wrong answers when faced with new situations. This research combines traditional physics rules with modern AI to make the predictions more reliable. The new method was tested on fluid movement problems and worked better than AI alone, especially when dealing with unfamiliar data. It also helps estimate how trustworthy the results are and can use simpler models to improve more complex ones.

physics-guided-machine-learning-using-si.scientist: Recent applications of machine learning, in particular deep learning, motivate the need to address the generalizability of the statistical inference approaches in physical sciences. In this Letter, we introduce a modular physics guided machine learning framework to improve the accuracy of such data-driven predictive engines. The chief idea in our approach is to augment the knowledge of the simplified theories with the underlying learning process. To emphasize their physical importance, our architecture consists of adding certain features at intermediate layers rather than in the input layer. To demonstrate our approach, we select a canonical airfoil aerodynamic problem with the enhancement of the potential flow theory. We include the features obtained by a panel method that can be computed efficiently for an unseen configuration in our training procedure. By addressing the generalizability concerns, our results suggest that the proposed feature enhancement approach can be effectively used in many scientific machine learning applications, especially for the systems where we can use a theoretical, empirical, or simplified model to guide the learning module.
physics-guided-machine-learning-using-si.student: Machine learning, especially deep learning, is increasingly used in physical sciences, but its predictions often struggle to generalize beyond the training data. This study proposes a modular framework that integrates physics-based knowledge into machine learning models to improve their accuracy. The key idea is to embed simplified physical theories, like potential flow theory for aerodynamics, into intermediate layers of the neural network rather than just the input. For example, in predicting airflow over an airfoil, the researchers added features derived from a panel method—a computational tool for fluid flow—during training. The results show that this approach addresses generalizability issues and could be applied to other scientific problems where theoretical or simplified models can guide the learning process.
physics-guided-machine-learning-using-si.layman: Scientists often use computer programs to predict how things like airplanes behave, but these programs can struggle when faced with new situations. This research combines basic physics knowledge with advanced computer learning to make better predictions. For instance, they used simple airflow rules to help a computer model predict how air moves around a wing. The results suggest this method can improve predictions in many areas of science where basic rules are already known.

digital-twin-values-challenges-and-enabl.scientist: Digital twin can be defined as a virtual representation of a physical asset enabled through data and simulators for real-time prediction, optimization, monitoring, controlling, and improved decision making. Recent advances in computational pipelines, multiphysics solvers, artificial intelligence, big data cybernetics, data processing and management tools bring the promise of digital twins and their impact on society closer to reality. Digital twinning is now an important and emerging trend in many applications. Also referred to as a computational megamodel, device shadow, mirrored system, avatar or a synchronized virtual prototype, there can be no doubt that a digital twin plays a transformative role not only in how we design and operate cyber-physical intelligent systems, but also in how we advance the modularity of multi-disciplinary systems to tackle fundamental barriers not addressed by the current, evolutionary modeling practices. In this work, we review the recent status of methodologies and techniques related to the construction of digital twins mostly from a modeling perspective. Our aim is to provide a detailed coverage of the current challenges and enabling technologies along with recommendations and reflections for various stakeholders.
digital-twin-values-challenges-and-enabl.student: A digital twin is a virtual copy of a physical object or system, built using data and simulations to predict, optimize, and monitor its real-world counterpart in real time. Recent progress in computing, physics-based modeling, AI, and data management has made digital twins more practical across many fields. Sometimes called computational megamodels or synchronized virtual prototypes, they are reshaping how we design and operate complex systems, like smart infrastructure or advanced manufacturing. This paper reviews current methods for building digital twins, focusing on modeling techniques. It outlines key challenges, enabling technologies, and offers recommendations for researchers, engineers, and policymakers to guide future development.
digital-twin-values-challenges-and-enabl.layman: Researchers are studying digital twins, which are virtual copies of real-world objects or systems, like a factory or a bridge. These copies use data and computer models to predict and improve how the real thing works. The study looks at how these digital twins are made today, what problems still exist, and what tools can help. It also gives advice to people who might use or build them in the future.

hybrid-analysis-and-modeling-eclecticism.scientist: Most modeling approaches lie in either of the two categories: physics-based or data-driven. Recently, a third approach which is a combination of these deterministic and statistical models is emerging for scientific applications. To leverage these developments, our aim in this perspective paper is centered around exploring numerous principle concepts to address the challenges of (i) trustworthiness and generalizability in developing data-driven models to shed light on understanding the fundamental trade-offs in their accuracy and efficiency and (ii) seamless integration of interface learning and multifidelity coupling approaches that transfer and represent information between different entities, particularly when different scales are governed by different physics, each operating on a different level of abstraction. Addressing these challenges could enable the revolution of digital twin technologies for scientific and engineering applications.
hybrid-analysis-and-modeling-eclecticism.student: Researchers often use either physics-based models, which rely on known physical laws, or data-driven models, which learn patterns from data. A newer approach combines both. This paper explores key ideas to tackle two main challenges: ensuring data-driven models are trustworthy and generalizable, and understanding the trade-offs between their accuracy and efficiency. It also examines how to smoothly integrate methods that transfer information between different systems, especially when these systems operate at different scales or follow different physical rules. Solving these issues could advance digital twin technologies—virtual replicas of physical systems—for science and engineering.
hybrid-analysis-and-modeling-eclecticism.layman: Scientists use two main ways to predict how things work: one based on known rules of nature, the other on patterns in data. A new method mixes both. This paper looks at how to make data-based predictions more reliable and widely useful, and how to balance their precision with speed. It also studies ways to connect different parts of a system, like linking a large-scale view to a small-scale one. Fixing these problems could help create better virtual copies of real-world systems, like engines or cities.

digital-twins-in-wind-energy-emerging-te.scientist: This article presents a comprehensive overview of the digital twin technology and its capability levels, with a specific focus on its applications in the wind energy industry. It consolidates the definitions of digital twin and its capability levels on a scale from 0-5; 0-standalone, 1-descriptive, 2-diagnostic, 3-predictive, 4-prescriptive, 5-autonomous. It then, from an industrial perspective, identifies the current state of the art and research needs in the wind energy sector. It is concluded that the main challenges hindering the realization of highly capable digital twins fall into one of the four categories; standards-related, data-related, model-related, and industrial acceptance related. The article proposes approaches to the identified challenges from the perspective of research institutes and offers a set of recommendations for various stakeholders to facilitate the acceptance of the technology. The contribution of this article lies in its synthesis of the current state of knowledge and its identification of future research needs and challenges from an industry perspective, ultimately providing a roadmap for future research and development in the field of digital twin and its applications in the wind energy industry.
digital-twins-in-wind-energy-emerging-te.student: This paper reviews digital twin technology—virtual models of physical systems used to simulate, predict, and optimize performance—and its application in wind energy. It defines capability levels for digital twins on a scale from 0 (standalone) to 5 (autonomous), where higher levels involve more advanced functions like prediction and autonomy. The study assesses the current state of digital twins in wind energy and identifies key challenges, grouped into four categories: lack of standards, data limitations, model inaccuracies, and industry resistance. The authors propose research-based solutions to these challenges and offer recommendations for stakeholders to improve adoption. The work synthesizes existing knowledge, highlights gaps, and provides a roadmap for future research and development in this area.
digital-twins-in-wind-energy-emerging-te.layman: Researchers studied how digital twins—virtual copies of real-world systems like wind turbines—are used in wind energy. They categorized these twins by how advanced they are, from simple models to fully self-operating ones. The study found that the biggest hurdles to making better digital twins are missing standards, poor data, weak models, and industry hesitation. The team suggests ways to tackle these problems and offers advice to help the technology catch on. Their work maps out where the field stands and what needs to be done next.

physics-guided-federated-learning-as-an-.scientist: Digital twins bring the potential to increase the efficiency of assets, systems, and processes by building virtual replicas through real-time data and modeling. However, data are often confidential and distributed, high-fidelity models based on physical principles tend to be slow and require detailed knowledge about the asset design that may not be available, simplified models lack accuracy, and data-driven models are not interpretable and limited to their training space. We demonstrate the interplay of two enabling technologies, namely federated learning and hybrid analysis and modeling, to combine the strengths of physics-based and data-driven models on distributed data sets that are kept confidential by different stakeholders. Throughout the work, an ensemble of physics-guided neural networks is designed, optimized, and validated to infer the parameters of digital twin components. The physics-guided neural network is injected with output from a simplified physics-based model in intermediate layers for increased performance, and the injection layer is optimized through weight regularization. The model is then integrated into a simulation of the digital twin asset and validated there. It is shown that the model outperforms the simplified physics-based and the data-driven models both on component and on asset level. In the final step, the physics-guided neural network is trained using federated methods, which allows training on confidential data owned by different stakeholders without requiring the stakeholders to share their data. We show that federated hybrid models can – with the right training strategy – by design achieve results that are always identical and potentially superior to models trained on a central data set. The problem chosen for this demonstration is the prediction of airfoil lift and drag coefficients based on the airfoil shape and the angle of attack, which is a task crucial for simulating wind turbines. Using the physics-guided neural network, the estimation of the airfoil coefficients experiences a speedup of several orders of magnitude compared to the high-fidelity simulation, and integration into blade element momentum theory shows that the turbine thrust, torque, and mechanical power can be accurately calculated. The federated approach makes it possible to extend the training of the model to any number of distributed confidential data sets from both simulations and experiments to further increase the model’s accuracy.
physics-guided-federated-learning-as-an-.student: Digital twins—virtual replicas of physical systems—can improve efficiency but face challenges: data is often private and scattered, physics-based models are slow and need detailed design knowledge, simplified models are inaccurate, and data-driven models lack interpretability. This study combines federated learning (a method for training models on decentralized, confidential data) and hybrid modeling (merging physics-based and data-driven approaches) to address these issues. Researchers designed an ensemble of physics-guided neural networks, enhanced by injecting outputs from a simplified physics model into intermediate layers, and optimized it via weight regularization. The model was validated in a digital twin simulation and outperformed both simplified physics-based and purely data-driven models at component and system levels. It was then trained using federated learning, achieving results identical or superior to centralized training. The demonstration focused on predicting airfoil lift and drag coefficients—a key task for wind turbine simulations—showing a speedup of several orders of magnitude compared to high-fidelity simulations and accurate turbine performance calculations.
physics-guided-federated-learning-as-an-.layman: Researchers wanted to create better virtual copies of real-world systems, like wind turbines, to improve their efficiency. The problem is that the data needed is often private, and existing models are either too slow, too simple, or hard to understand. They built a new kind of computer model that blends basic physics rules with machine learning, making it faster and more accurate. They also used a method that lets them train the model on private data from different sources without sharing the data itself. The result was a model that worked as well as or better than traditional ones, and it could predict how wind turbine parts perform much faster than before.

enhancing-elasticity-models-with-deep-le.scientist: With the recent wave of digitalization, specifically in the context of safety–critical applications, there has been a growing need for computationally efficient, accurate, generalizable, and trustworthy models. Physics-based models have traditionally been used extensively for simulating and understanding complex phenomena. However, these models, though trustworthy and generalizable to a wide array of problems, are not ideal for real-time. To address this issue, the physics-based models are simplified. Unfortunately, these simplifications, like reducing the dimension of the problem (3D to 2D) or linearizing the highly non-linear characteristics of the problem, can degrade model accuracy. Data-driven models, on the other hand, can exhibit better computational efficiency and accuracy. However, they fail to generalize and operate as blackbox, limiting their acceptability in safety–critical applications. In the current article, we demonstrate how we can use a data-driven approach to correct for the two kinds of simplifications in a physics-based model. To demonstrate the methodology’s effectiveness, we apply the method to model several elasticity problems. The results show that the hybrid approach, which we call the corrective source term approach, can make erroneous physics-based models more accurate and certain. The hybrid model also exhibits superior performance in terms of accuracy, model uncertainty, and generalizability when compared to its end-to-end data-driven modeling counterpart.
enhancing-elasticity-models-with-deep-le.student: In safety-critical fields like engineering, models must be fast, accurate, and reliable. Traditional physics-based models are trustworthy and adaptable but often too slow for real-time use, so they are simplified—e.g., reducing 3D problems to 2D or ignoring non-linear effects—which can reduce accuracy. Data-driven models (like machine learning) are faster and can be more accurate but lack transparency and struggle to generalize. This study proposes a hybrid method: using data-driven techniques to correct errors in simplified physics-based models. Tested on elasticity problems (which describe how materials deform), the hybrid approach improved accuracy and reduced uncertainty compared to both simplified physics models and purely data-driven models, while maintaining generalizability.
enhancing-elasticity-models-with-deep-le.layman: Scientists often use two types of models to predict how things behave: one based on physical laws and one based on data. The first is reliable but slow and often oversimplified, while the second is fast but hard to trust. This research combines both to fix the weaknesses of each. By using data to correct the oversimplified physical models, the team created a more accurate and dependable system. They tested it on problems involving how materials bend or stretch, and the new method worked better than either approach alone.

machine-learning-ml-based-reduced-order-.scientist: Multiple model reduction techniques have been proposed to tackle linear and non-linear problems. Intrusive model order reduction techniques exhibit high accuracy levels; however, they are rarely used as a standalone industrial tool because of the high level of expertise required in the construction and usage of these techniques. Moreover, the computation time benefit is compromised for highly non-linear problems. On the other hand, non-intrusive methods often struggle with accuracy in non-linear cases, typically requiring a large design of experiments and a large number of snapshots in order to achieve reliable performance. However, generating the stiffness matrix in a non-intrusive approach presents an optimal way to align accuracy with efficiency, combining the advantages of both intrusive and non-intrusive methods. This work introduces a minimally intrusive model order reduction technique that employs machine learning within a Proper Orthogonal Decomposition framework to achieve this alliance. By leveraging outputs from commercial full-order models, this method constructs a reduced-order model that operates effectively without requiring expert user intervention. The proposed technique is capable of approximating linear non-affine as well as non-linear terms. It is showcased for linear and non-linear structural mechanics problems.
machine-learning-ml-based-reduced-order-.student: Engineers often simplify complex models to save computation time, using either intrusive methods (highly accurate but expert-dependent and slow for non-linear problems) or non-intrusive methods (faster but less accurate, especially for non-linear cases). This study proposes a hybrid approach: a minimally intrusive model reduction technique that uses machine learning within a Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) framework. POD extracts dominant patterns from simulation data, and here, machine learning helps approximate non-linear terms. The method leverages outputs from existing commercial models, avoiding the need for expert input. It effectively handles both linear and non-linear structural mechanics problems, balancing accuracy and efficiency without requiring large datasets or manual adjustments.
machine-learning-ml-based-reduced-order-.layman: Researchers often simplify complex computer models to make them faster, but this can reduce accuracy. Some methods are precise but hard to use, while others are easier but less reliable. This study presents a new way to simplify models that keeps them both fast and accurate. It uses a mix of existing tools and machine learning to handle both simple and complex problems in engineering, without needing experts to adjust it every time.
